title: OpenAPI 3.1 Support
body:
Kubernetes support OpenAPI 3.0 for both [CRD structural schemas](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/custom-resources/custom-resource-definitions/#specifying-a-structural-schema) and for [REST API interface definitions](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/kubernetes-api/#openapi-interface-definition).

OpenAPI 3.1 has been available since early 2021. We get occasional questions about if Kubernetes will support OpenAPI 3.1. Let's use this issue to discuss.

## OpenAPI 3.1 Changes

JSON Schema version:
- OpenAPI 3.0 - subset of JSON Schema Draft 5.
- OpenAPI 3.1 - JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 (includes [draft 6](https://json-schema.org/draft-06/json-schema-release-notes) and [draft 7](https://json-schema.org/draft-07/json-schema-release-notes) changes)

The most significant breaking changes are:

| Feature | OpenAPI 3.0 (JSON Schema ~Draft 5) | OpenAPI 3.1 (JSON Schema 2020-12) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Nullability** | `nullable: true` (OAS-specific keyword) | `type: ["string", "null"]` |
| **Exclusive Limits** | `minimum: 10, exclusiveMinimum: true` (Boolean) | `exclusiveMinimum: 10` (Number) |
| **Schema Examples** | `example: "foo"` (Singular value) | `examples: ["foo", "bar"]` (Array of values) |

Some of the other noteworthy changes are:

| Feature | OpenAPI 3.0 (JSON Schema ~Draft 5) | OpenAPI 3.1 (JSON Schema 2020-12) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`$ref` Siblings** | Not allowed (e.g., `description` next to `$ref` is ignored) | **Allowed**. `description` can be a sibling. |
| **Conditional Logic** | Not supported (workarounds with `oneOf`/`allOf`) | **`if` / `then` / `else`** |
| **Property Name Validation** | Not supported. | **`propertyNames`** |
| **Strict "Open" Objects** | `additionalProperties: false` | **`unevaluatedProperties: false`** |
| **Constant Values** | `enum: ["value"]` (Workaround) | **`const: "value"`** |
| **Array Validation** | Basic `items` | **`prefixItems`** (for tuples), **`contains`** |

title: Improve WatchList Observability: Addressing Logging, Tracing, and Metric Gaps
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to propose addressing several observability gaps in the WatchList feature (introduced in [KEP-3157](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/3157-watch-list)). In Kubernetes 1.35 the controllers transitioned from the standard LIST operation to WatchList for fetching initial object sets, the  feature currently lacks the parity in logging and tracing required for effective production debugging.

**Overview of WatchList:**
WatchList allows controllers to bypass the initial `LIST` request in the List-Watch protocol by initiating a single `WATCH` request that includes the initial set of objects. While this reduces server-side memory spikes and improves scalability, the current streaming nature of the response bypasses existing discrete-step tracing and logging mechanisms.

### **Observability Comparison: LIST vs. WatchList**

| Feature | LIST (Legacy) | WatchList (New) | OSS Gaps to Address |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Initial log** | N/A | Emitted as a standard `WATCH` request. | Missing `audit-ID` field in the starting log entry, making it impossible to correlate with other logs. |
| **Access log** | Reports the `LIST` method with accurate latency. | Reported as `WATCH` after session completion. Latency reflects the entire session. | No specific log entry for the completion of the *initial listing* phase. `apf_init_latency` excludes serialization time. |
| **Trace log** | Detailed logs for each step exceeding 500ms. | No trace logs generated due to streaming processing. | Missing traces that can break down streamed response writing into Network, Compress, and Serialize stages. |
| **Latency metric**| `apiserver_request_duration_seconds` (STABLE). | `apiserver_watch_list_duration_seconds` (ALPHA). | Metric needs to reach **BETA** stability for reliable production use. |


Subtasks:
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136084
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136085
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136086
* Tracing WatchList
  * Add trace logs for WatchList
  * https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136002
  * Add timings into audit logs

### Why is this needed?

With Kubernetes 1.35, controllers will switch to WatchList by default. Without these improvements, performance debugging for large clusters (e.g., clusters with >40,000 nodes) becomes nearly impossible, as we lose the ability to determine if a slow initial sync is caused by serialization, compression, or network bottlenecks.

### **Example Logs for Reference**

#### **LIST Method (Legacy)**
**Access log:**
```text
I0102 09:50:22.075010 1 httplog.go:134] "HTTP" verb="LIST" URI="/api/v1/pods?limit=500&resourceVersion=0" latency="4.508309573s" userAgent="kube-controller-manager/v1.36.0" audit-ID="c736a782-3402-4072-8a25-c17f89598189" resp=200
```

**Trace log:**
```text
Trace[1456271344]: "List" audit-id:c736a782-3402-4072-8a25-c17f89598189,verb:LIST (total time: 4507ms):
Trace[1456271344]: ["cacher.GetList" 4507ms]
Trace[1456271344]: ["SerializeObject" 4502ms]
```

#### **WatchList Method (Current Gaps)**
**Initial log (Missing correlation):**
```text
I0102 09:37:41.848779 1 get.go:263] "Starting watch" path="/api/v1/pods" resourceVersion=""
```

**Access log (Latency reflects total session, not just initial listing):**
```text
I0102 09:39:25.708328 1 httplog.go:134] "HTTP" verb="WATCH" URI="/api/v1/pods?sendInitialEvents=true..." latency="1m43.859s" audit-ID="2f3e2ef1-e9ed-49ed-8963-65ddc0c50244" apf_init_latency="3.985s" resp=200
```

title: Don't delete a pod completely while preempting not bound yet pod
body:
Now, when preemption algorithm wants to delete victims, it only checks if the victim is waiting on permit - if it is, it's just rejected in that phase. But, if the victim is not there, the deletion API call is executed for such pod.

But then, this victim doesn't have to be bound yet, because it could wait in the PreBind phase for volume attachment or for some DRA stuff. Handling such scenario in better way could save us from making some API calls and won't require the victim to be recreated.

title: DRA: ResourceSlice controller - per-node reconciliation for network-shared resources (NodeSelector)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add an option to the [resourceslice controller](https://github.com/kubernetes/dynamic-resource-allocation/blob/master/resourceslice/resourceslicecontroller.go) (e.g. **`ReconcilePoolWithName`**) so that when it is set (e.g. to the node name):

- **Owner** remains Node (OwnerRef for GC when the node is removed).
- **Do not** set `ResourceSlice.Spec.NodeName` so the scheduler can use `NodeSelector` or `allNodes`.
- **Watch** all ResourceSlices for the driver (no `ResourceSliceSelectorNodeName` in list/watch), but in the informer **only enqueue work for slices whose `Spec.Pool.Name == ReconcilePoolWithName`**. Each node’s controller then reconciles only its own pool (e.g. pool name = node name).

**Backward compatibility:** when the option is empty, keep current behavior (node filter + NodeName when Owner is Node).

**Example 1 - initInformer:** when `poolName` is set, do not add node name to the field selector; in Add/Update/Delete handlers, ignore events where `slice.Spec.Pool.Name != c.poolName`:

```go
if c.owner != nil && c.owner.APIVersion == "v1" && c.owner.Kind == "Node" && c.poolName == "" {
        selector[resourceapi.ResourceSliceSelectorNodeName] = c.owner.Name
}
// In AddFunc / UpdateFunc / DeleteFunc:
if c.poolName != "" && slice.Spec.Pool.Name != c.poolName {
        return
}
```

**Example 2 - syncPool:** when `poolName` is set, do not set NodeName on the slice (keep OwnerRef for GC):

```go
if c.poolName != "" {
        nodeName = ""  // do not set ResourceSlice.Spec.NodeName
}
```

### Why is this needed?

We implemented a DRA USB plugin for **Deckhouse virtualization** with network sharing via USB/IP: USB devices from any node can be attached to pods on any other node ([github.com/deckhouse/virtualization](https://github.com/deckhouse/virtualization), `images/virtualization-dra`). Each node runs usbipd; with USB Gateway, a pod on node B can use a device that is physically on node A.

#### Flow (pod requests USB from another node)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Pod as Pod
    participant DRA as DRA (node with pod)
    participant usbipd as usbipd (node with USB)
    participant USB as USB device

    Pod->>DRA: ResourceClaim (device from another node)
    DRA->>usbipd: 1) Export(host, busID)
    usbipd->>USB: device available for export
    DRA->>usbipd: 2) Attach(host, busID) — vhci connects
    usbipd->>DRA: USB/IP link
    DRA->>DRA: device appears locally (vhci)
    DRA->>Pod: CDI / device into pod
```

We need ResourceSlices **without** `NodeName` (scheduler can place pods on any gateway node) but **with** `NodeSelector` (e.g. `usb-gateway=true`) and **OwnerRef to Node** (GC when the node with the device is removed).

**Current controller behavior:**

1. **If `Owner = Node`** - the controller sets `ResourceSlice.Spec.NodeName`. The API forbids both `NodeName` and `NodeSelector`. So we cannot use `NodeSelector` when the slice is node-owned; scheduling is forced to that single node.

2. **If we leave `NodeName` unset and use `NodeSelector`** - we must not filter list/watch by node. Then every controller instance (one per node) watches all ResourceSlices for the driver and reconciles all pools; they overwrite each other and conflict.

So: **NodeName set ⇒ no NodeSelector**. **NodeSelector without NodeName ⇒ controllers conflict.** There is no way to get “node-owned for GC, cluster-visible via NodeSelector” without this change.

**Validation:** I applied the two changes above locally and verified that the flow works (node-owned slices, no NodeName, NodeSelector for gateway nodes, no conflicts between nodes). We’d like this supported upstream so that “node-owned, cluster-visible” resources (USB/IP or any resource hosted on one node but usable on others) don’t require maintaining a fork.

title: Workload API gaps for disaggregated/multi-component inference workloads
body:
### Overview
The current Workload API in KEP-4671 supports intra-PodGroup gang scheduling effectively - all pods within a PodGroup (or PodGroup replica) can be required to schedule together. However, the design treats each `PodGroup` or `PodGroup` replica as fully independent scheduling units, which creates several gaps for workloads that require coordination across groups or replicas.

From the KEP:
> The individual PodGroups and PodGroup replicas are treated as independent gangs.
> As an example, if one of the groups can be scheduled and the other can't be - this is exactly what will happen.

The intent of this issue is to highlight these gaps and start a discussion, not to propose specific API changes or fixes. Additionally the gaps are explained in the context of disaggregated inference to ground them but are general gaps that would come up in a variety of AI workloads.

### Motivating Use Case: Disaggregated LLM Inference
In disaggregated inference architectures (prefill-decode separation), a functional serving instance requires both:
* **Prefill workers:** Handle prompt processing
* **Decode workers:** Handle token generation

A deployment is only functional if it has at least one of **each** worker type. These worker types may be single-node (representable by a Deployment or StatefulSet) or multi-node (representable by LWS or Grove PodCliqueScalingGroup). The gaps described below prevent expressing the scheduling requirements for these deployments.

### Gap 1: Inconsistent Semantics for `minCount` Across Single-Node vs Multi-Node Workers
The current API has inconsistent semantics for `minCount` depending on whether workers are single-node or multi-node.

* **Single-node case (e.g., Deployment or StatefulSet):** If I have a Deployment as a PodGroup where each replica is a single pod, I can assign all pods to the same PodGroup with the same (or no) `podGroupReplicaKey`. In this case, `minCount` effectively represents the minimum number of **replicas** I need scheduled.
* **Multi-node case (e.g., LeaderWorkerSet or Grove PodCliqueScalingGroup):** If I have an LWS as a PodGroup where each replica consists of multiple pods, the controller is expected to assign each pod a `podGroupReplicaKey` to distinguish replicas. In this case, `minCount` represents how many pods within a single LWS replica need to be scheduled - **not** how many LWS replicas need to be scheduled.

**Impact:** The semantics of `minCount` differ based on whether the PodGroup is representing a single-node or multi-node component, and there is no way to express "I need at least N complete multi-node replicas" for the LWS case. To me, this inconsistency is something that is important to address immediately as opposed to the fix being purely additive.

### Gap 2: No Inter-PodGroup Gang Constraints
Even if Gap 1 is addressed, there is no way to tie together minimum requirements across PodGroups into an all-or-nothing scheduling unit.

#### Single-node example
Even when replicas of prefill and decode workers are single pods, I cannot express "schedule at least 1 prefill pod AND at least 1 decode pod, or none at all." The current API allows me to guarantee that I get a given number of prefill pods or none, and a given number of decode pods or none, but these are independent guarantees. There is no way to express that I need at least 1 of each or none at all.

* *Risk:* The scheduler might schedule 10 prefill pods and 0 decode pods, resulting in a non-functional deployment.

#### Multi-node example
When workers themselves require multiple pods (e.g., a prefill worker spans 4 nodes for tensor parallelism), two levels of gang scheduling are needed:
1.  **Intra-group:** All pods within a single worker replica must schedule together
2.  **Inter-group:** At least 1 complete prefill replica AND at least 1 complete decode replica must schedule together, or none at all

The current API allows me to express intra-group constraints, but not the inter-group constraint that ties them together. Hierarchical gang scheduling is not supported, though adding support likely could be done in a purely additive way unlike gap 1.

> **Implied Requirement:** Scheduler should work to satisfy minimum requirements for all PodGroups before allocating resources beyond them.
> For instance if my application needs at least 1 prefill + 1 decode to function, but ideally wants 4 prefill + 2 decode, a situation should not occur where I schedule 2 prefills before I schedule 1 decode and then falsely end up failing scheduling for the entire workload when 1 prefill + 1 decode would’ve succeeded.

### Future Consideration: Hierarchical Topology Scheduling
This is less of a gap and more of a forward-looking consideration. The KEP mentions synergy between gang scheduling and topology-aware scheduling. As these features evolve, we should keep in mind that hierarchical topology requirements will emerge:

* **Topology requirements at the functional unit level:** The entire deployment (prefill + decode together) may have topology constraints - for instance the whole deployment being within a block.
* **Topology requirements at the PodGroup level:** Individual PodGroups like prefill or decode may have their own topology constraints - for instance each prefill worker being on the same nvl72 rack.
* **Cross-group affinity:** There may be preferences for scheduling prefill workers topologically closer to decode workers rather than to other prefill workers.

These requirements mirror the hierarchical nature of gang scheduling and should be considered as the API evolves.

title: Support dynamically resizing memory backed volumes
body:
### What would you like to be added?

This is a feature request for Kubernetes to resize memory-backed volumes without container restarts, similar to in-place pod resizing for CPU / memory.

### Why is this needed?

Ray project is working on an integration to use kuebrnetes in-place pod resizing in the Ray autoscaler. When upsizing memory in-place, we need to also resize the memory backed volume Ray uses for it's object store. This object store is typically configured to use ~30% of the memory requests in the Pod. Ray autoscaler can be responsible for setting the size but needs the ability to resize memory-backed volumes without restarts.

title: NCC-E003660-MRE: API Server Proxy Disables TLS Certificate
body:
### NCC-E003660-MRE: API Server Proxy Disables TLS Certificate
Validation
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
An attacker suitably positioned on the network may be able to intercept TLS connections
being made to pods, services or nodes from the API server proxy.

**Description**
When the proxy functionality in the Kubernetes API server is used, the TLS certificate for
the pod, service or node being accessed will not be checked by the API server. This could
allow an attacker suitably positioned on the network to intercept the TLS connection to
read or modify the traffic. The level of risk this presents will depend on the network
architecture of a particular cluster.

Note that this discussion refers to the connection made by the API server to the pod,
service or node which is the target of the proxy connection. The connection from the
client to the API Server is not affected by this issue.

For an example, please see the original finding on page 29 of the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Recommendation**
Consider whether it is possible to implement TLS certificate validation for pod, service and
node proxying. This would require a means of specifying the expected server certificate or
trust store.

If this is not possible, ensure that documentation for the relevant APIs makes it clear that
these connections are potentially vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

**Component**
kube-apiserver

**Location**
Function `CreateProxyTransport()` in file [release-1.24 server.go:L224](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.24/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go#L224-L234)

**Anything else we need to know?**
See umbrella issue [#118980](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118980) for current status of all issues created from these findings.
The vendor gave this issue an ID of NCC-E003660-MRE and it was finding 8 of the report under the kube-apiserver section.
The vendor considers this issue Medium Risk, High Impact, Low Exploitability
To view the original finding, begin on page 29 of the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Test Environment**
Kubernetes 1.24.3

title: Incorrect PodMemory usage after container termination
body:
### What happened? PodMemory metric continued to be available for few minutes after pod was removed from the node. ### What did you expect to happen? PodMemory metric should have been removed from the old pod instance as soon as new pod was destroyed or new pod was created. From initial understanding, kubelet/cAdvisor housekeepingInterval seems to be the static interval at which housekeeping should occur. If allowDynamicHousekeeping is enabled, cAdvisor determines the actual housekeeping interval based on houseKeepingInterval and maxHousekeepingInterval as shown in [manager/container.go#L481C1-L505C2](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/manager/container.go#L481C1-L505C2) with some jitter. Need to understand the behaviour of [statsCacheDuration](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.31.4/pkg/kubelet/cadvisor/cadvisor_linux.go#L55-L58) and maxHousekeepingInterval when kubelet is restarted. Does kubelet dump the cache data to disk before the package upgrade? Moreover, since these maintenance are happening for kubelet upgrades, does time to upgrade and bootstrap kubelet could lead to additional delay in housekeeping. One more weird observation I could find is, node uuid has changed twice, once while upgrading at 11 AM(which is relevant for this issue) and then again at 2 PM(which is unrelated). ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? This was observed during kubernetes upgrade. Node was drained and kubelet was upgraded. ### Anything else we need to know? **Context** In case of Kubernetes Upgrade related maintenances, pods are rescheduled or temporarily evicted from the node. It has been observed that the newly formed pod consumes approximately double the memory of the original pod at startup. Multiple alerts are raised due to this as it can violate set alerting thresholds. Below is the original query raising PodMemory alert for workload. We can notice the query is granular at pod level. ``` max_over_time( max by (workload) ( sum by (namespace, workload, pod) ( container_memory_working_set_bytes{cluster="",container!="",image!="",namespace=~"scorpius.*"} * on (namespace, pod) group_left (workload, workload_type) namespace_workload_pod:kube_pod_owner:relabel{cluster="",namespace=~"scorpius.*",workload_type="statefulset"} ) )[15m:] ) ``` From the graph view, we can see a sudden spike in memory usage before 11 AM when the pod got rescheduled. However, since the above query doesn't show the pod reschedule, we can fix it by adding pod uid into the query. ``` max_over_time( max by (workload, pod, uid) ( sum by (namespace, workload, pod, uid) ( container_memory_working_set_bytes{cluster="",container!="",image!="",namespace=~"scorpius.*"} * on (namespace, pod) group_left (uid) kube_pod_info{cluster="",namespace=~"scorpius.*",pod=~"uar-mapi-everest-grocery-2.*"} ) )[15m:] ) ``` Now, the below graph clearly shows data for earlier instance of pod grocery-2-0 is available till 11:10, well into the startup of new instances of pod grocery-2-0. This contributes to the overall memory usage since we are doing a join query with granularity of pod labels. You can also see that once the metrics for older instance stop relaying, the overall memory usage for pod grocery-2-0 drops down. While we have fixed the query to segregate container instances, we can see the cached metrics still getting emitted post 10:55 and before 11:10, after container is terminated. ``` max_over_time( max by (namespace, workload, name, pod) ( sum by (namespace, workload, pod, name) ( container_memory_working_set_bytes{cluster="", namespace=~"scorpius.*", container!="", image!="", pod=~"uar-mapi-everest-grocery.*"} * on(namespace, pod, name) group_left(uid) label_replace( kube_pod_container_info{namespace=~"scorpius.*", container="aerospike-server", pod=~"uar-mapi-everest-grocery.*"}, "name", "$1", "container_id", ".*://(.+)" ) * on (namespace, pod) group_left (workload, workload_type) namespace_workload_pod:kube_pod_owner:relabel{cluster="",namespace=~"scorpius.*",workload_type="statefulset"} ) ) [15m:]) ``` ### Kubernetes version

title: Let DRA drivers specify the order in which devices are considered during scheduling
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently the order in which the DRA allocator considers devices during scheduling is non-deterministic. Since the DRA allocator uses a first-fit algorithm, the order in which devices are considered can impact both the time required to schedule pods and which devices are selected.

We want to let DRA drivers specify the order in which the allocator will consider devices. This is discussed in more detail in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5773 and https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5794.

### Why is this needed?

This will allow faster scheduling and allocation of more appropriate devices.

title: kubelet marks the container Ready shortly which is killed for failing in StartupProbe

When a pod has StartupProbe and LivenessProbe but without ReadinessProbe, the pod will be marked Ready shortly if the application exits without an error after receiving exit signal because of the failure in StartupProbe.

application:
```
package main

import (
	"context"
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"net/http"
	"os/signal"
	"sync"
	"syscall"
	"time"
)

// healthStatus tracks the health state of the application
type healthStatus struct {
	mutex     sync.RWMutex
	isHealthy bool
	isStarted bool
}

func (h *healthStatus) setStarted() {
	h.mutex.Lock()
	defer h.mutex.Unlock()
	h.isStarted = true
	h.isHealthy = true
}

func (h *healthStatus) getStatus() (bool, bool) {
	h.mutex.RLock()
	defer h.mutex.RUnlock()
	return h.isHealthy, h.isStarted
}

var (
	port         = flag.Int("port", 80, "The port for the health check endpoint (default: 80)")
	fail         = flag.Bool("fail", false, "Never become started (default: false)")
	startupDelay = flag.Duration("startup-delay", 30*time.Second, "Time to wait before becoming healthy (default: 30s)")

	// Global health status tracker
	globalHealthStatus = &healthStatus{isHealthy: false, isStarted: false}
)

func main() {
	flag.Parse()

	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()

	fmt.Printf("Starting test application on port %d\n", *port)
	if *fail {
		fmt.Println("Application will never become healthy (--fail mode)")
	} else {
		fmt.Printf("Application will become healthy after %s\n", *startupDelay)
	}

	// Start health check server
	server := setupHealthServer(*port)

	// Start the startup process
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	wg.Add(1)

	go func() {
		defer wg.Done()

		if *fail {
			// In fail mode, never become healthy
			fmt.Println("Running in fail mode - will never become healthy")
			<-ctx.Done()
			return
		}

		// Simulate startup delay
		fmt.Printf("Starting up... will be ready in %s\n", *startupDelay)

		select {
		case <-time.After(*startupDelay):
			globalHealthStatus.setStarted()
			fmt.Println("Application is now healthy and ready!")
		case <-ctx.Done():
			fmt.Println("Startup interrupted by shutdown signal")
			return
		}

		// Keep running until shutdown
		<-ctx.Done()
	}()

	// Wait for shutdown signal
	<-ctx.Done()
	fmt.Println("Received shutdown signal, shutting down gracefully...")

	// Shutdown the health server
	shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
	defer cancel()

	if err := server.Shutdown(shutdownCtx); err != nil {
		fmt.Printf("Error during server shutdown: %s\n", err)
	}

	// Wait for startup goroutine to finish
	wg.Wait()

	fmt.Println("Application shutdown completed successfully")
}

// setupHealthServer sets up and starts the health check HTTP server
func setupHealthServer(port int) *http.Server {
	mux := http.NewServeMux()

	mux.HandleFunc("/healthz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		isHealthy, isStarted := globalHealthStatus.getStatus()

		if isHealthy && isStarted {
			w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
			_, _ = w.Write([]byte("OK"))
			fmt.Printf("[%s] Health check: OK\n", time.Now().Format("15:04:05"))
		} else {
			w.WriteHeader(http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
			_, _ = w.Write([]byte("Service Unavailable - still starting up"))
			fmt.Printf("[%s] Health check: Service Unavailable\n", time.Now().Format("15:04:05"))
		}
	})

	// Add a root handler for convenience
	mux.HandleFunc("/", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		isHealthy, isStarted := globalHealthStatus.getStatus()

		status := "starting up"
		if isHealthy && isStarted {
			status = "healthy"
		}

		response := fmt.Sprintf("Test Application Status: %s\nVisit /healthz for health check", status)
		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
		_, _ = w.Write([]byte(response))
	})

	server := &http.Server{
		Addr:              fmt.Sprintf(":%d", port),
		Handler:           mux,
		ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
	}

	go func() {
		fmt.Printf("Starting health check server on port %d\n", port)
		if err := server.ListenAndServe(); err != nil && err != http.ErrServerClosed {
			fmt.Printf("Health check server failed: %s\n", err)
		}
	}()

	return server
}
```

title: Provide CEL test tooling
body:
Today, we don't provide any guidance or tooling to make it easy or users of Kubernetes to test the CEL expressions they use in features such as:

- CRD Validation rules
- ValidatingAdmissionPolicy/MutatingAdmissionPolicy
- DRA Structured Parameters
- Autnn/Authz configurations
- matchConditions of admission webhooks

Testing utilities that set up the correct CEL environment for the above features and then write Go table tests for various inputs and CEL expressions would help the ecosystem make more effective use of CEL.

(This gap was mentioned in a recent knowledge sharing session, and I think we should follow up).

title: List watch request for Events with stale resourceVersion responds immediately without error (again)
body:
### What happened?

I am attempting to resume a watch stream for `Events` using the `watch` parameter together with a `resourceVersion` on a list request. However, when providing a stale `resourceVersion`, the server responds with HTTP 200 and immediately closes the connection. For example:

```
curl -i -k -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://$HOST/api/v1/events?watch=true&resourceVersion=1771345573854687008"
HTTP/2 200
audit-id: ...
cache-control: no-cache, private
content-type: application/json
x-kubernetes-pf-flowschema-uid: ...
x-kubernetes-pf-prioritylevel-uid: ...
date: Tue, 17 Feb 2026 16:41:18 GMT

// curl terminates 
```

This behavior appears to be specific to the `Event` resource. When I try the same request on `Pod` resources, I get a HTTP 200 with a 410 error message in the body as expected. For example:

```
curl -i -k -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://$HOST/api/v1/pods?watch=true&resourceVersion=1771343860357567024"
HTTP/2 200
audit-id: ...
cache-control: no-cache, private
content-type: application/json
x-kubernetes-pf-flowschema-uid: ...
x-kubernetes-pf-prioritylevel-uid: ...
date: Tue, 17 Feb 2026 16:42:44 GMT

{"type":"ERROR","object":{"kind":"Status","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{},"status":"Failure","message":"too old resource version: 1771343860357567024 (1771345494818591019)","reason":"Expired","code":410}}
```

This symptoms of this issue seem very similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/104171

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the events endpoint to return an error object in the response body indicating a 410 code when a stale `resourceVersion` is provided, as described in the documentation: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#efficient-detection-of-changes.

In that regard, I expected the `events` endpoint to behave consistently with the `pods` endpoint (and other resources) when handling stale `resourceVersion` values.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a new GKE cluster using the default settings and run the following curl commands against it:

```
curl -i -k -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://$HOST/api/v1/events?watch=true&resourceVersion=1"
```


```
curl -i -k -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://$HOST/api/v1/pods?watch=true&resourceVersion=1"
```

The issue is successfully reproduced if the events request returns immediately with no body and the pods request returns a body similar to:
```{"type":"ERROR","object":{"kind":"Status","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{},"status":"Failure","message":"too old resource version: 1 (1771345494818591019)","reason":"Expired","code":410}}```

title: kube-proxy iptables mode has 5-6x performance regression on aws-k8s-1.34 due to iptables-nft backend
body:
### What happened?

kube-proxy iptables mode sync latency is 5-6x slower on aws-k8s-1.34 nodes compared to aws-k8s-1.32/1.33 nodes.

  | Node Variant | iptables version             | Rule Sync Latency | iptables-save time |
  |--------------|------------------------------|-------------------|--------------------|
  | aws-k8s-1.32 | iptables v1.8.11 (legacy)    | 32-52ms           | 21ms               |
  | aws-k8s-1.33 | iptables v1.8.11 (legacy)    | 24-34ms           | -                  |
  | aws-k8s-1.34 | iptables v1.8.11 (nf_tables) | 172-248ms         | 61ms               |

  Test environment: Same EKS cluster , same kube-proxy version (v1.34.3-eksbuild.2), same workload (877 services, 2057 endpoints).

  Root cause: aws-k8s-1.34 switched from legacy iptables to iptables-nft (nftables kernel backend with iptables compatibility layer). Every iptables operation is now translated to nftables, adding significant overhead.

  Evidence from the nodes:
  # aws-k8s-1.32 (fast)
  $ iptables --version
  iptables v1.8.11 (legacy)

  $ ls -la /usr/sbin/iptables*
  # Points to legacy iptables binaries

  # aws-k8s-1.34 (slow)
  $ iptables --version
  iptables v1.8.11 (nf_tables)

  $ ls -la /usr/sbin/iptables*
  lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root  7 Jan 23 01:35 /usr/sbin/iptables -> xtables
  lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 17 Jan 23 01:35 /usr/sbin/iptables-nft -> xtables-nft-multi

### What did you expect to happen?

kube-proxy running in iptables mode should have similar rule sync performance on aws-k8s-1.34 nodes as on aws-k8s-1.32/1.33 nodes

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create an EKS cluster with mixed node groups:
    - Node group A: Bottlerocket aws-k8s-1.32 AMI
    - Node group B: Bottlerocket aws-k8s-1.34 AMI
  2. Deploy kube-proxy in iptables mode (EKS default)
  3. Deploy enough services to generate meaningful load (100+ services)
  4. Check kube-proxy logs on both node types:
  kubectl logs -n kube-system <kube-proxy-pod> | grep "SyncProxyRules complete"


### Anything else we need to know?

**Image I'm using:**

  - Bottlerocket OS 1.54.0 (aws-k8s-1.34) - kernel 6.12.63
  - Bottlerocket OS 1.54.0 (aws-k8s-1.32) - kernel 6.1.159 (for comparison)
  - Bottlerocket OS 1.54.0 (aws-k8s-1.33) - kernel 6.12.63 (for comparison)

title: Omitting patch version in go directives in go.mod
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Starting from Go 1.23, it is now possible to omit the patch version in go directives without `toolchain` in go.mod files.
link: https://github.com/golang/go/issues/62278#issuecomment-2062002018
I would like Kubernetes to consider omitting the patch version in its go directives (e.g., using `go 1.25` instead of `go 1.25.0`).

I've already opened a discussion in #k8s-code-organization.
https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/CHGFYJVAN/p1770986931001779

### Why is this needed?

I think Go's internal version comparison treats `go 1.25` as less than `go 1.25.0`. 
If Kubernetes includes the patch version, downstream projects would need to use an older, more minor Go version to omit the patch version.

title: Live container migration from one node to another to support long-running AI/ML workloads
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Building on the previous discussions in issue #3949, I'd like to propose adding ability to live migrate a container from one node to another. I believe this would be a valuable addition to those of us that use Kubernetes as a compute platform on which to run large scale batch jobs and model training. I have read the KEP by @adrianreber , but it only covers the "first part" of the required functionality - aka checkpointing the container for further analysis - and is more security oriented. The proposal here would be more geared AI/ML workloads that are expensive to restart, prone to exhausting resources on a single node and would benefit from being able to be transferred to another node and restarted from the current state. 

There are two specific cases I am thinking about: 

1. Move container from one node to a node with more resources if container is exhausting resources on original node
2. Move container from one node to another is original node is a spot node and has been pre-empted

### Why is this needed?

There are two primary types of AI/ML workloads that run on Kubernetes - live services that run model inference and service requests from users and batch jobs/tasks that are launched by an orchestrator and usually make up a a part of a more involved ML pipeline. Examples of things that happen inside containers in these tasks are things like - extracting data from a data store, manipulating the data in a process inside the container, long-running ingestion process ( for example, embedding vectors and indexing them into a vector store) training a model either using some custom framework or an open source framework like scikit-learn or PyTorch, writing data back to a datastore or uploading a model file to object storage. 

Due to their nature, these tasks are expensive to restart. For example, terminating and restarting a model training container might mean that you lose hours of work. Unfortunately, due to the nature of these tasks, it can be difficult to estimate up front how much resources these tasks take and very frequently, these containers exhaust the resources available on a node. Due to the computational requirements of these tasks and the cost of cloud computing, spot instances would offer a way to architect these platform more cost-effectively were it not for the potential interruptions that these tasks would incur were a spot instance to be pre-empted. 

Thus an easy-to use functionality that allows containers to be moved from one node to another would be very helpful in addressing some of the issues that make Kubernetes hard-to-use for AI/ML teams.

title: Dynamic update oom_score_adj for burstable Pods
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Dynamic update oom_score_adj for burstable Pods.  When global oom trigger, we should oom-kill container which usage is close to memory limit. 

### Why is this needed?

Current oom_score_adj of container is determined by creating. When global oom trigger, it should kill container which usage is close to memory limit.  The following scenario: 
1.  node memory total is 128Gi
2. pod-1 memory request is 62Gi, limit=100Gi,  which oom_score_adj  is  515. 
3. pod-2 memory request is 66Gi, limit=100Gi,  which oom_score_adj  is 484.

when pod-1 memory usage is 28Gi and pod-2 memory usage is 100Gi, pod-1 still oom be killed firstly. It seem like pod-2 should be killed firstly.

title: GracefulNodeShutdown fail to update Pod status for system critical pods.
body:
### What happened?

Pods with a  `system-cluster-critical` priority class  set are not evicted by Graceful node shutdown when a node is slated to be shutdown. Instead they are evicted by the Taint Manager once the tolerationSeconds period expires. 

### What did you expect to happen?

I'd expect the presence of priority classes to be orthogonal to whether or not Graceful node shutdown evicts the pods or not. If graceful node shutdown runs on node shutdown then pods should be evicted before Taint Manager runs. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run a deployment with the below tolerations
```
priorityClass: system-cluster-critical
```

Schedule a node shutdown or trigger a shutdown event using gdbus
```
gdbus emit --system --object-path /org/freedesktop/login1 --signal 'org.freedesktop.login1.Manager.PrepareForShutdown' true
```

Observe that pods from the deployment enter a "Terminating" state and have conditions indicating they were evicted by the Taint manager
```
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2024-04-22T14:30:26Z"
    message: 'Taint manager: deleting due to NoExecute taint'
    reason: DeletionByTaintManager
    status: "True"
    type: DisruptionTarget
```

The pod status is never updated to show TerminationByKubelet and stays in Running state until the eviction by Taint Manager

### Anything else we need to know?

Kubelet logs will indicate that the node shutdown manager finished terminating the pod but this doesn't get reflected in the API. 

```
shutdown_manager_linux.go:395] "Shutdown manager finished killing pod" pod="kube-system/coredns-5687d5bddb-fqlbh"
```

Pod in the API server
```
coredns-5687d5bddb-fqlbh                  1/1     Terminating   0          89m
```

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.29.3
Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
Server Version: v1.29.3
```

</details>

title: Writable cgroup for unprivileged containers
body:
### What happened?

Except for the case when the `privileged` field is enabled in a container `securityContext`, `cgroup` fs is mounted in `/sys/fs/cgroup` as read only. While this behavior is desirable for most workloads, it simply prevents further/nested containerization (e.g. docker/podman in kubernetes) inside kubernetes pods unless insecure and/or hairy and hacky ways are applied to expose writable cgroup inside an unprivileged container. As discussed in #112937 it seems that cgroup fs is mounted as is from the node/host in the case of privileged containers which is surprising to me since I thought even privileged containers are isolated in their own cgroup_namespace (i.e. just like they are in an isolated PID and network namespace)

### What did you expect to happen?

1. There should a way for unprivileged containers to enable writable cgroup.
2. At least for now privileged containers should be in their own cgroup_namespace and not see/be able to write to all cgroups of all other containers running in the same node (you can see other pods cgroups by just doing `ls /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/XXXX`)

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run a privileged container and use `kubectl exec -it` to see all other pods cgroups
2. Run an unprivileged container and use `cat /proc/mounts`, cgroup fs is read only

title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding fails to resolve ConfigMap params when resources are recreated in batch
body:
### What happened?

When testing a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding referencing a ConfigMap as params, the following behavior is observed:

When creating a batch (ConfigMap, Policy, and Binding are applied together), the validation works as expected. For example, a deployment exceeding the replica limit is denied with the correct message:

```
The deployments "failing-deployment" is invalid: : ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'demo-policy.example.com' with binding 'demo-binding-test.example.com' denied request: Too many replicas
```

If all three resources are then deleted together and recreated in batch, the policy fails with the following error:
```
The deployments "failing-deployment" is invalid: : ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'demo-policy.example.com' with binding 'demo-binding-test.example.com' denied request:
failed to configure binding: no params found for policy binding with `Deny` parameterNotFoundAction
```

However, if the resources are deleted one by one and then recreated (first ConfigMap, then Policy, then Binding), the validation works correctly.

After creating them one by one, even deleting and recreating them in batch does not reproduce the issue anymore, the policy continues to work


### What did you expect to happen?

After deleting and recreating the ConfigMap referenced by the ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding, the binding should automatically reload the new ConfigMap and continue enforcing the policy as before.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Apply the following resources

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: demo-policy-params
  namespace: default
data:
  maxReplicas: "5"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: "demo-policy.example.com"
spec:
  paramKind:
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiGroups:   ["apps"]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
      resources:   ["deployments"]
  validations:
    - expression: "int(object.spec.replicas) <= int(params.data.maxReplicas)"
      message: "Too many replicas"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: "demo-binding-test.example.com"
spec:
  policyName: "demo-policy.example.com"
  paramRef:
    name: demo-policy-params
    namespace: default
    parameterNotFoundAction: Deny
  validationActions: [Deny]
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: default
---

```

2. Create a deployment exceeding the replica limit
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: test
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: test
          image: busybox:latest
          command: ["sleep", "3600"]
```
The admission request is correctly denied with
`Too many replicas`

3. Delete the resources and recreate them. Two scenarios:
 a) If deleted and recreated one by one (ConfigMap, then Policy, then Binding): the policy continues to work correctly.
b) If deleted in batch and recreated in batch
`failed to configure binding: no params found for policy binding with `Deny` parameterNotFoundAction
`

This failure is consistently reproducible on Kubernetes v1.30.x, v1.31.x, v1.32.x, and v1.33.x.

### Anything else we need to know?

When the resources (ConfigMap, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding) are created in batch for the first time, the policy works as expected and the deployment is denied with the correct validation message.

If all three resources are then deleted together and recreated in batch, the policy no longer works and the deployment is denied with the following error:

```
ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'demo-policy.example.com' with binding 'demo-binding-test.example.com' denied request:
failed to configure binding: no params found for policy binding with `Deny` parameterNotFoundAction
```

If the resources are first deleted and recreated one by one (ConfigMap → Policy → Binding), the policy works. After that, even when deleting and recreating them in batch, the issue does not reproduce.

This behavior can be relevant for GitOps workflows, since many users do not apply resources manually but via automation tools, which typically create and delete resources in batch.

title: Scheduler: Support Plugin Influence Analysis for scoring observability
body:
### Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?:

/kind feature
/sig scheduling

### Motivation:

Currently, when multiple scoring plugins are enabled in the Kubernetes scheduler,
there is no built-in mechanism to understand which plugin actually influences the
final node selection.

Operators and developers often rely on plugin weights or raw scores to reason
about scheduling behavior. However, these signals do not accurately represent
real decision impact:

- A small score contribution may flip the winner
- A large score may have no effect on ranking
- Weight tuning is mostly trial-and-error
- Scheduling decisions are hard to explain or debug

This lack of observability makes it difficult to:

- Diagnose unexpected scheduling results
- Tune plugin weights safely
- Evaluate effectiveness of new plugins
- Remove ineffective plugins
- Explain scheduling behavior in production

We need a systematic, low-overhead, and interpretable way to quantify the real
influence of each scoring plugin on scheduling outcomes.

Current limitation (Problem Statement):

The scheduler today only exposes:

- per-plugin raw scores
- final aggregated score
- configured weights

But it does NOT expose:

- whether a plugin changed the winner
- how much a plugin perturbed rankings
- whether a plugin actually matters in practice

As a result, plugin influence cannot be directly measured.

Users must rely on manual experimentation or log inspection, which is time-consuming
and error-prone.

### What you expected to happen:

The scheduler should provide a built-in analysis capability that can:

- quantify per-plugin influence
- explain how rankings change if a plugin is removed
- help operators understand "why this node won"
- provide diagnostics without changing scheduling behavior

Ideally, this analysis should:

- be lightweight
- run after scoring
- not modify decisions
- be optional / configurable
- expose results via logs or metrics

### Proposed Solution:

Introduce a "Plugin Influence Analysis" feature in the scheduler.

After the scoring phase:

1. Record baseline total scores for all nodes
2. Compute baseline Top-K ranking and winner
3. For each plugin:
   - Temporarily remove its contribution (Leave-One-Out simulation)
   - Recompute ranking
   - Compare with baseline
4. Measure ranking differences
5. Output influence metrics

Metrics may include:

- whether winner changes
- top-K set similarity
- ranking displacement
- score spread / differentiating power

The results are emitted through logs (or metrics) for diagnostics only.

Important:

This is analysis-only and MUST NOT change scheduling behavior.

How to reproduce the problem today:

1. Enable multiple scoring plugins with different weights
2. Observe unexpected node selection
3. Attempt to determine which plugin caused the result

There is currently no direct way to answer this without manual experimentation.

### Anything else we need to know:

Context:

Modern clusters often enable many plugins (resource fit, topology spread,
locality, custom policies, etc.). Interactions between them are non-linear,
making reasoning difficult.

Leave-One-Out (counterfactual ablation) is a simple and efficient method to
measure true marginal influence while keeping all other conditions constant.

This approach:

- avoids recomputing plugin logic
- only subtracts scores
- has low overhead
- scales linearly with number of plugins

Benefits:

- Better observability
- Easier debugging
- Safer weight tuning
- Easier plugin validation
- No behavior change
- Low performance cost

### Long-term direction (Optional):

In the future, the influence metrics could also be used to:
- recommend weight adjustments
- detect ineffective plugins
- support automated tuning

title: Snapshot PodGroup state before initiating the scheduling cycle
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Workload scheduling plugins may need to check the already scheduled pods, e.g. to ensure that the pods to be scheduled are using the same topology domain. So we need to snapshot PodGroupStates before scheduling cycle.

### Why is this needed?

There's already WorkloadManager.PodGroupState, that can return scheduled pods.
It's currently used by the GangScheduling plugin to:
- Identify whether there are enough pods in the cluster to enqueue the pod group in PreEnqueue(): 
- Identify whether there are enough pods that are assumed or bound to proceed with binding in Permit(): 
- The plugin also uses it to assume/forget pods in Reserve/Unreserve.

There are a couple of problems with the WorkloadManager:
- It uses live cluster state, i.e. it can change during a single scheduling cycle, such that one plugin may see different state than the other while scheduling the same pod / podgroup
- It duplicates assume state, which normally lives in cache. If the WorkloadManager used the same assume state, there would be no need to assume/forget in GangScheduling plugin's Reserve/Unreserve, as it's already done in the core implementation: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/028015267e30a5f4f975c9a57f91f53ddd79eca5/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go#L200

One option is to simply snapshot the PodGroupState when we begin the workload scheduling cycle. However, if not done under the same lock as the regular snapshot, it can lead to inconsistent state with the SnapshotSharedLister. For example, PodGroupState may show that a pod is assigned on a node, but the node snapshot may not show that pod.

To avoid a situation like this, the snapshot of PodGroupState and the cache should be under the same lock. It could be useful to move the state managed by WorkloadManager to cache / snapshot, as it could simplify the state management and make it consistent.

title: Use Linux CFS burst to get rid of unnecessary CPU throttling
body:
<!-- Feature requests are unlikely to make progress as an issue.

Instead, please suggest enhancements by engaging with SIGs on slack and mailing lists.

A proposal that works through the design along with the implications of the change can be opened as a KEP:
https://git.k8s.io/enhancements/keps#kubernetes-enhancement-proposals-keps
-->

#### What would you like to be added:
Add [CFS burst](https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/162452036714.395.9249272896491500398.tip-bot2@tip-bot2/) configuration for pods' CPU limits

#### Why is this needed:
CPU throttling has been a headache for a long time. Even when pods' CPU utilization is far below its CPU limit, many long-tail cases still exist. Thus it is difficult for developers to choose the appropriate hard-limits.

Recently, the [CPU Burst](https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/162452036714.395.9249272896491500398.tip-bot2@tip-bot2/)  feature merged into Linux 5.14 has become a new option to solve unnecessary CPU throttling completely. Noticing that CPU throttling is caused by bursty CPU usage at 100-millisecond level, the CPU Burst feature allow possible burst usage when the average CPU utilization is below CPU limits.  Basically, this allowed the CFS Bandwidth Controller to borrow time against past underrun, at the cost of increased interference against the other system users.

The [proof](https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/YKe89Uda+uJdx4X0@hirez.programming.kicks-ass.net/) for using CPU burst in Linux is well-discussed, and the [interference](https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/5371BD36-55AE-4F71-B9D7-B86DC32E3D2B@linux.alibaba.com/) is calculated too. The result shows that when there are many cgroups or CPU is under utilized, the interference is limited.

title: option to suppress DNSConfigForming warning log messages and events
body:
### What would you like to be added?

A kubelet flag that will disable or otherwise prevent these warning messages from being printed.



### Why is this needed?

The condition that causes the DNSConfigForming "Nameserver limits were exceeded, some nameservers have been omitted, the applied nameserver line is" warning log messages and k8s events is well known:
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/82756
- https://github.com/kubermatic/kubeone/issues/1744
- http://jpetazzo.github.io/2024/05/12/understanding-kubernetes-dns-hostnetwork-dnspolicy-dnsconfigforming/
- https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/dns-debugging-resolution/#known-issues

However, in some network/cloud environments, having > 3 DNS servers is effectively considered correct or unavoidable and it is not always possible to limit. For example, AFAIK NetworkManager does not have an option to limit the number of DNS servers received via DHCP.  So this is generally considered to be a problem with no solution that you just have to live with.

However the issue with that is the constant noise and log pollution generated by these messages, from kubelet and any pods that use hostNetwork. It fills up syslog/journald on the nodes and contributes to unnecessary load (IOPS and storage) when the events are written in etcd, especially for large clusters, all of which is really unnecessary because the issue is considered harmless and can be safely ignored - so let's actually ignore it! _The noise produced by these warnings is worse than the actual condition that they are warning about._ So can we fully suppress these events and messages? There could be a kubelet option like `--ignore-dns-nameserver-limit-warning=True` to hide the warnings or `--force-truncate-nameservers=3`  to explicitly drop any nameservers after the first 3 so that we don't need to complain about them.

title: Remove last reference to deprecated wait.NewExponentialBackoffManager in csi_attacher.go
body:
## Summary

Remove the last remaining reference to the deprecated `wait.NewExponentialBackoffManager` function from the codebase, located in `pkg/volume/csi/csi_attacher.go`.

## Background

As part of the effort to remove the deprecated `wait.NewExponentialBackoffManager` API (see #136823), PRs #136824 and #137066 have already migrated other usages. The only remaining reference is in `csi_attacher.go:495`.

## Migration Pattern

Per the deprecation notice and the approach used in #136824, replace:

```go
backoffMgr := wait.NewExponentialBackoffManager(initBackoff, maxBackoff, resetDuration, backoffFactor, jitter, clock)

for {
    t := backoffMgr.Backoff()
    select {
    case <-t.C():
        // do work
    case <-ctx.Done():
        t.Stop()
        // handle timeout
    }
}
```

With:

```go
delayFunc := wait.Backoff{
    Duration: initBackoff,
    Cap:      maxBackoff,
    Steps:    math.MaxInt32,
    Factor:   backoffFactor,
    Jitter:   jitter,
}.DelayWithReset(clk, resetDuration)

for {
    select {
    case <-clk.After(delayFunc()):
        // do work
    case <-ctx.Done():
        // handle timeout
    }
}
```

## Location

- File: `pkg/volume/csi/csi_attacher.go`
- Function: `waitForVolumeAttachDetachStatusWithLister`
- Line: 495

## Related Issues/PRs

- #136823 - Original tracking issue
- #136824 - First migration PR (reflector)
- #137066 - Follow-up cleanup

title: kubelet starts workloads on a node that is currently in process of being shut down after it is restarted
When kube-controller-manager MarkPodsNotReady due to node disconnection, if the controller restarts unexpectedly, some Pods may not automatically update their status to notReady.
body:
### What happened?

When a node loses its heartbeat, kube-controller-manager marks the node and its pods as NotReady. However, if the kube-controller-manager unexpectedly exits during the batch marking of pods as NotReady, even if the kube-controller-manager automatically restarts later, it cannot continue to mark the remaining unhandled pods as NotReady.
The ready status of the pod is roughly as follows, some pods are NotReady, while others are Ready.:
```console
host-1:/home # kubectl get po -Aowide
NAMESPACE     NAME        READY   STATUS      RESTARTS      AGE   IP             NODE                 NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES
kube-system   pod-test-0  0/1     Running     0             26d   8.4.33.35      host-1               <none>           <none>
kube-system   pod-test-1  0/1     Running     0             26d   172.16.0.8     host-1               <none>           <none>
kube-system   pod-test-2  0/1     Running     0             26d   8.4.33.35      host-1               <none>           <none>
kube-system   pod-test-3  0/1     Running     0             26d   172.16.0.25    host-1               <none>           <none>
kube-system   pod-test-4  1/1     Running     0             26d   8.4.33.35      host-1               <none>           <none>
kube-system   pod-test-5  1/1     Running     0             26d   172.16.0.9     host-1               <none>           <none>
kube-system   pod-test-6  1/1     Running     0             26d   8.4.33.35      host-1               <none>           <none>
kube-system   pod-test-7  1/1     Running     0             26d   172.16.0.19    host-1               <none>           <none>
kube-system   pod-test-8  1/1     Running     0             26d   172.16.0.6     host-1               <none>           <none>
```

### What did you expect to happen?

When kube-controller-manager restarts automatically, it can continue to mark unhandled Pods as NotReady.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We need to simulate the kube-controller-manager exiting when it marks Pods as NotReady in bulk. The simplest way to reproduce this issue is to inject `os.Exit(1)` above the `MarkPodsNotReady` method in the `monitorNodeHealth` function of the file `pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/node_lifecycle_controller.go`.

```go
			switch {
			case currentReadyCondition.Status != v1.ConditionTrue && observedReadyCondition.Status == v1.ConditionTrue:
				// Report node event only once when status changed.
				controllerutil.RecordNodeStatusChange(logger, nc.recorder, node, "NodeNotReady")
				fallthrough
			case needsRetry && observedReadyCondition.Status != v1.ConditionTrue:
				os.Exit(1) // add here !!!
				if err = controllerutil.MarkPodsNotReady(ctx, nc.kubeClient, nc.recorder, pods, node.Name); err != nil {
					utilruntime.HandleErrorWithContext(ctx, err, "Unable to mark all pods NotReady on node; queuing for retry", "node", node.Name)
					nc.nodesToRetry.Store(node.Name, struct{}{})
					return
				}
```

title: NCC-E003660-JAV: Redirection of API Server Traffic to Kubelet
body:
### NCC-E003660-JAV: Redirection of API Server Traffic to Kubelet
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
A user with GET permissions on the `nodes/proxy` subresource and either PATCH on `nodes/status` or `CREATE` on nodes can manipulate the API Server into authenticating to itself, resulting in cluster-administrator permissions.

**Description**
The Kubernetes API server proxy is a feature which allows users to proxy requests through
the API server to workloads or nodes. The user’s own credentials are not proxied to the
destination, but if the API server recognizes the proxy target as a kubelet, it will
authenticate the request using its own client certificate. It is possible to abuse this
behavior to cause the API server to connect to itself using its own credentials (which
typically will have cluster administrator permissions), by temporarily modifying the cluster
state so that the API server directs proxied traffic to the wrong destination.
While this represents a potential privilege escalation to cluster administrator, the attack
does require significant existing permissions against nodes as a starting point.

For an example, please see the original finding on page 24 of the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Recommendation**
Consider whether it is possible to implement additional defensive measures to prevent
proxied requests being sent to the API server’s web port.

**Component**
kube-apiserver

**Anything else we need to know?**
See umbrella issue [#118980](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118980) for current status of all issues created from these findings.
The vendor gave this issue an ID of NCC-E003660-JAV and it was finding 7 of the report under the kube-apiserver section.
The vendor considers this issue Medium Risk, Medium Impact, Low Exploitability
To view the original finding, begin on page 24 of the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Test Environment**
Kubernetes 1.24.3

title: Make native scheduling workload-aware
body:
### What would you like to be added?

We would like to start a discussion and hopefully kick off an effort to pivot scheduling from the pod-based to workload-based. There are many things we are certain about, but there are also plenty of unanswered questions. We want to start from framing a problem, agreeing on goals and opening a discussion how to achieve those goals.

Please review [[External] Workload-aware scheduling](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1pZaQ4q9nhENFFIy-WjUhb89WCgJ7ZPcrKx-PIU8rOqA/edit?usp=sharing) doc and share your thoughts there.

Please note that there are two separate tabs, the first focused on framing the problem, the second on drawing a vision, which should help us to imagine how things could be organized even if we don't know all the details yet.

### Why is this needed?

There has been a lot of discussions and thoughts about making native scheduling workload-aware. It's needed not only to improve scheduling capabilities for workloads (finding a better placement), but also to make all necessary components aware of workloads to protect their integrity though their entire lifecycle. The second goal may be even more important as this is a big missing element in the Kubernetes ecosystem which even custom schedulers cannot address on their own.

title: Optimize volumemanager run loop
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Change how volume management tasks are scheduled to execute to reduce its overhead.

### Why is this needed?

There are two parts in volume management:

* populating the desired state of volumes
* reconciling the desired state and actual state

Both parts are scheduled to run for every [100ms](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7ec344dcef9a04920578aabe4e122bc0b3404afe/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/volume_manager.go#L58-L62), which might be unnecessary for nodes with very steady state (e.g. standalone kubelet). 

Two optimization options:

1. Just making the run interval configurable so the users can decide accordingly. However, this not only increases the configuration complexity but also increases the latency to reconcile the volumes
2. Making the populating first watch over pod changes, which can be a signal passed from kubelet PLEG/housekeeping so populating is only triggered when there are changes in pods. Then Also making reconciling watch over signals passed by populating, which only triggers a signal when there are differences populated. This optimization could be more complicated with trivial retries to ensure the reconciliation is successfully executed.

With optimization, I expect 1%~1.5% CPU per node reduced

title: kubectl logs should *not* fail while a pod is being started, because it makes for a terrible initial experience
body:
Currently the following can fail:

```
$ kubectl create -f pod.yaml 
pod "foo" created
$ kubectl logs -f foo
container "build" in pod "build" is waiting to start: ContainerCreating
```

For real world cases where it may take tens of seconds to pull the image, this is intensely frustrating to users because now they have to guess when the pod is started in order to debug it.

For users who specify `kubectl logs foo`, it may be ok to return immediately (we need to debate this).  `-f` is different because the expectation is to wait to see the results of the pod execution.

We need to fix the kubelet to return errors that allow clients to make the determination (probably by improving the types of errors returned by `validateContainerLogStatus` to include structured API errors) and ensure that the pod log (and other log endpoints, like deploy logs) can properly handle surfacing that.  Then we either need to change the logs endpoint for follow to have that behavior (reasonable) or change the clients (more work, harder to justify).  The other log endpoints should be have consistently.

We need to keep backwards compatibility in account on errors - right now we always return 400 Bad Request, but we could add detail causes.  The GenericHTTPResponseChecker would probably need to be wrapped with a more powerful PossibleAPIOrGenericHTTPResponseChecker that tested for JSON output and did the right thing.

title: startupProbe reports failed check attempt as Warning, but it should be Normal
body:
### What happened?

Let's say I have a containerized app which take about 75 seconds to start.
When a startupProbe is configured for its pod as below:
```
    startupProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /actuator/health/livenessState
        port: 9080
        scheme: HTTP
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
      successThreshold: 1
      timeoutSeconds: 3
```
it reports in Kubelet events Warning 7 times:
```
Events:
  Type     Reason     Age                From               Message
  ----     ------     ----               ----               -------
  Normal   Scheduled  38s                default-scheduler  Successfully assigned my-pod-86f77646d5-vd8ks
  Normal   Pulling    38s                kubelet            Pulling image "artifactory...."
  Normal   Pulled     32s                kubelet            Successfully pulled image "artifactory...." in 5.709s (5.709s including waiting). Image size: 232274542 bytes.
  Normal   Created    32s                kubelet            Created container my-pod
  Normal   Started    32s                kubelet            Started container my-pod
  Warning  Unhealthy  18s (x7 over 90s)  kubelet            Startup probe failed: Get "http://100.65.0.75:9080/actuator/health/livenessState": dial tcp 100.65.0.75:9080: connect: connection refused
```

That is logical, but **not practical nor semantic**.

The startupProbe's sole reason of existence **is to get** the initial **failures**. So it should not report them as `Warning`, because it's not wrong. If the app really did not start at the end, the probe which should report the problem should be the livenessProbe after the startupProbe reached its maximum (failureThreshold * periodSeconds), not the startupProbe. So the only `Warning` or `Error` situation the startupProbe should report, is if it exceeded its maximum livespan without any successful attempt.

### What did you expect to happen?

The startupProbe should not report failures, except at the end, if it exceeded its maximum livespan without any successful attempt.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

title: Pod status updates take longer to propagate to the API than necessary
body:
### What happened?

#107897 originally identified a number of inefficiencies in how pod status is reported back to the API:

1. Pods are queued in a channel and then processed one by one - this causes HoL blocking and writes every observed status change, but pod status is level driven (split into #116615 for inclusion into #115331)
2. Status is a GET then PATCH, but we now have server side apply and using it would reduce 2 RT to 1 RT and reduce QPS
3. We treat all status updates the same, when in reality certain transitions should be prioritized (unready -> ready, Running -> Succeeded|Failed)
4. Status is single threaded, and we could easily try multiple
5. It's hard to know when our status cache has been brought up to date (so that we can bypass a SSA attempt), we could use ResourceVersion tracking for that (apimachinery proposed allowing it to be parsed)

In general these contribute to #113606 and should be improved.

/sig node
/sig scalability

### What did you expect to happen?

Faster

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See kubelet logs.  Several e2e tests stress this flow, but we need a test that shows the improvements.

title: Race window between scheduler and device plugin restart in kubelet
body:
### What happened?

We restart a device plugin frequently as part of our design.

When a device plugin goes down, kubelet [marks the devices it was managing as unhealthy](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L240), removing it from allocatable, and preventing Pods from scheduling. However, it [keeps the resource in capacity for a grace period](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L415) in hopes that the device plugin will come back up and scheduled pods can keep running with no disruption.

Kube-scheduler reads node state and chooses nodes to schedule pods on based on allocatable resources.

If the device plugin restarts between the kube-scheduler decision and when kubelet tries to start allocating resources for the new Pod, then the pod is rejected and enters a Failed state.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod to either successfully schedule, or to stay in pending until the device plugin restarts

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I have not found a reliable reproducer. I think adding a large sleep before the lock acquisition [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L548) would widen the timing window significantly, but I could not figure out how to deploy a changed kubelet

title: kubelet nodeinfomanager does not reconcile CSINode ownerReference when Node is replaced with same name but different UID, leading to GC deletion
body:
### What happened? In our cluster, the node with same name got recreated, hence it should have the CSINode already there. notice kubelet start at `16:23:07.906` But, the GC collection of the CSINode happened after the new node was launched notice GC at `16:24:03.591`, that was done for instance ID `i-019f660891131cc51` When the kubelet on the new node started up, it failed to do any updates on CSINode making it eligible for GC shown above ### What did you expect to happen? When kubelet registers a CSI driver via tryUpdateCSINode in nodeinfomanager.go, and a CSINode object already exists for the node, kubelet should verify that the existing CSINode's ownerReference UID matches the current Node object's UID. If the UIDs do not match (e.g., the Node was replaced with the same name but a new UID), kubelet should either: * Delete the stale CSINode and recreate it with the correct ownerReference, or * Update the existing CSINode's ownerReference to reflect the current Node UID This would prevent the garbage collector from deleting a CSINode that was just successfully updated with valid driver registration info, simply because it still carried a stale ownerReference pointing to a previous Node UID that no longer exists. This is the same class of bug that was identified and fixed for Lease objects in #109777. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? This is a race condition that depends on GC timing relative to CSI driver registration. In the normal case, GC deletes the stale CSINode before the new kubelet's CSI driver registers, so tryUpdateCSINode takes the CreateCSINode() path and everything works. The bug manifests when GC is delayed. Theoretical steps to reproduce: ``` # 1. Identify your node name NODE_NAME=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') # 2. Record the current Node UID and CSINode ownerReference UID (should match) echo "Node UID: $(kubectl get node $NODE_NAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')" echo "CSINode ref: $(kubectl get csinode $NODE_NAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].uid}')" # 3. Delete the Node object (kubelet will re-register it automatically with a new UID) kubectl delete node $NODE_NAME # 4. Wait for the node to re-register kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready node/$NODE_NAME --timeout=120s # 5. Compare UIDs again — they will NOT match echo "New Node UID: $(kubectl get node $NODE_NAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')" echo "CSINode ownerRef UID: $(kubectl get csinode $NODE_NAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].uid}')" # 6. Wait for garbage collector to delete the stale CSINode (~30-60 seconds) echo "Waiting for GC to delete CSINode..." while kubectl get csinode $NODE_NAME &>/dev/null; do sleep 5 echo "CSINode still exists, waiting..." done echo "CSINode deleted by garbage collector" # 7. Confirm CSINode is gone and does not come back sleep 30 kubectl get csinode $NODE_NAME # Expected: Error from server (NotFound): csinodes.storage.k8s.io "" not found # 8. Create a PVC and pod to demonstrate the impact kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF' apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: csinode-repro-pvc spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce resources: requests: storage: 1Gi --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: csinode-repro-pod spec: nodeName: NODE_NAME_PLACEHOLDER containers: - name: app image: busybox command: ["sleep", "3600"] volumeMounts: - name: data mountPath: /data volumes: - name: data persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: csinode-repro-pvc EOF # Patch in the actual node name kubectl patch pod csinode-repro-pod --type=json \ -p="[{\"op\":\"replace\",\"path\":\"/spec/nodeName\",\"value\":\"$NODE_NAME\"}]" 2>/dev/null || true # 9. Observe the volume attachment failure kubectl describe pod csinode-repro-pod | grep -A5 "Events" # Expected: # Warning FailedAttachVolume attachdetach-controller # AttachVolume.Attach failed for volume "pvc-xxx" : # csinode.storage.k8s.io "" not found # 10. Cleanup kubectl delete pod csinode-repro-pod --force --grace-period=0 2>/dev/null kubectl delete pvc csinode-repro-pvc 2>/dev/null ``` ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version

title: possibility of resource reservation features
body:
### What would you like to be added?

What about the possibility of resource reservation? For example, in an online cluster with rescheduling capabilities, or when certain nodes (due to node maintenance or eviction from the cluster) need to be taken offline for some operational tasks. Suppose we have an online cluster with hundreds of nodes, and we use node labels to differentiate resource pools for different business units. If today I need to decommission a specific node or several nodes within a particular resource pool, I would need to "migrate" the pods on those nodes (i.e., evict the pods so they can be rescheduled to other nodes in different pools). We want to safely migrate the online services, so we are looking for a mechanism similar to "resource reservation." We want to preemptively reserve certain resources on the nodes before the pods are created, ensuring that our high-priority pods can definitely be scheduled successfully.

### Why is this needed?

For some high-priority pods, we want them to remain intact during node maintenance, which is very important to us. If we cannot preempt them, we will not evict them. 
I know this seems to be a very complicated problem in a large cluster, and I may not have considered it comprehensively. Or if there is already a similar feature, that would be great.
