title: Initialize kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total metric with 0
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total` metric is only created when the first error occurs. If a kubelet has never encountered a runtime operation error, the metric is absent from the `/metrics` endpoint.

This causes false positive alerts in monitoring systems that track metric absence. Our SLO alerting (using Pyrra) triggers pages when either `kubelet_runtime_operations_total` or `kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total` is missing:
```
absent(kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total{job="kubelet"}) == 1
```

The `kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total` counter should be initialized to 0 at startup, ensuring it's always present in the metrics output even when no errors have occurred.

### Why is this needed?

Prometheus counters should be initialized to 0 to ensure consistent presence.
Missing metrics trigger false alerts in SLO monitoring, especially on stable nodes that rarely encounter errors.

title: Policy for metric graduation and timely removal of deprecated metrics
body:
**Problem**:
We currently have a significant number of metrics that are stuck at [ALPHA](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/metrics/#list-of-alpha-kubernetes-metrics)  (450 as of v1.34) and [BETA](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/metrics/#list-of-beta-kubernetes-metrics) (23 as of v1.34)  stability levels, as well as deprecated metrics (8 as of v1.34) that have not been removed according to our deprecation timeline. This creates several issues:

1. User uncertainty: Users maybe wary of relying on alpha/beta metrics for production monitoring and alerting, yet many of these metrics have been at these levels for multiple releases
2. Technical debt: Deprecated metrics that linger beyond their expected removal timeline add maintenance burden and potential confusion
3. Lack of accountability: There is no clear ownership or process to ensure metrics progress through their lifecycle

We need some way of ensuring the following preferably by automation

1. Graduation tracking
    1. Metrics at ALPHA for more than N releases should either:
        1. Graduate to BETA (with required testing)
        2. Be deprecated and removed
    2. Metrics at BETA for more than M releases should either:
        1. Graduate to STABLE (with required testing and API review)
        2. Be deprecated

2. Deprecation enforcement
    1. Implement tooling/automation to identify metrics that have exceeded their deprecation timeline
    2. Create a release-blocking mechanism or regular audit process to ensure deprecated metrics are removed on schedule

3. Ownership
    1. Each metric should have a clear owning SIG responsible for its lifecycle
    2. Periodic reviews (e.g., quarterly) to assess metric status

**Questions**

1. What should be the maximum time a metric can remain at ALPHA before requiring action?
2. What should be the maximum time a metric can remain at BETA before requiring action?
3. Should we have exceptions for certain categories of metrics?
4. How do we handle metrics where the owning component/SIG is unclear?

/sig instrumentation

klog: Stripped file paths in --vmodule create ambiguity for duplicate filenames
body:
### What would you like to be added?

klog currently strips file paths to only show the base filename in log output (e.g., http.go). When multiple files in different packages share the same name (e.g., staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go and pkg/probe/http/http.go), it creates ambiguity.

We should investigate enhancing klog to provide a less ambiguous way to identify the source file for features like --vmodule.


### Why is this needed?

This ambiguity breaks fine-grained logging control. For example, with two files named http.go, it is impossible to use --vmodule to target only one of them. --vmodule=http.go=5 incorrectly applies verbosity 5 to both files, leading to log spam.

This also confuses external logging platforms that cannot distinguish the source of the logs.

title: `volumes[*].hostPath.type: Socket` doesn’t prevent the kubelet from creating a directory instead of waiting for a UNIX socket to be created.
body:
### What happened?

[`hostPath` volumes have different types](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/volumes/#hostpath-volume-types).
By default, no check is done. Whatever is found is bind-mounted and, if nothing exists, a directory is created on the host.
But, if the type is `Socket`, the kubelet is supposed to check that a UNIX socket exists at the expected location before starting the pod.

Yet, if the container restarts after the UNIX socket has disappeared, then a directory is created instead.
This leads to an unrecoverable issue because the directory will prevent the server from eventually re-creating the UNIX socket.

### What did you expect to happen?

If a container mounting a `Socket` `hostPath` restarts after the socket has been deleted, it should hang until the socket comes back.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod that mounts a socket:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: foo
  labels:
    app: foo
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: foo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: foo
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: sleeper
          image: busybox
          command:
            - sleep
            - infinity
          volumeMounts:
            - name: socket
              mountPath: /tmp/foo.sock
      volumes:
        - name: socket
          hostPath:
            path: /tmp/foo.sock
            type: Socket
```

The pod initially remains pending because there’s no UNIX socket at `/tmp/foo.sock`:


This is still fine.

Then, delete the UNIX socket from the node:

```console
# rm /tmp/foo.sock
# ls -l /tmp/foo.sock
ls: cannot access '/tmp/foo.sock': No such file or directory
```

And crash the container that mounts the socket to force its restart:

```console
# pkill -KILL -f "sleep infinity"
```

Then, once the container has restarted, `/tmp/foo.sock` becomes a directory:

```console
# ls -l /tmp/foo.sock
total 0
# ls -ld /tmp/foo.sock
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Nov 15 15:46 /tmp/foo.sock
```

### Anything else we need to know?

In real life, this bug affects situations where we have two pods communicating through a UNIX socket shared via a `hostPath` volume:
* A “server” pod has a `hostPath` volume for a directory on the host and creates a UNIX socket inside this directory.
* A “client” pod has a `hostPath` volume for the UNIX socket.

If the container of the “client” pod restarts while the “server” pod is cleanly redeployed (and the “server” process deletes the UNIX socket when shutdown), then a directory is created and it will prevent the “server” pod from re-creating it forever.

title: Enhancement: Marking a pending pod as failed after a certain timeout
body:
### What would you like to be added?

We would like to add configurable timeouts to allow pending pods to transition to failed.   

It would be ideal if it could be configurable based on container events or messages rather than a catch all timeout.  

A possible API could be as follows:

```
      - regexp: "Failed to pull image.*desc = failed to pull and unpack image"            # Suggests genuine problem with image name, no point in waiting around too long.
        gracePeriod: 90s
      - regexp: "Failed to pull image.*code = Unknown desc = Error response from daemon"  # Seen when image doesn't exist, no point in waiting around too long.
        gracePeriod: 90s
```

This can allow certain events/statuses to transition to failed.

### Why is this needed?

In the Armada project, we found that for batch users, it is useful to control how long Pods stay in pending before marking the pods as failed.  This allows for our scheduler to remove pods from the cluster and allow room for new pods to be scheduled.  This also allows users to be notified of invalid pods and they are able to resubmit their pods with correct configurations.  

We have discussed this idea in conjunction with the non goals of https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-apps/3329-retriable-and-non-retriable-failures#non-goals and @alculquicondor requested that I create an issue.

	// this node. So, we should remove their nomination. Removing their
	// nomination updates these pods and moves them to the active queue. It
	// lets scheduler find another place for them.
https://github.com/sanposhiho/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/preemption/preemption.go#L450-L458

We should un-nominate only necessary pods for better efficiency. i.e., let's say 10 nominated pods with 2 cpu on the node, and one high priority pod with 2 cpu triggers the preemption for the node. We should un-nominate only 1 pod, while keeping the nominations for other pods. 

### Why is this needed?

The nomination is a key element for efficient scheduling and we should try to keep them as much as possible.

### What would you like to be added?

GIVEN a job that has been executed like:

WHEN copying the output after the job has been completed:

This issue is almost 4 years old: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubectl/issues/454

title: DRA: DBC - happy path without binding failure in device attachment scenario
body:
## Summary One use case for DRA Device Binding Conditions is an attachement scenario where a fabric-attached device—such as a GPU connected via a PCIe or CXL switch—is provisioned when triggered by a ResourceClaim's request and subsequently attached. BindingConditions play a key role in waiting pod scheduling until the provisioning is complete. In this use case, the fabric device that is not yet attached to a node is represented as a separate ResourceSlice from devices already attached to the node. Once the fabric device is actually attached to the node, it should be exposed as a ResourceSlice for node-local. Thus, in an attachment scenario for fabric devices, a single device effectively appears to transition between ResourceSlices. The following section discusses the detailed approach to achieve this behavior. ## Device Attachment Scenario with Traditional Approach First, create a ResourceSlice for the fabric device, separate from the node-local one, as shown below. Do not explicitly specify `nodeName`; instead, use `nodeSelector` so that multiple nodes where the device could be attached match the criteria. This ResourceSlice should use the same `driverName` and GPU model name as the node-local one. This allows users to request devices via ResourceClaim without distinguishing between node-local and fabric devices. When a ResourceClaim is allocated to a fabric device within this ResourceSlice, the scheduler enters a wait state due to the BindingConditions. During this time, an external controller attaches the fabric device to an actual node. After the device is attached, it appears in the node-local ResourceSlice and is removed from the fabric device’s ResourceSlice. In this state, the ResourceClaim still has the fabric device allocated, so it needs to be updated so that the allocation information reflects the attached device. In the traditional approach, this was achieved by writing `BindingFailureConditions` to the ResourceClaim and invoking the scheduler to re-schedule. This caused the ResourceClaim allocation to be re-executed, resulting in a node-local device being allocated. In other words, this aims to achieve Pod scheduling onto the attached device through "multi-scheduling cycles".
ResourceSlice for fabric device 
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata:
  name: gpu.nvidia.com-7vg86
spec:
  devices:
  - attributes:
      productName:
        string: NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe
      type:
        string: gpu
    bindingConditions:
    - FabricDeviceReady
    bindingFailureConditions:
    - FabricDeviceReschedule
    - FabricDeviceFailed
    bindsToNode: true
    name: nvidia-a100-80-gpu0
  driver: gpu.nvidia.com
  nodeSelector:
    nodeSelectorTerms:
    - matchExpressions:
      - key: cohdi.io/nvidia-a100-80
        operator: In
        values:
        - "true"
  pool:
    generation: 1
    name: nvidia-a100-80
    resourceSliceCount: 1
**Problem** The following issues have been pointed out regarding this approach. - This scenario relies on a fail-and-reschedule approach, which is not the typical usage of this feature. - There should never be a situation where attachment fails during binding for reasons other than hardware failure. - When `BindingFailureConditions` is marked and the Pod is rescheduled, if other Pods are being created around the same time, race conditions could cause the attached device to be taken by another Pod. This approach carries a potential handoff issue. ## Resolution requiring discussion #### happy path - no setting of binding failures and forcing rescheduling This solution incorporates a handshake mechanism to ensure that the Pod is reliably allocated to the attached device. It can be divided into the following two steps. **First Step:** To prevent the attached device from being taken by another Pod, the feature `DRADeviceTaints` is used. The device taints must be guaranteed to be active at the point when the fabric device is attached and appears in the node-local ResourceSlice, and two methods have been proposed to achieve this. - Create a DeviceTaintRule before the device is attached - _pros_ This can be achieved with the current implementation without any additional enhancements. - _cons_ This has the potential race that the scheduler may schedule the Pod before the DeviceTaintRule has been applied to the device. In addition, there is no way to verify whether the DeviceTaintRule has been recognized by the scheduler. - Enable external augmentation of ResourceSlice attributes This approach is based on the following comment from @johnbelamaric. > Ensure that the first time the new device is published in the ResourceSlice, it is tainted with a ResourceClaim-specific taint. This prevents it from being "stolen". This may require coordination with the vendor driver (in the case of NVIDIA GPUs for example). This could be solved by allowing external agents to "augment" the driver attribute (and now taint) data. We have discussed this in the past in the context of node architects augmenting data about GPUs that the driver could not know, but the node architect does now. The simple mechanism I would use for this is a directory that drivers look in for JSON files that select and augment device attributes and taints. The on-node component here could write a file in there as part of the attachment process (prior to attachment). - _pros_ Since a taint is added when the vendor's DRA driver publishes a ResourceSlice, it ensures that the taint is effectively applied. - _cons_ Coordination with vendors and enhancements for the ResourceSlice creation process are needed. **Second Step:** Update the ResourceClaim to tolerate the taint and perform re-allocation. @johnbelamaric has proposed the following three options to achieve this. _Option 1 - Controller Re-allocates_ The controller managing binding conditions already has write access to the resource claim status. Therefore, couldn't it just re-write the allocation to the new device? I suppose this will lead to cache inconsistency inside the scheduler, so we would have to solve that somehow. _Option 2 - Scheduler Re-allocates_ Once binding conditions are met, we could re-run the allocation routine. To make sure the right device is picked, the controller creating the new device (via attachment or via some other provisioning method) could add a special DeviceTaint with the UUID of the ResourceClaim. This would prevent the device from getting stolen, and the scheduler plugin would know about this special taint and add a toleration. We could even add a special attribute or have a deterministic way to calculate the device name, so that the real allocation routine doesn't need to be run, it just needs to update the allocation reference and its internal cache. _Option 3 - Template Device_ We could add a new field on the Device that identifies it as a "template device". This would tell the scheduler - go ahead and pick this device, we will provision a device identical to this one. This is pretty similar to option 2, and the processing would be similar. But this flag lets the scheduler know that it needs to do this special processing, rather than always doing it. Unlike the approach of marking a failure, this method re-executes the allocation routine when the binding conditions are met, aiming to realize the attachment scenario in the typical way expected by BindingConditions. In other words, this is referred to as the ‘happy path.’ _Options 2_ and _3_ assume adding an additional CEL selection criterion to the DeviceRequest in the ResourceClaim as mentioned in @johnbelamaric comment below. > Update the ResourceClaim to a) tolerate the specific taint; b) can select _only_ the allocated device. This may require adding an additional CEL selection criteria to the DeviceRequest, that selects on a specific UID of the device. Another options for this second aspect would be to have the attachment controller know ahead of time the name of the driver/resource pool/device name - then it essentially just does the allocation and we move on. There could be a race at kubelet admission time, I am not sure. However, as noted in @pohly comments, it is confirmed that modifying the ResourceClaim spec is not allowed. Therefore, it is considered that _Option 1_ is likely to be recommended. > Note that a ResourceClaim.Spec is immutable. You cannot modify it once the ResourceClaim has been created. Since the details of the process for re-executing the allocation routine when the binding conditions are met are unclear, @johnbelamaric, could you please share any detailed ideas you might have about how this would work? In this issue, we want to discuss which of the two methods to ensure that taints are applied to attached devices and which approach to take among _Options 1–3_ to achieve the happy path, in addition, the details of how to implement it.

title: The Binding API does not validate node names, which can cause a pod with a finalizer to be stuck in deletion
body:
### What happened?

If a pod is created with a custom scheduler and a finalizer, and then bound through the Binding API to a node whose name contains uppercase characters, the API server accepts the request and set the node name to the invalid name.
The pod subsequently becomes stuck and cannot be deleted. Attempts to patch or remove finalizers fail with RCF‑1123 validation errors, preventing deletion through the API server and requiring manual removal from etcd.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod to be removable, or for the binding to be rejected in the first place.

If the patch request does not validate the node name, the finalizer should be removable, allowing the pod to be deleted.
If the Binding API validates the node name, then spec.nodeName would never be set to an invalid value, and therefore should not block pod deletion.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


1. Create a pod with a custom scheduler and a finalizer with spec [with-finalizer.yaml](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25052010/with-finalizer.yaml)
```bash
kubectl apply -f with-finalizer.yaml
```

2. Bind the pod to a node with upper case characters in its name [binding-with-finalizer.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25052011/binding-with-finalizer.json)

```bash
# Replace with your API Server, token and cacert
curl --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
     --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     --request POST \
     --data @binding-with-finalizer.json \
     --cacert ./ca.crt \
     https://APIServer/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/with-finalizer/binding 
```

3. The pod will be stuck as GC can't remove it.

4. Patch failed
```
kubectl patch pod with-finalizer   --type='json'   -p='[{"op": "remove", "path": "/metadata/finalizers"}]'
The Pod "busybox-on-specific-node" is invalid: spec.nodeName: Invalid value: "UPPER-NODES-11515560-VMSS000000": a lowercase RFC 1123 subdomain must consist of lower case alphanumeric characters, '-' or '.', and must start and end with an alphanumeric character (e.g. 'example.com', regex used for validation is '[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?(\.[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?)*')
```

title: failing device-plugin health checks causing kubelet SIGABRT by systemd watchdog during initialization.
body:
### What happened?

We have Kubelet, version 1.34, running in a systemd service, configured to expect watchdog updates atleast every 20 seconds. 

If the updateRuntimeUp function does not run to completion within this deadline, it causes the `device-plugin` health check to fail, causing watchdog updates to not be sent to systemd, which causes kubelet to crash-loop. 

In our case, the updateRuntimeUp function was blocked on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3ec72e2e973664a0690bc7122c9cd291702b5f36/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L3020

The device-plugin health check is failing because device manager service is initialized, but the device-plugin start is blocked by the delayed updateRuntimeUp. 




### What did you expect to happen?

device-plugin health check should not be expected to pass until kubelet is fully initialized?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

run kubelet with the recommended watchdog timeout of ~15 seconds, and cause updateRuntimeUp to be blocked on first start.

title: Allow go k8s client to accept KUBECONFIG env readily
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The kubeconfig environment variable typically uses a colon-separated format for specifying multiple paths. However, the Kubernetes Go client library currently only supports a single path. This inconsistency can be confusing for developers. To simplify things, let's make the Go client accept the colon-separated format for kubeconfig paths, making it consistent with the standard environment variable format.

KUBECONFIG env doc: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/access-application-cluster/configure-access-multiple-clusters/#set-the-kubeconfig-environment-variable

Following is the simple example to explain the issue:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0d439b43-0220-4501-bd25-eb72a56e425b)


### Why is this needed?

Currently, users have to do extra work to get the config-path value from `KUBECONFIG` env. The Go client library expects a single value, but the system environment variables for `KUBECONFIG` are separated by colons. Let's make the Go client accept the `KUBECONFIG` env value readily. This would make it consistent with how the system handles these variables and make things easier for developers

title: port kube-proxy nftables to netlink API (?)
body:
OK, so the arguments for using `nft` rather than the netlink API in the nftables kube-proxy backend were:

- The `nft` "API"/language is documented, the netlink API is not really.
- The bytecode used by actual nftables rules is even less documented than the netlink API.
- So if we use netlink/bytecode, it will be harder to understand what the code is doing, and harder to make changes.
- In particular, there is really no good way to use the netlink/bytecode API other than to invoke `nft` and see what it does (e.g., `nft --debug netlink`) and then copying that.
- ...and this changes depending on both CLI version and kernel version.
- (Seriously, just read through https://github.com/google/nftables/issues?q=is%3Aissue. Some of them are kind of horrifying.)
- `nft` is generally not good about being able to decompile nftables bytecode that it didn't write, so if we write rules with non-`nft`-generated bytecode, they will (at best) be invisible to admins using `nft list ruleset` and (at worst) may cause completely unrelated `nft` invocations to crash (as in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122743#issuecomment-1889932301).
- Theoretically, in the future knftables could switch from exec'ing `nft` to using `libnftables` instead, without needing to change API at all, because `nft` is just a thin wrapper around `libnftables`.

So what has changed?

Well, first, the idea that maybe we could eventually use `libnftables` seems to have failed; in particular, given the way that vendoring is used in the go ecosystem, linking against libnftables doesn't make it harder to build knftables, it makes it harder to build _everything that uses knftables_.

Second, `nft` itself has proven problematic in ways we didn't expect (eg, the pre-0.9.8 crashes mentioned above). [EDIT] Another example of this is that if the CLI adds new features (like OVS-style "cookies" for identifying rules), we generally can't use them, because we can't force people to have the new version of the CLI (whereas if we used netlink we might be able to just implement the feature ourselves).

Third, at very large scale, there's no getting around the inefficiency involved in serializing kube-proxy's internal state out to strings, passing that to `nft`, and having `nft` re-parse it all.

Fourth, I want to use the `owner` flag on kube-proxy's table (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/knftables/issues/28) but there's no good way to do that when using `nft`.

[EDIT] Fifth, CLI-syntax rules are effectively write-only anyway, because `nft` will often unmarshall the bytecode into a different form than you originally wrote it in (e.g., `mark & 0x4000` vs `meta mark and 0x00004000`), which may even depend on `nft` version, so (unlike with iptables) there's no way to find a rule you previously wrote other than by knowing its handle or abusing `comment`.

So really, none of the arguments against using the netlink API are any less valid than they were before, it's just that there are more arguments against using `nft` now too...

----

So if we move to netlink, how do we do that?

The obvious answer is to adopt https://github.com/google/nftables. Although it has warnings about being incomplete and API-unstable, there's a lot of foundational work there that it wouldn't make sense to duplicate. If necessary, we could fork it if they broke API in a way that was awkward for us.

Looking at kube-network-policies, this means we'll now have rules like:

```
	nft.AddRule(&nftables.Rule{
		Table: table,
		Chain: chain,
		Exprs: []expr.Any{
				&expr.Meta{Key: expr.MetaKeyL4PROTO, SourceRegister: false, Register: 0x1},
				&expr.Cmp{Op: expr.CmpOpEq, Register: 0x1, Data: []byte{unix.IPPROTO_UDP}},
				&expr.Payload{DestRegister: 0x1, Base: expr.PayloadBaseTransportHeader, Offset: 2, Len: 2},
				&expr.Cmp{Op: expr.CmpOpEq, Register: 0x1, Data: binaryutil.BigEndian.PutUint16(53)},
				&expr.Verdict{Kind: expr.VerdictAccept},
		},
	})
```

which, ugh. (That means "udp dport 53 accept" btw.) So, on the one hand, we mostly won't need to look at this, because we don't actually change the rules _that_ much. And on the other hand, ugh.

`nft --debug netlink` has a slightly nicer form of this:

```
  [ meta load l4proto => reg 1 ]
  [ cmp eq reg 1 0x00000011 ]
  [ payload load 2b @ transport header + 2 => reg 1 ]
  [ cmp eq reg 1 0x00003500 ]
  [ immediate reg 0 accept ]
```

Though if we accept rules in that format and then "compile" them we become inefficient when dealing with large rulesets again. We'd only want to do that if we could "precompile" everything only once. And we'd have to figure out some way to substitute in values correctly (eg, IP addresses).

(Also FWIW, the "`nft --json`" representation of that would be: `{ "match": { "op": "==", "left": { "payload": { "protocol": "udp", "field": "dport" } }, "right": 53 } }`.)

Anyway, we need to figure out a balance between "nice representation of rules/elements for the go code" and "nice representation for serializing to netlink messages without having to do extra work". Given that we only have to use a limited number of rule types in kube-proxy anyway, perhaps we could have a simpler (but still non-string-based) intermediate representation.

Using some sort of intermediate representation might also help with being able to keep the `runPacketFlowTests` in `pkg/proxy/nftables/proxier_test.go`, which I consider to be pretty important. (I could never have successfully implemented `MinimizeIPTablesRestore` without having added `runPacketFlowTests` to the iptables backend first.)

This possibly argues for keeping knftables (with an updated API) but making it a higher-level wrapper around google/nftables? Related: neither https://github.com/google/nftables nor https://github.com/networkplumbing/go-nft seems to have an equivalent of `knftables.Fake`.

Alternatively, we could give up on being able to test this sort of thing via unit tests, and instead test it via integration tests that create a separate network namespace for testing (like the CNI unit tests) and then actually create nftables rules, etc, there and then throw hand-crafted fake packets at them via a "raw" socket (like the k8s [conntrack/RST e2e test](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/test/images/regression-issue-74839)) and then intercept the output packets (via nf_queue like kube-network-policies) to make sure they are correct. This would be a bunch of work to implement, but it should do the job. (In fact, it would end up being mostly service-proxy-agnostic and could possibly be used by other projects too...)

/sig network
/area kube-proxy
cc @aojea @adrianmoisey @npinaeva

title: Mutable Job scheduling directives after suspension
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Allow modifying the scheduling directives of a Job template when the job is fully suspended.

Currently, as part of kubernetes/enhancements#2926, we allow the Job pod template to be modified only if the Job didn't start (`.status.startTime == nil`).

We could implement mutable scheduling directives after suspension if we set .status.startTime to nil when when we are confident that there all the running pods are at least terminating. This is possible because the job controller keeps an in-memory cache of the creations it issued (expectations) and `.status.active` takes into account the pods the job controller failed to remove.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dc3c9c0101563f95ca5d844c525a095b4a231dff/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1394-L1400

An alternate implementation would be to delay setting the Suspend condition to true until `.status.active==0` and allowing mutable pod conditions when this condition is true during validation (relax mutability).

### Why is this needed?

This would allow queueing controllers to redirect a workload to a different set of nodes after the workload was suspended (preempted).

title: Kubelet should ensure that node does not panic on OOM
body:
Linux can be configured to panic on OOM. This will impact QoS policy on kubelet since users can explicitly overcommit the node and kernel OOM killer is used to evict lower priority containers when the node is under memory pressure.

Specifically, kubelet needs to check the value of `/proc/sys/vm/panic_on_oom` and if it not equal to `0`, either 
1. Warn the user (event & logs) and mark the node `NotReady` (or)
2. disable `panic_on_oom` - `echo 0 > /proc/sys/vm/panic_on_oom`

https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/sysctl/vm.txt

cc @derekwaynecarr @kubernetes/goog-node

title: Kubelet admission check includes rejected pods in resource accounting, causing subsequent pods to be incorrectly rejected
body:
### What happened?

 The kubelet has a race condition in pod admission logic where rejected pods pollute the resource accounting for subsequent pod admissions.

  
  From Openshift CI logs:
  - Pod 1 (pod-out-of-cpu) requested 1000000000000000 millicores (intentionally absurd for testing)
  - Rejected at 03:12:06.086 with used: 759 millicores
  - Pod 2 (resize-test-kngwb) requested 20 millicores
  - Rejected at 03:12:06.220 (134ms later) with used: 1000000000000759 millicores
    - This is exactly: 1000000000000000 + 759

  The rejected Pod 1's CPU request was incorrectly included in the "used" calculation for Pod 2.

From kubelet logs (worker-2):
```
  Nov 06 03:12:06.086726 - Pod admission denied
    pod="e2e-pod-rejection-status-7203/pod-out-of-cpu"
    requested: 1000000000000000, used: 759, capacity: 3500

  Nov 06 03:12:06.220844 - Pod admission denied
    pod="e2e-pod-resize-tests-9859/resize-test-kngwb"
    requested: 20, used: 1000000000000759, capacity: 3500
```

title: Schema violations in patches result in empty API status error reason string
Input validation on client provided audit-id

Currently the API server accepts an audit-id as a request header even from unauthenticated clients. There seems to be almost no input validation for this and all kinds of special characters are allowed and reflected in the response:
![reflected_audit_id](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/05e035bb-7778-4e36-93bc-36391fd497e5)

This poses a risk to inject some malicious string which triggers a vulnerability in systems that process this audit-id. So the suggestion here is to limit this to some sensible set of characters.

This was reported to security@kubernetes.io and @cjcullen suggested to open it as a public issue for some discussion.

title: Feature Request: Reduce PSI Metric Cardinality to eliminate the impact to prometheus RSS
body:
**Summary**
I did a performance evaluation for enabling PSI at scale. with 500+ test containers on a cluster, enabling PSI causes Prometheus pod RSS increase up to 1.3+ GB on each Prometheus pod.
I noticed the "" and "POD" containers are included in the PSI metrics. Dropping them would eliminate approximately 66% of the PSI series.

**Analysis**
[PSI metrics](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/): Kubernetes lets you configure the kubelet to collect Linux kernel Pressure Stall Information (PSI) for CPU, memory, and I/O usage. The information is collected at node, pod and container level, exposed at the /metrics/cadvisor endpoint.

For each pod, PSI metrics are emitted not only for application containers but also for two additional containers:

- container="" (pause container - infra)
- container="POD" (pod cgroup)

Here is an example of one of the 3 PSI metrics for a pod
```
container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total{container="",id="/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-pod43e94c3b_60b2_463c_bb0c_bb10d153e49d.slice",image="",name="",namespace="node-density-heavy-0",pod="perfapp-1-1-bc966c69-h6c77"} 1.456709 1769503672619

container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total{container="POD",id="/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-pod43e94c3b_60b2_463c_bb0c_bb10d153e49d.slice/crio-d9ee10c5cdfc43b2bf36c7af5e34cffd4c353e09de52556c06ab98ee25d89310",image="",name="k8s_POD_perfapp-1-1-bc966c69-h6c77_node-density-heavy-0_43e94c3b-60b2-463c-bb0c-bb10d153e49d_0",namespace="node-density-heavy-0",pod="perfapp-1-1-bc966c69-h6c77"} 0 1769503667734

container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total{container="perfapp",id="/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-pod43e94c3b_60b2_463c_bb0c_bb10d153e49d.slice/crio-cf24cfb805081bc45e300e9c041d123b78bc97167e43831d83bb1b1c1bfd7609.scope",image="quay.io/cloud-bulldozer/perfapp:latest",name="k8s_perfapp_perfapp-1-1-bc966c69-h6c77_node-density-heavy-0_43e94c3b-60b2-463c-bb0c-bb10d153e49d_0",namespace="node-density-heavy-0",pod="perfapp-1-1-bc966c69-h6c77"} 1.295762 1769503671596
```

cAdvisor emits PSI metrics for every relevant cgroup. For a pod with a single application container, this means:
3 containers × 6 PSI metric types = 18 total PSI metrics per pod.

- container_pressure_cpu_stalled_seconds_total
- container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total
- container_pressure_memory_stalled_seconds_total
- container_pressure_memory_waiting_seconds_total
- container_pressure_io_stalled_seconds_total
- container_pressure_io_waiting_seconds_total

I investigated other container-level metrics and found inconsistent behavior—some include these two additional containers while others only include a subset of containers. 

Configure Prometheus metric relabeling to drop PSI metrics for non-application containers can help to reduce the prometheus resource consumption. But the kubelet.metricRelabelings field is not among the supported parameters in OpenShift until the 4.20 release.
The OpenShift Cluster Monitoring Operator only exposes a subset of Prometheus configuration parameters. According to the [Config Map Reference for the Cluster Monitoring Operator](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/monitoring_stack_for_red_hat_openshift/4.20/html-single/config_map_reference_for_the_cluster_monitoring_operator/index#clustermonitoringconfiguration%20%20https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/monitoring_stack_for_red_hat_openshift/4.20/html-single/config_map_reference_for_the_cluster_monitoring_operator/index):
"Not all configuration parameters for the monitoring stack are exposed. Only the parameters and fields listed in this reference are supported for configuration."

**Proposal**
Configure Kubernetes/cAdvisor/CRI-O to suppress PSI metrics for pause and pod cgroups("" and "POD" containers ) at the source. 
Dropping the "" and "POD" containers would eliminate approximately 66% of the PSI series from the source.

**Open Question**
- Is there strong reason to avoid dropping "" and "POD" containers because they are still meaningful to PSI metrics?
- The effort to drop them v.s. the additional resource consumption them bring.

- [ ] set performance thresholds to prevent regressions

### Why is this needed?

When adding new features to the "experimental" allocator we are not directly breaking "normal" usage of DRA because that uses the "incubating" allocator. If there is one, we might not be able to implement an experimental feature in a way that allows promoting it later.

title: Start static pod take long time if APIServer down
body:
#### What happened:

I have a kubelet configured to connect to a local APIServer that run as a static pod managed by kubelet, if this APIServer goes down or get edited and I have a bunch of Pod (not static ones) that use PVCs kubelet will take a lot of time to schedule APIServer static pod again.

So in kubelet logs I have a bunch of
```
Jul 07 10:45:21 HP-DL380-01_21014 kubelet[15723]: E0707 10:45:21.318938   15723 kubelet.go:1684] Unable to attach or mount volumes for pod "kube-apiserver-bootstrap_kube-system(c4786b9c39e0789c7ef802f731bf115b)": unmounted volumes=[k8s-encryption etc-pki k8s-certs ca-certs], unattached volumes=[k8s-encryption etc-pki k8s-certs ca-certs]: timed out waiting for the condition; skipping pod
Jul 07 10:45:21 HP-DL380-01_21014 kubelet[15723]: E0707 10:45:21.318963   15723 pod_workers.go:191] Error syncing pod c4786b9c39e0789c7ef802f731bf115b ("kube-apiserver-bootstrap_kube-system(c4786b9c39e0789c7ef802f731bf115b)"), skipping: unmounted volumes=[k8s-encryption etc-pki k8s-certs ca-certs], unattached volumes=[k8s-encryption etc-pki k8s-certs ca-certs]: timed out waiting for the condition
```

#### What you expected to happen:

Static pods to be scheduled properly and in a short amount of time even if APIServer is down

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

Basically a simple Kubernetes deployment with a bunch of Pods on a specific node with a bunch PVCs then just edit static manifest of APIServer

#### Anything else we need to know?:

I investigated it a bit and it seems it's due to kubelet that iterate on all pods the same way, no matter if it's a static pod or not and also if the Pod kubelet want to deploy has a PVC he will try to get PVC information from APIServer (that may be down and so it will timeout).

To me, kubelet should either, first try to schedule all static Pods before doing other Pods, or handle static Pods and "classic" Pods in 2 different loops in parallel.

"""Workaround""": As a simple "workaround" to just make APIServer come back a bit faster, I did restart kubelet

#### Environment:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.20.6 (but also tested with 1.21.2 and we have the same issue)
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`): CentOS 7.9.2009
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): 3.10.0-1160.el7.x86_64
- Install tools:
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug):
- Others:

title: Kubelet removes non-Kubernetes images.
body:
### What happened?

We also hit by this issue. We're using Flatcar Linux which is quite barebone so we are using a few containers to augment it. Unfortunately kubelet removes the images when they are not in active use. For example we a have a cronjob which uses an image we pulled and specially tagged. That images isn't used by any pods at all but kubelet choose to remove it under disk pressure. It is very annoying.

It would be nice to have a setting which says that "you can touch images only if the tag is starting with this prefix" or similar.

Even if you are using another Linux distribution then you might want to install something which isn't available in the distribution itself. Using a container is a very likely way to go and you don't expect that something which never belonged to the Kubernetes cluster will be removed by kubelet. It's very unintuitive.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet won't remove images which aren't belongs to it.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Pull some images from the command line.
* Fill up the local disk to create a DiskPressure "situation".
* Wait until kubelet removes the images - by the documentation it does in every five minutes.

### Anything else we need to know?

I created this new ticket because the old one (#103255) I found gets closed by k8s-ci-robot.

We are still using Kubernetes 1.21 as because of the faulty etcd-client lib used in 1.22 and 1.23 we cannot upgrade our clusters. The fix appeared in 1.24 but never backported to 1.22 or 1.23 which left us no possible upgrade paths.

title: ContainerStatus imageID is inconsistent / badly documented
body:
### What happened?

the `imageID` property on ContainerStatus seems inconsistent on clusters running different CRI implementations (or the same CRI implementation with different configuration), which makes it impossible to actually tell which container image is being used.

On GKE, `imageID` is a repo digest, though often to a "fat manifest", so to figure out which container is actually used you have to check the node architecture.

```
  - containerID: containerd://6eed9a2af53b5a56f39328fe1349395e56a0d01b443780a5d3ded56c3690a7e5
    image: gke.gcr.io/k8s-dns-kube-dns:1.22.12-gke.0
    imageID: gke.gcr.io/k8s-dns-kube-dns@sha256:b18b51683f6633979434a24ca2341e3b6bab8af0167b1be6b43f901aa615b38e
```

On Kind, it seems to actually be an Image ID from the image configuration object, so it is not possible to resolve on a container registry beyond hoping the `image` property isn't pointing to a moving target and then matching the image ID of the resolved image.

```
  - containerID: containerd://058f852ac99502198092865c214c548c871f20e1ac5d9c9e75b2f4ae4ed9622c
    image: registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.9.3
    imageID: sha256:b19406328e70dd2f6a36d6dbe4e867b0684ced2fdeb2f02ecb54ead39ec0bac0
```

```
$ docker image inspect registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.9.3 | jq .[0].Id
"sha256:b19406328e70dd2f6a36d6dbe4e867b0684ced2fdeb2f02ecb54ead39ec0bac0"
```

The field is simply documented as "ImageID of the container's image.". This is insufficient and should be changed if the content of the field being implementation dependent is intentional.

### What did you expect to happen?

`imageID` has predictable behavior and ideally can be used to identify the exact image used (repo digest or single-arch manifest digest)

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

`kind create cluster`

get any pod

pull the same image, compare `imageID` provided with config and manifests

### Anything else we need to know?

body:
### What happened?

Below was stack trace of crash:
```
kubelet[2767716]: runtime: program exceeds 10000-thread limit
kubelet[2767716]: fatal error: thread exhaustion
 kubelet[2767716]: runtime stack:
 kubelet[2767716]: runtime.throw({0x468f19a?, 0x46cba0?})

 kubelet[2767716]: runtime.startm(0xc0001a8a00, 0x0)
```
From kubelet logs, Validated around 10000 threads, majority are with this stack trace
```
 kubelet[2767716]: goroutine 63494 [select, 39 minutes]:
 kubelet[2767716]: k8s.io/kubernetes/vendor/github.com/godbus/dbus/v5.(*signalChannelData).deferredDeliver(0xc00201c1e0, 0xc0008fa778?)
 kubelet[2767716]:         vendor/github.com/godbus/dbus/v5/default_handler.go:332 +0x69
 Aug 04 18:36:09  kubelet[2767716]: created by k8s.io/kubernetes/vendor/github.com/godbus/dbus/v5.(*signalChannelData).deliver
 kubelet[2767716]:         vendor/github.com/godbus/dbus/v5/default_handler.go:327 +0xea
```
```
Top shows kubelet using ~80GB of memory (as well as enormous CPU utilization)

    PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU  %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND
2849677 root      20   0  264.2g  78.5g  64520 S  5983   3.9  10338:12 kubelet
```
### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet not to crash and keep memory and thread footprint low


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

By injecting error in loginD or dbus logic, this should be reproducible.


### Anything else we need to know?

Traced down the kubelet where [these threads ](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/vendor/github.com/godbus/dbus/v5/default_handler.go#L331)are getting created in Loop:
Reference to kubelet code: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.24/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L181
 ```
// Start starts the node shutdown manager and will start watching the node for shutdown events.
func (m *managerImpl) Start() error {
	stop, err := m.start()
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	go func() {
		for { >>> NEVER ENDING FOR LOOP, Till m.start send stop()
			if stop != nil {
				<-stop
			}

			time.Sleep(dbusReconnectPeriod)
			klog.V(1).InfoS("Restarting watch for node shutdown events")
			stop, err = m.start()
			if err != nil {
				klog.ErrorS(err, "Unable to watch the node for shutdown events")
			}
		}
	}()

func (m *managerImpl) start() (chan struct{}, error) {
	systemBus, err := systemDbus() >>>> Created Dbus thread to deliver signal which we see in logs
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	m.dbusCon = systemBus

	currentInhibitDelay, err := m.dbusCon.CurrentInhibitDelay()
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err        >>> If Error happens here or anywhere below, Dbus connections are not closed, thereby threads of dbus just keeps hanging
	}

      .....
       .....
	........
}
```

title: kubelet: deprecate the podresources API endpoint v1alpha1
body:
The [podresources API](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/08/23/kubelet-podresources-api-ga/) currently support the `v1alpha1` and `v1` endpoint. The `v1` endpoint is a strict superset of the `v1alpha1` with only a key change: it lists only running pods (see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132028).

Listing only running pods addresses arguably a very early implementation issue of the API, and makes a concurrent device manager call no longer needed. This alone would significantly simplify the resource managers kubelet flows.

The simplification potential and the fact the APIs almost completely overlap is a strong incentive to deprecate the old endpoint.

Prerequisite for the deprecation:
- expose metrics to clearly signal the endpoint version usage; if achievable with existing metrics, document how.
- run user surveys to learn why migration is not happened or is challenging

title: Lack of Visibility Into Previously Applied VAC Parameters During PVC Transitions
body:
Apologies in advance if this has already been discussed, decided, or implemented elsewhere. If there is already a recommended approach or existing mechanism that addresses this, I would appreciate being pointed to it.

When a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) changes its volumeAttributesClassName, the external-resizer triggers a CSI ControllerModifyVolume operation based on parameters defined in the target VolumeAttributesClass (VAC). However, Kubernetes does not store or expose the previously applied VolumeAttributesClass (VAC) parameters anywhere—neither on the PVC nor the PV. Events are ephemeral and eventually purged, and any annotations added by components or users may be overwritten over time. Since VAC parameters are driver‑opaque and immutable by design, there is no built‑in Kubernetes mechanism to retrieve or reconstruct the earlier attributes that were applied to the underlying volume.

VACs can be changed on PVCs at any time, but administrators have no visibility into what attributes were previously applied to the underlying volume.

This creates an operational blind spot for users and cluster admins who need to understand the cumulative modifications performed on a volume via VAC transitions.

Can we consider adding one or more of the following enhancements to external-resizer?

A mechanism (status field) where resizer records the effective parameters applied during the last successful modify operation.
A validation/warning mechanism when the new VAC lacks parameters that were previously applied.
An optional feature gate to enable detailed audit logging for modify operations.

This would significantly improve operational clarity for administrators and reduce misconfigurations when using VolumeAttributesClass for dynamic volume modification.

title: HPA wrongly assumes that terminated pods have an utilization of 100%
body:
### What happened?

A pod that terminated was considered by the HPA controller to be at its target utilization.

The controller logic ([1](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed9572d9c7733602de43979caf886fd4092a7b0f/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L106-L120), [2](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed9572d9c7733602de43979caf886fd4092a7b0f/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L211-L223)) is such that, while scaling up, it conservatively considers that a pod for which we couldn't get the utilization metric from a metrics API are at their target utilization. (On scale down, the assumption is conservatively that the utilization is 0.)

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the controller to assume that a terminated pod has an utilization of 0.

This is [already correctly handled for pods that terminated with a failure](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed9572d9c7733602de43979caf886fd4092a7b0f/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L383), but the case where a pod terminated successfully isn't handled.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a Deployment with pods that terminate (without a failure) and observe that an HPA targetting this Deployment will assume that terminated pods are at target utilization.

### Anything else we need to know?

Handling the case where the pod is terminated normally [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed9572d9c7733602de43979caf886fd4092a7b0f/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L383) will fix this.

title: k8s deployment remove duplicate `tolerations` but not `affinity`
body:
### What happened?

If we create a deployment with duplicate toleration the pod spec doesn't reflect the duplicate values, but the same doesn't happen to duplicate node affinities,

Deployment tolerations:
```
      tolerations:
      - effect: NoSchedule
        key: "key1"
        operator: Equal
        value: "true"
      - effect: NoSchedule
        key: "key1"
        operator: Equal
        value: "true"

```

Pod tolerations:
```
  tolerations:
  - effect: NoSchedule
    key: "key1"
    operator: Equal
    value: "true"
```


Deployment Affinity == Pod affinity :
```
      affinity:
        nodeAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
            - matchExpressions:
              - key: "key1"
                operator: Exists
              - key: "key1"
                operator: Exists
            - matchExpressions:
              - key: "key1"
                operator: Exists
              - key: "key1"
                operator: Exists
```


### What did you expect to happen?

Desired affinity:
```
      affinity:
        nodeAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
            - matchExpressions:
              - key: "key1"
                operator: Exists
```

Create a normal deployment with placements(tolerations and affinity)

body:
**What would you like to be added?**

We have a few options:

1. Introduce a kubelet-server started by using `httpServer.Serve(YourTLSConfig)` with a x509.Config wrapper to update TLS config periodically. 
2. Set `GetConfigForClient` in `TLSOptions.Config` when initializing TLSOptions for kubelet. For reloading CA, use a cache which either lazy loads the CA (and cert + key) from disk with a TTL OR Implement a separate process which periodically sync the cache.
3. Move kubelet towards using the [k8s.io/apiserver](http://k8s.io/apiserver%60) `SecureServing` structures to set up its TLS handler if possible 


**Why is this needed?**

It will enable CA rotation for kubelet clients without requiring kubelet restarts.

title: Listing doesn't fail if a resource of the returned set permafails to transform
body:
### What happened?

If data transformation suddenly starts failing on a resource from a set that is returned by a List() query, the user is not notified of these failures, but is presented with the latest known version of the resource. That happens even after new, properly readable resources get added and appear in the returned set.

Get() fails correctly on the failing resource.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected `List()` to notify me about issues reading a resource.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. run the API server with etcd encryption turned on
2. rewrite your EncryptionConfiguration by replacing the key in the encryption provider
3. wait for the changes to take effect - `Get()` a resource that was previously encrypted until the `Get()` fails with an internal error
4. issue a `List()` request that contains the resource that was previously failing on `Get()`

Alternatively, you can apply the patch from the attachment that adds an integration test and 
[0001-list-broken-proof.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/17202520/0001-list-broken-proof.txt)

```
make test-integration WHAT=./test/integration/controlplane/transformation GOFLAGS="-v" KUBE_TEST_ARGS='-run ^TestBrokenTransformations$'
```

### Anything else we need to know?

I wonder if it would be possible to allow `.patch` attachments so that patches don't have to be sent as .txt files.

title: [Feature] Use InPlacePodVerticalScaling for Deployments/ReplicaSets/StatefulSets when only resources.requests/limits change
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Support for updating resources.requests or resources.limits on Deployments, ReplicaSets, and StatefulSets using InPlacePodVerticalScaling if those are the only fields that differ from the current template. This should apply when the InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate is enabled, aligning the behavior with Jobs (see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132436) and with the context of user workloads managed by higher-level controllers.

Reference prior related discussions:
- Flux2 issue describing the need for in-place resizing for workloads, not just Jobs: https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/issues/5693
- Kubernetes issue discussing extension to Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132436

This feature would allow resource vertical scaling for Deployments/ReplicaSets/StatefulSets without a rolling restart, leveraging the resize subresource when ResizePolicy allows.

### Why is this needed?

The current InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature is useful in Jobs context, but operators and users deploying with Deployments, ReplicaSets, or StatefulSets have similar needs to scale pod resources in place (for example, to match sideways autoscaling recommendations, rebalance resource usage after initialization, or to allow for vertical adjustment of long-running pods).

At the moment, updating only the resources.requests or resources.limits for these controllers always results in a pod restart, even when in-place resize is technically supported. Relaxing this will reduce unnecessary restarts and will bring feature parity to Pod-backed workloads, that are very rare.

Several orchestration tools (such as Flux, see https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/issues/5693) and user workloads would benefit from native support for in-place resource adjustment.

This could be implemented as a specific strategy if needed.

title: kubelet TopologyManager Stalls on Large NUMA Systems (e.g. Nvidia GB200 Compute Tray with 34 NUMA nodes)
body:
### What happened?

When scheduling a pod (e.g. KubeVirt virt-launcher pod) that requests a PCI device on a very large NUMA system, kubelet’s TopologyManager never finishes computing topology hints and the pod is effectively stuck in admission:

- The pod is scheduled to the node.
- kubelet never reaches the device Allocate call for the requested resource.
- From a higher-level consumer (KubeVirt in our case), the virt-launcher pod stays in Pending and the VM remains in Starting with Ready = False.
- kubelet is responsive, but many goroutines are stuck in topology hint generation.

In our environment this manifests as:

- KubeVirt VM with a hostDevice (GPU, InfiniBand or NVMe) never transitions to Running, even though the node has the capacity and the device is free.
- Disabling TopologyManager or constraining the NUMA fan-out immediately lets the VM start

### What did you expect to happen?

kubelet should compute topology hints in bounded time, even on systems with many NUMA nodes (in a case GB200 with 34 NUMA nodes where only 2 NUMA nodes have CPUs, the rest are for HBM/NVLink), and call device-plugin Allocate so that pods/VMs using PCI host devices can start.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

## High-level repro:
1. Use a host with a large NUMA topology  
    Example: Nvidia GB200-class system with 34 NUMA nodes visible to the OS.
 
2. Run Kubernetes with kubelet configured roughly as follows:
```yaml
kubeReserved:
  cpu: "2"
  memory: 4Gi
  ephemeral-storage: 20Gi
systemReserved:
  cpu: "2"
  memory: 8Gi
  ephemeral-storage: 20Gi
topologyManagerPolicy: best-effort
topologyManagerScope: pod
topologyManagerPolicyOptions:
  prefer-closest-numa-nodes: "true"
  max-allowable-numa-nodes: "34"
cpuManagerPolicy: static
reservedSystemCPUs: "0-3,72-75"
cpuManagerPolicyOptions:
  distribute-cpus-across-numa: "false"
```
3. Deploy a device plugin that:
- Advertises a PCI resource (e.g. GPU, InfiniBand or NVMe) as a kubelet device resource.
- Exposes the device with topology information referencing many NUMA nodes (up to 34 in our case).

4. Create a Pod
Requests one unit of that device resource.
Uses Guaranteed QoS (requests == limits for CPU/memory) so that TopologyManager participates fully.
 
5. Observe
- The pod is scheduled to the node.
- kubelet never calls Allocate on the device plugin for that resource.
- The pod stays in Pending indefinitely.
- KubeVirt-specific repro (how we hit it)
- Instead of a raw pod, create a KubeVirt VirtualMachineInstance that uses hostDevices:
```yaml
devices:
   hostDevices:
    - deviceName: nvidia.com/GB100_HGX_GB200
      name: gpu1
```
The pod (if using KubeVirt, it is virt-launcher pod for a VM) is scheduled to the large NUMA node but stays Pending forever. The pod stuck at Pending, (if using KubeVirt, the VM status remains Starting) and never reaches Ready, despite sufficient resources.


### Anything else we need to know?

## Root cause analysis

- The kubelet TopologyManager asks each hint provider (CPU, memory, device) to compute topology hints over the set of NUMA nodes that the kubelet knows about.
- For the device plugin case, generateDeviceTopologyHints ends up calling bitmask.IterateBitMasks across a bitmask spanning all NUMA IDs known to the machine, not just those relevant to the requested device.
- With 34 NUMA nodes this becomes effectively an exponential search (O(2^n)) over the 34-bit mask.
- On a GB200 host with 34 NUMA nodes and a device plugin that advertises per-node topology across those nodes, generateDeviceTopologyHints spends unbounded time iterating combinations that are not actually schedulable for the requested device.
- While TopologyManager is doing this, kubelet never reaches the device Allocate call, so pods/VMs that need that device are permanently stuck in admission.

## Evidence observed

- Goroutine dumps from kubelet show many workers blocked under TopologyManager/device-manager paths, repeatedly calling IterateBitMasks on a large bitmask.
- No calls to Allocate are observed for the affected device resource while the system is in this hung state.
- If we disable TopologyManager, then virt-launcher pods immediately proceed and the KubeVirt VM starts successfully.

### Kubernetes version

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.34.2
Kustomize Version: v5.7.1
Server Version: v1.34.2
```

Bare metal, GB200 compute tray

title: PROPOSAL: Include image labels in ContainerStatus
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:
/kind feature

Currently the [ContainerStatus](https://github.com/kubernetes/api/blob/8ab7c6a2fbd1724a52514855629cec31a8f86929/core/v1/types.go#L2183) API object reports the image and image ID, for example:
```
Image:         gcr.io/google_containers/kube-proxy-amd64:v1.9.6
Image ID:      docker-pullable://gcr.io/google_containers/kube-proxy-amd64@sha256:dd647b619b75882f217a21a6e2c473deb77cba1cfb20461da0084ed78d951af1
```

It's a not-uncommon practice for folks to include labels in their image metadata, for example vendor information or version control references that help link the image back to its source. I'd love to be able to get this information out of Kubernetes in a single step without having to resort to scripting multiple tools (for example `kubectl get pod` to get the image ID and then `docker inspect` to get the labels out of the image config). I believe that this is a common concept across container formats, for example this seems to be analogous to [annotations](https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/blob/master/annotations.md) in the open containers spec.

As it turns out, the image label information is available in the Docker API responses that are used to populate the `ContainerStatus` in `pkg/kubelet/dockershim/convert.go`. I don't know if the same is true for other runtimes.

I'd like to make an attempt at plumbing this data all the way up the stack so that it could eventually be exposed in `kubectl describe pod` or in some mystical future the k8s dashboard, but I'd need some help with what seems like pretty basic questions, like:

1. Do folks agree that this is a potentially-worthwhile activity that they'd be willing to support? Who could / should I ask questions of?
2. Where would I start looking for documentation on how to extend the API? Is it as simple as "edit [core/v1/types.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/api/core/v1/types.go), run <something that calls `go-to-protobuf`>, $$$?" or is there more involved?
3. Assuming I get something that seems like it could work, where should I go to learn how to write some integration tests, or if I wanted to see the smoke come out where would I go to learn how to build a cluster that uses the code from a local build?

ps: I know that Kubernetes assigns some labels to the container that represent the k8s labels and annotations and I'll need to filter those out somehow so they're not double-reported.

pps: I expect that this would need to be broken up into a series of PRs in order to be considered and reviewed efficiently. At the moment I'd be up for doing the support for Docker, but I don't have any experience with other runtimes (yet) so I'd be pretty hesitant to go there. Maybe someone with more experience will see this and get inspired?

title: Priority for static Pods
body:
### What would you like to be added?

There should be an official, and ideally documented (see https://github.com/kubernetes/website/issues/46859) way to run a static Pod with a non-zero priority.

Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/103587 asserts that Pods should not reference API objects, but the kubelet's mirror Pods are rejected at admission time if they have a `.spec.priority` (by the API server, in conjunction with the [`Priority`](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/admission-controllers/#priority) admission controller).

We might document that we only support built-in PriorityClassNames for static Pods (deprecating the use of any other value for static Pod `.spec.priorityClassName`). Omitting the priority class entirely is fine, I think, albeit not a great idea.

I'm filing this even though there are lots of similar issues because I'm worried that https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131837 may actually make this **harder**.

Similar issues:
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/22212
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/40573
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/58379
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/58471
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/80489
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/89966



### Why is this needed?

People want to specify the priority of static Pods
 
- You might want to specify whether it is node-critical or cluster-critical, to avoid problems such as a node-critical static Pod getting shut down, and thus preventing a graceful shutdown of a control plane component

- You might want the node-critical static Pods to start first

Also:
- You might want to do odd things, like run a static Pod but only when nothing else wants the capacity. Maybe you like SETI@Home but not DaemonSets.

title: Support cpu.idle (SCHED_IDLE) for BestEffort QoS to improve isolation and node utilization
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**: 

- /kind feature 

- /sig node

**Motivation**:
Currently, Kubelet sets `cpu.shares` to `2` for the top-level BestEffort QoS cgroup. The goal is to allow BestEffort tasks to utilize free CPU cycles (improving node utilization) while minimizing the impact on Guaranteed and Burstable workloads.

However, relying solely on `cpu.shares` (even with a minimal value) provides "weight-based" isolation. In high-load scenarios, this can still lead to latency interference for high-priority tasks.

Since Linux Kernel 5.4, significant improvements have been made to `SCHED_IDLE` (Reference Patch: `sched/fair: Improve the scheduling of SCHED_IDLE tasks`).
* **Better Isolation**: `cpu.idle` (SCHED_IDLE) ensures that tasks are treated with truly "idle" priority. They only run when there is absolutely no other higher-priority task to run. This offers significantly better isolation for Guaranteed/Burstable pods compared to simply lowering `cpu.shares`（cgroup v2 `cpu.weight`）.
* **Safe Colocation**: It allows safe colocation of BestEffort batch jobs with latency-sensitive services without the risk of performance degradation for the latter.

**Current Barrier (The Conflict)**:
We are currently attempting to utilize `cpu.idle` for BestEffort pods using external agents/extensions on  nodes. However, this conflicts with Kubelet's current initialization logic, causing Kubelet to fail to start.

In Cgroup v1, when `cpu.idle` is set to `1`:
1.  The kernel forces `cpu.shares` to `1` (minimal weight).
2.  The kernel locks `cpu.shares` from being modified.

In Cgroup v2, when `cpu.idle` is set to `1`:
1.  The kernel forces `cpu.weight` to `0` (minimal weight).
2.  The kernel locks `cpu.weight` from being modified.
 
Because Kubelet hardcodes the enforcement of `cpu.shares = 2` or `cpu.weight = 1`   for BestEffort, it crashes during startup if `cpu.idle` is already enabled by an external tool or previous configuration:

For Example in Cgroup v1: 
> "Failed to start ContainerManager" err="failed to initialize top level QOS containers: failed to update top level BestEffort QOS cgroup : failed to write \"2\": write /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu,cpuacct/kubepods.slice/kubepods-besteffort.slice/cpu.shares: invalid argument"



**What you expected to happen:** Kubelet should start successfully even if `cpu.idle` is enabled for the BestEffort cgroup. Kubelet should either detect that `cpu.idle` is enabled and skip setting `cpu.shares` or `cpu.weight`, or handle the write error gracefully.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):**

1. On a node with a Kernel supporting `cpu.idle` interface (Linux).

2. Manually (or via an external agent) set `cpu.idle` to `1` for the BestEffort slice:

```
Bash

echo 1 > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu,cpuacct/kubepods.slice/kubepods-besteffort.slice/cpu.idle

```
3. Restart Kubelet.
4. Observe the startup failure.

5. Manual verification of the conflict:

```
Bash

# echo 2 > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuacct/kubepods.slice/kubepods-besteffort.slice/cpu.shares
-bash: echo: write error: Invalid argument
```
**Anything else we need to know:**

- **Context:** We use `cpu.idle` (SCHED_IDLE) for BestEffort tasks to utilize the enhanced scheduling isolation provided by Linux Kernel 5.4+ (Patch: `sched/fair: Improve the scheduling of SCHED_IDLE tasks`). This is often a superior alternative to low `cpu.shares` for maximizing node utilization without interfering with high-priority workloads.

- **Kernel Behavior:** When `cpu.idle` is configured to `1`, the kernel forces `cpu.shares` to `1` and `cpu.weight` to `1` and forbids modification, leading to the Invalid argument error when Kubelet tries to write min shares(or weight)

- **Workaround:** Setting `cpu.idle` back to `0` allows Kubelet to start.

**Proposed Solution:**

1. **Short-term fix (Resilience)**: Modify the Kubelet `qos_container_manager` logic. Before attempting to set `cpu.shares` for the BestEffort cgroup, check if cpu.idle is configured (if the interface exists).

    If `cpu.idle == 1`: Skip setting `cpu.shares` and `cpu.weight` (accept the kernel's forced value).

    If `cpu.idle == 0` or file does not exist: Proceed with setting `cpu.shares` to `2`and `cpu.weight` to `1`.

2. **Long-term feature**: Add native support in Kubelet configuration to support `cpu.idle` (SCHED_IDLE) for BestEffort pods, allowing users to opt-in to this scheduling policy directly via Kubelet rather than relying on external agents.

**Benefits:**

**Superior QoS**: Provides strict priority isolation for Guaranteed/Burstable pods, reducing tail latency in colocation scenarios.

**Resilience**: Prevents Kubelet startup failures for users attempting to use SCHED_IDLE via custom tuning agents.

title: Auto-approved but unissued kubelet client CSRs persist indefinitely
body:
### What happened?

An incident was triggered by unexpectedly high etcd storage usage on production Kubernetes clusters. Initial analysis revealed that the majority of the space was consumed by a large number of Certificate Signing Requests (CSRs).

Using `etcdctl`, the top resource consumers in etcd were identified:

| Resource Type | Count |
|---------------|-------|
| **CertificateSigningRequests** | **520,858** |
| Events | 1,395 |
| CRDs (Calico) | 1,005 |
| ReplicaSets | 864 |
| RoleBindings | 473 |
| Services | 428 |
| Pods | 416 |

This overwhelming number of CSRs was far beyond what could be explained by normal node provisioning or rotation activity. A sample of 1,000 CSRs showed an average size of **1,192 bytes**, meaning the CSRs alone were consuming **~592 MiB** of etcd space—nearly a third of the 2 GiB etcd limit.

This dates on the resources showed the build up had been happening for years, with one being generated for each node every 15 minutes.

On examination they were all of the type:

```
apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
kind: CertificateSigningRequest
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2025-07-09T06:51:01Z"
  generateName: csr-
  name: csr-jllx7
  resourceVersion: "296695671"
  uid: 0f6d31fd-c8ed-465e-ac45-e283f453f56c
spec:
  groups:
  - system:nodes
  - system:authenticated
  request: 
  signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet
  usages:
  - digital signature
  - client auth
  username: system:node:octavia
status:
  conditions:
  - lastTransitionTime: "2025-07-09T06:51:01Z"
    lastUpdateTime: "2025-07-09T06:51:01Z"
    message: Auto approving self kubelet client certificate after SubjectAccessReview.
    reason: AutoApproved
    status: "True"
    type: Approved
```

TLS Bootsrapping was disabled in our kubeadm config, and setting `rotateCertificates: false` had no effect.

Because we don't rely on the kubelet + controller-manager auto certificate handling mechanism for our nodes, the kubelets continued to issue client CSRs and the controller kept approving them.

We narrowed down the root cause to some cluster role bindings that were created automatically by kubeadm.

CRBs in question:
```
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: kubeadm:node-autoapprove-certificate-rotation
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: system:certificates.k8s.io:certificatesigningrequests:selfnodeclient
subjects:
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Group
  name: system:nodes 
```
and
```
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2023-10-09T23:54:31Z"
  name: kubeadm:node-autoapprove-bootstrap
  resourceVersion: "90650499"
  uid: 7d2c0095-b8c1-4b7d-baac-0f7b8edd0ec5
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: system:certificates.k8s.io:certificatesigningrequests:nodeclient
subjects:
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Group
  name: system:bootstrappers:kubeadm:default-node-token
```

Combined with [no logic in the CSR cleaner controller code accounting for the scenario of kubelet CSR's getting approved with certificates not issued](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.30/pkg/controller/certificates/cleaner/cleaner.go#L53-L61) means no GC and a build up over time of approved CSRs. 

Mitigation is to manually remove these cluster role bindings and to delete all old approved CSRs... all half million of them.

Is there is an alternative way to deal with the problem we're missing? If so the documentation could use an update.

Otherwise we propose the cleaner be updated with a condition to also remove **Approved** but not Issued CSRs in line with the documentation.
If there is a reason why we would not want to remove them in such a short period of time as the **Approved** GC timeline in the documentation, at least treating them the same as **Pending** i.e. 24hrs.


### What did you expect to happen?

- We expected these would get garbage collected in line with the GC policy where ["Approved requests: automatically deleted after 1 hour](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/certificate-signing-requests/#request-signing-process)" 
 
- if this condition is not included by design, documentation should be updated to explain it.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- kubeadm configured without TLS bootstrapping and with self managed certificate issuing
- Assert these [these cluster role bindings](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/kubelet-tls-bootstrapping/#approval) allowing the kube controller to auto approve the certificates.
  - `kubeadm:node-autoapprove-certificate-rotation`
  - `kubeadm:node-autoapprove-bootstrap`
- Wait 15 minutes and run check that kubelet CSRs that get created are now moving into an `Approved` state but never get issued certificates `kubectl get csr --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.status.conditions[]?.type=="Approved" and (.status.certificate|length==0)) | .metadata.name'`
- After exceeding 24 hours later they should still persist and be growing in count.

### Anything else we need to know?

HashiVault used for certificate signing. Not so much relevant but does gives context in our use case.

### Kubernetes version

<details>
```console
Client Version: v1.30.8
Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
Server Version: v1.30.8
```
</details>


### Cloud provider

N\A - Bare metal.

```console
$ cat /etc/os-release

NAME="Ubuntu"

```

title: PQC hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) support is missing in etcd component
body:
### What happened?

kubernetes 1.33 is missing to support PQC hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) in etcd because
etcd is still using go version 1.23 version which does not supports this PQC key exchange 

etcd version 3.5.21 is mentioned as module dependency as per https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.33/go.mod#L62

and go version 1.23 is used in etcd(3.5.21)  as per https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/v3.5.21/go.mod#L5



### What did you expect to happen?

I see that in etcd, go version is bumped to 1.24.6 in https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/20527 .

etcd version consisting of this bump will be added in kube 1.33 version or will be part of kube 1.34 only?
