title: Feature Request: Use e2e --prefix flag to identify namespaces/resources created by an e2e run
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Enable the existing e2e framework --prefix flag (defined in TestContext) to be applied to namespaces created during e2e test execution, so that all resources created by an e2e run can be deterministically identified.

### Why is this needed?

1. Downstream CI systems, hosted environments, and long-running clusters executing upstream e2e tests need a reliable and supported mechanism to identify and clean up all resources created by a specific e2e run.
2. After e2e run on the environment, it leaves many cluster-scoped / namespace-scoped resources, which affect the cluster state for the next execution. Right now, we don't have any specific way to identify all leftover resources after e2e run, so we need some logic to identify such resources for clean up. 

**Currently:**

Namespace names vary per test

There is no common identifier tying them to a run

Cleanup often relies on heuristics (time-based, managedFields, etc.)

The framework already exposes a --prefix flag, but it has no effect today.

**Background / Current State**

**Prefix flag exists:**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/framework/test_context.go#L427

Originally introduced (GCE use case), but usage later removed:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/899cf360bad0d9575124a46da455e048b6dfbeb1

Flag is still passed by e2e scripts but currently unused:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/hack/ginkgo-e2e.sh#L278

Namespace creation flow today

Most e2e namespaces are created via:

CreateTestingNS
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/framework/util.go#L323

Although comments suggest using NewFramework, the call chain eventually reaches CreateTestingNS.

The namespace base name comes from hardcoded test definitions, for example:

taints.go (taint-single-pod)
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/node/taints.go#L161

**Other examples:**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/kubectl/exec.go#L57

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e_node/proc_mount_test.go#L40

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/storage/testsuites/capacity.go#L90

**As a result:**

Namespace naming is test-specific

There is no run-level grouping mechanism

**Proposed enhancement (for discussion)**

CreateTestingNS already has access to TestContext and uses other context variables:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/framework/util.go#L362

**Proposal:**

When TestContext.Prefix is non-empty, prepend it to the namespace base name

title: Improve the jitter value for kubelet's serviceAccountToken projected volume source
body:
The current jittering logic in [kubelet token_manager](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd68c5f2409fec7176e6172d6f9d97bd6447c4da/pkg/kubelet/token/token_manager.go#L42) refreshes the token once it has 20% of its lifetime remaining, with 10 seconds of jitter.

Experimentally, this doesn't seem to be enough to really blunt spikes of refresh requests that come from many workloads having a synced refresh.  This can occur when:

* A large deployment is scaled up.  All the new replicas will have synced-up refresh traffic.
* A kubelet restarts.  Because kubelet only holds the tokens in an in-memory cache, it will need to acquire new tokens for all pods on the node after it restarts.  After that, all of the pods will have synced-up refresh traffic.

As an example, here's serviceaccount/token API traffic from a real cluster.  Note how there is a repeating spike every 48 minutes, which is what we would expect from the "refresh after 80%" logic, and the default setting of token lifetime for 1 hour.  Effective jittering logic would be noticeably smoothing these peaks.

We should increase the `maxJitter` value.  Perhaps 5 minutes would be a good value.

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/1017202/133a6c5c-5a6b-4ad1-a1e8-ffb29fae3059)

/sig auth
/kind bug

title: [Umbrella] kubelet/containermanager tech debt payback
body:
Over the past few months, especially during the review process of the pod level resources, in-place resize et. al., a number of tech-debt issues emerged, leading to poor dev experience and suboptimal maintainability.
These issues didn't cause any bug directly, but lead to longer development time, longer reviews and, indeed, higher than necessary maintainership cost. Essentially, we gathered accidental complexity and tech debt which we should pay back to keep the subcomponent healthy.

Therefore, here's a list of (somehow) low hanging fruits.

- [ ] resource managers should have better APIs and don't force consumers to second-guess using the nodeConfig objects. PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128728
- [ ] cpumanager fake Manager should sit in its own subpackage, like client-go
- [ ] cpumanager fake Manager should return a concrete type, not an interface
- [ ] memorymanager fake should sit in its own subpackage, like client-go
- [ ] memorymanager fake Manager should return a concrete type, not an interface
- [ ] provide a simpler way to create a functional cpumanager for testing of other components (e.g. container manager)
- [ ] provide a simpler way to create a functional memorymanager for testing of other components (e.g. container manager)
- [ ] streamline the layout of `cm`: move qos_container_manager in its own subpackage (`pkg/kubelet/cm/qos`)
- [ ] streamline the layout of `cm`: move node_container_manager in its own subpackage (`pkg/kubelet/cm/node`)

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Performance degradation in latency-sensitive services due to CPU affinity loss upon guaranteed QoS Pod scaling down
body:
### What happened?

For the latency-sensitive service in guaranteed QoS Pod, each worker has core affinity with a CPU. 
When the workload decreases, some workers are removed, and the worker's affinity CPUs becoming idle. 
When the Pod scaling down, these idle CPUs were excepted to be removed.
If the busy CPUs which run the busy worker are removed, the performance will be decreased for latency-sensitive services.
For example:
At the begin, there are 2 CPUs (CPU 1 anf CPU 11) are allocated to the Pod when Pod creation.
When the workload increases, Pod scale up, and 4 additional CPUs (CPU 2,12,3,13) are allocated to the Pod, add another 4 workers and set core affinity to each CPU.
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a19807c3-ba8d-40cd-8313-078f5b1afe07)

When the workload decreases, remove worker 4 and worker 5, CPU 3 and CPU 13 are idle, 
Ideal case:
When Pod scale down, idle CPU 3 and CPU 13 are excepted to be removed. the workers not be affected.
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/75cad118-4ff5-457f-b38e-b5b94c48bac1)

Non-ideal case:
When Pod scale down, busy CPU 2 and CPU 12 are removed. the worker2 and worker3 will be affected because of CPU migration due to CPU affinity loss.
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/978b2bbc-f7b3-44b6-9598-2cc9d320810c)

### What did you expect to happen?

When Pod scale down, idle CPU 3 and CPU 13 are removed, and busy CPUs are not removed.

So, we need some method or option to let container tell kubelet which CPU should be keep.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

title: Can't mount iscsi volume with openiscsi from target that does not automatically inform your initiator about changes in that session.
body:
### What happened?

Can't mount iscsi volume in pod. 

I'm creating pod with iscsi volume from NAS using config:
```
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: iscsipd2
spec:
  containers:
  - name: iscsipd-ro
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: "/mnt/iscsipd"
      name: iscsipd-rw
  volumes:
  - name: iscsipd-rw
    iscsi:
      targetPortal: <portalhost/port>
      iqn: <IQN>
      lun: 1
      fsType: ext4
      readOnly: false
```

Pod fails to start reporting:
```
  Warning  FailedMount             2s (x7 over 3m28s)  kubelet                  MountVolume.WaitForAttach failed for volume "iscsipd-rw" : failed to get any path for iscsi disk, last err seen:
Timed out waiting for device at path /dev/disk/by-path/<portal-IQN-Lun> after 30s
```

iSCSI server is Synology NAS which uses open iscsi 2.0-876.

It is possible to mount LUNs onto the host itself manually.

### What did you expect to happen?

Volume mounted.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproducing could be tricky if you don't have version of iscsi that shows similar behaviour.


When kubelet mounts iSCSI volume it executes the following command sequence
(starts here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/642efbb595df18bcac54e1e53ab3d1d4df1569aa/pkg/volume/iscsi/iscsi_util.go#L339)

```
iscsiadm -m discoverydb -t sendtargets -p <portal> -I default -o new
iscsiadm -m discoverydb -t sendtargets -p <portal> -I default --discover
iscsiadm -m node -p <portal> -T <target> -I default -o update -n node.session.scan -v manual
iscsiadm -m node -p <portal> -T <target> -I default --login
iscsiadm -m node -p <portal> -T <target> -o update -n node.startup -v manual
```
After this it will wait for device path to appear once iscsid service on the node attaches to LUN. This unfortunately doesn't happen. The reason is `node.session.scan` being set to `manual` which was introduced in #90982 to address different issue. It is happening because my server doesn't notify initiator about new luns in session when `manual` option is set.

The solution is to rescan active iSCSI session to discover LUN which would trigger device file creation.
The test was to just execute
```
sudo iscsiadm -m node -p <...> -T <...> -I default -R
```
while `kubelet` was waiting for device file.
I then added
```
diff --git a/pkg/volume/iscsi/iscsi_util.go b/pkg/volume/iscsi/iscsi_util.go
index b51127aa92f..239cb075aef 100644
--- a/pkg/volume/iscsi/iscsi_util.go
+++ b/pkg/volume/iscsi/iscsi_util.go
@@ -376,6 +376,12 @@ func (util *ISCSIUtil) AttachDisk(b iscsiDiskMounter) (string, error) {
                                        klog.Warningf("Warning: Failed to set iSCSI login mode to manual. Error: %v", err)
                                }
 
+                               // For targets that don't notify initiator about LUNs added to session we need to trigger recans
+                               _, err = execWithLog(b, "iscsiadm", "-m", "node", "-p", tp, "-T", b.Iqn, "-I", b.Iface, "-R")
+                               if err != nil {
+                                       klog.Warningf("Warning: Failed to trigger rescan of LUNs in session. Error: %v", err)
+                               }
+
                                // Rebuild the host map after logging in
                                portalHostMap, err := b.deviceUtil.GetISCSIPortalHostMapForTarget(b.Iqn)
                                if err != nil {

```
to `kubelet` unconditionally after `--login` command to fix the issue. While it works, I'm sure there might be cases where this behaviour is undesirable, some internet people mentioned rescan being slow. Nevertheless it would be nice to have an option to do rescan either based on config or when mount can't be found within certain time threshold.

### What would you like to be added?

From https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134793#discussion_r2465710724:

> As it stands now, we always set Requests. Would it make sense to detect the special case of "config applies to all requests" and then unset the field to take advantage of "if empty, all requests"? This applies to both class and request configs.
>
> I think the "all requests" check can be simplified to a length check: if a config has as many requests name as there are top-level requests, then it covers all. We can ignore sub-requests because each request is satisfied by exactly one sub-request.

/assign @LionelJouin 

### Why is this needed?

Shorter, more readable allocation results. Semantically it's equivalent.

title: DRA: Non-pod references in ReservedFor prevents removal of pod references
body:
### What happened?

The `status.reservedFor` field in the `ResourceClaim` resource allows for references to arbitrary objects, but only pod references are set by the scheduler and managed by the resourceclaim controller. This involves removing references to a pod when it terminates.

When a non-pod reference is added to the ReservedFor list, either before or after the scheduler adds a pod reference, the pod reference is no longer removed by the resourceclaim controller when the pod terminates.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected that the pod reference would be removed, but that the non-pod reference would remain.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Set up the DRA example driver with Kind as described in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver?tab=readme-ov-file#demo, but don't apply any of the demo workloads.

Apply the following ResourceClaim and Pod:
```
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  name: single-gpu
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
    - name: gpu
      exactly:
        deviceClassName: gpu.example.com
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod0
  labels:
    app: pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ctr0
    image: ubuntu:22.04
    command: ["bash", "-c"]
    args: ["export; trap 'exit 0' TERM; sleep 9999 & wait"]
    resources:
      claims:
      - name: gpu
  resourceClaims:
  - name: gpu
    resourceClaimName: single-gpu
```

Wait until the pod is running.

Edit the ResourceClaim to add the non-pod reference in the `ReservedFor` list:


title: DRA: Scheduler CEL evaluation fails with "no such key" when accessing nested attributes without existence check
body:
### What happened?

I am using DRA with a CEL selector to filter devices based on driver attributes. When writing an expression that accesses a nested field within `device.attributes`, the scheduler encounters a CEL runtime error if the specific driver key does not exist on the device, rather than evaluating the expression to false.

The following expression fails during the DynamicResources filter plugin execution:

```
cel:
  expression: 'device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].sharingStrategy == "runai-fractions"'
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the expression to evaluate to false for devices that do not possess the gpu.nvidia.com attribute, allowing the scheduler to simply skip those devices.

Instead, the scheduler treats this as a hard runtime error, preventing the claim from being allocated even if valid devices exist, or logging significant errors during the filter phase.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: DeviceClass
metadata:
  name: gpu.nvidia.com
spec:
  selectors:
  - cel: 
      expression: "device.driver == 'gpu.nvidia.com'"
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata:
  name: kind-control-plane-gpu-devices-slice
spec:
  nodeName: kind-control-plane
  driver: gpu.nvidia.com

  pool:
    generation: 1
    resourceSliceCount: 1
    name: kind-control-plane-gpu-pool

  devices:
  - name: gpu-0
    bindsToNode: true

  - name: gpu-1
    attributes:
      sharingStrategy:
        string: runai-fractions
    bindsToNode: true
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  name: kind-control-plane-gpu-runai-fractionable-claim-1
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
    - name: gpu-runai-fractionable
      exactly:
        deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com
        capacity:
          requests:
            memory: 10Gi
        selectors:
        - cel:
            expression: 'device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].sharingStrategy == "runai-fractions"'
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: fraction-pod-1
spec:
  resourceClaims:
  - name: fraction-claim
    resourceClaimName: kind-control-plane-gpu-runai-fractionable-claim-1
  containers:
  - name: fraction-container
    resources:
      claims:
      - name: fraction-claim
    image: ubuntu:latest
    command: [ "/bin/bash", "-c", "--" ]
    args: [sleep Infinity"]
```

title: Pod affinity implementation with multiple rules does not match documentation
body:
### What happened?

When using multiple rules in `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution`, they must currently both match the same pod, or else the pod will not be able to be scheduled.

This makes it impossible to use pod affinity to require that a pod be placed on the same node as multiple other separate pods.

### What did you expect to happen?

The [API documentation](https://kubespec.dev/kubernetes/v1/Pod) says this:

> When there are multiple elements, the lists of nodes corresponding to each
> podAffinityTerm are intersected, i.e. all terms must be satisfied.

So I expected that since both rules can be satisfied for the node, the pod should be scheduled on that node.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Assuming a single node cluster:

```yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: required-a
  labels:
    name: required-a
spec:
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: required-b
  labels:
    name: required-b
spec:
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: affinity-test-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
  affinity:
    podAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            name: required-a
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            name: required-b
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
```

title: TOB-K8S-004: Pervasive world-accessible file permissions
body:
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/wg-security-audit/findings/Kubernetes%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Description**
Kubernetes uses files and directories to store information ranging from key-value data to certificate data to logs. However, a number of locations have world-writable directories:

```
cluster/images/etcd/migrate/rollback_v2.go:110:	if err :=
os.MkdirAll(path.Join(migrateDatadir, "member", "snap"), 0777); err != nil {
cluster/images/etcd/migrate/data_dir.go:49:		err := os.MkdirAll(path, 0777)
cluster/images/etcd/migrate/data_dir.go:87:	err = os.MkdirAll(backupDir, 0777)
third_party/forked/godep/save.go:472:	err := os.MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(dst), 0777)
third_party/forked/godep/save.go:585:	err := os.MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(name), 0777)
pkg/volume/azure_file/azure_util.go:34:	defaultFileMode = "0777"
pkg/volume/azure_file/azure_util.go:35:	defaultDirMode  = "0777"
pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go:41:const perm os.FileMode = 0777
```
Figure 7.1: World-writable (0777) directories and defaults

Other areas of the system use world-writable files as well:
```
cluster/images/etcd/migrate/data_dir.go:147:	return ioutil.WriteFile(v.path, data, 0666)
cluster/images/etcd/migrate/migrator.go:120:	err := os.Mkdir(backupDir, 0666)
third_party/forked/godep/save.go:589:	return ioutil.WriteFile(name, []byte(body), 0666)
pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go:306:			if err := m.osInterface.Chmod(containerLogPath, 0666); err != nil {
pkg/volume/cinder/cinder_util.go:271:			ioutil.WriteFile(name, data, 0666)
pkg/volume/fc/fc_util.go:118:	io.WriteFile(fileName, data, 0666)
pkg/volume/fc/fc_util.go:128:			io.WriteFile(name, data, 0666)
pkg/volume/azure_dd/azure_common_linux.go:77:			if err = io.WriteFile(name, data, 0666); err != nil {
pkg/volume/photon_pd/photon_util.go:55:	ioutil.WriteFile(fileName, data, 0666)
pkg/volume/photon_pd/photon_util.go:65:			ioutil.WriteFile(name, data, 0666)
```
Figure 7.2: World-writable (0666) files

A number of locations in the code base also rely on world-readable directories and files. For example, Certificate Signing Requests (CSRs) are written to a directory with mode 0755 (world readable and browseable) with the actual CSR having mode 0644 (world-readable):

```
// WriteCSR writes the pem-encoded CSR data to csrPath.
// The CSR file will be created with file mode 0644.
// If the CSR file already exists, it will be overwritten.
// The parent directory of the csrPath will be created as needed with file mode 0755.
func WriteCSR(csrDir, name string, csr *x509.CertificateRequest) error {
    ... 
    if err := os.MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(csrPath), os.FileMode(0755)); err != nil {
        ...
    }   

    if err := ioutil.WriteFile(csrPath, EncodeCSRPEM(csr), os.FileMode(0644)); err != nil {
       ... 
    }   
    ...
}
```
Figure 7.3: Documentation and code from cmd/kubeadm/app/util/pkiutil/pki_helpers.go

**Exploit Scenario**
Alice wishes to migrate some etcd values during normal cluster maintenance. Eve has local access to the cluster’s filesystem, and modifies the values stored during the migration process, granting Eve further access to the cluster as a whole.

**Recommendation**
Short term, audit all locations that use world-accessible permissions. Revoke those that are unnecessary. Very few files truly need to be readable by any user on a system. Almost none should need to allow arbitrary system users write access. 

Long term, use system groups and extended Access Control Lists (ACLs) to ensure that all files and directories created by Kuberenetes are accessible by only those users and groups that should be able to access them. This will ensure that only the appropriate users with the correct Unix-level groups may access data. Kubernetes may describe what these groups should be, or create a role-based system to which administrators may assign users and groups.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

See #81146 for current status of all issues created from these findings.

The vendor gave this issue an ID of TOB-K8S-004 and it was finding 8 of the report.

The vendor considers this issue Medium Severity.

To view the original finding, begin on page 32 of the [Kubernetes Security Review Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/wg-security-audit/findings/Kubernetes%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Environment**:

- Kubernetes version: 1.13.4

title: Kubectl apply does not remove manually added env vars, causing permanent drift between manifest and live Deployment
body:
### What would you like to be added?

What happened?

We manage Deployments declaratively using kubectl apply (server-side apply) from GitOps pipelines.

In production, a user manually edited a Deployment (kubectl edit deployment) and added an extra environment variable directly under:
spec.template.spec.containers[].env

Later, the Deployment was redeployed using kubectl apply -f <manifest.yaml> with a manifest that does not contain this manually added env var.

Despite successful apply and no reported conflicts, the manually added environment variable remains present in the live Deployment.

This results in permanent configuration drift between the manifest and the cluster state.


### Why is this needed?

We expected the live Deployment to exactly match the applied manifest, such that:
Environment variables not present in the manifest are removed from the Deployment
kubectl apply enforces declarative state, even for mergeable lists like env
The applied manifest becomes the source of truth

In short:
After apply, the cluster state should be fully in sync with the manifest.

**How can we reproduce it**
1. create a deployment

    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: sample-app
    spec:
      replicas: 1
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app: sample
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: sample
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: app
            image: nginx
            env:
            - name: Testing
              value: "working"
    
    kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

2. Manually edit the Deployment

    kubectl edit deployment sample-app
  
    env:
    - name: Testing2
      value: workingNot

  kubectl describe deployment sample-app

3. Re-apply the original manifest
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

4. Observe the result
kubectl describe deployment sample-app
❌ Testing2=workingNot still exists, even though it is not in the manifest.

**Anything else we need to know?**
Even tried with the below commands 
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml --server-side --force-conflicts --field-manager=gitops
Still it is not able to remove the additional env variables. 

There is currently no supported way to say:
“This list must exactly match the manifest.”
using kubectl apply

**Kubernetes version**
1.32.6

**Cloud provider**
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)

title: Add `apisever_watch_decode_errors_total` metric to track watch stream decode failures
body:
### What happened?

#### Problem statement
Currently, `apiserver_storage_decode_errors_total` only tracks CRUD decode errors. Watch decode errors are unmonitored, making it impossible to validate whether decode errors are caused by unreachable webhook(`conversion_webhook_call_failure`) or potential data corruption.

#### Use Case: Detecting Data Corruption
When investigating decode errors, operators need to distinguish:

1. Webhook-induced decode errors (expected) - webhook validation/mutation failures that prevent proper encoding
2. Potential Data corruption (critical) - actual corruption in etcd or during transmission

#### Detection method
If: webhook_failures == storage_decode_errors + watch_decode_errors
Then: All decode errors are webhook-induced (no data corruption)


If: storage_decode_errors + watch_decode_errors > webhook_failures  
Then: **Potential** Data corruption detected! (decode errors exceed webhook failures)


### What did you expect to happen?

Add `apiserver_watch_decode_errors_total` to complete observability:

```
watchDecodeErrorCounts = compbasemetrics.NewCounterVec(
    &compbasemetrics.CounterOpts{
        Namespace:      "apiserver",
        Name:           "watch_decode_errors_total",
        Help:           "Number of watch event decode errors split by object type",
        StabilityLevel: compbasemetrics.ALPHA,
    },
    []string{"group", "resource"},
)
```
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8c9c67c000104450cfc5a5f48053a9a84b73cf93/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L759
```
func decodeObj(codec runtime.Codec, versioner storage.Versioner, data []byte, rev int64, groupResource schema.GroupResource, key string) (_ runtime.Object, err error) {
	obj, err := runtime.Decode(codec, []byte(data))
	if err != nil {
		...
		metrics.RecordWatchDecodeError(groupResource)
		klog.V(2).Infof("Watch decoding %s \"%s\" failed due to %v", groupResource, key, err)
		return nil, err
	}
	...
	return obj, nil
}
```

Benefits:

- Enable corruption detection: Can now validate `conversion_webhook_call_failure` == `total_decode_errors`
- Complete observability: All decode paths are monitored
- Better alerting: Alert on decode_errors > webhook_failures for real corruption



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Update config to use unexisting webhook to introduce webhook failure

### Anything else we need to know?

1.35 (theoretically any version enabled listWatch cacher Decode path)

title: goroutine leak in DynamicPluginProber (PersistentVolumeAttachDetachController)
body:
DynamicPluginProber is used by two controllers:
- PersistentVolumeAttachDetachController
- SELinuxWarningController (disabled by default)

This plugin creates an fsnotify watcher: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/flexvolume/probe.go#L50

The fsnotify watcher has a `Run()` function that fetches indefinitely with no way to stop:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/util/filesystem/watcher.go#L77-L93

/cc @tchap 
/sig storage

title: Create New Test Cases for Pod Lifecycle Events
body:
**What should be added?**
This issue focuses on writing new test cases that cover Pod lifecycle events in Kubernetes. The aim is to create a suite of tests that thoroughly document and validate the behaviours throughout the Pod lifecycle. These tests will ensure that Pods function correctly during various phases, including creation, deletion, probe handling, restart policies, and termination scenarios.

Tasks:
- [ ] Create a new directory structure to organise tests by area and behaviour: test/e2e_node/AREA/BEHAVIOUR-SHORTNAME_test.go
 
**Write test cases for the following Pod lifecycle behaviours:**

Pod Phases:

- [ ]  Pending 
- [ ]  Running
- [ ]  Succeeded
- [ ]  Failed
- [ ]  Unknown

Container States:

- [ ]  Waiting
- [ ]  Running
- [ ] Terminated

Lifecycle Hooks:

- [ ] postStart Hook
- [ ] preStop Hook

Probes:

 - [ ] Liveness Probe
 - [ ] Readiness Probe 
 - [ ] Startup Probe

Restart Policies:

 - [ ] Always
 - [ ] OnFailure
 - [ ] Never

Pod Termination

 - [ ] Graceful Termination
 - [ ] Forced Termination

CrashLoopBackOff

- [ ] Test how Kubernetes handles retries when containers fail repeatedly and enter backoff.

Pod Conditions:

- [ ] PodScheduled: 
- [ ] Initialised
- [ ] ContainersReady:
- [ ] Ready

Fault Recovery:

- [ ] Initial Container Failure
- [ ] Repeated Failures

Node Failure and Pod Eviction:

- [ ] Test what happens when Pods are evicted due to node failure or resource shortages.
Pod Garbage Collection:
- [ ] Test the behaviour of the Kubernetes garbage collector when removing terminated Pods.

Sidecar Containers and Pod Shutdown:

 - [ ] Test how Kubernetes handles the termination order of sidecar containers during Pod shutdown.

**Expected Outcome:**
A set of well-organised and documented test files that demonstrate key Pod lifecycle behaviours, ensuring Pods function as expected throughout their lifecycle.

title: SAST. Potential bugs
body:
1. In /cmd/kubeadm/app/cmd/reset.go [on line 106 of the newResetData function](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kubeadm/app/cmd/reset.go#L106) an uninitialized initCfg pointer is declared. 
The initCfg pointer is initialized [on line 139](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kubeadm/app/cmd/reset.go#L139) when calling the FetchInitConfigurationFromCluster function, if the FetchInitConfigurationFromCluster function returned a tuple of nil, err, then the function is not exited. On [on line 170](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kubeadm/app/cmd/reset.go#L170) a potential nil dereference may occur when accessing the ClusterConfiguration field.
2. In [pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox_linux.go on the line 57](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox_linux.go#L57) is the cpuRequest pointer, which is initialized when the condition for equality of the variable cpuRequestExists is true on line 58. When [calling the calculateLinuxResources](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox_linux.go#L66) function and passing cpuRequest as an argument, a null pointer may be dereferenced.
3. In [/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/cp/cp.go on the line 304](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/cp/cp.go#L304 ) opens a bidirectional read-start channel, in case of exit [on line 316](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/cp/cp.go#L316), the goroutine for closing allocated resources does not close. Resource leakage is possible.
4. In [/pkg/registry/core/serviceaccount/storage/token.go on the line 98](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/core/serviceaccount/storage/token.go#L98 ) the name parameter is used in the error, although the namespace parameter was validated. It might be more correct to use namespace on line 98.
Could you tell me please, am I right in evaluating these static analyzer triggers as TP?

title: projected serviceAccountToken do not honour defaultMode or readOnly: true (tested in 1.30)
body:
### What happened?

We have a container which needs to start as root today (because we install packages, mount a docker socket and the like). But then we change uid to a lower privilege user for the rest of time. 

That user needs access to a projected serviceAccountToken to access another service. The user cannot read the file because its mode is rw-------.

So, we set defaultMode on the projected volume definition, but this has no effect.

We also had readOnly: true in the mount definition, and that seems to not have effect either, as the mode was still rw------- not r--------.

<details>

<summary>Sample Pod definitions</summary>

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: with-mode
  namespace: robertc-scratch
spec:
      containers:
      - command:
        - sleep
        - "604800"
        image: ubuntu
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        name: test
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          runAsUser: 0
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /secrets/token
          name: token
      volumes:
      - name: token
        projected:
          defaultMode: 292
          sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: with-readonly
  namespace: robertc-scratch
spec:
      containers:
      - command:
        - sleep
        - "604800"
        image: ubuntu
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        name: test
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          runAsUser: 0
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /secrets/token
          name: token
          readOnly: true
      volumes:
      - name: token
        projected:
          sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token

```

</details>

The test I did in making a SSCCE was to run this:
```
kubectl --namespace robertc-scratch exec -ti with-mode -- ls -l /secrets/token/..data/
total 4
-rw------- 1 root root 1414 Jan  3 17:45 token
@rbtcollins ➜ /workspaces/infrastructure (rbt/agent-permissions-3) $ kubectl --namespace robertc-scratch exec -ti with-mode -- ls -l /secrets/token/..data/
total 4
-rw------- 1 root root 1414 Jan  3 17:45 token
```

We checked the [documentation ](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/projected-volumes/#introduction) and it describes defaultMode with no restrictions on its relevance to difference sources. The API reference is no more useful.




### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the defaultMode setting to apply to the serviceAccountToken. All the same reasons one might want a different mode for a projected secret or config map also apply to a projected serviceAccountToken.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See above.

### Anything else we need to know?

Probably not ;) .

title: Panic when comparing two interface.
body:
### What happened?

When I used ArgoCD, I found [this line](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/strategicpatch/patch.go#L955) will result in panic if two compared values are `map[string]interface`. The call was initiated from [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/strategicpatch/patch.go#L2105). If the passed in entry does not follow the schema, it may result the two compared values are `map[string]interface` and will raise panic.

### What did you expect to happen?

From the function `CreateThreeWayMergePatch`'s comments, it should either return the error said the input does not follow the schema or do the comparison. Panic should not be raised. I proposed reflect.DeepEqual could be used instead of "=="

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

If the struct does not follow the schema and give one field as map[string]interface instead of string, and calling `CreateThreeWayMergePatch`, the panic will be raised.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: TopologySpreadConstraint not acting well When multiple deployments rollout at same time
body:
### What happened?

TopologySpreadConstraint not acting well When multiple deployments rollout at same time

### What did you expect to happen?

All deployments should have 1 pod locate in each az

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Pre-requisites: a 2 az cluster,  2 replicas deployments with 1 pod in each az.

1. apply topologySpreadConstraint with maxSkew=1 and whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule. to all deployments
2. rollout all deployments at same time

After deployment rollout some deployment have 2 pods locate in 1 az for sometimes

### Anything else we need to know?

According to [87621](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/87621#issuecomment-579613755)  `"update" event comes before "add" event, and then the real "delete" event comes` but there might be some other circumstances

title: OpenAPI loading double-buffering (or triple-buffering)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

While inspecting the code for https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/discovery/cached/disk/cached_discovery.go, it appears that we buffer the OpenAPI response _twice_ as a []byte, once in io.ReadAll when we are reading it for parsing, and once in the HTTP caching layer.

Arguably we need 3x the memory because our json parser is not streaming, so we retain the []byte while we unmarshal into the OpenAPI types.

Given we are writing it to disk anyway, we should probably just write to a temp file.

### Why is this needed?

This is inefficient, and is visible in memory profiles.

I think we can also eliminate two library dependencies from our stack (possibly even 3).: https://github.com/gregjones/httpcache is archived.  diskv has not had many updates in years.  diskv pulls in google/btree, so we might also be able to eliminate that.

title: feature request: add Kind/ResourceScope support in APIService model
Ceph RBD CSI volume statistics missing from kubelet endpoints after upgrade to v1.34.0
body:
### What happened?

After upgrading from Kubernetes v1.33.4 to v1.34.0, all CSI volume statistics disappeared from both kubelet `/stats/summary` and `/metrics` endpoints. CSI volumes continue to function normally, but monitoring data is completely unavailable.

### What did you expect to happen?

CSI volumes should appear in kubelet's `/stats/summary` endpoint with `availableBytes`, `capacityBytes`, and `usedBytes` data, and corresponding `kubelet_volume_stats_*` metrics should be available at the /metrics endpoint.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Upgrade a cluster from Kubernetes v1.33.x to v1.34.0
2. Ensure you have active Ceph RBD CSI volumes
3. Check kubelet metrics: `kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/metrics" | grep kubelet_volume_stats`
4. Check stats summary: `kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/stats/summary" | jq '.pods[].volume[].name'`
5. Observe: Zero CSI volumes in both endpoints, only non-CSI volumes like "tmp", "kube-api-access-*" appear

### Anything else we need to know?

- Similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/98476
- CSI operations work: 24,000+ successful NodeGetVolumeStats calls logged
- CSI driver responds correctly: Returns valid data `"usage":[{"available":90295296,"total":92500992,"unit":"BYTES","used":108544}]`
- Kubelet collection metrics increment: `kubelet_volume_metric_collection_duration_seconds_count{metric_source="rbd.csi.ceph.com"}` shows successful attempts
- Volume stats metrics missing: `grep kubelet_volume_stats` returns nothing from `/metrics`
- Stats summary incomplete: Only non-CSI volumes appear in `/stats/summary`

title: Refactor pkg/scheduler/backend/queue tests to use mocks instead of a real metric registry
body:
/kind cleanup

Tests in pkg/scheduler/backend/queue (example: TestPendingPodsMetric https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/scheduling_queue_test.go#L3298) test metric export using `k8s.io/component-base/metrics/testutil.GatherAndCompare`, also calling real  `metrics.Register` and using real `MetricAsyncRecorder`.
This should be refactored to use a mock/fake MetricAsyncRecorder and verify calls to this object, as opposed to verifying actual metrics collected.
As a safety measure, a single simple test case that verifies collected metrics can be left in the code in its current shape (e.g. `TestPendingPodsMetric_add pods to activeQ and unschedulablePods`), but the main test logic should be based on mocks.

title: genfeaturegates: Add linkCode and linkKEPs to json output for consistency with markdown
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The recently added [genfeaturegates tool](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/genfeaturegates/genfeaturegates.go) outputs feature gate information in both Markdown and json formats. However, I noticed that the json output is missing `linkCode` and `linkKEPs` fields that are present in the markdown output.

Markdown output includes:
- `[code](https://cs.k8s.io/?q=...&repos=kubernetes/kubernetes)`
- `[KEPs](https://cs.k8s.io/?q=...&repos=kubernetes/enhancements)`

JSON output currently lacks these links.

### Why is this needed?

I'm working on k/docs (kubernetes/website) and discovered this inconsistency.
Having consistent output between formats would help tools and documentation that consume the json output.

### Proposal

Unless there is a specific reason for omitting these fields from json, I would like to add `linkCode` and `linkKEPs` fields to match what's already in the Markdown output.

title: tracker: improve the kubelet test coverage
body:
There is a strong and growing consensus in sig-node about the need of increasing the test coverage in the kubelet, improving the current testsuite about coverage and reliability. See for example the [April 26 sig-node meeting notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Ne57gvidMEWXR70OxxnRkYquAoMpt56o75oZtg-OeBg/edit#heading=h.d9zp2j5jvkke) and the [April 27 sig-node CI subgroup meeting notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fb-ugvgdSVIkkuJ388_nhp2pBTy_4HEVg5848Xy7n5U/edit#heading=h.2v8vzknys4nk).

This work has already begun and there are already some PR posted (see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108024#pullrequestreview-954083698). This is a great start. There are more areas in the kubelet, especially in the container manager and resource manager area, that can use better unit test coverage.

Besides the obvious benefits of documenting and preserving the current behaviour, adding tests is meant to lower the barrier for future work and contributions.

Examples of some areas which can benefit of more tests:

- k/k/pkg/kubelet/cm/internal_container_lifecycle.go
- k/k/pkg/kubelet/cm/internal_container_lifecycle_linux.go
- k/k/pkg/kubelet/cm/pod_container_manager_linux.go
- k/k/pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go
- everything coverage-driven (check [test code coverage](https://go.dev/blog/cover) and build from there)
- error paths in general
-  e2e tests in general

title: setcap build image shouldn't require a shell
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Building with a more vanilla setcap image shouldn't require a shell in the image to run the command 


in `build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile`

```sh
# We apply cap_net_bind_service so that kube-apiserver can be run as
# non-root and still listen on port less than 1024
RUN setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /${BINARY}
```

this command requires the `SETCAP_IMAGE` have a shell in order to:
1) RUN a command that isn't in the form of ["/usr/sbin/setcap", "..."] 
2) shell expand the `${BINARY}` argument


### Why is this needed?

By making this change you can eliminate the need of having a shell in the setcap image:


```diff
diff --git a/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile b/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile
index 27129d29bd9..acfe8c26f22 100644
--- a/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile
+++ b/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile
@@ -20,11 +20,11 @@ ARG SETCAP_IMAGE
 # to setup qemu for the builder.
 FROM --platform=linux/$BUILDARCH ${SETCAP_IMAGE}
 ARG BINARY
-COPY --chmod=755 ${BINARY} /${BINARY}
+COPY --chmod=755 ${BINARY} /set_cap_binary
 # We apply cap_net_bind_service so that kube-apiserver can be run as
 # non-root and still listen on port less than 1024
-RUN setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /${BINARY}
+RUN ["setcap", "cap_net_bind_service=+ep", "/set_cap_binary"]
 
 FROM --platform=linux/$TARGETARCH ${BASEIMAGE}
 ARG BINARY
-COPY --from=0 /${BINARY} /usr/local/bin/${BINARY}
+COPY --from=0 /set_cap_binary /usr/local/bin/${BINARY}
```

title: Deletion of resources can fail due to etcd size limit
body:
Steps:

- Create a resource that is just barely within the etcd size limit
- Delete the resource, which triggers an update to etcd to record the intent to delete the resource
- Because the update adds fields like deleteTimestamp, the size of the resource increases
- When the size exceeds the etcd size limit, the update-to-record-intent-to-delete fails to be recorded to etcd, causing the deletion operation to fail

title: kubelet static pod initialization doesn't replicate API defaulting+PrepareForCreate+PrepareForUpdate
body:
When kubelet reads pod manifests from disk, it bypasses API server defaulting / strategy initialization

It tries to replicate that by:
1. decoding with defaulting (which replicates API server defaulting): 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a90cf500049d228f5ee4d217c4714028eb9c5f35/pkg/kubelet/config/common.go#L115-L122

2. applying its own calculated versions of generated fields like uid / generated name / etc:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a90cf500049d228f5ee4d217c4714028eb9c5f35/pkg/kubelet/config/common.go#L60-L82

However, it is missing any fields set at pod creation time by podStrategy#PrepareForCreate:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a90cf500049d228f5ee4d217c4714028eb9c5f35/pkg/registry/core/pod/strategy.go#L86-L110

This is likely to break assumptions in the kubelet that every pod it encounters has gone through those strategy methods. We should consider having the kubelet call both of those functions on static pods.

cc @tallclair @thockin 
/sig node
/kind bug

title: Make healthCheckNodePort Optional for On-Premises LoadBalancer Services with externalTrafficPolicy: Local
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Introduce a way to disable automatic allocation of healthCheckNodePort for LoadBalancer services when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set, particularly for on-premises environments where external load balancers do not rely on this port.

### Why is this needed?

In on-premises Kubernetes/OpenShift clusters using MetalLB with BGP and external load balancers (e.g., F5), the healthCheckNodePort is not used. However, Kubernetes still allocates and exposes this port when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set.

**This leads to:**

Unnecessary open ports on nodes.
Potential security concerns.
Port exhaustion risks in large-scale clusters.
Operational confusion for administrators.
There is currently no native way to disable this behavior while preserving externalTrafficPolicy: Local, which is often required for source IP preservation.

**Proposed Solution**
Introduce an opt-out mechanism for healthCheckNodePort allocation, such as:

**Option 1: Annotation-based opt-out**

metadata:
  annotations:
    service.kubernetes.io/disable-healthcheck-nodeport: "true"

**Option 2: API field**

spec:
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  disableHealthCheckNodePort: true

**Risks and Mitigations**
Misconfiguration could lead to traffic being sent to unhealthy nodes if the external load balancer is not properly configured.
Clear documentation and validation should accompany the feature to ensure safe usage.
**Additional Context**
This enhancement would benefit on-premises setups where:

MetalLB is used with BGP.
External load balancers perform their own health checks.
healthCheckNodePort is not required and adds unnecessary complexity.

title: Informer/Reflector in client-go do not support receiving resources in Table format
Improve error messages for CEL validation
body:
### What would you like to be added?

When I use CEL validation as of today I get messages that not easy to parse for users, e.g.

```
* spec.name: Invalid value: "string": name must consist of lower case alphanumeric characters
* spec.pods: Invalid value: "array": entries in pods must be unique
```

More specifically, looks “string” or "array" is not reporting the actual value of the field but the field type.

This can be reproduced by creating a kind cluster (I used K8s v1.32.0), applying the following CRD:

```
---
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  annotations:
    controller-gen.kubebuilder.io/version: v0.18.0
  name: testresources.test.cluster.x-k8s.io
spec:
  group: test.cluster.x-k8s.io
  names:
    kind: TestResource
    listKind: TestResourceList
    plural: testresources
    singular: testresource
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1beta1
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        description: TestResource defines a test resource.
        properties:
          apiVersion:
            description: |-
              APIVersion defines the versioned schema of this representation of an object.
              Servers should convert recognized schemas to the latest internal value, and
              may reject unrecognized values.
              More info: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#resources
            type: string
          kind:
            description: |-
              Kind is a string value representing the REST resource this object represents.
              Servers may infer this from the endpoint the client submits requests to.
              Cannot be updated.
              In CamelCase.
              More info: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#types-kinds
            type: string
          metadata:
            type: object
          spec:
            description: TestResourceSpec defines the resource spec.
            properties:
              name:
                maxLength: 253
                minLength: 1
                type: string
                x-kubernetes-validations:
                - message: name must consist of lower case alphanumeric characters
                  rule: self.matches('^[a-z0-9]*$')
              pods:
                items:
                  maxLength: 256
                  minLength: 1
                  type: string
                maxItems: 32
                minItems: 1
                type: array
                x-kubernetes-list-type: atomic
                x-kubernetes-validations:
                - message: entries in pods must be unique
                  rule: self.all(x, self.exists_one(y, x == y))
            required:
            - name
            type: object
          status:
            description: TestResourceStatus defines the status of a TestResource.
            properties:
              availableReplicas:
                format: int32
                type: integer
              readyReplicas:
                format: int32
                type: integer
              replicas:
                format: int32
                type: integer
              upToDateReplicas:
                format: int32
                type: integer
              version:
                maxLength: 256
                minLength: 1
                type: string
            type: object
        type: object
    served: true
    storage: true
    subresources:
      status: {}
```

And then the following yaml to create an invalid resource

```yml
apiVersion: test.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: TestResource
metadata:
  name: invalid
spec:
  name: $__
  pods:
    - foo
    - foo
```


FYI there was some discussion in https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C02TTBG6LF4/p1750091061651119 about this issue, capturing here some relevant points:

<details>
@sbueringer 
I would probably expect from a user pov that no message prefix is added if message or messageExpression is set

@erikgb 
From a developer POV I think it is nice to get some context automatically injected into the error message. :wink: But I would prefer the invalid value to be echoed, and not the type. So I agree there is a bug somewhere.

@JoelSpeed 
When you add an XValidation, you can specify the type of the error, whether it's Invalid, Forbidden etc, that is where this context is coming from, I wonder if this is specifically an issue with Invalid, or whether the same also applies to Forbidden or other error types

@liggitt 
maybe something like this would work
```diff
diff --git a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/schema/cel/validation.go b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/schema/cel/validation.go
index 575fd5e2e9a..2a3f7ca29df 100644
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/schema/cel/validation.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/schema/cel/validation.go
@@ -476,15 +476,16 @@ func (s *Validator) validateExpressions(ctx context.Context, fldPath *field.Path
 						return errs, -1
 					} else {
 						klog.V(2).ErrorS(msgErr, "messageExpression evaluation failed")
-						addErr(fieldErrorForReason(currentFldPath, sts.Type, ruleMessageOrDefault(rule), rule.Reason))
+						addErr(fieldErrorForReason(currentFldPath, obj, ruleMessageOrDefault(rule), rule.Reason))
 						remainingBudget = newRemainingBudget
 					}
 				} else {
-					addErr(fieldErrorForReason(currentFldPath, sts.Type, messageExpression, rule.Reason))
+					// messageExpression is expected to embed the value if desired
+					addErr(fieldErrorForReason(currentFldPath, field.OmitValueType{}, messageExpression, rule.Reason))
 					remainingBudget = newRemainingBudget
 				}
 			} else {
-				addErr(fieldErrorForReason(currentFldPath, sts.Type, ruleMessageOrDefault(rule), rule.Reason))
+				addErr(fieldErrorForReason(currentFldPath, obj, ruleMessageOrDefault(rule), rule.Reason))
 			}
 		}
 	}
@@ -675,7 +676,13 @@ func fieldErrorForReason(fldPath *field.Path, value interface{}, detail string,
 	case apiextensions.FieldValueDuplicate:
 		return field.Duplicate(fldPath, value)
 	default:
-		return field.Invalid(fldPath, value, detail)
+		displayValue := value
+		switch value.(type) {
+		case map[string]any, []any:
+			// avoid outputting complex structured field values
+			displayValue = field.OmitValueType{}
+		}
+		return field.Invalid(fldPath, displayValue, detail)
 	}
 }
```
needs good tests and such
</details>
/sig api-machinery
/cc @liggitt 

### Why is this needed?

Improve UX when CRD implements validation rules using CEL

title: Improve tracing observability for streamed responses (KEP-3157 and KEP-5116)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to propose an improvement to the Kubernetes tracing system to provide more granular visibility into streamed responses. Specifically, I propose wrapping each io.Writer in a wrapper that measures both the latency and the number of bytes processed at each stage of the response writing process.

This improvement would allow the tracing system to break down the overall latency into distinct categories:

1. Network: Time spent sending data over the network.
2. Compress: Time spent in the compression layer (e.g., gzip).
3. Serialize: Time spent serializing objects into the response format.

Each stage should report the accurate size of the data processed and its individual latency. 

Proof of concept: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136001

**Integration with Tracing:** Initial PoC hardcodes the steps, however we could make the implementation generic and properly integrate streamed/concurrent operation into the tracing framework.

**Performance Consideration:** Adding time.Now() and time.Since() calls to each writer call introduces a negligible overhead of approximately 100ns per call. For a response containing 100,000 objects, the total cost would be roughly 10ms.

/cc @wojtek-t @mborsz @richabanker @p0lyn0mial @jpbetz 
/sig scalability
/sig api-machinery
/sig instrumentation

### Why is this needed?

The current implementation of Kubernetes tracing assumes that all computation is executed in clear, discrete steps. However, with the introduction of KEP-5116 (Streaming Encoding for LIST Responses) and KEP-3157 (WatchList), the existing traces have become ineffective for performance debugging.

Currently, traces for streamed responses:

* Mix compression, encoding, and network latencies into a single reported value.
* Show inaccurate values for object sizes (e.g., reporting only the size of the first chunk instead of the total data).

Without this improvement, it is impossible to determine whether a slow response is caused by network bottlenecks, serialization overhead, or compression delays.

**Before**

Streamed response writing results in traces mixing compressing, encoding and network. As result it only shows combined latency and inaccurate values of sizes. As measured on client side, the size presented in "About to start writing response" writer:*gzip.Writer,size:201240 227ms” is incorrect as it’s not the amount of data compressed, but the size of the first chunk. 

```
Trace[1461829279]: ["SerializeObject" audit-id:e2ed459c-4f3c-47e4-abb3-099e8a4ad38d,method:GET,url:/api/v1/namespaces/0/pods,protocol:HTTP/2.0,mediaType:application/vnd.kubernetes.protobuf,encoder:{"encodeGV":"v1","encoder":"protobuf","name":"versioning"} 9230ms (12:49:16.965)
Trace[1461829279]:  ---"About to start writing response" writer:*gzip.Writer,size:201240 227ms (12:49:17.192)
Trace[1461829279]:  ---"Write call succeeded" size:1006056694 9003ms (12:49:26.196)]
Trace[1461829279]: ---"Writing http response done" count:10000 0ms (12:49:26.196)
Trace[1461829279]: [9.244573577s] [9.244573577s] END
```

**After:**

With improved tracing we see three separate latencies: Network, Compress and Serialize. Each shows individual latency measurement and accurate size of data processed. Here we can see that gzip archives around a 5x compression ratio, which checks out on client side.

```
Trace[2139214577]: ["SerializeObject" audit-id:858bb641-5ba4-44d5-8e6a-d60e6609d4ed,method:GET,url:/api/v1/namespaces/0/pods,protocol:HTTP/2.0,mediaType:application/vnd.kubernetes.protobuf,encoder:{"encodeGV":"v1","encoder":"protobuf","name":"versioning"} 9246ms (13:54:00.023)
Trace[2139214577]:  ---"Network" size:188001850 2796ms
Trace[2139214577]:  ---"Compress" size:1006056312 4966ms
Trace[2139214577]:  ---"Serialize" count:10000 1483ms
Trace[2139214577]:  ---"Write call succeeded" 0ms (13:54:09.270)]
Trace[2139214577]: [9.251880697s] [9.251880697s] END
```
**Bonus WatchList:**
```
I0102 15:08:04.102809       1 trace.go:250] Trace[1455537276]: "SerializeObject" audit-id:bfdf3082-2666-44b7-b8cc-0208147aa063,method:GET,url:/api/v1/namespaces/0/pods,protocol:HTTP/2.0,mediaType:application/vnd.kubernetes.protobuf;stream=watch,encoder:{"encodeGV":"v1","encoder":"raw-protobuf","name":"versioning"} (02-Jan-2026 15:08:00.061) (total time: 4041ms):
Trace[1455537276]: ---"Network" size:1003095731 3031ms
Trace[1455537276]: ---"Serialize" count:10000 986ms
Trace[1455537276]: [4.041542797s] [4.041542797s] END
```

title: preStop sleep continues after PID 1 exits
body:
### What happened?

I've configured the podSpec of a Job to include a preStop sleep lifecycle hook. If the Pod is asked to terminate before it completes, the preStop sleep begins and runs for its full duration - even if the Pod completes its processing and PID 1 exits before the preStop sleep is complete. The Pod remains in "Terminating" and the Job remains in "Running" state until the preStop sleep finishes, which delays the completion of the Job.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the preStop sleep to end when PID 1 in the Pod exits. The Job should be marked as complete at that time and the Pod should finish terminating. This is the behavior when a preStop exec is used to run the sleep command in the container's shell.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Define a Job with a preStop sleep lifecycle hook:

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sleep-job
spec:
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - command:
          - /bin/sleep
          - "60"
          image: busybox:latest
          name: sleep-container
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              sleep:
                seconds: 120
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
      restartPolicy: Never
```

Apply the manifest and then delete the resulting Pod. Observe that the Pod is now in "Terminating" state. The preStop sleep will have begun.

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl apply -f sleep-job.yaml 
job.batch/sleep-job created
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           6s         6s

NAME                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Running   0          6s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl delete pods sleep-job-qh2qk
pod "sleep-job-qh2qk" deleted
^Cwedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           24s        24s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          24s
```

After 60 seconds the Pod should complete but instead it remains in Terminating state and the Job shows 0 completions. Only after 2 minutes has elapsed (from the time the `delete` command was issued) does the Pod finish terminating and the Job shows a completion.

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           59s        59s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          59s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           69s        69s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          69s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           2m19s      2m19s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          2m19s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Complete   1/1           2m21s      2m22s
```


### Anything else we need to know?

This kind of configuration is useful to ensure that batch jobs run to completion even if they are asked to terminate for whatever reason (maintenance, preemption, autoscaler consolidation, etc.). The fact that the Job takes longer to complete when the Pod is asked to terminate is problematic when timely completion of the Job is desired. Imagine that the Job takes an hour instead of a minute and so the prestop sleep is set to 3600. Then imagine that the Pod is asked to terminate at minute 59. The duration of the Job will now be 119 minutes instead of 60.

Using a preStop exec to run /bin/sleep produces the expected behavior where the Pod finishes terminating and the Job shows as complete when PID 1 in the container exits. Of course this won't work in a shell-less container which AFAIK is the reason the preStop sleep was introduced.

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: exec-job
spec:
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - command:
          - /bin/sleep
          - "60"
          image: busybox:latest
          name: exec-container
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["/bin/sleep", "120"]
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
      restartPolicy: Never
```

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl apply -f exec-job.yaml 
job.batch/exec-job created
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           4s         4s

NAME                 READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Running   0          4s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl delete pods exec-job-k62r4
pod "exec-job-k62r4" deleted
^Cwedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           23s        23s

NAME                 READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Terminating   0          23s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           55s        55s

NAME                 READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Terminating   0          55s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           61s        61s

NAME                 READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Terminating   0          61s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Complete   1/1           63s        64s
```

title: List watch request for Events with stale resourceVersion responds immediately without error
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


#### What happened:
Per the [documentation on using watches](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#efficient-detection-of-changes) I attempted to resume a timed out watch for `events.k8s.io/v1` `Event` objects by issuing a new List request with the `watch` parameter set and the `resourceVersion` set to the last `Event` object I'd received on the watch.

However, by the time I issued the new request that `resourceVersion` was stale.  The response I received from the K8S API was an immediate HTTP 200 with an empty request body.  (This confused the K8S library I was using which was expecting a 410 Gone error in that case, and resulted in a busy-loop of retrying over and over which put strain on the K8S API server.)

#### What you expected to happen:
I expected the watch request to receive a response with some form of `410 Gone` error (either in the HTTP status code or as some form of JSON error object in the response body).  This is the documented behavior, and I was able to verify that this is what happens for other resource types like Secrets.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

##### How to reproduce the failure for Events
Ensure there are recorded events in the Kubernetes cluster, e.g., `kubectl -n YOUR-NS-HERE get events.events.k8s.io` yields a non-empty output.

Then request a watch for events with a known stale `resourceVersion`.
```
$ curl -i -kE k3s.client.pem 'https://localhost:6443/apis/events.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/YOUR-NS-HERE/events?&watch=1&resourceVersion=1'      
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Thu, 05 Aug 2021 15:58:57 GMT
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

```

Note that even though the `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header is given, the K8S API server closes the connection immediately after serving an empty response.

##### How to reproduce correct behavior for an alternate Resource type (e.g., a Secret)
```
$ curl -i -kE k3s.client.pem 'https://localhost:6443/api/v1/namespaces/YOUR-NS-HERE/secrets?&watch=true&resourceVersion=1'                                                                                                          HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Thu, 05 Aug 2021 15:58:40 GMT
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

{"type":"ERROR","object":{"kind":"Status","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{},"status":"Failure","message":"too old resource version: 1 (1126176)","reason":"Expired","code":410}}
```

#### Anything else we need to know?:

#### Environment:

title: Fix panic when allocate gpu parallelly
Inconsistent fieldPath in CRD validation rules
body:
### What happened?

While validating the contents of an additionalProperties object (a map), I noticed that a rule's fieldPath renders differently depending on where the rule is placed.

Rule `size(self.pairs.bar) > 1` is reported as `spec.pairs[bar]`, while
rule `size(self.bar) > 1` is reported as `spec.pairs.[bar]`. Notice the dot between `pairs` and `bar`.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected a rule's fieldPath to render consistently at any depth of the CRD schema.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This CRD has two rules, one on `spec` and one on `spec.pairs`. Both have a fieldPath that intends to reference `spec.pairs[bar]`.

```yaml
---
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: foos.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  names:
    kind: Foo
    listKind: FooList
    singular: foo
    plural: foos
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          apiVersion:
            type: string
          kind:
            type: string
          metadata:
            type: object
          spec:
            type: object
            x-kubernetes-validations:
            - rule: 'size(self.pairs.bar) > 5'
              fieldPath: .pairs.bar
            properties:
              pairs:
                type: object
                additionalProperties: { type: string }
                maxProperties: 10
                x-kubernetes-map-type: granular
                x-kubernetes-validations:
                - rule: 'size(self.bar) > 1'
                  fieldPath: .bar
```

This CR fails those validation rules causing `kubectl apply --server-side` to return the following:

```
The Foo "example" is invalid: 
* spec.pairs[bar]: Invalid value: "object": failed rule: size(self.pairs.bar) > 5
* spec.pairs.[bar]: Invalid value: "object": failed rule: size(self.bar) > 1
```

```yaml
---
apiVersion: example.com/v1
kind: Foo
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  pairs:
    bar: x
```

### Anything else we need to know?

It is also possible to spell the fieldPaths with brackets, but the result is the same:

```yaml
- rule: 'size(self.pairs.bar) > 5'
  fieldPath: .pairs['bar']

- rule: 'size(self.bar) > 1'
  fieldPath: "['bar']"
```

title: Error-level logs incorrectly use verbosity levels
body:
Currently, some components in Kubernetes have been migrated (or partially migrated) to [contextual logging](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/3077-contextual-logging/README.md). However, an incorrect pattern was introduced during the migration: Error-level logs are being called with verbosity methods (e.g., .V()).

The underlying package go-logr/logr, which contextual logging relies on, ignores the verbosity level when printing Error-level logs. For example, in the statement `logger.V(8).Error(nil, "Readiness probe already exists for container", "pod", klog.KObj(pod), "containerName", c.Name)`, the error log will be printed regardless of the verbosity level set.

This can lead to error log flooding, which may hinder users' ability to review normal logs for troubleshooting. More critically, according to the [Kubernetes logging policy](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/logging.md#what-method-to-use), logs should only be recorded when the information requires action from an administrator. This directly contradicts the practice of setting verbosity levels for Error logs, as administrators using the default logging level might miss these actionable errors. Therefore, these instances need to be fixed.

title: sendInitialEvents returns events other than ADDED prior to initial BOOKMARK
body:
### What happened?

I am adding support for sendInitialEvents to our kubernetes client so I am very closely observing the data to verify the reliability of the feature before moving to it. I was recording the raw data into a file while testing so that I could confirm my expectations. What I found is that when starting these watches, I receive a large number of ADDED events in a row, then just before the BOOKMARK is sent, some MODIFIED or DELETED events may get sent unexpectedly.



### What did you expect to happen?

On the [api concepts](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/) page, it says:
> On the client-side the initial state can be requested by specifying sendInitialEvents=true as query string parameter in a watch request. If set, the API server starts the watch stream with synthetic init events (of type `ADDED`) to build the whole state of all existing objects followed by a [`BOOKMARK` event](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#watch-bookmarks) (if requested via `allowWatchBookmarks=true` option). The bookmark event includes the resource version to which is synced. After sending the bookmark event, the API server continues as for any other watch request.

title: Inability to receive WatchBookmarks from the etcd storage implementation
body:
### What happened?

In general, clients can request `WatchBookmark` events by specifying the `allowWatchBookmarks` query parameter. However, the server is not obliged to deliver any `WatchBookmark` events, as described in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/956-watch-bookmark#proposal

The motivation for this approach is that the frequency of `WatchBookmark` events from a storage system like etcd can be very high. As the number of watch requests increases, so does the server load.

In practice, watch requests destined for the watch cache will receive the events, while those destined for the etcd storage implementation will not.

I would like all storage implementations to be compatible and provide the same set of capabilities. This would make life easier for developers and end users, as the behaviour of the system would be consistent regardless of the actual storage used to handle a request.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would like all storage implementations to be compatible and provide the same set of capabilities. This would make life easier for developers and end users, as the behaviour of the system would be consistent regardless of the actual storage used to handle a request.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Today when you do `k get --raw '/api/v1/namespaces/default/events?watch=true&allowWatchBookmarks=true'` against a cluster built from the `master` branch you won't get any bookmark events.

title: Proposal: Kubelet to add a preset label for Swap enabled nodes
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add swap labels to swap-enabled nodes to allow admin to target swap demanding pods selectively for scheduling on specific nodes.

eg:

```
 node.kubernetes.io/swap-behavior: "LimitedSwap"
```

This follows precedent in kubelet auto-adding hardware/os features as node-label metadata. eg: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/node/node-labels/#preset-labels

### Why is this needed?

This is desirable to ensure that only specific swap needing Pods run on swap setup nodes with certain isolation. 

Swap labels doesn't replace but will be additive to other swap scheduling improvements and/or NodeCapabilities in Kubernetes as it also enables efficient filtering and monitoring of swap provisioned nodes.

title: The pod has been successfully removed, but the volume’s project quota mapping still remains on the node
body:
### What happened?


I enabled the `LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring` feature gate. 
I was able to successfully create a pod using the YAML file, with `hostUsers` set to `false`. However, after the pod was deleted, the project quota information for the pod’s volume still remained in `/etc/project` and `/etc/projid`.

After adding some debug logs to the kubelet, I noticed that `ed.pod.Spec.HostUsers` is `nil` in the code below. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/93248f9ae092f571eb870b7664c534bfc7d00f03/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go#L538

As far as I know, since version 1.31, the kubelet checks if a user namespace is in use before assigning or clearing quotas. That means `ed.pod.Spec.HostUsers=nil` would bypass the entire quota teardown process.


### What did you expect to happen?

The Project ID is an attribute of the directory and is removed when the directory is deleted. However, the tear down process should still be handled properly to avoid side effects such as memory leaks.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Here’s what I actually did:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ephemeral-pod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
  hostUsers: false
  containers:
  - name: demo-container
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo Hello World && sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests:
        ephemeral-storage: "5Mi"
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: "5Mi"
    volumeMounts:
    - name: test-storage
      mountPath: /mnt/temp
  volumes:
  - name: test-storage
    emptyDir: {}
```
```console
$ k get pod ephemeral-pod -o yaml | grep uid
  uid: d7b0b7f3-608d-4a30-ae29-60093eb69e9
$ k delete pod ephemeral-pod
pod "ephemeral-pod" deleted from kube-system namespace
$ cat /etc/projects 
1048577:/var/lib/kubelet/pods/d7b0b7f3-608d-4a30-ae29-60093eb69e95/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/test-storage
$ cat /etc/projid 
volume1048577:1048577
```
