title: CREATE request for already existing object is denied with `exceeded quota`
body:
### What happened?

CREATE request for already existing object is denied with `exceeded quota` by the ResourceQuota admission plugin.

### What did you expect to happen?

CREATE request for already existing object (and when the resourcequota is exhausted) to be denied with `already exists` (`409 Conflict`).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a test namespace `foo`
   ```
   k create ns foo
   ```

2. Create a resourcequota that allows only 1 Pod.
   ```yaml
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: ResourceQuota
   metadata:
     name: resource-quota
   spec:
     hard:
       pods: "1"
   ```

    ```
    k -n foo create -f resource-qouta.yaml
    ```

3. Create a Pod

   ```yaml
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Pod
   metadata:
     name: nginx
   spec:
     containers:
     - name: nginx
       image: nginx:1.14.2
       ports:
       - containerPort: 80
   ```

   ```
   k -n foo create -f pod.yaml
    ```

4. Try to create the Pod again and make sure that it fails with `exceeded quota`

   ```
   k -n foo create -f pod.yaml
   Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "pod.yaml": pods "nginx" is forbidden: exceeded quota: resource-quota, requested: pods=1, used: pods=1, limited: pods=1
   ```

### Anything else we need to know?

On server side we have an admission component (let's call it "authorizer") similar to the kubelet's [`NodeAuthorizer`](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/node/) . The "authorizer" allows certain verbs on resources only if there is a "relation" between the requesting component and the requested resource - similar to the NodeAuthorizer that allows operations for secrets, configmaps, pvcs, pv related to pods bound to the kubelet's node. This authorizer would actually reject a GET request for non-existing object. That's why the client's strategy is "create or get and patch". We rely on the CREATE request to return `already exists` (`409 Conflict`).

title: Sometime Liveness/Readiness Probes fail because of net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
body:
**What happened**:
In my cluster sometimes readiness the probes are failing. But the application works fine.
```
Apr 06 18:15:14 kubenode** kubelet[34236]: I0406 18:15:14.056915   34236 prober.go:111] Readiness probe for "default-nginx-daemonset-4g6b5_default(a3734646-77fd-11ea-ad94-509a4c9f2810):nginx" failed (failure): Get http://172.18.123.127:80/: net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
```

**What you expected to happen**:
Successful Readiness Probe.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
We have few clusters with different workloads.
Only in cluster with big number of short living pods we have this issue.
But not on all nodes.
We can't reproduce this error on other our clusters (that have same configuration but different workload).
How i found the issue?
I deployed a daemonset:
```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: default-nginx-daemonset
  namespace: default
  labels:
    k8s-app: default-nginx
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      name: default-nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: default-nginx
    spec:
      tolerations:
      - operator: Exists
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:latest
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: "1Gi"
          requests:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: "1Gi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
```
Then i started to listen events on all pods of this daemonset.
After a couple of time i received next events:
```
Warning  Unhealthy  110s (x5 over 44m)  kubelet, kubenode20  Readiness probe failed: Get http://172.18.122.143:80/: net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
Warning  Unhealthy  11m (x3 over 32m)  kubelet, kubenode10  Readiness probe failed: Get http://172.18.65.57:80/: net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
....
```
Those events where on ~50% of pods of this daemonset.

On the nodes where the pods with failed probes was placed, I collected the logs of kubelet.
And there was errors like:
```
Apr 06 14:08:35 kubenode20 kubelet[10653]: I0406 14:08:35.464223   10653 prober.go:111] Readiness probe for "default-nginx-daemonset-nkwkf_default(90a3883b-77f3-11ea-ad94-509a4c9f2810):nginx" failed (failure): Get http://172.18.122.143:80/: net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
```

I was thinking that sometimes the nginx in pod really response slowly.
For excluding this theory, I created a short script that curl the application in pod and store response time in a file:

title: Streaming connections (SPDY and WebSockets) do not support custom dialers
body:
/kind bug
/sig api-machinery
/triage accepted

Even though there is a field in the `rest.Config` that specifies a custom `Dial` function, SPDY and WebSocket connections do not support these custom dialers.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/59f3aa1e342a469e838133417edab825c0cfe7e7/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/config.go#L152-L153

This functionality has never worked for either SPDY or WebSockets. Either we 1) explicity disallow this functionality for streaming connections, or 2) create the functionality for both streaming protocols.

This issue will keep track of our decisions/progress.

Related issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112847

title: NetworkPolicy tests for blocking north/south traffic
body:
The NP docs point out that [NP's semantics for north/south traffic are not very clearly defined](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/#behavior-of-ipblock-selectors):

> Cluster ingress and egress mechanisms often require rewriting the source or destination IP of packets. In cases where this happens, it is not defined whether this happens before or after NetworkPolicy processing, and the behavior may be different for different combinations of network plugin, cloud provider, `Service` implementation, etc.
> 
> In the case of ingress, this means that in some cases you may be able to filter incoming packets based on the actual original source IP, while in other cases, the "source IP" that the NetworkPolicy acts on may be the IP of a `LoadBalancer` or of the Pod's node, etc.
> 
> For egress, this means that connections from pods to `Service` IPs that get rewritten to cluster-external IPs may or may not be subject to `ipBlock`-based policies.

However, what's _not_ ambiguous is that a pod which is fully isolated for ingress should not accept E/W _or_ N/S traffic. Regardless of how the ingress/LB/cloud handles the traffic, it should end up getting blocked. (Well, unless it gets masqueraded to the pod's node IP, because then it hits that exception to the rules.)

Unfortunately we can't say the same for egress; I think we assume that a pod-to-service-IP connection will be allowed to reach kube-proxy even if the pod is fully isolated-for-egress, but we explicitly don't require that `ipBlock` policies get applied after service proxying.

Anyway, we should be able to add a test to `test/e2e/network/netpol/network_policy.go` that confirms that cluster-ingress traffic to a fully isolated-for-ingress pod is not allowed. In particular, if we create a LoadBalancer Service with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`, and a NetworkPolicy blocking all ingress to that Service's Pods, then we should not be able to connect to the service via either the LoadBalancer IP/name or via its NodePort (on one of the correct nodes).

/sig network
/area network-policy
/priority backlog
/help
/good-first-issue

title: Add `x-kubernetes-sensitive-string` extension to CRDs
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The x-kubernetes-sensitive-string extension in a Custom Resource Definition (CRD) provides a way to indicate to Kubernetes and other components that the values in a particular field should be treated as sensitive and protected.

When a field is marked as sensitive using this extension, Kubernetes and other components will take additional precautions to protect the field's value, such as:

Redacting the field's value in log output
Hiding the field's value in API responses by default
Masking the field's value in API objects stored in etcd
These precautions help prevent sensitive information from being accidentally leaked, either through logs or through API responses, which could compromise the security of your application and data.

In addition to providing these security benefits, marking a field as sensitive using the x-kubernetes-sensitive-string extension can also provide clarity to users and administrators about which fields contain sensitive information and should be treated with care.

### Why is this needed?

Currently, there are no ways to pass sensitive information to the CR.

title: emulatedStorageVersion incorrectly maintains n-1 compat for alpha API transitions
body:
#### What happened?

The `emulatedStorageVersion` function in `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/storage/resource_encoding_config.go` uses `MinCompatibilityVersion` (n-1) to select the storage version for all API resources. This is correct for beta→GA transitions where the n-1 server needs to read the stored data, but incorrect for alpha→beta transitions.

For alpha→beta, the function selects the alpha version for storage to maintain n-1 compat. However, alpha APIs have no compatibility guarantees, so there is no value in maintaining n-1 compat with them. Beta should be used immediately when introduced.

This forces every alpha→beta transition to add a manual override in `NewStorageFactoryConfigEffectiveVersion` (`pkg/kubeapiserver/default_storage_factory_builder.go`), which is error-prone and requires cleanup the following release.

#### What did you expect to happen?

`emulatedStorageVersion` should automatically select beta for storage as soon as it is introduced at the emulation version, without requiring manual overrides.

#### Affected scenarios:
- **alpha→beta**: should store as beta immediately (currently stores as alpha)
- **alpha→alpha**: should store as latest alpha at emulation version (currently may fall through to wrong group-level version)
- **new beta/alpha resources**: should store correctly without overrides (currently may fall through to wrong group-level version)

/sig api-machinery
/kind bug

title: add tests for scheduler-perf itself
body:
/sig scheduling
/kind cleanup

[scheduler-perf](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/test/integration/scheduler_perf) has few tests for itself at the moment; we roughly check the behavior with `-tags performance, short` or `-tags integration-test, short`, which could miss some potential issues with it.
scheduler-perf right now serves a crucial role for the scheduler to keep our targets in various metrics, and we're adding more and more features into it. Unless we have proper testing for it, the more features we add into it, the more likely we could break some existing parts without noticing it since the reviewing would get more and more difficult.

So, this issue aims to add tests for it. I guess it also requires some refactoring, especially around [`runWorkload`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1bbe775d5ffb131636193fe0bc15a8fcc0cd6fd6/test/integration/scheduler_perf/scheduler_perf.go#L1270), which is currently huge.

title: Consider exposing node labels via downward api
body:
**What keywords did you search in Kubernetes issues before filing this one?** (If you have found any duplicates, you should instead reply there.): downward api node labels

---

**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?** (choose one): Feature request

<!--
If this is a BUG REPORT, please:
  - Fill in as much of the template below as you can.  If you leave out
    information, we can't help you as well.

If this is a FEATURE REQUEST, please:
  - Describe *in detail* the feature/behavior/change you'd like to see.

In both cases, be ready for followup questions, and please respond in a timely
manner.  If we can't reproduce a bug or think a feature already exists, we
might close your issue.  If we're wrong, PLEASE feel free to reopen it and
explain why.
-->

I think the downward API should support exposing the node labels on which the pod it is running. While I understand that the Pod should not be coupled too much with the node it is scheduled to. But I think there are certain scenarios that require the pod  to have more information about it's host.

- ***failure-zones*** like rack names on premise or availability zones in cloud
- ***instance-types*** for adapting thread settings per instance type
- other labels like local ssd storage available 

This helps applications that are cloud-native to understand where they are located. While this could be achieved using API calls to the node object, I think it should be supported by the downward API. A node object would expose way more information that should not be available to any pod. In OpenShift's default configuration there is access to the Node objects prevented by default.

@mattbates @smarterclayton @bprashanth

title: Fake dynamic client pluralizes "Gateway" as "gatewaies" instead of "gateways"
body:
### What happened?

When using the fake dynamic client from client-go to test resources from the Gateway API (or any resource named “Gateway”), the client fails with the following error:
```text
panic: coding error: you must register resource to list kind for every resource you're going to LIST when creating the client.  See NewSimpleDynamicClientWithCustomListKinds or register the list into the scheme: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1, Resource=gateways out of map[gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1, Resource=gatewaies:GatewayList gateway.networking.k8s.io/version, Resource=gatewaies:GatewayList group2/version, Resource=gatewaies:GatewayList] [recovered]
```

The fake client internally pluralizes Gateway → gatewaies (staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/meta/restmapper.go: UnsafeGuessKindToResource()),
but the actual resource name in Kubernetes is gateways.

This makes List() calls fail even if the Scheme and GVR are correctly registered.

### What did you expect to happen?

The fake dynamic client should respect the correct plural form defined in the resource or Scheme,
or at least allow overriding the plural form without panicking.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go
import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"testing"

	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/unstructured"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/schema"
	"k8s.io/client-go/dynamic/fake"
)

func newUnstructured(apiVersion, kind, namespace, name string) *unstructured.Unstructured {
	return &unstructured.Unstructured{
		Object: map[string]interface{}{
			"apiVersion": apiVersion,
			"kind":       kind,
			"metadata": map[string]interface{}{
				"namespace": namespace,
				"name":      name,
			},
		},
	}
}

func TestListbug(t *testing.T) {
	scheme := runtime.NewScheme()

	client := fake.NewSimpleDynamicClient(scheme,
		newUnstructured("gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1", "Gateway", "default", "name-foo"),
		newUnstructured("group2/version", "Gateway", "default", "name2-foo"),
		newUnstructured("gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1", "Gateway", "default", "name-bar"),
		newUnstructured("gateway.networking.k8s.io/version", "Gateway", "default", "name-baz"),
		newUnstructured("group2/version", "Gateway", "default", "name2-baz"),
	)

	listFirstWithOutNamesapce, err := client.Resource(schema.GroupVersionResource{Group: "gateway.networking.k8s.io", Version: "v1", Resource: "gateways"}).List(context.TODO(), metav1.ListOptions{})
	listFirstWithNamesapce, err2 := client.Resource(schema.GroupVersionResource{Group: "gateway.networking.k8s.io", Version: "v1", Resource: "gateways"}).Namespace("default").List(context.TODO(), metav1.ListOptions{})

	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err2 != nil {
		t.Fatal(err2)
	}

	fmt.Printf("Number of items: %d", len(listFirstWithOutNamesapce.Items))
	fmt.Printf("Number of items: %d", len(listFirstWithNamesapce.Items))
}
```

title: [FG:EventedPLEG] lastSyncTime race and latency regression
body:
I was benchmarking pod startup latency, and noticed that the evented PLEG latency was unexpectedly _worse_ than not the evented PLEG. The latency is close to the slower 5s global sync time, so I suspect that it's missing the events and falling back to the (slower) global sync:

Generic: First Sync -> Running: Avg=1.773, StdDev=0.234
EventedPLEG: First Sync -> Running: Avg=4.854, StdDev=0.221

I suspect that what's happening is that the events from container state transitions are picked up by the evented PLEG right away, which modifies them in the cache. However, the `lastSyncTime` is not set until _after_ the pod sync completes. If the cache has already been asynchronously updated from events, then the modified time for the pod cache will be **before** the `lastSyncTime`, which means that on the next iteration `GetNewerThan` will need to wait for the next global relist to get a "newer" result from the cache:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1879769b9354b6e47a13dac831aec6fe3e0368b6/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1271-L1280

/sig node
/cc @HirazawaUi

title: correct the usage of ephemeral storage volumes in the eviction message
body:
### What happened?

In k8s 1.32 cluster, I created a pod with `emptydir` volume and continuously wrote data into the `emptydir` volume to trigger node eviction. However, the event generated during the eviction is as follows:
```
115s        Warning   Evicted                       pod/test-xxxxxsas-b966b9bd4-pzbbc                        The node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage. Threshold quantity: 94576558032, available: 92034400Ki. Container container-1 was using 122Ki, request is 0, has larger consumption of ephemeral-storage.
```
The reported `122Ki` value only includes the usage of `rootfs` and `logs`, without accounting for the usage of volumes such as `emptydir`. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/39c640fe9051b60bacbacf47f64cb697fb807861/pkg/kubelet/eviction/helpers.go#L1262
This may lead to user confusion: why is the pod being evicted when it appears to be using so little ephemeral storage?
Therefore, it is necessary to include the consideration of `emptydir` in the eviction message.

/sig node
friendly ping @pacoxu  @kannon92 

### What did you expect to happen?

the eviction message contains the correct usage of ephemeral storage volumes

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a pod with `emptydir` volume

title: Shift-left validation for cel expressions
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently, CEL expressions are validated only at runtime when a resource is submitted to the cluster. To address this, we propose expanding the existing[ kubectl-validate](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubectl-validate) repository to provide a shift-left validation tool that allows users to test CEL expressions against incoming object files locally before deploying them.

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QzEXIEdAjbPtaFnAtuHzot16Lp2X4vTpQ1AokfPFv1w/edit?tab=t.0

### Why is this needed?

Kubernetes has increasingly leveraged Common Expression Language (CEL) to enhance policy enforcement and resource allocation. Features such as ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and Dynamic Resource Allocation rely on CEL to define the matching resources and how resources should be validated. However, one major challenge is the lack of a shift-left validation tool that enables developers and operators to test CEL expressions against real objects before deploying them to a cluster.

title: Test flake: TestStalePodDisruption/stale_pod_disruption times out waiting for DisruptionTarget to be set to False
body:
### Which jobs are flaking?

`pull-kubernetes-unit` ([Prow log](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/137336/pull-kubernetes-unit/2028488280995008512))

### Which tests are flaking?

`TestStalePodDisruption/stale_pod_disruption` in `k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controller/disruption`

### Since when has it been flaking?

Observed on 2025-03-02 in PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137336. This is a recurrence of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112594 (closed 2022-09-21).

### Testgrid link

N/A (observed in presubmit)

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The test creates a pod with a `DisruptionTarget=True` condition (no `DeletionTimestamp`), advances the fake clock past the 2-minute `stalePodDisruptionTimeout`, adds the pod to the indexer, and then polls for the controller to set `DisruptionTarget=False`. The poll times out after 30 seconds:

```
=== RUN   TestStalePodDisruption/stale_pod_disruption
    disruption_test.go:1560: Failed waiting for worker to sync: timed out waiting for the condition, (-want,+got):
          []v1.PodCondition{
              {
                  Type:               "DisruptionTarget",
                  ObservedGeneration: 0,
        -         Status:             "False",
        +         Status:             "True",
                  LastProbeTime:      {},
                  ... // 1 ignored and 2 identical fields
              },
          }
--- FAIL: TestStalePodDisruption/stale_pod_disruption (30.01s)
```

**Race condition analysis:** The test starts the controller with `go dc.Run(tCtx)` ([disruption_test.go:1543](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/disruption/disruption_test.go#L1543)) and then immediately adds the pod to the informer indexer ([disruption_test.go:1548](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/disruption/disruption_test.go#L1548)). The flow for stale pod cleanup is:

1. `addPod` event handler calls `nonTerminatingPodHasStaleDisruptionCondition()` to check if the condition is stale
2. If stale, it enqueues the pod into `stalePodDisruptionQueue` via `enqueueStalePodDisruptionCleanup()` with `AddAfter(key, d)`
3. The `stalePodDisruptionWorker` goroutine picks it up and calls `syncStalePodDisruption()`
4. `syncStalePodDisruption()` patches the pod condition to `False`

The flake occurs because:
- There is no synchronization ensuring the controller's `Run()` goroutine has fully started and its informer event handlers are registered before the pod is added to the indexer
- The `addPod` event may fire before the informer caches have synced (line 476), or the `stalePodDisruptionWorker` goroutine (line 487) may not yet be running
- The pod is added directly to the indexer (`GetIndexer().Add()`) rather than through the informer's normal flow, which may bypass event delivery depending on timing
- Since the fake clock is advanced *before* the pod is added (line 1547), the `nonTerminatingPodHasStaleDisruptionCondition` check correctly computes `waitFor=0`, but if the event is missed entirely, the cleanup never gets enqueued

### Anything else we need to know?

This is a recurrence of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112594, which was closed in September 2022. The underlying race condition between controller startup and pod indexer insertion appears to still exist.

title: DRA: scale testing for GA of structured parameters
body:
Before going GA in 1.34, we want to do some scale testing to ensure that there are no surprises as real deployments ramp up. We might want to run this testing regularly to avoid regressions. Here's a proposal what we could measure and how.

* Kwok vs. real cluster: the DRA driver on each node and the kubelet both need to do a GET to retrieve ResourceClaims. The driver also has an active watch for ResourceSlices. If we can afford the costs, then using a real cluster would be more realistic.
* Driver: DRA example driver, with 8 fake GPUs per node.
* Workload: 1/8th of RAM on a node, 1 GPU per pod requested via a ResourceClaimTemplate. Initially fill up the cluster to 90% utilization with permanently running pods, then measure the steady state of constantly scheduling short-lived pods at a certain rate. Measuring the steady state, in contrast to a simpler "fill up a cluster as quickly as possible" scenario, covers the work that the resource claim controller needs to do after pod termination (= deallocating claims) and thus ensures that that controller is also scalable. Using a ResourceClaimTemplate includes the extra latency for creating the ResourceClaim.
* Measurements: [pod startup latency](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/sig-scalability/slos/pod_startup_latency.md), resource consumption of control plane components
* Baseline: pod without a  claim

It is not clear from https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/sig-scalability/slos/pod_startup_latency.md what exactly the workload behavior is, in particular the cluster utilization. Scheduling gets slower as the cluster fills up because the scheduler has to evaluate more nodes. Ideally we want to be comparable. cc @Huang-Wei and @wojtek-t for advice.

/cc @johnbelamaric

title: [Bug] Pod not scheduled although there is a node matching all hard pod affinity terms
body:
### What happened?

A pod (`pod-x`) is supposed to be scheduled on a node (only) when:

- another pod with `label-1: x` **and**
- yet another pod with `label-2: x`

are already running on that node.

This should be possible by using _multiple_ pod affinity terms in `spec.affinity.podAffinity.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` like this:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod-x
spec:
  affinity:
    podAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              label-1: "x"
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
        - labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              label-2: "x"
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
  containers:
    - name: c1
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.8
```

For testing purposes the two prerequisite pods may be created like this:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod-a
  labels:
    label-1: "x"
spec:
  containers:
    - name: c1
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.8
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod-b
  labels:
    label-2: "x"
spec:
  containers:
    - name: c1
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.8
  affinity:
    podAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              label-1: "x"
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
```

What actually happens is that **`pod-x` is not scheduled at all**:

```
NAME    STATUS    NODE
pod-a   Running   ip-10-250-74-235.ec2.internal
pod-b   Running   ip-10-250-74-235.ec2.internal
pod-x   Pending   <none>
```

Status of `pod-x`:

```yaml
status:                                                                                                                                                                                     
  conditions:                                                                                                                                                                               
  - lastProbeTime: null                                                                                                                                                                     
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-03-13T09:49:54Z"                                                                                                                                              
    message: '0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn''t match pod affinity rules.                                                                                                          
      preemption: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.'                                                                                                     
    reason: Unschedulable                                                                                                                                                                   
    status: "False"                                                                                                                                                                         
    type: PodScheduled                                                                                                                                                                      
  phase: Pending                                                                                                                                                                            
  qosClass: BestEffort                                                                                                                                                                      
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The [API reference](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1/#PodAffinity) says:

> requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution ([]PodAffinityTerm)
> ...
> When there are multiple elements, the lists of nodes corresponding to each podAffinityTerm are intersected, i.e. all terms must be satisfied.

This means, each affinity term should be resolved to a list of matching nodes independently of other affinity terms, and the results are intersected to yield the nodes where the pod to be scheduled is feasible. This corresponds to the [algorithm](https://github.com/kubernetes/design-proposals-archive/blob/main/scheduling/podaffinity.md#algorithm) (step 1a) described in the pod affinity design proposal.

In my example the pod affinity terms would resolve to two lists:

- `["ip-10-250-74-235.ec2.internal"]`
- `["ip-10-250-74-235.ec2.internal"]`

The intersection of those yields:

- `["ip-10-250-74-235.ec2.internal"]`

**Expected Result**: `pod-x` is feasible on node `ip-10-250-74-235.ec2.internal` and gets scheduled there.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create the pods:

    ```bash
    kubectl create -f - <<EOF
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: pod-a
      labels:
        label-1: "x"
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: c1
          image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.8
    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: pod-b
      labels:
        label-2: "x"
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: c1
          image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.8
      affinity:
        podAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - labelSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  label-1: "x"
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: pod-x
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - labelSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  label-1: "x"
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
            - labelSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  label-2: "x"
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      containers:
        - name: c1
          image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.8
    EOF
    ```

2. Check the pods' status:

    ```bash
    kubectl get pods
    ```
    
    Output:

    ```
    NAME    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
    pod-a   1/1     Running   0          86s
    pod-b   1/1     Running   0          85s
    pod-x   0/1     Pending   0          85s
    ```

3. Inspect the reason for `pod-x` not being scheduled:

    ```bash
    kubectl get pod pod-x -o yaml
    ```

    ```yaml
    ...
    status:
      conditions:
      - lastProbeTime: null
        lastTransitionTime: "2025-03-13T14:48:28Z"
        message: '0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn''t match pod affinity rules.
          preemption: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.'
        reason: Unschedulable
        status: "False"
        type: PodScheduled
      phase: Pending
      qosClass: BestEffort
    ```

### Anything else we need to know?

As soon as a _single_ pod, e.g. `pod-a`, matches both pod affinity terms, `pod-x` _gets_ scheduled. This proves that the pod affinity terms as such are understood correctly. However, considering only nodes that match _all_ affinity terms evaluated with a _single_ pod is not compliant to the API spec and design proposal.

### Kubernetes version

Tested with:

* v1.31.5
* v1.29.1

title: Inaccurate metric scheduler_plugin_execution_duration_seconds in large cluster
Extended resources could not be zeroed while node has been recreated
body:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7436ca32bc766ff202109a7541d2e7bb41ee7d13/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L181

the `reconcileExtendedResource` check with devicemanager to see if there is no checkpoints to  decide whether to zero out ER, but while kubelet start, the checkpoint dir could not be empty as the kubelet.sock will be created first

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7436ca32bc766ff202109a7541d2e7bb41ee7d13/pkg/kubelet/checkpointmanager/checkpoint_manager.go#L105

the `ListCheckpoints ` list all file except ones which has prefix ".",  but not filter the sock files, so `kl.containerManager.ShouldResetExtendedResourceCapacity`  will always return false


### What did you expect to happen?

title: Add geofencing to prevent running this software in California in order to avoid legal liabilities from AB 1043
body:
Reference:
https://www.troutmanprivacy.com/2025/10/analyzing-californias-digital-age-assurance-act/

AB 1043 requires operating systems to collect user's age, and applications (like Kubernates) to receive age bracket signals, whether they use them or not. User, in this case, roughly referring to someone who installs Kubernates on a computer. But the law is vague for this use case.

Just by knowing the user's age, Kubernates will become legally responsible under other sets of laws like CCPA which prohibit collection of minor's personal information, and provide hefty fines for violations.

It is in the project's, and the world's, best interest to prohibit use of Kubernates inside of the state of California, so there are no lawsuits under these regulations. Hopefully with enough resistance these laws will be overturned when their impracticality is realized.

title: Kubelet device manager: Improve reconciliation/cleanup for failed Pods to avoid stale allocation state
body:
### What would you like to be added?

### Background

PR #130172 fixes a specific bug where allocatedDevices was not restored after devicesToAllocate failed, which could lead to repeated UnexpectedAdmissionError.

During review, a broader concern was identified: Pods that fail allocation/admission may linger, and device manager state (e.g. partial allocatedDevices) may not be proactively reconciled or cleaned up.

This issue tracks that architectural concern separately from the targeted bugfix.

### Problem

When allocation/admission fails:

Partial device allocation state may remain.

Cleanup relies on Pod lifecycle transitions.

If a failed Pod remains “active”, stale state may persist and impact subsequent Pods.

The current model is not fully transactional and can be brittle under failure scenarios.

### Scope of this issue

Evaluate whether additional proactive reconciliation is needed.

Consider cleanup strategies for failed/lingering Pods.

Improve test coverage for failure and recovery paths.

/sig node
/area kubelet

title: Potential cache inconsistency during leader election causing resource overcommitment
body:
We encountered an issue in kube-scheduler where, during leader election, the newly elected standby instance does not re-sync its cache and event handlers before starting scheduling operations. This may cause the new leader to miss Pods scheduled by the previous leader in the final moments before election, potentially leading to unexpected resource overcommitment (e.g., assigning Pods to nodes whose allocated resources were already consumed by unsynced Pods).

We are aware of the `DelayCacheUntilActive` configuration, which delays Informer startup until leadership is acquired. However, this approach significantly increases failover latency, as the standby scheduler cannot begin scheduling until the full cache sync completes after election—impacting cluster scheduling availability during failover.

**Key Concerns:**
1. Without cache re-sync post-election: Risk of stale cache → resource conflicts/overcommitment
2. With `DelayCacheUntilActive`: Extra scheduling downtime during failover

**Questions for the Community:**
1. Is there an officially recommended pattern to safely reconcile cache state after acquiring leadership without delaying scheduling readiness?
2. Are there plans to enhance the leader election workflow (e.g., lightweight delta sync, cache validation hook) to address this trade-off?
3. Has this scenario been discussed in prior scheduler reliability improvements (e.g., #XX)?

We appreciate any insights or guidance on robust patterns to ensure cache consistency during scheduler failover while minimizing scheduling downtime. Thank you for your support! 🙏

title: [Declarative Validation] Support matching short-circuited errors from DV with HV short circuited and child nodes errors.
body:
### **Problem**
During the migration of `RoleBinding.RoleRef` to declarative validation (referencing [PR #137094](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137094)), a parity issue was identified between handwritten validation (HV) and declarative validation (DV) short-circuiting behavior. 

Currently, DV may short-circuit on a field (e.g., for immutability), while existing HV might return both an immutability error for that field and additional validation errors for its child nodes. 

Manually refactoring all existing HV code to align perfectly with the DV short-circuiting graph is "not worth the effort" as it "could introduce bugs into the existing validation code and would require significant bandwidth from API approvers for review".

### **Proposed Solution**
The goal is to update the declarative validation framework's error matcher to accept these differences as equivalent. We should "change the error matcher to match short-circuited errors from DV with short-circuited errors from HV and errors from child nodes". 

By implementing this support in the framework, we can achieve parity without needing to refactor complex handwritten validation logic.

### **Example Case**
*   **Field:** `RoleBinding.RoleRef`
*   **DV Result:** Returns an immutable error for the `RoleRef` field and short-circuits.
*   **HV Result:** Returns an immutable error for the `RoleRef` field AND "required" errors for `RoleRef.Kind` and other child fields.
*   **Desired Behavior:** The framework should treat the DV result as a valid match for the HV result.

### **Context**
*   **Part of:** KEP-5073 declarative validation migration tracking issue [#136785](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136785).
*   **Related PR:** [#137094](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137094).

title: [Windows] usageNanoCores reported by /stats/summary occasionally higher than number of vCPUs available
body:
### What happened?

Hi there! 
We recently discovered a potential anomaly in what is being reported by the kubelet `/stats/summary` endpoint for Windows nodes where in containers with generally high CPU usage, the `usageNanoCores` metric reported was occasionally higher than the total number of vCPUs available (so in a node having 2 vCPUs, the `usageNanoCores` metric could be `3_000_000_000` or higher - we captured 22 cores at one point). The container spec included resource request/limts for CPU. We did not see anything similar in Linux nodes. I'm also willing to believe this is inherent in how core usage is measured for Windows as opposed to Linux, but figured it was worth reporting. This was found for containers on both Windows LTSC 2019 & 2022 nodes.

This issue was initially reported to us from a real customer workload & we were able to reproduce it by spinning up some containers that logged out random numbers on the respective nodes & running a script that scraped `usageNanoCores` from the`/stats/summary` endpoint for those nodes every 10 seconds.

From what I can tell, the kubelet should be using CRI (containerd, `"containerRuntimeEndpoint":"npipe:////./pipe/containerd-containerd"`) for pod/container metrics rather than CAdvisor.

title: Support longer (maybe pseudo-permanent?) Service Session Affinity
body:
### What would you like to be added?

According to our session affinity timeout docs: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/networking/virtual-ips/#session-stickiness-timeout if timeout is not specified we set it to 3 hours by default: https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/core/v1#ClientIPConfig

So if we do:
```
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP
```
it is auto converted into:
```
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP
  sessionAffinityConfig:
    clientIP:
      timeoutSeconds: 10800
```

So currently it seems there cannot be a session affinity without a timeout. Why was it designed this way? Can we change this to support being able to express affinity without timeout or permanent affinity? Maybe we do 
`service.Spec.SessionAffinityConfig.ClientIP.TimeoutSeconds = 0` to convey its permanent session affinity? However not sure if that becomes an API backwards incompatible change since `0` is not allowed as of today as a value.

/sig network

### Why is this needed?

IoT Edge use case where clients send sparse packets but still want to hit the same backend. Users should not have to worry about the timeout being max a day, they should have a way to say "permanent affinity".

title: Kubernetes endpoint validation
body:
### What happened?

Scenario:

In a setup of multiple kube-apiserver, one of the apiserver's advertise address is configured to `127.0.0.1`. When the apiserver starts up, it saves the ip into etcd registry directly without validation, followed by endpoint object update. However, the endpoint object update fails due to the validation [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.25.15/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L6176). The validation rejects the update when endpoint is localhost or link local address. 

Since the IP is already persisted into etcd registry, other apiservers cannot update the endpoint object anymore. This results in one apiserver mis/configuration to block all endpoint updates until the apiserver is taken out of service. If the other healthy apiservers restart or change IP, the kubernetes endpoint object IPs become stale.

Potential solution: Flip the order of endpoint update. Update the endpoint object followed by the update to etcd registry.
Alternative: Duplicate the validation [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c28c2009181fcc44c5f6b47e10e62dacf53e4da0/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L284) in `checkEndpointSubsetFormatWithLease` 

### What did you expect to happen?

A misconfigured apiserver advertise address should not block all apiservers from updating their IP.

title: Race condition on pod eviction due to taint manager
body:
### What happened?

When running Kubernetes on AWS (EKS) version 1.24, we have a strange random race condition with the kube-controller-manager service, specifically the taint_manager component.

We use AWS autoscaler and cilium as CNI. At startup, all of our nodes have a taint with the key node.cilium.io/agent-not-ready, the value true, and the effect NoExecute. This taint is deleted by cilium when the node is ready. Once the taint is deleted, the scheduler can bind a pod to the node. However, the kube-controller-manager cannot see that the taint has been deleted and evicts the pod even though the taint no longer exists.

I have traced all of the logs and calls to the Kubernetes API or other components and have attached the history.

```
# kube-scheduler
I0809 00:12:58.755233      11 schedule_one.go:265] "Successfully bound pod to node" pod="default/test" node="ip-10-1-1-1.ec2.internal" evaluatedNodes=22 feasibleNodes=1

# kube-controller-manager
I0809 00:12:58.756918      10 taint_manager.go:353] "Not all taints are tolerated after update for pod on node" pod="default/test" node="ip-10-1-1-1.ec2.internal"
I0809 00:12:58.757005      10 taint_manager.go:106] "NoExecuteTaintManager is deleting pod" pod="default/test"
I0809 00:12:58.757713      10 event.go:294] "Event occurred" object="default/test" fieldPath="" kind="Pod" apiVersion="" type="Normal" reason="TaintManagerEviction" message="Marking for deletion Pod default/test"
I0809 00:12:58.763628      10 event.go:294] "Event occurred" object="default/test" fieldPath="" kind="Pod" apiVersion="" type="Normal" reason="TaintManagerEviction" message="Cancelling deletion of Pod default/test"

# kube-api-server 
2023-08-09T00:12:02.033236Z CREATE NODE ip-10-1-1-1.ec2.internal BY -- creating node with taint {"key":"node.cilium.io/agent-not-ready","value":"true","effect":"NoExecute"},{"key":"node.kubernetes.io/not-ready","effect":"NoSchedule"}
2023-08-09T00:12:29.099571Z PATCH NODE ip-10-1-1-1.ec2.internal BY system:serviceaccount:kube-system:node-controller (kube-controller-manager) -- removing taint node.kubernetes.io/not-ready
2023-08-09T00:12:58.748851Z PATCH NODE ip-10-1-1-1.ec2.internal BY system:serviceaccount:kube-system:cilium-operator (cilium-operator-aws) -- removing taint node.cilium.io/agent-not-ready
2023-08-09T00:12:58.763226Z DELETE PODS test BY system:serviceaccount:kube-system:node-controller (kube-controller-manager)
```

title: [InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Deferred resizes can prevent other pods from being scheduled / resized
body:
When the kubelet is making a decision about whether a new resize can be allocated, or the scheduler is scheduling a new pod, it uses max(spec, allocated, actual) of pods to determine how much resources they are using.

This means that if a resize comes in that is too large, and ends up deferred, from the node's perspective we are already "committed" to those resources. That means a pending resize can prevent new smaller pods from being scheduled to this node, or other smaller resizes from succeeding, even though there may be space that is available. 

Additionally, when `describe`ing the node, a deferred resize causes the node to appear overcommitted: 

```
Allocated resources:
  (Total limits may be over 100 percent, i.e., overcommitted.)
  Resource           Requests       Limits
  --------           --------       ------
  cpu                13150m (109%)  500m (4%)
```

The behavior is confusing, but I'm on the fence about whether it is incorrect. If we change the behavior, it could lead to smaller resizes generally being favored while larger resizes starve.

With the resize allocation decision with the kubelet, I'm not sure if there is a good alternative without introducing a race condition. But if we consider moving the allocation decision to the scheduler, would it then be sufficient to just look at max(allocated, actual) when making fit decisions? 

/sig node
/priority backlog

This issue was brought to me by @adrianmoisey from VPA, opening an issue to capture thoughts and discussions.

title: [Declarative Validation] Decide Policy on Unknown +k8s: Tags in Code Generators
body:
### What would you like to be added?

We need to decide on a consistent policy for how code generators in `kubernetes/kubernetes` (specifically `validation-gen`, but this likely applies more broadly) handle unrecognized `+k8s:` prefixed tags in comments.  Currently, `validation-gen` silently ignores unknown tags.  We need to decide whether to:

1.  **Ignore unknown `+k8s:` tags:**  (Current behavior) This allows older generators to process code that includes newer tags they don't understand, maintaining backwards compatibility.  The downside is that typos in tag names will go undetected.

2.  **Warn on unknown `+k8s:` tags:** This would provide a middle ground, alerting users to potential typos or misconfigurations without breaking existing workflows.  The downside is that users might ignore warnings.

3.  **Fail (error) on unknown `+k8s:` tags:** This would prevent typos and ensure that all tags are explicitly understood by the generator. The downside is that it breaks backwards compatibility: older generators would fail when processing newer code, even if the newer tags are irrelevant to that generator.

This decision impacts `validation-gen` directly but probably should be a consistent policy across all code generators.


### Why is this needed?



This issue was raised during review of PR #130349, which introduces the `validation-gen` code generator. See this comment thread:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130349#discussion_r1970588825 

The main trade-off is between:

*   **Strictness/Correctness:**  Failing on unknown tags prevents typos and ensures that all declared behavior is understood.
*   **Backwards Compatibility/Flexibility:**  Ignoring unknown tags allows older generators to process newer code without modification.

Without a consistent policy, we risk introducing subtle bugs or unexpected behavior due to misspelled or misunderstood tags.  A decision will inform how we handle tags going forward, and whether existing generators need to be updated. Also, the answer to this question will determine if a linter rule should be created to enforce this behaviour.

title: [InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Move feasibility checks to admission
body:
This is an umbrella issue to track the work of moving feasibility checks to admission.

Resizes can be considered infeasible for the following reasons:
- The requested resources exceed the node's total capacity.
- The pod is running on a node with an OS that does not support resize (like windows).
- The pod is a static pod.
- The feature gate is disabled on the node.
- Resize is not supported in combination with a few other features, which are:
  - Swap
  - Static CPU manager
  - Static memory manager


For infeasible resizes, the admission controller accepts the resize patch, with the feasibility check subsequently performed by the kubelet prior to resource allocation. If the resize is deemed infeasible, the kubelet adds a PodResizePending / Infeasible condition to the pod. An optimization we can make is to instead move these feasibility checks to admission, instead of accepting the patch and waiting for the kubelet to reject the resize.

The first 3 are trivial to move to admission. The remaining ones can be handled using the node declared features framework once we have commitment to implement those features so that we have a feature gate that we can tie the NDFs to.

Deployment stuck indefinitely when scaling during rolling update with maxSurge=0 due to stale annotations
body:
### What happened?

When a Deployment is scaled down during an in-progress rolling update (with maxSurge=0),
  the deployment controller gets stuck in an infinite loop and the rolling update never completes.

  The issue occurs because:
  1. During a rolling update, ReplicaSet annotations (deployment.kubernetes.io/desired-replicas)
     are set to the initial deployment size
  2. If the deployment is scaled down while the update is in progress, the replica count changes
     but the annotations remain stale
  3. isScalingEvent() detects the annotation mismatch and returns true, causing the controller
     to call sync() instead of rolloutRolling()
  4. scale() checks if replica counts match and returns early without updating annotations
     (lines 303-304 in pkg/controller/deployment/sync.go)
  5. scaleReplicaSetAndRecordEvent() also has an early return when replicas match (lines 400-401)
  6. The annotations are never updated, creating an infinite loop

  This prevents the rolling update from proceeding. Pods remain on the old version indefinitely, and there are no error messages.

  **Impact:** Applications cannot be updated, security patches cannot be deployed, and the
  deployment appears healthy while being completely stuck.

### What did you expect to happen?

The deployment controller should update ReplicaSet annotations even when replica counts
  already match the desired state. After scaling during a rolling update, the controller should:

  1. Detect the annotation mismatch
  2. Update the stale annotations to match the current deployment.spec.replicas
  3. Continue with the rolling update by calling rolloutRolling()
  4. Create a new ReplicaSet with the updated template
  5. Complete the rolling update successfully

  The annotations should be kept in sync with deployment.spec.replicas regardless of whether
  the replica count changed, to ensure isScalingEvent() correctly identifies true scaling
  events versus stale annotation states.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

### Automated Reproduction

  Run this automated verification script which reproduces the bug from scratch:

  ```bash
  curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/SDkie/eb9527f434b5556fdf77f9a4207c56fc/raw/b9195d738eb5b99b8f1931818699ebe0378b9be9/gistfile1.txt | bash
```

  The script will:
  - Create a kind cluster
  - Deploy a test application with maxSurge=0, maxUnavailable=1
  - Simulate the stale annotation condition
  - Trigger a rolling update
  - Demonstrate that the update is blocked

title: kubelet system-reserved unexpectedly sets memory.max in system-reserved-cgroup under systemd
body:
### What happened?

When starting kubelet with config `system-reserved=memory=1.5Gi` as part of [reserved
compute resources](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/reserve-compute-resources/#system-reserved), running under `systemd`, with a `system-reserved-cgroup=systemreserved` (as per [Recommended Cgroups Setup](system-reserved-cgroup=systemreserved), that cgroup (`systemreserved`) has it's memory.max set to the value of `system-reserved=memory`, away from the default which is `memory.max=max`:

*Without* `system-reserved=memory=1.5Gi`:

```
[root@k8s-node1 systemreserved.slice]# pwd
/sys/fs/cgroup/systemreserved.slice
[root@k8s-node1 systemreserved.slice]# cat memory.max 
max
```


*With* `system-reserved=memory=1.5Gi`:
```
[root@k8s-node1 systemreserved.slice]# pwd
/sys/fs/cgroup/systemreserved.slice
[root@k8s-node1 systemreserved.slice]# cat memory.max 
1610612736 # 1.5Gi
```

### What did you expect to happen?

When I write `system-reserved=memory=1.5Gi` to the kubelet config, I don't expect that to result in `systemreserved` services
(service units within `systemreserved`, such as `sshd`, and any other system service within that cgroup to be collectivly *limmited* with a `memory.max` which sets a [*hard limit*](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#:~:text=Memory%20usage%20hard%20limit) on these systemreserved services when they previously were not. This feels the *opposite* of what is intended- it should be the inverse (non systemreserved should 'back off' in the face of memory pressure to allow for 1.5G for the `systemreserved` cgroup.
 
Having `memory.max` set that may lead to these `systemreserved` services being *more likely* to be OOM killed since they get altered away from their default `memory.max=max`.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Start kubelet with --config (or args) with the following:

> Please note you have to restart the entire node to reset (kubelet does not clean up reset `system-reserved=memory=x` back to `max` after removing /restarting kubelet).

Apply the config to your kubelet start behaviour:

```
--system-reserved=memory=1.5Gi
--enforce-node-allocatable=pods,system-reserved
--system-reserved-cgroup=systemreserved
```

Ensure you have created the cgroup `systemreserved`, for example, by adding `Slice=systemreserved` to sshd:

File: /usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service
```
[Unit]
Description=OpenSSH server daemon
Documentation=man:sshd(8) man:sshd_config(5)
After=network.target sshd-keygen.target
Wants=sshd-keygen.target

[Service]
Type=notify
EnvironmentFile=-/etc/sysconfig/sshd
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/sshd -D $OPTIONS
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID
Slice=systemreserved.slice
KillMode=process
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=42s

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```
And reload your systemd daemon/restart sshds etc. (`systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart sshd`)

Observe memory.max being set:

```
[root@k8s-node1 systemreserved.slice]# cd /sys/fs/cgroup/systemreserved.slice
[root@k8s-node1 systemreserved.slice]# cat memory.max 
1610612736 # 1.5Gi
```

### Anything else we need to know?

I suspect Kubernetes needs to account for the Allocatable memory somewhere, which might by why `memory.max` is being altered?


Chris Down's suggestions may be relvant here, if kubelet *needs* to edit the cgroup, perhaps `memory.low` is more appropriate, and/or perhaps even
better allowing more fine grained control over which memory max/min/low get set rather than `--memory=` which doesn't appear to allow that level of expression.

> Our ultimate goal here is to keep the workload running ... so
what if could could encode that rather than sprinking memory.max everywhere? ... memory.low is a funamental different way about how we've controled memory for the last ~50 years. Instead we should just say how much memory the applications which we want to protect need, and let the system sort it out. ... memory.low hooks into the kernel's reclaiming structure in order to protect some memory for a cgroup. src: https://youtu.be/kPMZYoRxtmg?feature=shared&t=1242

title: Improve efficiency of requeuing unschedulable pods when a pod is added for gang scheduling
body:
### What would you like to be added?

With cluster events, we need to check whether we can requeue unschedulable pods into active queue or backoff queue more efficiently.

/sig scheduling
/assign
/cc @macsko 

### Why is this needed?

When it comes to gang scheduling, when Pod/Add event happens, it should also check unschedulable pods (because the newly added pod, along with unschedulable pods grouped together may complete the gang/workload).

Workaround was introduced is to use "MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue()" inside the "Add/Pod" cluster event. But this would run queuing hints for all plugins subscribing to such event, while we are only concerned with "GangScheduling" plugin for this particular case.

### References

A relevant issue was mentioned earlier in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/127290 and has pull request that wasn't merged/accepted https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127387 because it adds many lines of code and there was no strong reason to do so.

But with gang scheduling being introduced, this seems to be beneficial.

title: kubectl apply --dry-run=client doesn't seem very dry
body:
### What happened? When I try to do some linting with `kubectl apply --dry-run=client` (with no config to simulate no available remote API) I first get ```console $ kubectl apply --dry-run=client -k overlays/preprod/ error: error validating "overlays/preprod/": error validating data: failed to download openapi: Get "http://localhost:8080/openapi/v2?timeout=32s": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connect: connection refused; if you choose to ignore these errors, turn validation off with --validate=false ``` This seems to make sense; and the [--validate](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_apply/#options) docs seem reasonable in explaining `--validate=false` > "false" or "ignore" will not perform any schema validation, silently dropping any unknown or duplicate fields. Adding that flag, I a priori expected that I'd get some sort of "linting" that at least `kubectl` was parsing everything OK. However, it still fails ```console $ kubectl apply --dry-run=client -k overlays/preprod/ --validate=false -o yaml E0224 14:11:56.939647 112987 memcache.go:265] "Unhandled Error" err="couldn't get current server API group list: Get \"http://localhost:8080/api?timeout=32s\": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connect: connection refused" ... repeats, a lot ... unable to recognize "overlays/preprod/": Get "http://localhost:8080/api?timeout=32s": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connect: connection refused ... also repeats ... $ echo $? 1 ``` So with `--dry-run=client --validate=false` this is still trying to get to the API. Now I realise that AI is just regurgitating what it has seen and telling me what I want to hear, but perhaps that is illustrative that the broad consensus of what people _think_ this tool does. Note the documentation on `--dry-run` doesn't actually say this about API access > Must be "none", "server", or "client". If client strategy, only print the object that would be sent, without sending it. If server strategy, submit server-side request without persisting the resource. but it kind of _implies_ that it doesn't need API access. I'll be happy to propose a change with clarification of this, but I'd like to establish what the truth is before doing that :) Is it expected that `--dry-run=client` will not _send_ any information to the server, but still requires authenticated server access to complete successfully? What is the real interaction of `--validate=false` with this? ### What did you expect to happen? I expected `kubectl apply --dry-run=client --validate=false` to be a form of linting without authenticated access ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version Client Version: v1.33.5-dispatcher Kustomize Version: v5.6.0 ```

title: Refactor: Unify the pattern of the string concatenations spanning the line breaks
body:
/kind cleanup

#### Why we need it:

ref: #131286 

There are two types of string concatenations spanning the line breaks.

1. Insert whitespace / `\n` at the last of the upper line
```go
fs.StringVar(&o.ServiceAccounts.JWKSURI, "service-account-jwks-uri", o.ServiceAccounts.JWKSURI, ""+
	"Overrides the URI for the JSON Web Key Set in the discovery doc served at "+
	"/.well-known/openid-configuration. This flag is useful if the discovery doc "+
	"and key set are served to relying parties from a URL other than the "+
	"API server's external (as auto-detected or overridden with external-hostname).")
```
2. Insert whitespace / `\n` at the beginning of the lower line
```go
fs.StringVar(&o.ServiceAccounts.JWKSURI, "service-account-jwks-uri", o.ServiceAccounts.JWKSURI, ""+
	"Overrides the URI for the JSON Web Key Set in the discovery doc served at"+
	" /.well-known/openid-configuration. This flag is useful if the discovery doc"+
	" and key set are served to relying parties from a URL other than the"+
	" API server's external (as auto-detected or overridden with external-hostname).")
```

The inconsistency of the concatenation sometimes causes the missing whitespace, like this.
https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-apiserver/#:~:text=%2D%2Dservice%2Daccount%2Djwks%2Duri
![IMG_0253](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e73b832f-a732-4492-91c9-03ee83216409)

With a few inspections, I assumed the first one (Insert whitespace / `\n` at the last of the upper line) is the current majority.
All the second patterns can be searched by a regex `[^" (]"\+\n` (and excluding the line ends with `\n`)

### What happened?

We found that after the kubelet process restarts, some pods dependent on device plugins may enter the UnexpectedAdmissionError state.
The reason is that when the kubelet restarts, it retrieves the pod list from the apiserver and begins processing the pods. At this point, the device plugin has not yet had the chance to register, which can cause the pods to enter an UnexpectedAdmissionError state. As a result, the containers are killed, and the workload then pulls up a new replica.
Assuming the service has only two replicas, the aforementioned reasons may lead to the pod being rebuilt, during which the service will be interrupted.

Containers should not exit due to kubelet restarts.

title: API proxy strips URL query params when proxying websocket connections
body:
Tested on Kubernetes 1.14 (minikube 1.0). To reproduce:

1. deploy pod with a websocket server running:

    ```bash
    kubectl run wsserver --generator=run-pod/v1 --rm -i --tty --image ubuntu:disco -- bash -c \
      "apt-get update && apt-get install -y wget && \
      wget https://github.com/vi/websocat/releases/download/v1.4.0/websocat_1.4.0_ssl1.1_amd64.deb && \
      dpkg -i webso*.deb && \
      websocat -vv -s 0.0.0.0:8000"
    ```

2. in host shell outside minikube run the following websocat command to connect to the websocket server in your wsserver pod:

    ```bash
    websocat --binary --ws-c-uri=wss://192.168.99.100:8443/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/wsserver:8000/proxy/test?foo=what - ws-c:cmd:'socat - ssl:192.168.99.100:8443,verify=0,cafile=$HOME/.minikube/ca.crt,cert=$HOME/.minikube/client.crt,key=$HOME/.minikube/client.key'
    ```
3. check the output of the server-side websocat and notice that **the query params are missing**: `[DEBUG websocat::ws_server_peer] Incoming { version: Http11, subject: (Get, AbsolutePath("/test")), headers: ...`
4. exec into your pod with the websocket server, and issue a local websocket connect.

    ```bash
    kubectl exec wsserver websocat ws://localhost:8000/test?foo=what
    ```

5. check output of the service-side websocat, now **the query params are present as to be expected**: `[DEBUG websocat::ws_server_peer] Incoming { version: Http11, subject: (Get, AbsolutePath("/test?foo=what")), headers: ...`

title: Kubelet watchdog: improve logging visibility and add internal timeouts
body:
### What would you like to be added?

### **1\. Log SdNotify failure at Error (currently V(5))**

Currently when `hc.watchdog.SdNotify(false)` fails, the err is logged at `v=5`.

Change this to a `log.ErrorS(..)` event, since this is an exceptional, infrequent and an error scenario.This failure would be captured by standard logging levels, whereas the current level of 5 is typically filtered.

Reference : [https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.34/pkg/kubelet/watchdog/watchdog\_linux.go\#L149-L152](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.34/pkg/kubelet/watchdog/watchdog_linux.go#L149-L152)  

### **2\. Implement timeout for doCheck()**

In `doCheck()`, we run checks in a serial fashion. As we continue to add checks, these stack up, and the aggregate completion time needs to finish before `watchdogVal`.

It would be beneficial to place a timeout for each check to complete within a fraction of `hc.interval`. That way, a long-running check will return an error, causing the specific stalling check to be logged and preventing the entire loop from hanging silently.

Reference [https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.33/pkg/kubelet/watchdog/watchdog\_linux.go\#L157-L163](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.33/pkg/kubelet/watchdog/watchdog_linux.go#L157-L163)

### **3\. Add timeout to hc.watchdog.SdNotify()**

When we call `hc.watchdog.SdNotify()`, the kubelet connects, writes, and closes a session with systemd's unix domain socket. Currently, the kubelet does not apply a timeout to this action.

If this takes longer than `hc.interval`, `SdNotify` blocks, and the heartbeat is never sent or logged. Guarding this with a timeout and logging the failure would provide a clue that the issue lies with the systemd socket interaction rather than the Kubelet internals.

Reference [https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.33/pkg/kubelet/watchdog/watchdog\_linux.go\#L139](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.33/pkg/kubelet/watchdog/watchdog_linux.go#L139) 

### Why is this needed?

The introduction of kubelet’s systemd watchdog healthcheck has improved the way in which we monitor the health of the service.

But we’ve seen that kubelet may fail to send its heartbeat for a number of reasons (deadlock, misbehaving systemd, VM migration pause, host performance issues, etc). The outcome of such a failure, which is triggered by a `SIGABRT` and subsequent restarts of the Kubelet are logged and visible to the operator. But the root cause of the event is not clear, making it hard to identify what is causing the kubelet to fail.

The changes summarized here provide additional logging and guardrails for kubelet internals that may help identify the root of the issue quicker.

title: Configure memory overcommit behavior on node
body:
### What would you like to be added?

#### Background:

From kernel [documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/vm/overcommit-accounting), there is a parameter `vm.overcommit_memory` to control the overcommit behavior with following values:
* 0 - never overcommit, kernel default
* 1 - always overcommit, kubelet default
* 2 - overcommit is allowed with specified amount of physical RAM defined by `vm.overcommit_ratio' (percentage) or `vm.overcommit_kbytes' 


#### Kubelet Implementation:

Kubelet has override the paramter `vm.overcommit_memory=1` in [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.1/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L452), with context in #14935. This ensures the memory overcommit policy to never fail on the node, and let the OOM killer handle real memory allocations. 

#### Feature Request:

Sometimes users want to run memory sensitive workloads and control the overcommit size, can we make the sysctl configurable so that users could change based on their use case?

title: StatefulSet: support resize pvc storage in K8s v1.11
body:
/kind feature


**What happened**:
With k8s v1.11 the [new feature "Resizing Persistent Volume"](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2018/07/12/resizing-persistent-volumes-using-kubernetes/)   was prompted to beta. 

I tried to update the field "statefulset.spec.volumeClaimTemplates.spec.resources.requests.storage" by increasing the storage size from 3Gi to 4Gi, however received following error message.

"The StatefulSet "es-data" is invalid: spec: Forbidden: updates to statefulset spec for fields other than 'replicas', 'template', and 'updateStrategy' are forbidden."


**What you expected to happen**:
The storage size defined in volumeClaimTemplates should be updated using the new feature in v 1.11. 

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Try following yaml file. Note that you might need to change the "storageClassName" field according to your cluster setup.

Once the deployment finished, try to change the field "statefulset.spec.volumeClaimTemplates.spec.resources.requests.storage" to e.g. 4Gi.

then applying the same yaml file will result in above error.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 80
    name: web
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: nginx
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx # has to match .spec.template.metadata.labels
  serviceName: "nginx"
  replicas: 2 # by default is 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx # has to match .spec.selector.matchLabels
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 10
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: k8s.gcr.io/nginx-slim:0.8
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          name: web
        volumeMounts:
        - name: www
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: www
    spec:
      accessModes: [ "ReadWriteOnce" ]
      storageClassName: "default"
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 3Gi
```

title: HPA e2e tests not running in parallel as intended
body:
Although #131091 was intended to enable the HPA e2e tests to run in parallel, it appears that they are still running serially. According to the [test-infra](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-autoscaling/sig-autoscaling-config.yaml#L386) configuration , the autoscaling tests are not currently executed in parallel.

According to @maxcao13, downstream (e.g., OpenShift) environments that attempted to remove the serial labels saw all 31 HPA tests run concurrently, leading to resource exhaustion and broken tests.

It’s currently unclear what the expected upstream behavior or outcome should be - whether the HPA tests are meant to run fully in parallel or only partially, depending on infrastructure capacity. Another possible approach could be to trim down the resources that each HPA test uses, allowing more tests to run concurrently without overwhelming the cluster.

/sig autoscaling
/kind cleanup
cc @adrianmoisey 
/assign @maxcao13

title: Validating Admission Policy: Uniform workload type policy enforcement
body:
This is a feature suggestion for ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP).  It may depend on other enhancements to workload types before it becomes tractable.

Writing a VAP that verifies all PodSpecs is difficult/impossible.  PodSpecs are embedded in multiple built-in types (Deployments, Jobs...) as well as CRDs.

Even writing a VAP to validate the containers in Pod requires writing validation code in triplicate to handle `containers`, `initContainers` and `ephemeralContainers`.

Writing a VAP against Pod and all the other built-in types that embed PodSpec is even more difficult and is at risk of not validating types that are introduced AFTER the VAP is authored.

If CRDs were to clearly identify where PodSpecs were embedded, and VAP had a way to match "all resources that embed PodSpec", this could become feasible.

This idea has come up multiple times and relates to topics such as CRX and "workload type embedding", so I'd like to open this tracker to allow for discussion.

/sig api-machinery

cc @cici37 @cheftako @thockin

title: WAS: Retry binding API calls on pod group binding cycle
body:
### What would you like to be added?

some slack discussion: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0AHLJ0EAEL/p1775561714916009

Just add a few retries (with some backoff) at the pod group binding cycle's pod binding API calls. 
How many retries? -> That is a open question. 

Options in my mind:
- always the same max retries. 
- decide the max retry proportionally to the group size.
- retries workloads that meet some criteria, like gang and/or bigger than a certain size, etc.

### Why is this needed?

When it comes to WAS, binding API call failures due to temporary network issue or kube-apiserver instability are the expensive issue (especially for huge workloads) because
- We need to reschedule pods that failed at binding API call again with another WAS scheduling cycle. WAS is expensive.
- Gang could end up with a stuck issue if users don't have any rescheduling component (descheduler, Kueue's PodsReadyTimeout, etc)
  - Example: One-rack-sized gang job pods get scheduled to rack-A. But, more than half bindings have failed (they go back to the queue). Smaller jobs later came and take over the remaining empty capacity on rack-A. The first job never lands until smaller jobs complete at the same timing, which could be nearly impossible.
  - Note: if the pod group has some scheduled pods, the scheduler tries to bind all the other pods onto the same domain. i.e., in this example, all the remaining pods have to go to rack-A. 

So, the reliability of binding API calls matters more than usual pod-by-pod scheduling. Of course, retries don't solve the issue completely, but it would reduce the chance for workloads to get into these troubles at least.

Adding a few retries (which might lengthen the binding cycle time) makes sense to me because:
- If some temporary network issue or kube-apiserver instability happen, even if we immediately push failed pods back to the queue and proceed to next schedulings of other pods, next bindings might fail with the same reason. "immediately pushing back" doesn't give any value for us.
- The pod group binding for big workloads takes time anyway. Adding some few retry API calls doesn't matter. 

Alternatively or additionally, we can use NNN to preserve the previous decisions _to some extent_, but NNN is easy to get taken over. The bigger workload it is, the more likely it could hit the temporary binding failures, the more likely its NNN could be taken over by others (simply because it has tons of pods), therefore the more they need a reliable binding retry anyway for such failure mode.

/sig scheduling

title: Daemonset Rollout can get stuck when the Controller chooses bad nodes
body:
### What happened?

The Daemonset Controller can pick broken nodes during a rollout causing the rollout to get stuck and require Admin intervention.

When the Daemonset controller is choosing a node, the underlying node health is not clear until Daemonset attempts the rollout.  For example, a stuck node can exhibit normal behavior such as appearing `Ready`, having `Running` Pods, ect...  However, when the Daemonset attempts to rollout a new Pod, the Pod can get stuck.  The Daemonset has no realistic chance to rollout this Pod without Admin intervention on the Node.

In a large enough cluster (500+ nodes), it's common to discover many stuck nodes during a rollout.  Each time the Daemonset controller chooses a bad node, it negatively impacts the rollout.  The worst case is the rollout gets completely stuck as the `maxUnavailable` capacity is completely consumed by stuck nodes.

In all of these scenarios, admin intervention is required to manually adjust the `maxUnavailable` to account for the discovered stuck nodes during the rollout.
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
spec:
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 5%
```

### What did you expect to happen?

When the Daemonset controller discovers a stuck node, it should report its observation (in a location so that admins/providers can observe) and deprioritze this node's pod rollout until later on.  Eventually, the rollout will get stuck, but only after all the health nodes have been upgraded. 

The Daemonset controller shouldn't need to manage the lifecycle of the node as that's external, but it would be useful if it knew about it.  Having the admin manually change `maxUnavailable` side steps this larger issue - sharing node health.  These such scenarios can exist in many forms because it's difficult to sync the real-world state of the node with the control-plane when they are distributed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This is a scenario where you can observe the daemonset controller behavior.
- Create a 5 node cluster
- The node are all in `Ready` state
- Attempt a daemonset rollout with `maxUnavailable` set to `1`
- Rollout hits a stuck kubelet and Pod is unable to be deleted
- Daemonset rollout hangs forever until admin intervenes
