title: kubectl drain stuck in eviction retry loop even after pod is no longer on the drained node
body:
### What happened?

Hi everyone,
I wanted to raise a potential issue (or at least a discussion point) around the behavior of kubectl drain when eviction requests are throttled.

The behavior: When kubectl drain is triggered, it attempts to evict all pods on the target node. If the eviction API returns a 429 Too Many Requests (typically because of a blocking PodDisruptionBudget), the drain command retries the eviction every 5 seconds — indefinitely.
The problem: During this retry window, if the pod gets rescheduled or moved to a different node and come up with same name(in statefulset) by an external factor (e.g., a controller, a preemption, or manual intervention), kubectl drain has no awareness of this. It continues to retry eviction for a pod that no longer belongs to the node being drained — potentially blocking the drain operation forever.

Is this a known limitation? Is there a design reason why this check isn't done today?
Thanks!


https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C09NXKJKA/p1774538968085579

### What did you expect to happen?

On each retry iteration, kubectl drain should verify whether the pod still has spec.nodeName set to the node being drained. If the pod has moved, it should either skip that pod or consider it "done" from the drain's perspective.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a statefulset with n number of pods
- Drain the underlying node and make sure PDB never allows the pod to get evicted.
- Manually delete the pod so that it gets scheduled on another node
- Drain will still delete that pod even if that pod is no longer running on the drained node.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Backward incompatibility of OpenAPI changes
body:
### What happened?

This [commit](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131755/changes#diff-33ef32bf6c23acb95f5902d7097b7a1d5128ca061167ec0716715b0b9eeaa5f6) removed rest friendly name conversion for OpenAPI model names and now requires addition of `k8s:openapi-model-package` annotation for the correct model names to be autogenerated. This change can be backward incompatible. For extension APIServers that dont explicitly add the required annotation, the generated OpenAPI model names may incorrectly contain ~1 characters instead of “/” due Json escaping logic [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-openapi/blob/4e65d59e963e749fa7939999518f9e90682983c3/pkg/builder/openapi.go#L130-L133). This produces an invalid OpenAPI schema. 

In OpenAPI V2, the specification is an aggregated document across all API’s. An invalid schema generated by an Extension APIServer is not validated before corresponding APIService is created. This means the incorrect schema propagates to aggregated specification causing failures that affect interactions with all API’s - including the core API’s served by kube-apiserver. Any client that uses OpenAPI V2 by default (like helm) would be impacted while performing OpenAPI validation against the aggregated schema.

References highlighting impact due to this behavior: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-load-balancer-controller/issues/4543 and https://github.com/karmada-io/karmada/pull/7255

### What did you expect to happen?

1. Backward compatibility is maintained even when `k8s:openapi-model-package` is not explicitly specified. Retain the logic for rest friendly model name generation to maintain backward compatibility when the required annotation is not present.
2. Validate the OpenAPI schema from an extension API server before creating the corresponding APIService, to prevent runtime failures.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Setup an extension apiserver without `k8s:openapi-model-package` annotation. [Sample-apiserver](https://github.com/kubernetes/sample-apiserver/blob/master/pkg/apis/wardle) could be used by removing the annotation within `doc.go` files and generating the updated open api definition. 
2. Build, deploy and register this as extension apiserver within a kubernetes cluster. 
3. Observe the corrupted aggregated OpenAPI V2 spec for the cluster. 
```
kubectl get --raw /openapi/v2 > /tmp/openapi_v2.json
grep '~1' /tmp/openapi_v2.json
```
4. Attempt to run any command that performs OpenAPI validation, this would fail.  
Example: `kubectl apply -f some-pod.yaml`

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

Issue not specific to a kubernetes version. 1.33 - 1.35, all versions are impacted when relying on kubernetes clients that default to OpenAPI V2. 


### Cloud provider

Issue not specific to a cloud provider

title: Pods that consume "devices" via Device Plugin always fail when Node reboots even if it implements `plugins_registry` interface
body:
### What happened?

When node reboots, Pods that consume **devices** via Device Plugin always fail.

Even if I implement device plugin with ability to use `/var/lib/kubelet/plugins_registry` directory, it fails too.

Below is my flow of inspection to understand current implementation of `kubelet` related to the device plugin interface.

***

I tested below cases:
- Only `kubelet` restarts
- Only `containerd` restarts
- Both `kubelet` and `containerd` restart

All of 3 cases do not make any error. It only happens when node reboots.

***

Device Health status is provided using `healthDevices`.
- [When `kubelet` starts, it restores from checkpoint, but both `healthDevices` and `unhealthyDevices` set to empty set.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L506-L532)
- [`healthyDevices` will be supplied through this code block.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L259-L318)
    - Right now, there is no other code block that supplies `healthyDevices`.

About Device Plugin Registration
- [Device Plugin can be registered to `kubelet` through this code block.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/plugin/v1beta1/handler.go#L41-L44)
    - Plugin sends request to `kubelet`.
- After registration, dedicated client will be created and [run at another goroutine](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/plugin/v1beta1/handler.go#L78-L80).
- [As I mentioned above, `healthyDevices` can only be injected through this code block](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L271-L318).
    - However, initialization always happens at the beginning of this code block.
- To summarize it, **there is no way to supply health devices before device plugin registration**.

***

About `PluginManager` and `plugins_registry`
> `pluginmanager` runs a set of asynchronous loops that figure out which plugins need to be registered/unregistered based on this node and makes it so.
- [`plugins_registry` is used at `PluginManager`. The first usage can be found here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L848-L851).
- [In `PluginManager`, registration of Device Plugin watcher (NOT the DEVICE PLUGIN) happens.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1581-L1582)
    - [For device plugin, this code block implements Device Plugin watcher interface.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/plugin/v1beta1/server.go#L40-L45)
- [After registration of watcher, `PluginManager` runs.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/plugin_manager.go#L108-L124)
    - Inside that code block, we can find `go pm.reconciler.Run(stopCh)`. We can jump to [this section](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/reconciler/reconciler.go#L85-L91).
- [In the `reconcile()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/reconciler/reconciler.go#L111-L165), it syncs `desiredStateOfWorld` and `actualStateOfWorld`.
- [In this code block, all unix sockets exist in the `/var/lib/kubelet/plugins_registry` are managed through `AddOrUpdatePlugin()` method.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/pluginwatcher/plugin_watcher.go#L187-L200)

All of above steps are executed BEFORE entering `syncLoop()`.

***

So my thought was, If I implement device plugin to deal with `plugins_registry`, it can be registered to `kubelet` before other pod run.
- [`GetInfo(...)`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L91) and [`NotifyRegistrationStatus(...)`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.31/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L166) GRPC interface have to be implemented.

However, even if I implemented above things, same problem happens.
- When node reboots, all containers are in stopped state.
- `kubelet` is in charge of re-run stopped containers in that node.
- Before entering `syncLoop()`, 2 GRPC interface will be called.
    - However, because device plugin pod is in stopped state, above GRPC call fails.
    - Due to failure of above GRPC call, device plugin registration before entering `syncLoop()` also fails too.

To solve this problem, I have to run the device plugin using other method (e.g. systemd daemon), that can't be managed by kubelet.

### What did you expect to happen?

To be honest, I know the current problem but don't know the nice solution.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Prepare device plugin (e.g. [`NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin)) and run any Pod consumes that device (e.g. NVIDIA GPU).

After Pod successfully created and run without any problem, DO node reboot (e.g. just type `sudo reboot`).

After node reboots, you can see error message like below.
```
Allocate failed due to no healthy devices present; cannot allocate unhealthy devices nvidia.com/gpu, which is unexpected
```

### Anything else we need to know?

This issue has been discussed in [this Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1709610711920639).

body:
# Problem 

There is a case:
t0: container liveness probe failed, readiness probe still succeed for some reason, kubelet starts to do pre-stop
t1: pre-stop done, kubelet starts to stop container
between t0 and t1, readiness probe didn't failed,  pod is still ready, traffic is forwarded to  the abnormal container.

title: Scale max pod backoff time with the number of unscheduled pods in the cluster
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Instead of using statically configured `pod_max_backoff_seconds`, allow the kube-scheduler to dynamically compute this value, based on the actual load, taking into consideration number of unscheduled (or unschedulable) pods and potentially average scheduling throughput.

/sig scheduling

### Why is this needed?

In large clusters, the default 10 seconds max backoff time value is too low and can lead to unschedulable pods starvation issue, when a large quantity of unschedulable, but high priority pods occupy all scheduling cycles, starving lower priority pods. Configuring a good static value is a hard process and should be automated on scheduler side to mitigate such issues.

title: A mechanism to fail a Pod that is stuck due to an invalid Image
body:
### What would you like to be added?

A mechanism to set a Pod into phase=Failed when the image pull has failed for a number of times (perhaps configurable).
Currently, the Pod just stays in phase=Pending

### Why is this needed?

This is especially problematic for Jobs submitted through a queueing system.

In a queued environment, the time when the job starts running (pods created) might be hours or even days after the Job is created. Then, the user that submitted the job might not realize their mistake until it's too late. Since these Pods block resources in the cluster, it might cause other pending Jobs not to start.

If the Pods stay in phase=Pending, the job controller cannot do anything about them, as it only does "failure handling" once the Pods actually terminate with a phase=Failed.

body:
### What happened?

The CSI driver mount may show this error which prevents the volume to be mounted to the pod on Windows.

```
E0215 06:30:42.244047    4176 nestedpendingoperations.go:348] Operation for "{volumeName:kubernetes.io/csi/csi.vsphere.vmware.com^3a8ec4cb-cd82-4e6a-826a-3ff0b998d347-4f75432b-3c45-42a4-b205-176a45bf7237 podName: nodeName:}" failed. No retries permitted until 2025-02-15 06:32:44.2440476 -0800 PST m=+373.590890801 (durationBeforeRetry 2m2s). Error: MountVolume.MountDevice failed for volume "pvc-4f75432b-3c45-42a4-b205-176a45bf7237" (UniqueName: "kubernetes.io/csi/csi.vsphere.vmware.com^3a8ec4cb-cd82-4e6a-826a-3ff0b998d347-4f75432b-3c45-42a4-b205-176a45bf7237") pod "win-webserver-new-57df95657d-58p96" (UID: "bc613216-d761-4d4f-8677-b00249bff5fd") : kubernetes.io/csi: attacher.MountDevice failed to create dir "\\var\\lib\\kubelet\\plugins\\kubernetes.io\\csi\\csi.vsphere.vmware.com\\a2d2504ecac0aea11a8ddbfe72ebd253579aa79a98c6133b71a9a26200d740b8\\globalmount":  path \var\lib\kubelet\plugins\kubernetes.io\csi\csi.vsphere.vmware.com\a2d2504ecac0aea11a8ddbfe72ebd253579aa79a98c6133b71a9a26200d740b8\globalmount exists but is not a directory
```

The current logic to detect whether the volume is a mount point on Windows is not reliable any longer.


### What did you expect to happen?

kubelet should ensure the CSI volume mounted correctly on Windows after crashing.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Relaunch kubelet after CSI volume is mounted.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is related to the volume mount point check on Windows.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c2529e844395f8895ae809fa1a5775ea8181fd20/pkg/util/filesystem/defaultfs.go#L93-L94

This didn't work on Windows with NTFS.
A more reliable way to do the check is recommended by Windows documentation
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/determining-whether-a-directory-is-a-volume-mount-point
as demonstrated in this csi-proxy PR.
https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy/blob/c55b906bb336e30e8074a41a2063543647fb6c91/pkg/os/volume/api.go#L408-L447

Another approach could be checking `ModeIrregular` from `Lstat`.

title: Preloaded image pull spec poisoned by a pulled image
body:
### What happened?

This seems to be a corner case in the "Ensure secret pulled images" [feature](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2535).

1. pre-load an image from repo X behind kubelet's back
2. deploy pod A, which references the image from repo X, **without** specifying a pull secret and with `imagePullPolicy: Never`; delete pod A
3. deploy pod B, referencing the same (in terms of identical content digest)  image but from a different repo Y, **using** a pull secret and default `imagePullPolicy`; delete pod B
4. deploy the same pod A again -> get `Container image "X..." is not present with pull policy of Never`

### What did you expect to happen?

Step (4) should continue working if step (1) did.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Note: @SergeyKanzhelev suggested using agnhost/fakeregistryserver, but I was unable to make the container runtime reach a pod running on the same cluster 🤷🏻 So here is a recipe using my private toy repo on quay. But any non-public repo will do.

# Preparation

1. Prepare an image. You can use any image (does not even need to run properly) that you can get both:
- preloaded on the cluster behind kubelet's back from repository X, and
- present on a private OCI repository Y.

Here is how I did it, after giving up on trying to get the multi-arch `registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10.1` mirrored (`error from registry: manifest invalid` 🙈).

```
$ echo foo >> README.md
$ cat > Dockerfile.foo <<EOF
FROM scratch
COPY ./README.md .
EOF
$ docker build -f Dockerfile.foo . --tag quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo
$ docker tag quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo
$ docker push quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo # X
$ docker push quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo # Y
```

2. Get the image preloaded on a node. I used [image-prefetcher](https://github.com/stackrox/image-prefetcher):

```
$ go run github.com/stackrox/image-prefetcher/deploy@v0.4.3 --version v0.4.3 --namespace t foo > foo-prefetch.yaml
$ echo quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo > image-list.txt
$ kubectl create ns t
$ kubectl create -n t configmap foo --from-file=images.txt=image-list.txt
$ kubectl apply -f foo-prefetch.yaml
```

# Run pod A

```
$ cat > pod-a-never.yaml << EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: testpod-a-never
  namespace: t
spec:
  nodeName: gke-mowsiany-test1-default-pool-1e8c798d-q93d # just to make things deterministic
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: test
    args:
    - foo
    imagePullPolicy: Never
    image: quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo
EOF
$ kubectl apply -f pod-a-never.yaml 
pod/testpod-a-never created
$ kubectl describe -f pod-a-never.yaml
[...]
Events:
  Type     Reason   Age   From     Message
  ----     ------   ----  ----     -------
  Normal   Pulled   6s    kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Container image "quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo" already present on machine and can be accessed by the pod
  Normal   Created  6s    kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Container created
[...]
$ kubectl delete -f pod-a-never.yaml 
pod "testpod-a-never" deleted from t namespace
```

# Run pod B

```
$ cat > pod-b-pull.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: testpod-b-pull
  namespace: t
spec:
  nodeName: gke-mowsiany-test1-default-pool-1e8c798d-q93d
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: test
    args:
    - foo
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    image: quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo
  imagePullSecrets:
  - name: mowsiany-robot1-pull-secret
EOF
$ kubectl -n t create -f ~/Downloads/mowsiany-robot1-secret.yml # Attached below
$ kubectl apply -f pod-b-pull.yaml 
pod/testpod-b-pull created
$ kubectl describe -f pod-b-pull.yaml 
[...]
Events:
  Type     Reason   Age   From     Message
  ----     ------   ----  ----     -------
  Normal   Pulling  7s    kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Pulling image "quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo"
  Normal   Pulled   7s    kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Successfully pulled image "quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo" in 285ms (285ms including waiting). Image size: 4601 bytes.
[...]
$ kubectl delete -f pod-b-pull.yaml 
pod "testpod-b-pull" deleted from t namespace
```

# Run pod A again

```
$ kubectl apply -f pod-a-never.yaml 
pod/testpod-a-never created
$ kubectl describe -f pod-a-never.yaml 
[...]
Events:
  Type     Reason             Age              From     Message
  ----     ------             ----             ----     -------
  Warning  ErrImageNeverPull  3s (x3 over 4s)  kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Container image "quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo" is not present with pull policy of Never
  Warning  Failed             3s (x3 over 4s)  kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Error: ErrImageNeverPull
```


### Anything else we need to know?

1. [Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1775037474294369)
2. After running pod B, the following file appears in `/var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled` on the node:

```

gke-mowsiany-test1-default-pool-1e8c798d-q93d /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled # grep -l mowsiany *|xargs jq .

  "lastUpdatedTime": "2026-04-02T11:02:13Z",
  "imageRef": "sha256:6446253dd96b1a1ec4a6d69fe9859961929c3a6c79a17f119f4f5021693d998b",
  "credentialMapping": {
    "quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv": {
      "kubernetesSecrets": [
        {
          "uid": "3d2a7cfc-3554-49b5-9fdb-7da367b705e3",
          "namespace": "t",
          "name": "mowsiany-robot1-pull-secret",
          "credentialHash": "8d80430d4f9c305461e11e35e4faa310611ca4d577265b2d18859ce5679eb9c0"
        }

```

What I’m seeing (k8s v1.32): • When the controller emits many Events for the same CR, kubectl describe and kubectl get events only show a limited subset (roughly ~15–20). • The later events get missed (it looks like only the “first ~20” appear). • If I remove some intermediate events (emit fewer), the events near the end start appearing, but again it caps around ~20 total. • I also notice events sometimes appear very late (e.g., 20+ minutes after they were emitted), even though the cluster creation finished in <1 minute and all events were emitted in the first minute. • Commands tried: kubectl get events --watch --field-selector involvedObject.name= kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name= -A kubectl describe Question: Is there a reliable way to verify that all Events are actually being emitted (beyond what kubectl get/describe shows? title: NCC-E003660-WV3: Privilege Escalation via `nodes/proxy` Permission
body:
### NCC-E003660-WV3: Privilege Escalation via `nodes/proxy` Permission
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
A user with permissions on the `nodes/proxy` subresource in a cluster has full permissions
against the kubelet API on any node by proxying requests through the API server, and can
execute commands in any pod. This may represent privileges beyond those expected by
the cluster administrator, and this situation is not explained in the Kubernetes
documentation.

**Description**
The Kubernetes API server proxy is a feature which allows users to proxy requests through
the API server to workloads or nodes. When a proxy request is made to the kubelet service
on a node, the API server’s own client certificate (which in a typical cluster is a user in the
`system:masters` group) is used to authenticate the request. This effectively allows a user with `get` permissions against the `nodes/proxy` subresource to make `GET` requests to the kubelet
API as `system:masters` (and equivalent for `create`, `patch`, etc.). It is not clear from the
Kubernetes documentation that giving a user permission to make proxied requests to nodes is effectively permitting them to run arbitrary commands against any pod (as can be achieved using the Kubelet API’s `/exec` endpoint).

**Recommendation**
Ensure that the Kubernetes documentation makes it clear that permissions on the `nodes/
proxy` subresource are powerful, overriding other permissions against nodes (as shown
above) and permitting commands to be run in pods.

**Component**
kubelet


**Anything else we need to know?**
See umbrella issue [#118980](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118980) for current status of all issues created from these findings.
The vendor gave this issue an ID of NCC-E003660-WHE and it was finding 18 of the report under the kube-apiserver section.
The vendor considers this issue Medium Risk, High Impact, Low Exploitability
To view the original finding, begin on page 49 of the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Test Environment**
Kubernetes 1.24.3

title: [Scheduling] OpportunisticBatching: redundant synchronous RunFilterPlugins call in batchStateCompatible for low-resource pods
body:
/kind bug
/sig scheduling

### What happened?

When OpportunisticBatching (KEP-5598) is enabled, `batchStateCompatible` performs a synchronous
`RunFilterPlugins` call on the `lastChosenNode` to validate whether the cached batch state is
still usable (i.e., the previously chosen node is now full).

For pods with low resource requirements that do not fill up a node, this check always passes
(not rejected), causing `batchStateCompatible` to always return `false`. This means:

1. **The synchronous `RunFilterPlugins` call is pure overhead** — it runs on the critical
   scheduling path, adds latency, and never yields a useful result for these pods.
2. **The same node is filtered twice** — once synchronously in `batchStateCompatible`, and again
   in the parallel `findNodesThatPassFilters` pipeline (since `lastChosenNode` is part of
   `allNodes`).
3. **The batch cache is flushed every cycle** — preventing any future batching even though the
   pod signatures match.

This is a common scenario in production clusters with many small pods (microservices, batch
workloads, etc.), where the batching optimization provides no benefit but introduces consistent
per-cycle overhead.

### What did you expect to happen?

The `batchStateCompatible` check should not introduce synchronous overhead on the critical
scheduling path when the optimization cannot provide any benefit (i.e., when pods don't fill
up nodes).

### Code reference

```go
// pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/batch.go, line 218-222
status := b.handle.RunFilterPlugins(ctx, state, pod, lastChosenNode)
if !status.IsRejected() {
    b.logUnusableState(logger, cycleCount, metrics.BatchFlushNodeNotFull)
    return false
}
```

###  Proposed optimization

Option A: Cheap pre-check before RunFilterPluginsBefore calling RunFilterPlugins on lastChosenNode, perform a lightweight resource comparison

(pod's resource requests vs. node's remaining allocatable capacity). If the node clearly has
sufficient resources, skip the expensive RunFilterPlugins call entirely. This is O(1) and
avoids running all filter plugins.Caveat: This only covers resource-based filters and may miss non-resource filters (affinity,
taints, etc.), but it would eliminate the overhead for the common case.

Option B: Include lastChosenNode validation in the parallel filtering pipeline

Include lastChosenNode validation in the parallel filtering pipelineWhen batch state exists but validity is uncertain, include the lastChosenNode filter result
as metadata from the parallel findNodesThatPassFilters execution. After parallel filtering
completes, retroactively determine batch validity for the NEXT scheduling cycle. This shifts
the validation cost from a synchronous pre-check to being amortized within the existing
parallel workload.

title: watcherStream.buf in apiserver can grow indefinitely
body:
### What happened?

The [watcherStream.buf](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d3b9c54bd952117924fb0790f6989c0d30715b19/vendor/go.etcd.io/etcd/client/v3/watch.go#L243) in apiserver can [grow indefinitely](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d3b9c54bd952117924fb0790f6989c0d30715b19/vendor/go.etcd.io/etcd/client/v3/watch.go#L867). When this happens, ConsistentReadFromCache feature will wait for 3s and hope the cache to catch and then delegate to etcd.
One scenario that this can happen: high pod revision churns (pod mutation) and high number of watch requests.
There's no metric or logs that indicate the backlog in this buffer.

Enabling `ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode` FG doesn't help much.

### What did you expect to happen?

1. We may want to have a queue depth metric for this buffer. But I'm not sure if it is practical when it's an etcd vendor library code.
2. If metric is not possible, we should at least add some log to show the queue depth for the buffer
3. We may want to take some action when the buffer is too big. e.g. restart this etcd watch.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

It may not be the minimum to reproduce, but the steps I use:
1. Generate pod mutation load: about 150 pod revisions/sec where each pod size is about 50KB.
2. Create watch requests load: 40 pod watch requests/sec

title: [Declarative Validation] Feature: Add `+k8s:multipleOf` declarative validation tag
body:
Add a new `+k8s:multipleOf=<int>` declarative validation (DV) tag that enforces a numeric field's value must be an exact multiple of the specified number. This corresponds to the OpenAPI/JSON Schema `multipleOf` keyword.

## Motivation

OpenAPI/JSON Schema supports `multipleOf` as a standard validation keyword. DV currently has no equivalent. This is needed for fields like integer resource quantities where values must be whole units, or alignment/granularity requirements.

## Kubernetes API Example

**Integer resource quantity validation** in `pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go`:

```go
// Handwritten validation today:
if helper.IsIntegerResourceName(resource) {
    if value.MilliValue()%int64(1000) != int64(0) {
        allErrs = append(allErrs, field.Invalid(fldPath, value, isNotIntegerErrorMsg))
    }
}
```

This validates that millivalue representations of integer resources are multiples of 1000 (i.e., whole units). With the proposed tag:

```go
type ResourceList struct {
    // +k8s:multipleOf=1000
    MilliCPU int64
}
```

## OpenAPI Semantics

- **OpenAPI keyword:** `multipleOf`
- **Go type in JSONSchemaProps:** `*float64`
- **Spec behavior:** Value must be divisible by the factor with no remainder. Factor must be **strictly positive** (zero and negatives are rejected).
- **Float support in OpenAPI:** Yes — OpenAPI `multipleOf` supports float factors (e.g., `0.01`). The kube-openapi validation uses special float64 precision handling (`IsFloat64AJSONInteger()`) and has separate `MultipleOf()` (float), `MultipleOfInt()` (int64), `MultipleOfUint()` (uint64) implementations.

## DV Design Considerations

- **Integer-only vs. float:** Existing DV numeric tags (`+k8s:minimum`, `+k8s:maximum`) only accept **Go integer types** and parse values via `util.ParseInt()`. DV could follow this pattern (integer-only `multipleOf`) which covers the primary k8s use cases. Float support could be added later if needed.
- **Type checking:** Should use `types.IsInteger(t)` like existing numeric limits in `limits.go` to restrict to integer fields.
- **Validation function:** For integer types, a simple modulo (`value % factor != 0`) suffices. No need for the float precision handling that OpenAPI's `MultipleOf()` uses.
- **Zero and negative factors:** Should be rejected at code generation time (lint error), consistent with OpenAPI spec.

## Implementation Notes

- Should be implemented in `validators/limits.go` alongside existing numeric validation tags
- Should generate a call to a new validation function in `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/validate`
- Validator file: `staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/limits.go`

/sig api-machinery
/triage accepted
/area api-validation

title: Migrate DRA components to support granular authorization on status updates
body:
/triage accepted
/sig auth node network
/wg device-management
/good-first-issue

@liggitt @aojea @dims @pohly @johnbelamaric 

AI generated migration guide with list of potentially impacted components.

---

# DRA Granular Status Authorization: Migration Guide

Starting in Kubernetes v1.36, the `DRAResourceClaimGranularStatusAuthorization` feature gate
(beta, on-by-default) enforces fine-grained authorization checks for `ResourceClaim` status
updates. Components that previously only needed `update`/`patch` on `resourceclaims/status`
now require additional permissions on **synthetic subresources** depending on which status
fields they modify.

Reference: #134947, https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/55070

---

## What changed

| Old permission | New additional permission required | Who needs it |
|---|---|---|
| `resourceclaims/status` `update`/`patch` | `resourceclaims/binding` `update`/`patch` | Schedulers, allocation controllers (anything modifying `status.allocation` or `status.reservedFor`) |
| `resourceclaims/status` `update`/`patch` | `resourceclaims/driver` `associated-node:update`/`associated-node:patch` | Node-local DRA drivers (ServiceAccount bound to a specific node via pod-bound token) |
| `resourceclaims/status` `update`/`patch` | `resourceclaims/driver` `arbitrary-node:update`/`arbitrary-node:patch` | Control-plane DRA drivers, network controllers, or any component managing device status across nodes |

The existing `resourceclaims/status` permission is **still required** — it remains the "front door".
The new synthetic subresources are **additional** checks on top of it.

These new permissions can be added **now** in preparation for 1.36, they are inert in earlier versions of Kubernetes.

---

## Migration by component type

### Node-local DRA drivers

These run as DaemonSets with a ServiceAccount whose token is bound to the node (via a pod
scheduled on that node). They update `status.devices` for their own driver.

**Add this rule to the driver's ClusterRole:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/driver"]
  verbs: ["associated-node:update", "associated-node:patch"]
  resourceNames: ["<your-driver-name>"]  # e.g. "dra.example.com"
```

**Keep the existing rule:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]
```

### Control-plane DRA drivers / multi-node controllers

These run as Deployments (not node-bound). They update `status.devices` for their driver
from a central controller.

**Add this rule to the controller's ClusterRole:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/driver"]
  verbs: ["arbitrary-node:update", "arbitrary-node:patch"]
  resourceNames: ["<your-driver-name>"]  # e.g. "dra.example.com"
```

**Keep the existing rule:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]
```

### Schedulers

These modify `status.allocation` and `status.reservedFor` when binding claims to nodes.

**Add this rule to the scheduler's ClusterRole:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/binding"]
  verbs: ["update", "patch"]
```

**Keep the existing rule:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]
```

> Note: The built-in `system:kube-scheduler` ClusterRole is updated automatically
> by the bootstrap policy when the feature gate is enabled. Only custom schedulers
> need manual updates.

### Operators / virtual clusters that proxy all ResourceClaim operations

These need **all** of the above depending on what operations they proxy.

**Add both rules:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/binding"]
  verbs: ["update", "patch"]
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/driver"]
  verbs: ["associated-node:update", "associated-node:patch", "arbitrary-node:update", "arbitrary-node:patch"]
```

### Components that only read status or manage non-status fields

No changes needed. The new checks only apply to **writes** to `status.allocation`,
`status.reservedFor`, and `status.devices`.

---

## Projects to update

### DRA Drivers

- [ ] [kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-cpu](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-cpu) — `manifests/base/clusterrole-dracpu.part.yaml` - @back1ash

title: Readiness probe stops too early at eviction
body:
### What happened?

When kubelet evicts a pod, the ready condition doesn’t get `NotReady` during the pod termination even if a `readinessProbe` is configured.

### What did you expect to happen?

A readiness probe works during a pod termination so that the pod gets `NotReady` as early as possible.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use this `readiness.yaml`:
```
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: readiness-script-configmap
data:
  readiness-script.sh: |
    #!/bin/sh
    handler() {
      rm /tmp/ready
      sleep 20
    }
    touch /tmp/ready
    trap handler SIGTERM
    while true; do
      sleep 1
    done
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: null
  labels:
    run: readiness-container
  name: readiness-test
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - sh
    - /script/readiness-script.sh
    image: busybox
    name: readiness
    readinessProbe:
      exec:
        command:
        - cat
        - /tmp/ready
      initialDelaySeconds: 3
      periodSeconds: 3
    volumeMounts:
    - name: readiness-script
      mountPath: /script
  - command:
    - sh
    - -c
    - for i in `seq 100`; do dd if=/dev/random of=file${i} bs=1048576 count=1 2>/dev/null; sleep .1; done; while true; do sleep 5; done
    name: disk-consumer
    image: busybox
    resources:
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: "100Mi"
      requests:
        ephemeral-storage: "100Mi"
  volumes:
  - name: readiness-script
    configMap:
      name: readiness-script-configmap
```

Create resources and wait an eviction happens:
```
$ kubectl create -f readiness.yaml; kubectl get pods readiness-test -w
configmap/readiness-script-configmap created
pod/readiness-test created
NAME         	READY   STATUS          	RESTARTS   AGE
readiness-test   0/2 	ContainerCreating   0      	0s
readiness-test   1/2 	Running         	0      	3s
readiness-test   2/2 	Running         	0      	7s
readiness-test   0/2 	Error           	0      	46s
readiness-test   0/2 	Error           	0      	47s

```

When deleting this pod, the readiness probe works during termination:
```
$ kubectl create -f readiness.yaml; (sleep 15; kubectl delete pod readiness-test) & kubectl get pods -w
configmap/readiness-script-configmap created
pod/readiness-test created
[1] 137999
NAME             READY   STATUS              RESTARTS   AGE
readiness-test   0/2     ContainerCreating   0          0s
readiness-test   1/2     Running             0          2s
readiness-test   2/2     Running             0          6s
pod "readiness-test" deleted
readiness-test   2/2     Terminating         0          15s
readiness-test   1/2     Terminating         0          21s
readiness-test   0/2     Terminating         0          45s
readiness-test   0/2     Terminating         0          45s
readiness-test   0/2     Terminating         0          45s
readiness-test   0/2     Terminating         0          45s

```


### Anything else we need to know?

I guess this issue is caused as follows:

At eviction, a pod phase is set to `PodFailed` internally in `podStatusFn` before stopping containers in the pod:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0d8f996aa9a1667d5994f10e03de5be21bf205e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2026-L2029
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0d8f996aa9a1667d5994f10e03de5be21bf205e0/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L605-L608

Because the internal pod phase is `PodFailed`, the probe worker finishes working without probing containers at termination:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd68c5f2409fec7176e6172d6f9d97bd6447c4da/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L203-L216

title: Relinquish leadership during zonal outage
body:
### What happened?

A kubernetes cluster deployed in AWS is subject to occasional zonal [outages](https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/technology/pes/). In the most kubernetes cluster setup usecases(e.g kops), all control plane components(e.g kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager) are setup as static pods. Depending on how the cluster is setup further, there could be more components(e.g webhooks, authenticator, cloud-controller-manager, etc) running as static pods too. If the kubernetes control plane(master) instances are part of a zone experiencing outage, the cluster can have undesired experience based on behavior of the specific component failing during the outage.

During zonal outages that do not affect apiserver to etcd connectivity, any controller that depends on leader election and is currently hosted on an instance in the affected zone continues to renew its lease. Continuing to hold the lease is fine as long as the controller's workload is only dependent on apiserver objects. In cases where the controller's work depends on aws api calls(e.g. cloud-controller-manager), success of the controller is not guaranteed. In such cases the workloads would benefit from lease transfer.

As an operator of clusters in AWS, it might be beneficial if there was a way to indicate the controllers using abstract rules (that work across cloud) to exclude controllers from taking lease if certain rules match. The rule can be created as a separate api object that cluster admin can control. During zonal outages, the operator can refer to the aws status page and indicate any lease based controllers to evacuate from the bad zone. 

What are your thoughts on the idea. Is there any prior art around this to explore.

title: API Server: Health checks cause "http2: stream closed" errors in aggregated API servers
body:
### What happened?

Our project (Calico) deploys an aggregated API server, `calico-apiserver`. We've observed that `calico-apiserver` periodically logs errors, approximately every 30-60 seconds, indicating that a client is aborting its connection.

The errors in the calico-apiserver log look like this:
```
... level=error msg="Unhandled Error" error="apiserver was unable to write a JSON response: http2: stream closed" klog-logger=calico-apiserver
... level=error msg="Timeout or abort while handling" URI=/apis/projectcalico.org/v3 auditID=a948aada-6f9c-498d-a638-53ffaf0662c3 error="<nil>" klog-logger=calico-apiserver method=GET 
... level=error msg="Post-timeout activity" error="<nil>" klog-logger=calico-apiserver method=GET path=/apis/projectcalico.org/v3 result="<nil>" timeElapsed=5.234003ms
```

### What did you expect to happen?

There should be no "http2: stream closed" or "Timeout or abort" errors in the aggregated API server logs.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Install a cluster with Calico's aggregated API server and watch the `calico-apiserver` logs.

### Anything else we need to know?

With verbose logging enabled, we can confirm the errors on the `calico-apiserver` are emitted at the same time as the periodic health checks from the `kube-apiserver`.

- The `kube-apiserver` log shows it sent 5 requests and successfully received 5 200 OK responses.

- The `calico-apiserver` log for the exact same timeframe shows that all requests are received for processing. However, one or two of them fail during the response phase with an `http2: stream closed` error.

The [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.33/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/controllers/status/remote/remote_available_controller.go#L311) shows that the `kube-apiserver`'s health check client closes the HTTP stream as soon as it receives the response headers. This prevents the calico-apiserver from successfully writing the full API resource list in the response body, causing the `stream closed` error on the server side. 

The error messages on `calico-apiserver`  are benign, because the health check's goal is only to verify a successful status code, which the `kube-apiserver` client does receive before it closes the connection.

title: Whether pod deletion should enqueue the deployment again when there is only evicted pod left
body:
### What happened?

For example, there is one deployment with below configuration. 
```
progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
replicas: 1
strategy:
   type: Recreate
```
Due to resource exhaustion on the node, the node evicted pods of this deployment. The running pod is owned by the rs 'nginx-deployment-dfbd8fcd5'
Around 13:46, the deployment is patched and due to the "recreate" strategy, the old pod started to be deleted. The deployment status is updated but nothing new which triggers the deployment is "stuck".
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.22.3/pkg/controller/deployment/progress.go#L111 
Because the "lastUpdateTime" + "progressDeadlineSeconds" > current time, the deployemnet is added to the "delayQueue"  
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.22.3/pkg/controller/deployment/progress.go#L186

the deployment "status.conditions" is below
```
   - lastTransitionTime: "2021-11-14T13:26:08Z"
      lastUpdateTime: "2021-11-14T13:44:57Z"
      message: Created new replica set "nginx-deployment-dfbd8fcd5"
      reason: NewReplicaSetCreated
      status: "True"
      type: Progressing
```
After the old pod is deleted, the deployment is still not enqueue immediately because there is still evicted pods left
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.22.3/pkg/controller/deployment/deployment_controller.go#L372

Whether this is expected behavior or we should continue to create new RS once old active old pod is deleted? Because in "rolloutRecreate" function, when the controller checks if there is pod pod running it doesn't count the evict pod
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.22.3/pkg/controller/deployment/recreate.go#L109

### What did you expect to happen?

deployment controller continues to create new rs if there is only evicted pod left 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a deployment with "recreate" strategy and trigger pod eviction
2. Patch the deployment
2. When  the "lastUpdateTime" + "progressDeadlineSeconds" > current time, even the old pod is deleted, the new rs is not created until it reaches the result of  "lastUpdateTime" + "progressDeadlineSeconds"

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Zone-aware down scaling behavior
body:
### What happened?

During scale-in we have an interesting zone unbalance behavior for hpa workloads.

We use topology spread `maxSkew: 1` in our deployment, but during the night
when scale-in happens we have sometimes only 1 pod for a workload spanning 3 zones
 with minreplica 9.

relevant deployment snippet:
```yaml
       topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              # This is kind of stupid, but would work for now. Ideally we should just stop filtering out the pods in
              # kube-system in our admitters, since we've never really had any issues with them.
              parent-resource-hash: 71556441059f2d033fb06b1e73df03598c7ecaa6
```

Impact: one pod has high CPU usage during low number of pods time:
![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/50872/9ee227cb-7ff7-4618-ba45-1a6a7491edec)
The HPA data during the same period of time:
![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/50872/e1f7d7e1-5d05-413b-a349-2504c32b0370)

We could track it back that the pod with high CPU usage is the only one in the affected zone and the rest of the pods are split into the other 2 zones.


We are now collecting more data to have better visibility. You can already see the "miss behavior" in the picture, which shows 2 zones have 7 pods and 1 zone has 5 pods:
![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/50872/bb1536d5-4f17-435d-b8f7-36aa51b957b5)


### What did you expect to happen?

I expect that scale-in respects somehow topology spread `maxSkew: 1` behavior, so in the pods by zone split picture I would expect at most `+/- 1` pod by zone, but I see 2.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

As far as I know scale-in happens by subresource API call to replicaset, so I guess you can reproduce it by manipulating a test that has a deployment with a similar config like shown above. You would need to have maybe 9 pods with an even split by zone. The pods in one zone should have a modified creation(?) timestamp, such that these are the newest that will be terminated first at scale-in. After applied modification you can scale to 7 and you should observe the zone split from 3,3,3 going down to 3,3,1

### Anything else we need to know?

Deployment for reference:
https://github.com/zalando-incubator/kubernetes-on-aws/blob/dev/cluster/manifests/skipper/deployment.yaml#L73-L81

There might be some related issues, but none which were precise enough to show the impact.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107598
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115911
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123541
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-apps/2255-pod-cost

title: Introduce `ReevaluationHint` in QHint for a single node scheduling constraint optimization
body:
/assign
/sig scheduling
/cc @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-misc @macsko @dom4ha 
 

## Summary

Introduce a new return value `ReevaluationHint` in QHint so that we don't have to re-evaluate all nodes at the scheduling retries.

## Motivation

We can roughly divide our scheduling constraints into two groups: "single node constraint" or "cross-node (or node unrelated) constraint".

For example, resource requirement is "single node constraint" because if node-a doesn't have enough CPU for pod-a, node-a is filtered out in the scheduling cycle, that is, node-a's filtering result is determined only by node-a's status.
And, pod topology spread is "cross-node constraint" because if domain-a, which node-a belongs to, has too many Pods matching topology spread, node-a is filtered out, that is, node-a's filtering result is determined by not only node-a's status, but also by other nodes' status too.

Let’s think about the requeueing scenarios of the resource fit plugin (single node constraints).
There are four registered events:
- Node/Add: Node is newly added. In this case, the Pod might be schedulable on the new node.
- Node/UpdateNodeAllocatable: Node got more resources. In this case, the Pod might be schedulable on the updated node.
- Pod/Delete: The running Pod is deleted, In this case, the Pod might be schedulable on the node where the deleted Pod was running on.
- Pod/UpdatePodScaleDown: 
  - The existing Pod is scaled down: In this case, the Pod might be schedulable on the node where the scaled-down pod is running on.
  - The unschedulable Pod itself is scaled down: In this case, the Pod might be schedulable on any nodes.

In all cases, we can determine which node(s) to re-evaluate in the next scheduling cycles.

Currently, every scheduling cycle (basically) always evaluates all the nodes.
If we could reduce the number of nodes to re-evaluate, that could be a significant performance optimization for the second or later scheduling cycles.

## Goals

- Allow QHint to return which node(s) to re-evaluate, change the scheduling cycles to consider them, and improve the scheduling latency for Pods with a single node scheduling constraint.

## Non-Goals

<!--
What is out of scope for this proposal? Listing non-goals helps to focus discussion
and make progress.
-->

- Cross nodes scheduling constraint is out-of-scope for now. But, see `Future ideas` section at the bottom.
  - Given the cross node scheduling constraints are only PodAffinity and PodTopologySpread in the default scheduler, we can still get a huge benefit only with a single node scheduling constraint support.

## Proposal

### Design Details

#### QHint interface change

Change QHint interface to return which node(s) to re-evaluate.

```go
type ReevaluationHint struct {
  // NodeNames has the names of nodes which should be re-evaluated in the next scheduling cycle.
  // Empty means all nodes.
  NodeNames sets.Set[string]
}

type QueueingHintFn func(logger klog.Logger, pod *v1.Pod, oldObj, newObj interface{}) (QueueingHint, ReevaluationHint, error)
```

#### Scheduling queue change

We need to run QHints for Pods that are already in backoffQ or activeQ,
otherwise some nodes that should be re-evaluated might be overlooked.

The queue would aggregate all ReevaluationHint(s) that are returned from QHints,
and store them in PodInfo or somewhere so that the next scheduling cycle can refer to them. 
### User Stories

<!--
Detail the things that people will be able to do if this proposal is implemented.
Include as much detail as possible so that people can understand the "how" of
the system. The goal here is to make this feel real for users without getting
bogged down.
-->

#### Story 1

There are 5k nodes in the cluster.
Pod-a is created, but a scheduling for Pod-a fails because all Nodes don't have enough CPU for this Pod.
A moment later, one Pod on Node-a is removed and now Node-a may have enough CPU for Pod-a, thus the scheduler retries the scheduling for this Pod.
We currently (basically) re-evaluate all nodes in the next scheduling cycle.

But, after this enhancement, QHint from the resource fit plugin returns Queue for this Pod/Delete event, and also it returns Node-a in ReevaluationHint.
And, at the next scheduling cycle, 4999 Nodes are pre-filtered out by ReevaluationHint, and the scheduling cycle only re-evaluate Node-a
We can save the calculation for 4999 Nodes.

### Risks and Mitigations

#### QHint calculation cost and possible negative impact on the scheduling throughput

As mentioned earlier, the number of QHint runs would increase because we have to run QHints for Pods in activeQ/backoffQ as well.
As we experienced recently, the latency of event handling could impact the scheduling throughput negatively, mainly because of the shared lock in the queue.

We need to carefully evaluate if this enhancement really improves the throughput with some PoC.

## Future ideas

### Cross node scheduling constraint support

Actually, we might be able to do the same for some cross node constraints too.
We can add LabelSelector in ReevaluationHint.

```go
type ReevaluationHint struct {
  // NodeNames has the names of nodes which should be re-evaluated in the next scheduling cycle.
  // Empty means all nodes.
  NodeNames sets.Set[string]
  // LabelSelector has the selector for nodes which should be re-evaluated in the next scheduling cycle.
  // Empty means all nodes.
  LabelSelector *labels.Selector
}
```

And, for example, let’s say a Pod failed with PodTopologySpread because the spreading is like: zone-a:zone-b:zone-c = 2:3:4 (maxSkew: 1). In this case, PodTopologySpread rejects all nodes in zone-b and zone-c.

And, supposing a new matching Pod is added to zone-a, which makes zone-a:zone-b:zone-c = 3:3:4.
In this case, QHint from PodTopologySpread could return the labelselector for zone-a and zone-b.

But, the problem is that, then QHint has to know the current spreading situation (2:3:4) to return the label selector.
We currently have a internal policy where QHint shouldn’t look up resources other than the ones given from the QHint paramters (= QHint should only use pod, oldObj, and newObj to return results) so that we can prevent QHints to be too complicated and slow.
So, if we want to do this, we probably have to loosen this policy.

Those are why I don’t want to include the cross node scheduling constraints in the first step.
We should see if this idea is really worthy only with single node constraints first, and then we can discuss those stuff later.

### Concurrent scheduling cycles

In the long term, this enhancement could be a first step for the concurrent scheduling cycles, our dream.
As long as `NodeNames` is not overlapped, we can run the evaluations for multiple Pods concurrently since the scheduling results won't be conflict.

title: Implement a kubelet oomwatcher that does not depend on /dev/kmsg
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The kubelet currently needs access to /dev/kmsg , and this is only used in oom_watcher_linux. Currently, enabling KubeletInUserNamespace can ignore the creation error and creates the kubelet with a nil oomWatcher, but this should be possible to improve on. 

This issue would be to write an implementation of the oomwatcher that does not depend on /dev/kmsg, but which can depend on cgroups v2 since the feature flag requires it. One option is to poll memory.events in the top level cgroups, which is an approach that containerd and slurm also use. Though this would only report that an oomkill event happened and in what cgroup without reporting its pid.

### Why is this needed?

Anything that runs rootless or in a completely isolated container can't use the kernel log buffer since it is global per kernel, needs CAP_SYSLOG in the root user namespace, and is hard to virtualize. This is an issue for running kubernetes in docker, kubernetes in an unprivileged LXC, or just normal rootless kubernetes.

This issue can hopefully also be a useful reference in any linux kernel mailing list discussions about the oom killer, since getting information about oomkill events as an unprivileged user is a recurring issue

title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy CEL validation rules do not seem to expand `__dot__` and `__slash__` as written in the documentation
body:
### What happened?

Given the rule:
```
"!has(object.metadata.labels) || (has(object.metadata.labels) && !object.metadata.labels.helm__dot__sh__slash__chart == 'other')"
```
does not seem to expand the \_\_dot\_\_ and \_\_slash\_\_ because it gives the error 
```
Error from server (Invalid): error when creating "manifests/test.yaml": secrets "test" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'block-helm-other' with binding 'block-helm-other' denied request: expression '!has(object.metadata.labels) || (has(object.metadata.labels) && object.metadata.labels.helm__dot__sh__chart__chart == 'other')' resulted in error: no such key: helm__dot__sh__chart__chart
```
And of course just guarding it with another has() macro doesn't work since that will just return false.

You end up with
```
!has(object.metadata.labels) || (has(object.metadata.labels) && !has(object.metadata.labels.helm__dot__sh__chart__chart)) || (has(object.metadata.labels) && !has(object.metadata.labels.helm__dot__sh__slash__chart) && !object.metadata.labels.helm__dot__sh__slash__chart.startsWith('other'))
```
for example but that lets everything pass because `!has(object.metadata.labels.helm__dot__sh__slash__chart)` is returns true.

### What did you expect to happen?

This should block anything with the label like this:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: "test"
  labels:
    helm.sh/chart: other
```

instead it doesn't stop this at all.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The policies
```yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: "block-helm-other"

      resources:   ["*"]
```

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
```

title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy using CRDs as paramKind can fail due to 30s discovery mechanism
body:
### What happened?

When a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is using CRDs as paramKind, it can result in `failed to find resource referenced by paramKind` error if the custom resource is created around the same time as the vap resource. This could result in new resources getting blocked by this vap because it thinks the custom type does not exist assuming fail policy is set to `fail`. 

As discussed with @alexzielenski on slack:
> It can take up to 30s for the discovery mechanism to pickup the change to the CRD list

### What did you expect to happen?

Allow retries on CRD list to resync without breaking the vap. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A example of failed unit test https://github.com/open-policy-agent/gatekeeper/actions/runs/8070764571/job/22048871826?pr=3289 the test tries to create a custom resource after the vap resource is created and this new resource is blocked because it thinks the custom type referenced by paramKind does not exist

title: [InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Relaxing immutability of Pod Templates resources/limits
body:
### What would you like to be added?

As In Place Pod Vertical scaling is maturing, there is interest in using this feature for apps or batch workloads.

I can imagine a world where someone wants to change an existing job to lower the cgroups of a workload or scale up. One interest is to rebalance workloads to match their actual utilization. As stated in the in place pod vertical scaling, some apps have high startup resources and then they are able to have their resources scaled down. Most of these workloads do not use pods but higher level objects so it is important to consider how this feature will eventually work with higher level controllers like Jobs, Deployments and StatefulSets. 

Another use case I have heard is the ability to patch/update workloads before they are scheduled. Some use cases I've heard are using an external service to select requests/limits for workloads based on model size or historical data. One implementation idea is to submit a Job in a suspended state and allow the service to patch the Job to reflect the intended state of the resource request and unsuspend with the updated request. This is forbidden today in validation logic so it would be worth considering how to relax this.

For Job, Deployment, and StatefulSet we assume PodTemplates are immutable. In some cases, for Job, we did relax the immutability for scheduling directives but we did not change resource/requests. I was curious how we can start the discussion on how to relax this to further enable In Place Pod Vertical scaling and other use cases where the workloads have not yet been scheduled.

I am opening this up to see how we could tackle this overall.

One possibility is to take this in smaller KEPS:

- [KEP - 1]: Relax immutability of container requests/limits when suspended for Jobs
- [KEP - 2]: In Place Pod Resizing of Job while running.
- [KEP - 3]: In Place Pod Resizing of Deployments
- [KEP - 4]: In Place Pod Resizing of StatefulSets


### Why is this needed?

See above.

title: Add suspend subresource
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add `suspend` subresource to allow agnostically suspending/restarting apps, especially jobs. This is similar to the `scale` subresource.


### Why is this needed?

This is useful to develop job management operators (such as job queueing controllers) that aim to control when to start/stop jobs, whether that being the k/k [batch/v1.Job](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/#suspending-a-job) API or custom defined jobs.

The idea is that given only a reference to the job, the controller can start/stop jobs just like HPA is able to scale up/down apps that implement the scale subresource (see [scaleTargetRef](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/horizontal-pod-autoscaler-v2/#HorizontalPodAutoscalerSpec), which identifies CRDs for HPA).

/sig apps
/sig scheduling

title: NodeDeclaredFeatures are not dynamically updated when container runtime features change
body:
This issue is introduced from #135828.

In #135828, I integrated the `RuntimeFeatures` of the container runtime into `NodeDeclaredFeatures`, so that we can make decisions earlier and avoid scheduling pods to nodes where the container runtime does not support certain `RuntimeFeatures`. But after the changes in #135828, the kubelet only discovers the container runtime features once at startup (i.e., in NewMainKubelet).

This means that if the container runtime's features change after the kubelet has started (for example, after an in-place upgrade of the container runtime, a runtime feature like `UserNamespacesHostNetwork` becomes available), the kubelet will still report stale declared features in the node status and use these stale features for pod admission and pod update validation.

However, currently this only affects a single feature gate, `UserNamespacesHostNetwork`, and it is still in the alpha stage. We don't need to solve this in v1.36.

/kind bug
/triage accepted
/sig node

title: [Declarative Validation] Add `+k8s:pattern` declarative validation tag
body:
Add a new `+k8s:pattern=<regex>` declarative validation (DV) tag that validates a string field matches the specified regular expression pattern. This corresponds to the OpenAPI/JSON Schema `pattern` keyword.

## Motivation

OpenAPI/JSON Schema supports `pattern` as a standard validation keyword for string regex matching. Many Kubernetes API fields use regex pattern validation in handwritten code. A `+k8s:pattern` tag would enable declarative migration of these validations and provide OpenAPI schema parity.

## Kubernetes API Example

**`ISCSIPersistentVolumeSource.IQN`** in `pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go`:

```go
// Handwritten validation today:
var iscsiInitiatorIqnRegex = regexp.MustCompile(`iqn\.\d{4}-\d{2}\.([[:alnum:]-.]+)(:[^,;*&$|\s]+)$`)
var iscsiInitiatorEuiRegex = regexp.MustCompile(`^eui.[[:alnum:]]{16}$`)
var iscsiInitiatorNaaRegex = regexp.MustCompile(`^naa.[[:alnum:]]{32}$`)

if strings.HasPrefix(iscsi.IQN, "iqn") && !iscsiInitiatorIqnRegex.MatchString(iscsi.IQN) {
    allErrs = append(allErrs, field.Invalid(fldPath.Child("iqn"), iscsi.IQN,
        "must be valid format starting with iqn, eui, or naa"))
}
```

With the proposed tag:

```go
type ISCSIPersistentVolumeSource struct {
    // +k8s:pattern=^(iqn\.\d{4}-\d{2}\..+|eui\.[[:alnum:]]{16}|naa\.[[:alnum:]]{32})$
    IQN string
}
```

## OpenAPI Semantics

- **OpenAPI keyword:** `pattern`
- **Go type in JSONSchemaProps:** `string`
- **Spec behavior:** The string value must match the regex. OpenAPI formally specifies ECMA-262 regular expressions.
- **Kubernetes reality:** kube-openapi's actual validation uses **Go's `regexp` package (RE2 engine)**, not ECMA-262 (see `vendor/k8s.io/kube-openapi/pkg/validation/validate/rexp.go`). Compiled regexes are cached for performance.

## DV Design Considerations

- **Regex engine:** DV generates Go code, so it will naturally use Go's RE2 engine. This is consistent with how kube-openapi already validates patterns. However, this means:
  - **No lookahead/lookbehind** assertions (RE2 limitation vs. ECMA-262)
  - **No backreferences** (RE2 limitation)
  - **Guaranteed linear-time** execution (RE2 advantage — no ReDoS risk)
  - This should be documented so API authors know the constraints.
- **Compile-time validation:** Invalid regex patterns should be caught at code generation time (lint error), not at runtime. The existing kube-openapi validation handles invalid patterns gracefully at runtime, but DV can do better.
- **Performance:** Regex should be compiled once as a **package-level variable** (using `VariableGen`) — similar to how `+k8s:enum` generates package-level sets. Do not compile on every validation call.
- **Type restriction:** Should only apply to string types, consistent with `+k8s:format` and `+k8s:maxLength` (which check `t != types.String`).
- **Relationship to `+k8s:format`:** A field could have both `+k8s:format` and `+k8s:pattern`. These are independent constraints (format checks semantic validity, pattern checks syntactic shape). No conflict.

## Implementation Notes

- Should be implemented as a new validator file (e.g., `validators/pattern.go`)
- Validator file: new `staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/pattern.go`


/sig api-machinery
/triage accepted
/area api-validation

title: [Declarative Validation] Add `k8s-cidr` format to `+k8s:format` declarative validation tag
body:
Add support for a `k8s-cidr` format value in the existing `+k8s:format` declarative validation (DV) tag to validate that a string field contains valid CIDR notation (e.g., `192.168.1.0/24` or `2001:db8::/64`). This corresponds to the OpenAPI `format: cidr` keyword.

## Motivation

CIDR notation validation is common across Kubernetes networking APIs (NetworkPolicy, Service CIDR allocation, ClusterCIDR, etc.). OpenAPI supports `format: cidr` as a format. Adding this to DV enables declarative validation of CIDR fields currently validated with handwritten code.

## Kubernetes API Example

**`IPBlock.CIDR`** in `pkg/apis/networking/validation/validation.go`:

```go
// Handwritten validation today:
func ValidateIPBlock(ipb *networking.IPBlock, fldPath *field.Path, opts NetworkPolicyValidationOptions) field.ErrorList {
    allErrs := field.ErrorList{}
    if ipb.CIDR == "" {
        allErrs = append(allErrs, field.Required(fldPath.Child("cidr"), "").MarkCoveredByDeclarative())
        return allErrs
    }
    allErrs = append(allErrs, apivalidation.IsValidCIDRForLegacyField(
        fldPath.Child("cidr"), ipb.CIDR, opts.AllowCIDRsEvenIfInvalid)...)
    _, cidrIPNet, err := netutils.ParseCIDRSloppy(ipb.CIDR)
    // ...
}
```

With the proposed format:

```go
type IPBlock struct {
    // +k8s:required
    // +k8s:format=k8s-cidr
    CIDR string
}
```

## OpenAPI Semantics

- **OpenAPI format:** `cidr`
- **kube-openapi strfmt:** registered in `strfmt/default.go`, validated with `net.ParseCIDR()`
- **Format:** `<ip-address>/<prefix-length>` for both IPv4 and IPv6

## DV Design Considerations

- **Sloppy vs. strict parsing:** Similar to the `k8s-ip` ratcheting concern — existing Kubernetes CIDR fields use `netutils.ParseCIDRSloppy()` which tolerates leading zeros in IP octets. The DV format should use sloppy parsing (e.g., `k8s-cidr` → `CIDRSloppy()`) to match historical behavior. A strict variant could be added later.
- **Relationship to `k8s-ip`:** CIDR validation is closely related to IP validation — a CIDR is an IP address plus prefix length. If `k8s-ip` is blocked on ratcheting concerns, `k8s-cidr` may face the same issue. These should be evaluated together.
- **IPv4/IPv6 variants:** Consider whether to add `k8s-cidrv4` and `k8s-cidrv6` for fields constrained to a specific address family.
- **Naming convention:** Follows existing `k8s-` prefix pattern.

## Implementation Notes

- Should be added to the format switch in `validators/format.go`
- Runtime validation function should use `net.ParseCIDR()` or `netutils.ParseCIDRSloppy()`
- High priority — CIDR is used extensively in NetworkPolicy, Service CIDR allocation, and cluster networking
- Validator file: `staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/format.go`

/sig api-machinery
/triage accepted
/area api-validation

title: [Declarative Validation] Add `+k8s:maxProperties` declarative validation tag
body:
Add a new `+k8s:maxProperties=<int>` declarative validation (DV) tag that enforces a maximum number of keys in a map field. This corresponds to the OpenAPI/JSON Schema `maxProperties` keyword.

## Motivation

OpenAPI/JSON Schema supports `maxProperties` as a standard validation keyword. DV currently has no equivalent. Several Kubernetes API map fields have upper bounds on the number of entries for resource/performance reasons, currently enforced with handwritten validation.

## Kubernetes API Example

**`StorageClass.Parameters`** in `pkg/apis/storage/validation/validation.go`:

```go
// Handwritten validation today:
const maxProvisionerParameterLen = 512

if len(params) > maxProvisionerParameterLen {
    allErrs = append(allErrs, field.TooLong(fldPath, "" /*unused*/, maxProvisionerParameterLen))
    return allErrs
}
```

With the proposed tag:

```go
type StorageClass struct {
    // +k8s:maxProperties=512
    Parameters map[string]string
}
```

## OpenAPI Semantics

- **OpenAPI keyword:** `maxProperties`
- **Go type in JSONSchemaProps:** `*int64`
- **Spec behavior:** The object (map) must have at most the specified number of properties/keys.

## DV Design Considerations

- **Map types only:** Same as `+k8s:minProperties` — only meaningful for `map` types in Go, since struct fields are fixed at compile time. Type check should restrict to `types.Map` kind.
- **Relationship to `+k8s:maxItems`:** `+k8s:maxItems` validates slice/array length and uses the **ShortCircuit flag** to stop further validation if the limit is exceeded (prevents DoS via oversized inputs). `+k8s:maxProperties` should similarly consider short-circuiting — an oversized map should skip per-key/per-value validation.
- **Value parsing:** Should use `util.ParseInt()` like other limit tags. Value must be non-negative.

## Implementation Notes

- Should be implemented in `validators/limits.go` alongside existing min/max tags
- Consider using `ShortCircuit` flag like `+k8s:maxItems` to avoid validating entries in oversized maps
- Should generate a call to a validation function in `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/validate`
- Validator file: `staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/limits.go`

/sig api-machinery
/triage accepted
/area api-validation

title: Eviction signal is not hugepages aware
body:
### What happened?

On nodes with hugepages configured, the kubelet's memory.available eviction signal overstates real available regular memory by the total hugepage reservation. This causes eviction to fire later than the configured threshold intends, causing OOM kills.

The root cause is that AvailableBytes is computed as root_cgroup.memory.limit - root_cgroup.memory.workingSet, where:
- memory.limit is set to MemTotal from /proc/meminfo (includes hugepage-reserved RAM)
- memory.workingSet comes from the memory cgroup controller (does not track hugetlb allocations — those use a separate controller)

This creates "phantom" available bytes equal to the hugepage reservation. The kernel's own MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo does not have this problem because hugepage-reserved pages are removed from the buddy allocator's free pool at boot and never appear in MemFree.

### What did you expect to happen?

memory.available should reflect memory available for regular (non-hugepage) allocations. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Configure a node with hugepages.
Query the kubelet summary API: kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/stats/summary".
Observe node.memory.availableBytes — it exceeds what is physically available as regular memory by exactly the hugepage reservation.

### Anything else we need to know?

The issue can be fixed by subtracting the node's total hugepage capacity from AvailableBytes in the summary stats provider (pkg/kubelet/server/stats/summary.go) before the stats are consumed by the eviction manager. This is a minimal, targeted adjustment at the point where NodeStats.Memory is constructed. It aligns the kubelet's computation with the kernel's own MemAvailable accounting.

### Kubernetes version

This issue is long existing and reproducible on v1.35/master

title: runtime.Scheme.AddKnownTypeWithName has undocumented panic paths
[declarative validation] Support grouping of operation-specific validations
body:
### Description

Currently, validation-gen treats each validation tag as an independent logical unit. For tags that only apply to specific operations (like +k8s:update=, +k8s:immutable, and the proposed +k8s:monotonic), the generator emits a series of independent function calls. Each of these runtime functions is then responsible for checking the operation type (op.Type) internally.

For a field with multiple such tags, the generated code looks like this:
```go
errs = append(errs, validate.Immutable(ctx, op, fldPath, obj, oldObj)...)
errs = append(errs, validate.UpdateValue(ctx, op, fldPath, obj, oldObj, ...)...)
errs = append(errs, validate.Monotonic(ctx, op, fldPath, obj, oldObj)...)

```

Each of these functions begins with an identical `if op.Type != operation.Update { return nil }` check. This leads to redundant branching and less efficient, less readable generated code.

### Proposal

We should enhance `validation-gen` to recognize cohorts of validators that share the same operation constraints and group them into a single conditional block in the generated code.
The ideal output would look like this:
```go
if op.Type == operation.Update {
    errs = append(errs, validate.Immutable(ctx, op, fldPath, obj, oldObj)...)
    errs = append(errs, validate.UpdateValue(...)...)
    errs = append(errs, validate.Monotonic(...)...)
}

```

### Complexity: The Intersection with Short-Circuiting

The primary challenge is managing the intersection between Operation Cohorts and the existing `ShortCircuit` grouping.
- **State Gating**: Structural checks (like +k8s:optional) often short-circuit if a value is nil.
- **Operation Gating**: Operation checks (like +k8s:monotonic) only run on Update.

If a field has an `optional` check (always) and a `monotonic` check (Update-Only), the generator must ensure that the `Update` block correctly respects the outcome of the `optional` block, and vice-versa.

**Impact: This would improve the performance of validation (by reducing branching in the hot path) across Kubernetes**

title: Do built-in types still need an internal type?
body:
My understanding is that the internal's purposes are:

1. Hub type for conversion
2. Allow all handwritten validation to be written only once against a single type
3. Provides a server only type that is not exported to clients

(1) can be achieved without the internal type. We could pick a versioned type (storage type seems like a good candidate) to use as the hub type.

(2) can also work with a hub type. More importantly, with declarative validation this becomes less relevant.

(3) I'm not aware of any APIs that need this. Today, the internal types ~always matches a versioned type, usually the most stable type.

/sig api-machinery

title: Support for Topology Aware Routing in winkernel proxier
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Topology Aware Routing was introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/99522 and at the time of introduction it was introduced for `iptable` and `ipvs` proxiers. The feature is in beta since 1.23 but support is missing for Windows worker nodes.

### Why is this needed?

Windows worker nodes are supported by various distributions and cloud providers. A lot of them already automatically set `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` based on the service provider's availability zone information for these nodes. if you have a multi-zone environment with Windows worker nodes, it is not possible to benefit from Topology Aware Routing, therefore all the benefits highlighted in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-network/2433-topology-aware-hints are missed. If the cluster has active Linux workloads in these zones, interacting with these services through Windows workload may actually turn out to be costly - both performance & bandwidth wise.

It looks like there may not be a technical blockers (HNS, for eg) to have this. Today all the endpoint registration logic in winkernel proxier resides in `syncProxyRules` where iTP, eTP policies are evaluated - this diverges from iptables, ipvs proxiers that have evolved to use `CategorizeEndpoints` from `topology.go` for this purpose, which also handles selection of endpoints matching node's topology zone. 

If there are technical reasons for this not being supported, the lack of support should be documented and tracked.
