
title: `kubectl apply` (client-side) removes all entries when attempting to remove a single duplicated entry in a persisted object
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:
/kind bug

Lists in API objects can define a named property that should act as a "merge key". The value of that property is expected to be unique for each item in the list. However, gaps in API validation allow some types to be persisted with multiple items in the list sharing the same value for a mergeKey property.

The algorithm used by `kubectl apply` detects removals from a list based on the specified key, and communicates that removal to the server using a delete directive, specifying only the key. When duplicate items exist, that deletion directive is ambiguous, and the server implementation deletes all items with that key.

Known API types/fields which define a mergeKey but allow duplicate items to be persisted:

PodSpec (affects all workload objects containing a pod template):
* `hostAliases` (#91670)
* `imagePullSecrets` (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/91629)
* `containers[*].env` (this issue, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/86163, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/93266, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/106809, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/121541, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122121)
* `containers[*].ports` (#86273,  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/93952, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113246, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134470)
* `volumes` (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/78266)
* ~~`containers[*].volumeMounts`~~ (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/35071 changed the merge key from name to mountPath, which was [a breaking change](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/36024#issuecomment-261169033), but mountPath is at least required to be unique)

Service
* `ports` (name+protocol required to be unique on create in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/47336, but still has issues on update in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/59119, #97883, and mergeKey is still only name, xref https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/47249)

Original report

===

**What happened**:
For `deployment` resource:

A container has defined environment variable with name `x` that is duplicated (there are two env vars with the same name, the value is also the same).

When you fix the `deployment` resource descriptor so that environment variable with name `x` appears only once and push it with `kubectl apply`, deployment with no environment variable named `x` is created and therefore no environment variable named `x` is passed to replica set and pods.

**What you expected to happen**:
After fixing the `deployment`, environment variable with name `x` is defined in the `deployment` once .

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. create deployment with container with duplicated environment variable
1. `kubectl apply` it
1. fix deployment removing one of duplicated environment variable definitions
1. `kubectl apply` it
1. `kubectl get deployment/your-deployment -o yaml` prints deployment without

nope

title: Discrepancy between `kubectl top pod` and the sum of Rss in `/proc/[pid]/smaps`
body:
We encountered inconsistencies among various memory metrics in our production environment. On the front-end monitoring page, we use `kubectl top pod` to display memory usage. Its output is as follows:
```
kubectl top pod clickhouse-keeper-0 
NAME                  CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)   
clickhouse-keeper-0   1314m        7117Mi   
```
Afterwards, we entered the pod:
```
kubectl exec -it clickhouse-keeper-0 bash
```
We then checked the cgroup memory statistics inside the pod, which showed:
```
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.stat

total_pgmajfault 297
total_inactive_anon 0
total_active_anon 6906904576
total_inactive_file 1098760192
total_active_file 551292928
total_unevictable 0
```
Finally, we examined the Rss metric in the `smaps` file of the pod's only process, summed it up, and the result was:
```
grep Rss /proc/1/smaps | awk '{sum+=$2} END {print sum " kB"}'
5579016 kB
```
The anonymous huge page memory usage was:
```
grep AnonHuge /proc/1/smaps | awk '{sum+=$2} END {print sum " kB"}'
3330048 kB
```
Based on the data above, the memory usage value from `kubectl top pod` is largely consistent with the `Rss` value from the `cgroup` inside the pod. However, there is a significant discrepancy compared to the sum of `Rss` from the `smaps` of that process inside the pod.

What I would like to know is: Why is there a difference between the sum of RSS in `smaps` and the memory usage reported by `kubectl top pod`?

Looking forward to your reply. Thanks.

title: informer and any other things depends on tools/cache.Reflector may suffer unexpected memory consumption
body:
### What happened?

Let's revisit Reflector work flow:
1. `Reflector.ListAndWatch` called `list` https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/b2097e607c196a94c5e1100cb073fa0e8277fd7e/tools/cache/reflector.go#L254-L257
2. `list` collects `items` via `meta.ExtractList` and called `syncWith` to store all items into the memory kv store https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/b2097e607c196a94c5e1100cb073fa0e8277fd7e/tools/cache/reflector.go#L441-L446
3. `meta.ExtractList` is using reflect to get each item and copy them to another slice https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/915d89afb4cbcaca892b455a5550495411a37a84/pkg/api/meta/help.go#L169

Here is the problem, `meta.ExtractList` use [`items.Index`](https://pkg.go.dev/reflect#Value.Index) to get each item as a pointer, usually equals to `&podList.Items[i]` or something else, this item is then being put to store by its key, but it still keep  referrence to the whole podList object which may consume lots of memory when in a large cluster(in my case, 10,000 pods consumes 400MiB around), so the store will keep all podList and delta pods from `watch` which may double the memory consumption in some edge case, e.g. whole podLists from `list` each of which has one item still alive in store and nearly whole pods from `watch`, nearly all pods have two copy in store, one from list and one from watch.

I'm using [controller-runtime](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-runtime), which depends on [`sharedIndexInformer`](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache#NewSharedIndexInformer), which depends on Reflector so i found this problem but can not fix it easily.

You can verify this memory "leak"(i dont have better word to describe this problem) in this mini program:

```go
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
	"strings"

	v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/meta"
)

func main() {
	const cnt = 10000
	podList := v1.PodList{
		Items: make([]v1.Pod, cnt),
	}
	list, _ := meta.ExtractList(&podList)
	fmt.Printf("Type: %T\n", list[0])

	str := string(bytes.Repeat([]byte("a"), 20_000))
	for i := 0; i < cnt; i++ {
		podList.Items[i].Annotations = map[string]string{"foo": strings.Clone(str)}
	}
	var memStats runtime.MemStats
	runtime.ReadMemStats(&memStats)
	fmt.Println("podList alive:", memStats.HeapInuse)

	pod := &podList.Items[100]
	podList = v1.PodList{}
	runtime.GC()
	runtime.ReadMemStats(&memStats)
	fmt.Println("podList dead, pod alive:", memStats.HeapInuse)
	runtime.KeepAlive(pod)

	pod = nil
	runtime.GC()
	runtime.ReadMemStats(&memStats)
	fmt.Println("pod dead:", memStats.HeapInuse)
}
```

It will output as below:
```
Type: *v1.Pod
podList alive: 219521024
podList dead, pod alive: 219529216
pod dead: 1220608
```



### What did you expect to happen?

See above full description

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See above full description

title: The generator for swagger docs removes some (but not all) of the line breaks, breaking the markdown
body:
### What happened?

When generating the [networking/v1/types_swagger_doc_generated.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/api/networking/v1/types_swagger_doc_generated.go) from [networking/v1/types.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/api/blob/master/networking/v1/types.go), some of the line breaks in the input documentation comments are removed (while others are kept).
From this we get https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/api/openapi-spec/swagger.json, which in turn is used to generate https://github.com/kubernetes/website/tree/main/content/en/docs/reference/kubernetes-api.
In the final documentation (e.g. https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/service-resources/ingress-v1/#IngressSpec), the result is that list formatting is broken.

### What did you expect to happen?

Line breaks in the input are kept for the Markdown processor. (Or the removal is at least smart enough to not remove relevant line breaks.)

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Input in [types.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/api/networking/v1/types.go#L461-L476):

```go

	// PathType determines the interpretation of the Path matching. PathType can
	// be one of the following values:
	// * Exact: Matches the URL path exactly.
	// * Prefix: Matches based on a URL path prefix split by '/'. Matching is
	//   done on a path element by element basis. A path element refers is the
	//   list of labels in the path split by the '/' separator. A request is a
	//   match for path p if every p is an element-wise prefix of p of the
	//   request path. Note that if the last element of the path is a substring
	//   of the last element in request path, it is not a match (e.g. /foo/bar
	//   matches /foo/bar/baz, but does not match /foo/barbaz).
	// * ImplementationSpecific: Interpretation of the Path matching is up to
	//   the IngressClass. Implementations can treat this as a separate PathType
	//   or treat it identically to Prefix or Exact path types.
	// Implementations are required to support all path types.
	PathType *PathType `json:"pathType" protobuf:"bytes,3,opt,name=pathType"`
```
This becomes in [types_swagger_doc_generated.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/api/networking/v1/types_swagger_doc_generated.go#L33):

```go
var map_HTTPIngressPath = map[string]string{
	...,
	"pathType": "PathType determines the interpretation of the Path matching. PathType can be one of the following values: * Exact: Matches the URL path exactly. * Prefix: Matches based on a URL path prefix split by '/'. Matching is\n  done on a path element by element basis. A path element refers is the\n  list of labels in the path split by the '/' separator. A request is a\n  match for path p if every p is an element-wise prefix of p of the\n  request path. Note that if the last element of the path is a substring\n  of the last element in request path, it is not a match (e.g. /foo/bar\n  matches /foo/bar/baz, but does not match /foo/barbaz).\n* ImplementationSpecific: Interpretation of the Path matching is up to\n  the IngressClass. Implementations can treat this as a separate PathType\n  or treat it identically to Prefix or Exact path types.\nImplementations are required to support all path types.",
	...
}
```
We can here see that the first 3 line breaks are removed, the later ones are still there (escaped as \n).

In the generated markdown, [ingress-v1.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/website/blob/main/content/en/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/service-resources/ingress-v1.md?plain=1#L110-L122), this results in this:
```markdown
      - **rules.http.paths.pathType** (string), required

        PathType determines the interpretation of the Path matching. PathType can be one of the following values: * Exact: Matches the URL path exactly. * Prefix: Matches based on a URL path prefix split by '/'. Matching is
          done on a path element by element basis. A path element refers is the
          list of labels in the path split by the '/' separator. A request is a
          match for path p if every p is an element-wise prefix of p of the
          request path. Note that if the last element of the path is a substring
          of the last element in request path, it is not a match (e.g. /foo/bar
          matches /foo/bar/baz, but does not match /foo/barbaz).
        * ImplementationSpecific: Interpretation of the Path matching is up to
          the IngressClass. Implementations can treat this as a separate PathType
          or treat it identically to Prefix or Exact path types.
        Implementations are required to support all path types.
```

Instead, it should be this:
```markdown
      - **rules.http.paths.pathType** (string), required

        PathType determines the interpretation of the Path matching. PathType can
        be one of the following values:
        * Exact: Matches the URL path exactly.
        * Prefix: Matches based on a URL path prefix split by '/'. Matching is
          done on a path element by element basis. A path element refers is the
          list of labels in the path split by the '/' separator. A request is a
          match for path p if every p is an element-wise prefix of p of the
          request path. Note that if the last element of the path is a substring
          of the last element in request path, it is not a match (e.g. /foo/bar
          matches /foo/bar/baz, but does not match /foo/barbaz).
        * ImplementationSpecific: Interpretation of the Path matching is up to
          the IngressClass. Implementations can treat this as a separate PathType
          or treat it identically to Prefix or Exact path types.
        Implementations are required to support all path types.
```

The same is happening for several other cases, this is just the one where I noticed it on the [website](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/service-resources/ingress-v1/#IngressSpec).

### Anything else we need to know?

This investigation was triggered by https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/35203 (which pointed me to "this is generated").

title: Enabling Graceful node shutdown in Kubernetes, preStop hook for statefulset unfinished
body:
### What happened?

Execute OS reboot， trigger kubernetes graceful node shutdown
kubelet exec preStop hook，but statefulset preStop hook unfinished
kubelet log show statefulset pod exec preStop hook，but delete and set gracePeriod=2

title: [InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Unnecessary ResizeCompleted event emitted when PLR FG is enabled
body:
### What happened?

After I create a pod using a Kubernetes deployment in an empty Kind cluster, I see an in-place update event that seems unnecessary:

```bash
kubectl get events --watch -A

default              0s          Normal    ResizeCompleted           pod/hamster-deployment-57445548f6-r27rn          Pod resize completed: {"containers":[{"name":"hamster1","resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"10m","memory":"10Mi"}}},{"name":"hamster2","resources":{}},{"name":"hamster3","resources":{}}],"generation":1}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I don't expect to see an in-place update after deploying the pod to the cluster.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```bash
KIND_VERSION="kindest/node:v1.35.0@sha256:452d707d4862f52530247495d180205e029056831160e22870e37e3f6c1ac31f"

kind create cluster --image=${KIND_VERSION} --config <(cat <<EOF
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
featureGates:
  "InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScaling": true
  "NodeDeclaredFeatures": true
EOF
)
```

```yaml
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  labels:
    app: hamster
  name: hamster-deployment
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hamster
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hamster
    spec:
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 100Mi
      containers:
      - name: hamster1
        image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.1
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 10m
            memory: 10Mi
      - image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.1
        name: hamster2
      - image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.1
        name: hamster3
EOF
```

### Anything else we need to know?

* I don't have anything like Vertical Pod Autoscaler that should trigger in-place updates at any level (container or pod).
* related slack thread: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C06FSK01BGU/p1773818099854269

title: Possible name collision between RS and STS controllers
body:
### What happened?

ReplicaSet and StatefulSet both manages pod, and ReplicaSet creates pods by attaching a 5-letter hash to it's name:
```shell
$ kubectl get rs 
NAME                 DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
collision-test-113   1         1         1       17m
$ kubectl get pods
NAME                       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
collision-test-113-87797   1/1     Running   0          17m
```
Once in a while, the hash contains only digits like the example here.
However, StatefulSet creates pod by attaching the ordinal based on the config (starting from 1 if unspecified):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: collision-test-113   # the deployment that got the numeric hash
spec:
  serviceName: collision-test-113
  replicas: 1
  ordinals:
    start: 87797    # e.g. 748291
  #..
```
They may collide if the suffix matches each other.
```shell
$ kubectl describe pod collision-test-113-87797 
Name:             collision-test-113-87797
# ...
Controlled By:  ReplicaSet/collision-test-113
$ kubectl describe sts collision-test-113      
Name:               collision-test-113
Replicas:           1 desired | 0 total
Pods Status:        0 Running / 0 Waiting / 0 Succeeded / 0 Failed
Events:            <none>
# ..
```

The collision may be rare unless you manually specify the `sts.spec.ordinal.start`, but it may happen more frequently in large scale deployment if the sysadmin happens to give the same name to ReplicaSet and StatefulSet.

### What did you expect to happen?

No collision

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

`$ cat batch.sh `
```shell
#!/bin/bash
PREFIX="collision-test"
COUNT=500

# Step 1: Create ReplicaSets directly
for i in $(seq 1 $COUNT); do
  kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
  name: $PREFIX-$i
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: $PREFIX-$i
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: $PREFIX-$i
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
EOF
done

echo "Waiting for pods to be scheduled..."
sleep 15

# Step 2: Find purely numeric hashes
echo "Scanning for numeric hashes..."
kubectl get pods --no-headers | awk '{print $1}' | grep "^$PREFIX" | while read podname; do
  hash=$(echo "$podname" | rev | cut -d'-' -f1 | rev)
  rs=$(echo "$podname" | rev | cut -d'-' -f2- | rev)

  if [[ "$hash" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
    echo "FOUND! RS: $rs | Hash: $hash | Full pod: $podname"
  fi
done
```

After a pod with numeric hash is found, update the config below

`$ cat sts.yml`
```yml
cat sts.yml 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: collision-test-113   # the deployment that got the numeric hash
spec:
  serviceName: collision-test-113
  replicas: 1
  ordinals:
    start: 87797
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: sts
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: sts
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx
```

### Kubernetes version

```console
kubectl version
Client Version: v1.35.3
Kustomize Version: v5.7.1
Server Version: v1.35.0
```

### Anything else we need to know?

A similar bug https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/41153 caused by name collision. It's hard to fix because there is no separation mechanism in object names between different CR.

The root cause here is ReplicaSet uses automatically generated names but StatefulSet uses fixed names. It's very hard to avoid collision in string if they share the same naming space. We prevent it by forcing the CR prefix in both ReplicaSet and StatefulSet controller in our project (adding `replicaset-` and `statefulset-` respectively). I think one possible solution here is to let StatefulSet controller also attach auto-generated suffix to avoid collision.

title: [Umbrella][Declarative Validation] Enable Declarative Validation for APIs
body:
### Objective

To complete the migration to declarative validation by applying the necessary internal code changes to every **unversioned API Kind and its Subresources** in the codebase that has not yet been migrated. This process must be tracked by individual commits for each unit of work.

### Contribution Workflow

To contribute to this effort, please pick an unchecked item from the migration checklist below and create a pull request. Each pull request should enable declarative validation for a single resource or a group of related subresources.

The process for each item involves the following steps:

1.  **Enable Validation Generation:** Add the `+k8s:validation-gen` tag to the `doc.go` file for the corresponding API group (e.g., `pkg/apis/{group}/{version}/doc.go`).

title: ServerSideApply: empty object {} converted to null and causing failure in schema validation
body:
### What happened?

We are using ArgoCD Application CRD, in their [documentation](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/auto_sync/), to set automatic sync with selfHeal we need to specify

```yaml
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      selfHeal: true
```

Later, we want to disable selfHeal, the issue we found is that we cannot change the existing manifest to 

```yaml
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    automated: {}
```

using server-side apply,

It will give an error saying the `{}` converted to `null` and thus become invalid according to the schema

Although ArgoCD provide an alternative solution by updating the manifest to

```yaml
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      enabled: true
```

We still think that ServerSideApply should work for `{}` too

### What did you expect to happen?

The apply should be successfully

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We can reproduce this by creating the following simple CRD

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: hellos.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  names:
    kind: Hello
    plural: hellos
    singular: hello
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                automated:
                  type: object
                  properties:
                    selfHeal: { type: boolean }

```

Applying the following manifest is successful

```bash
bash$ kubectl apply --server-side -f- <<EOF
apiVersion: example.com/v1alpha1
kind: Hello
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  automated:
    selfHeal: true
---
apiVersion: example.com/v1alpha1
kind: Hello
metadata:
  name: example2
spec:
  automated: {}
EOF
```

this is to prove that apiserver can store empty object

```bash
bash$ kubectl get hello -o json | jq '.items[].spec'
{
  "automated": {
    "selfHeal": true
  }
}
{
  "automated": {}
}
```

but change the `example` to have empty object will fail

```bash
bash$ kubectl apply --server-side -f- <<EOF
apiVersion: example.com/v1alpha1
kind: Hello
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  automated: {}
EOF
The Hello "example" is invalid: spec.automated: Invalid value: "null": spec.automated in body must be of type object: "null"
```

title: Give an indication in container events for probe failure as to whether the failure was ignored due to FailureThreshold
body:
Probes of all kinds currently support FailureThreshold (and SuccessThreshold), these properties allow a user to specify that Kubernetes should not take action in response to a failed probe unless it fails a successive number of times.

This is useful for  end-users as it allows them to mitigate the effects of any probes that "flake" by requiring successive failure.

When a probe fails in Kubernetes, we emit a container event indicating this here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L110 and end-users can consume these events via the API for their own purposes. This event is emitted regardless of whether the FailureThreshold has been reached or not.

Currently when a user consumes a probe failure event they have no way of knowing whether the event resulted in action on the control plane (because the event can be ignored due to FailureThreshold, and information on this is not included in the event). This can lead to users assuming there is a problem and a container/pod was restarted when nothing occurred.

I think we should expose the keepGoing value from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L203 in the emitted event somehow, my preferred solution is to emit the probe failure event in the worker rather than where it currently sits in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L110 - there is also the option of passing some information down the stack into the prober from the worker (such as making the FailureThreshold/SuccessThreshold decision in the prober) but I'm worried about separation of concerns, happy to hear what other folks think :)

Also of note is that FailureThreshold/SuccessThreshold is the only filter I can see where a probe can be ignored after being run (and therefore emitting a container event)

I’m happy to write this PR once we’re confident in our approach :)

title: TopologySpreadConstraints - Scaling Pods during rolling updates can cause pods to be stuck in Pending
body:
### What happened?

We have a stateful application that requires pods to be evenly spread across zones. Each pod required a persistent volume (AWS EBS volume) to store data. To deploy this application we use a StatefulSet with the following Pod Topology Spread Constraint:

```
topologySpreadConstraints:
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            name: my-app
        maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
```

During rolling updates, we update multiple pods from the same zone. For that, we use a custom controller ([zone-aware-controllers-for-k8s](https://github.com/aws/zone-aware-controllers-for-k8s)), but it would be possible to archive something similar using the [StatefulSets’ Max Unavailable](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2022/05/27/maxunavailable-for-statefulset/) alpha feature available on Kubernetes 1.24+.

When the application happens to be scaled (e.g manually or by the HPA) during a rolling updated, we have noticed old Pods getting stuck on Pending because of topology spread constraints + volume node affinity conflict: 

```
 Warning  FailedScheduling   40s   default-scheduler   0/34 nodes are available: 26 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector, 4 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints, 4 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict.
```

Example: 

Initial state (zone : pods).
- ZoneA : [PA1, PA2, PA3, PA4]
- ZoneB : [PB1, PB2, PB3, PB4]
- ZoneC : [PC1, PC2, PC3, PC4]

Assuming that we update 2 pods in Zone A:
- ZoneA : [PA1, PA2, **PA3(Terminating)**, **PA4(Terminating)**]
- ZoneB : [PB1, PB2, PB3, PB4]
- ZoneC : [PC1, PC2, PC3, PC4]

Now, scale the number of pods by the same number of pods getting updated. Noticed that new replicas are placed on Zone A first (scheduler seems to ignore the pods that are getting terminated/updated).
- ZoneA : [PA1, PA2, PA3(Terminating), PA4(Terminating), **PA5**, **PA6**]
- ZoneB : [PB1, PB2, PB3, PB4]
- ZoneC : [PC1, PC2, PC3, PC4]

In the end, some pods that were getting updated will be stuck in Pending as they can't be rescheduled into another zone because of the volume node affinity conflict (those pods can only be scheduled on ZoneA which is the zone in which their EBS volumes exists). 
- ZoneA : [PA1, PA2, PA3, **PA4(Pending)**, PA5, PA6]
- ZoneB : [PB1, PB2, PB3, PB4]
- ZoneC : [PC1, PC2, PC3, PC4]

Note that in this specific example PA3 will be scheduled on ZoneA as it satisfy `maxSkew = 1`, but PA4 will get stuck.

### What did you expect to happen?

Statefulset Pods getting restarted/updated are considered when scheduling new Pods.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The easier way to reproduce this is probably by deleting multiple pods from the same zone and, while new pods are getting recreated, try to scale the number of replicas. For example: 

- Create a Statefulset with PersistentVolume and the above TopologySpreadConstraint. 
- Scale the Statefulset so you have multiple pods per zone (e.g 12 pods distributed in 3 zones)
- Delete multiple pods from a single zone
- While pods are getting recreated, try to scale the number of replicas
- Notice that all (or majority) of new replicas are placed on the zone in which pods were deleted
- Notice that old pods are stuck in Pending

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: Support `objectSelector` filtering for Webhooks on CONNECT Operations (e.g., `pods/exec`)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Enable support for the `objectSelector` field in `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` for webhooks that handle `CONNECT` operations, such as `pods/exec`. This would allow webhook invocations to be filtered based on pod labels, similar to how `objectSelector` works for `CREATE` and other operations.

### Why is this needed?

We are currently using a `ValidatingAdmissionWebhook` to intercept `CONNECT` operations (e.g., `pods/exec`) across the entire cluster. However, this broad scope is inefficient and introduces unnecessary overhead. We want to scope the webhook to only target specific pods based on labels, reducing impact and avoiding unintended side effects in case the webhook pods are down. 

**For example, if the webhook pods are unavailable, all `pods/exec` operations throughout the cluster are blocked; effectively making the entire cluster inaccessible for interactive debugging or remote command execution.**

While the `objectSelector` field works as expected for `CREATE` operations, it appears to be unsupported or non-functional for `CONNECT` operations. For example, using the following configuration causes the webhook not to trigger at all, even for matching pods:

```yaml
objectSelector:
  matchLabels:
    controller.devfile.io/creator: "foo"
```

It is currently documented that resources that cannot have labels are not supported for matching https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/extensible-admission-controllers/#matching-requests-objectselector

This issue has been previously discussed in:
- #91732 – originally raised but closed due to inactivity
- #132287 – related discussion on webhook filtering limitations, where I got feedback to use `namespaceSelector`

Actually, `namespaceSelector` does not help in our scenario, as our workloads often share namespaces. We require pod-level granularity, which only objectSelector can provide.

Supporting `objectSelector` for CONNECT operations would bring consistency to webhook behavior and allow for more precise and efficient admission control logic.

If there is an alternative way to achieve this targeted behavior, we would appreciate any guidance.

title: Migrate "Good First Migration" Required Fields to Declarative Validation
body:
### What would you like to be added?

This issue tracks a number of identified "good first migration" cases from handwritten Go code to Declarative Validation tags (+k8s:required) as part of KEP-5073.  This issue aims to be a more narrowed down list with specific fields and validation tags than the list of types tracked in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134280. The goals is to have users more easily able to aid in the migration by first having a set of "Good First Migration" cases with minimal migration friction and build from there.

For more information on the tasks here, the Declarative Validation work group (guiding this and similar issues) has open discussion in kubernetes Slack channel: #sig-api-machinery-dev-tools

We are targeting fields that meet the "Good First Migration" criteria:
1.  **Validation Logic:** Simple `Required` checks (e.g., `if len(field) == 0 { return Required }` or `if ptr == nil { return Required }`).
2.  **Versioning:** The field exists at the same path across all API versions (typically v1).
3.  **Nesting:** The field is close to the root of the struct or part of a struct that is **always** validated (not a pointer that might be nil). This avoids having to check field path parents for short-circuiting logic.
4.  **Not Optional:** The field is not marked `+optional` in `types.go`.
5.  **Status:** The field has not yet been migrated (does not currently have a `+k8s:` tag).

### IMPORTANT! - PR Structure
The ideal PR structure for a PR contributing a DV tag migration is:

Commit # 1: IF NOT ALREADY WIRED UP FOR DV - Wire up the apigroup, add empty test and empty generated file. 

Commit # 2: Use a single DV tag on a single field. E.g. Add `+k8s:required` to required field. Includes generated code and robust test cases. Emphasis on test-cases -- we want enough to prove that a field is correct, but we don't want to duplicate all the per-tag tests (e.g. a k8s-short-name field has dozens of corner cases, but we really only need a few). We want each case to be as short and specific as possible, which is why the "tweak" pattern and the use of Origin for Invalid() errors is so important. Specify as little as possible to be sufficiently precise. Newcomers need guidance on this.

Commits # 3...N: Use DV tags on the same field, one per commit; repeat until that field is done or all that is left is not handled by DV yet. Includes generated code and tests for each field. (not the case for the specific examples below as they are for single tag migrations)

Commits N+1...M: Repeat the above for more fields. (not the case for the specific examples below as they are for single field migrations)

The emphasis is on lots of small commits. Maintaining commit discipline is hard but worthwhile.

If DV exposes bugs in the existing testing or the hand-written validation itself (!!), those should be fixed as a PR of its own or as commits at the front of the PR.

### Resources

*   **KEP:** [KEP-5073: Declarative Validation](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/5073-declarative-validation)
*   **Migration Guide:** [Review the "Migrating Handwritten Validation" section in the README](https://github.com/jpbetz/validation-gen/blob/main/staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/README.md#2-migrating-handwritten-validation-to-declarative-validation)

### Task List

The following fields have been identified as good candidates for the initial migration.


#### Storage (`storage.k8s.io`)

*   [ ] **VolumeAttachment.Spec.Attacher**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.Attacher` (string)
    *   **Location:** `staging/src/k8s.io/api/storage/v1/types.go`
    *   **Current Validation:** `pkg/apis/storage/validation/validation.go` (`validateAttacher`)
    *   **Analysis:** `Attacher` is a direct string field on `VolumeAttachmentSpec`. It is not marked optional. Validation checks `len(attacher) == 0`. `VolumeAttachment` is a top-level resource. Safe to migrate.

#### AdmissionRegistration (`admissionregistration.k8s.io`)

*   [ ] **ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding.Spec.PolicyName**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.PolicyName` (string)
    *   **Location:** `staging/src/k8s.io/api/admissionregistration/v1/types.go`
    *   **Current Validation:** `pkg/apis/admissionregistration/validation/validation.go` (`validateValidatingAdmissionPolicyBindingSpec`)
    *   **Analysis:** `PolicyName` is a direct string field. It is not marked optional. Validation checks `len(spec.PolicyName) == 0`. Safe to migrate.

*   [ ] **ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding.Spec.ValidationActions**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.ValidationActions` ([]ValidationAction)
    *   **Location:** `staging/src/k8s.io/api/admissionregistration/v1/types.go`
    *   **Current Validation:** `pkg/apis/admissionregistration/validation/validation.go` (`validateValidationActions`)
    *   **Analysis:** This is a slice field. It is not marked optional. Validation checks `len(actions) == 0`. Safe to migrate.

#### FlowControl (`flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io`)

*   [ ] **FlowSchema.Spec.PriorityLevelConfiguration.Name**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.PriorityLevelConfiguration.Name` (string)
    *   **Location:** `staging/src/k8s.io/api/flowcontrol/v1/types.go`
    *   **Current Validation:** `pkg/apis/flowcontrol/validation/validation.go` (`ValidateFlowSchemaSpec`)
    *   **Analysis:** `PriorityLevelConfiguration` is a struct type (not a pointer) embedded in `Spec`, so it is always present. `Name` inside it is a string and not optional. Validation checks for empty name. The struct `PriorityLevelConfigurationReference` appears to only be used in this context. Safe to migrate.

#### Autoscaling (`autoscaling/v1`)

*   [ ] **HorizontalPodAutoscaler.Spec.ScaleTargetRef.Kind**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.ScaleTargetRef.Kind` (string)
    *   **Location:** `staging/src/k8s.io/api/autoscaling/v1/types.go`
    *   **Current Validation:** `pkg/apis/autoscaling/validation/validation.go` (`ValidateCrossVersionObjectReference`)
    *   **Analysis:** `ScaleTargetRef` is a struct (not a pointer) in `HorizontalPodAutoscalerSpec`, so it is always traversed. `Kind` is a string field in `CrossVersionObjectReference`. It is not marked optional. Validation checks `len(ref.Kind) == 0`.
    *   **Hierarchy Note:** `CrossVersionObjectReference` is also used in v2 `MetricSpec` (`ObjectMetricSource`). In both cases, `Kind` is required. Adding the tag to the v1 struct definition is safe and correct.

*   [ ] **HorizontalPodAutoscaler.Spec.ScaleTargetRef.Name**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.ScaleTargetRef.Name` (string)
    *   **Location:** `staging/src/k8s.io/api/autoscaling/v1/types.go`
    *   **Current Validation:** `pkg/apis/autoscaling/validation/validation.go` (`ValidateCrossVersionObjectReference`)
    *   **Analysis:** Same as `Kind`. `Name` is required in all usages of this struct.

#### Certificates (`certificates.k8s.io`)

*   [ ] **CertificateSigningRequest.Spec.Usages**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.Usages` ([]KeyUsage)
    *   **Location:** `staging/src/k8s.io/api/certificates/v1/types.go`
    *   **Current Validation:** `pkg/apis/certificates/validation/validation.go` (`validateCertificateSigningRequest`)
    *   **Analysis:** `Usages` is a slice. It is not marked optional. Validation checks `len(csr.Spec.Usages) == 0`. Safe to migrate.


### How to Migrate a Field

1.  **Locate the Versioned Type:** Find the `types.go` file for the versioned API (e.g., `staging/src/k8s.io/api/storage/v1/types.go`).
2.  **Add the Tag:** Add `// +k8s:required` above the field definition.
3.  **Generate:** Run `hack/update-codegen.sh validation`.
4.  **Update Strategy:** In the resource's `strategy.go` (usually in `pkg/registry/<group>/<resource>/`), update the `Validate` function to use `rest.ValidateDeclarativelyWithMigrationChecks`.
5.  **Verify:**
    *   Ensure unit tests pass.
    *   Run `declarative_validation_test.go` (add one if missing) to prove equivalence.
6.  **Mark Covered:** In the original `validation.go`, find the manual check and append `.MarkCoveredByDeclarative()`.

Example of marking hand-written validation code:
```go
if len(t.Provisioner) == 0 {
    allErrs = append(allErrs, field.Required(fldPath.Child("provisioner"), "")).MarkCoveredByDeclarative()
}
```

7. **If new API group being plumbed for DV** - wire up API group and all associated versions for fuzz testing in [pkg/api/testing/validation_test.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9720186a466cc627b0417433fb1f66cd1dd96f94/pkg/api/testing/validation_test.go#L32-L50)
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9720186a466cc627b0417433fb1f66cd1dd96f94/pkg/api/testing/validation_test.go#L32-L50

### Why is this needed?

This helps onboard the community to DV, improves the APIs touched, and helps in the process of getting Declarative Validation to it's stated goal of migrating ~50% of existing hand-written code to DV over 5 releases -> improved API readability and more declarative APIs

title: RV vs object-wide logical clock
body:
(followup from SIG API Machinery meeting of 2022-09-21)

(note, I'm keeping this text up to date so you don't have to read all the discussion below if you don't want to)

We are trying to unblock a class of caching behaviors, example PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/112202

The problem is that today there is no way for a client to know which of two object states is "more recent". This makes it very hard to e.g. put the result of a write into a cache ahead of seeing the corresponding watch event.

(Aside: doing this destroys the property that listing out of cache always gives you a group of objects that actually co-existed in the server at some point in time. Not everyone needs this property, but we will probably ask that an in-tree assumption / write-through cache gives the option to restore this property. I'll refer to this as the "cross-object ordering problem".)

## Option 1: Relax prohibition on clients parsing resourceVersion.

Today we tell clients that they may compare RV as a string, only for equality. In practice, some clients actually do parse it anyway, and we already suffer the downside of not being able to change what we store in the string.

So this option is to tell clients that they may parse RV as a positive integer of up to 63 bits. The resulting integers may be compared to determine recency, but *only* between objects within the same collection (resource). RV comparison between collections is still invalid and at least some clusters are actually configured in a way that would break clients attempting this comparison.

Pros:
* People already do this. We lose almost no flexibility to change this in the future (we already lost it)
* Easy to see how this could solve the cross-object ordering problem (you can directly compare RV from objects in the same collection)
* No control plane changes needed, client changes compatible with old clusters.
 
Cons:
* Ugly; we would never do it this way if we started fresh
* 63 bits is slightly constraining for alternative DB implementations (but it's already that way)

## Option 2:
Alternatively, we could add a field to metadata, `.objectVersion`; this field would be a 63 bit int, a per-object logical clock. The server would enforce that it functions like the current `.generation` field, but for changes in the whole object, not just spec.

Pros:
* This design is much more aesthetic
* 63 bits is enough for a single object (especially since no-op changes won't increment this)
* [EDIT: perhaps in a few years we could start being more stringent about RV handling?]

Cons:
* Requires server changes, clients have to wait for a new version. ~Code has to take care for no-op updates.~ [EDIT: storage-layer changes aren't actually needed, only an api change]
* ~slight storage size increase.~ [EDIT: no, actually etcd already stores this for us]
* More difficult to solve the cross-object ordering problem (you have to wait for object X to hit at least objectVersion Y, instead of waiting to see any object with RV > Z)
* RV situation is probably not improved [EDIT: not in the short term at least].
* [EDIT: Awkward / not clear how to make this useful / play nice with other preconditions (including RV)]

## Recommendation

I recommend we select option 1, update documentation, and call it a day. [EDIT: but option 2 is back in the running after these updates...]

/sig api-machinery

title: [kubectl] server-side apply with --force-conflicts should warn about any conflicts it is forcing
body:
### What would you like to be added?

`kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts` should provide a way to display any conflicts being overridden so that users--especially those migrating to SSA--can detect, investigate and address them without causing a disruption to their service (or need to revert to CSA). Perhaps this could even be the default behaviour. If it can't, I suggest `--force-conflicts=warn`

/sig api-machinery
/sig cli

### Why is this needed?

One of the biggest changes for end users migrating to server-side apply (SSA) from client-side apply (CSA) is the notion of field ownership conflicts. Indeed, the need to identify and resolve them may be a barrier to migrating to SSA, particularly when a central entity determines the apply strategy in CD pipelines they manage for an entire organization. Users can get around the problem to some extent by setting `--force-conflicts=true`, but then they don't even know whether or not conflicts are occurring. This functionality could be used to make the migration path smoother. It could also be a helpful tool in developing a strategy to automate opt-in to SSA in the long term.

Note: clients other than kubectl could likely also benefit from this information being exposed in the response

title: Two names for one thing: flowcontrol and API Priority and Fairness
body:
### What happened?

In the rush to alpha, we merged the code with an inconsistency: we used the term "flow control" in some places, "API Priority and Fairness" in others.  These two terms are used interchangeably for the same thing.  This is unnecessarily confusing.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected to use one term consistently.

I think "API Priority and Fairness" is the better choice.  The term "flow control" is broad and misleading. I did a web search for "flow control". The first hit was https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flow_control_(data) . As you would expect from the words, the concepts there are around controlling rate rather than concurrency. The techniques listed on that web page do not include things like APF. While it is true that the two are connected, so controlling either has an effect on the other, the problem with the term "flow control" is that it suggests that rate rather than concurrency is being directly controlled.

Look at the name of the feature gate.  Look at the user-facing documentation.  Look at the API group name.  Look at the code directory structure.

title: DNS intermittent delays of 5s
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:
/kind bug

**What happened**:
DNS lookup is sometimes taking 5 seconds.

**What you expected to happen**:
No delays in DNS.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

1. Create a cluster in AWS using kops with cni networking:
```
kops create cluster     --node-count 3     --zones eu-west-1a,eu-west-1b,eu-west-1c     --master-zones eu-west-1a,eu-west-1b,eu-west-1c     --dns-zone kube.example.com   --node-size t2.medium     --master-size t2.medium  --topology private --networking cni   --cloud-labels "Env=Staging"  ${NAME}
```
2. CNI plugin:
```
kubectl apply -f "https://cloud.weave.works/k8s/net?k8s-version=$(kubectl version | base64 | tr -d '\n')"
```
3. Run this script in any pod with that has curl:
```
var=1
while true ; do
  res=$( { curl -o /dev/null -s -w %{time_namelookup}\\n  http://www.google.com; } 2>&1 )
  var=$((var+1))
  if [[ $res =~ ^[1-9] ]]; then
    now=$(date +"%T")
    echo "$var slow: $res $now"
    break
  fi
done
```
**Anything else we need to know?**:
1. I am encountering this issue in both staging and production clusters, but for some reason staging cluster is having a lot more 5s delays.
2. Delays happen both for external services (google.com) or internal, such as service.namespace.
3. Happens on both 1.6 and 1.7 version of kubernetes, but did not encounter these issues in 1.5 (though the setup was a bit different - no CNI back then).
4. Have not tested with 1.7 without CNI yet.

title: Explore user network namespace for rootless network testing
body:
Unprivileged network namespaces allow users to create network namespaces and behave as a root inside those namespaces.

This allows to create nftables rules , nested user namespaces and network interfaces

```
lrwxrwxrwx 1 nobody nogroup 0 Feb 28 13:46 /proc/self -> 153429

```

Currently, for our kube-proxy testing, for complex testing we rely on the great work done by @danwinship with the nftablesTracer, that allows to simulate the packet traversal of the installed nftables rules.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/73f54b67b29d77601b0bd42ad8b4992925b9df47/pkg/proxy/nftables/helpers_test.go#L150-L178

However,  simulators will never be as reliable as the real thing and also can have the problem to drift if the simulated logic changes.

Using unprivileged network namespaces can COMPLEMENT current testing , not replacing, as these namespaces has some security issues and are relatively new, so maybe are not able to run in each system.

We can just create a predefined topology to emulate the most complex feature and run table tests and multiple combinations just with `go test. ./pkg/proxy/nftables/...`  ... this can be very useful for things like endpoints termination or topology awareness, where all the possible combinations  are hard to test with e2e

```
ns-pod1 ---- ns-kproxy. ---- ns-pod2
                               |
                               |
                               L----- ns-pod3      
```

### References

### What would you like to be added?

For people dealing with extremely high-throughput batch work (i.e 1000's jobs / second, lasting 1-2 mins each), etcd starts to become a real problem. There should be an in-k8s solution to this.

title: Refactor emptydir setup layering in pkg/volume/emptydir
body:
#### What would you like to be added / why is this needed?

Refactor `pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go` so directory setup and medium-specific mounts are layered clearly, and add focused tests for behavior that was only covered indirectly.

**Problem**

- `setupTmpfs` and `setupHugepages` implicitly required `setupDir` to run first, but the call pattern was inconsistent: for default medium, `setupDir` ran directly; for memory-backed and hugepages volumes, `setupTmpfs` / `setupHugepages` called `setupDir` internally. That mixed “mount” helpers with directory creation and made responsibilities unclear.
- `setupDir` had no dedicated unit tests for its permission checks and `chmod` correction logic.

**Proposed approach**

- Always create the directory in `SetUpAt` first, then run the medium-specific mount (`setupTmpfs` / `setupHugepages`) without those functions calling `setupDir` internally.
- Add `os.Stat` preconditions in `setupTmpfs` and `setupHugepages` so missing directories fail fast with clear errors (extra `stat` is O(1) and negligible vs existing `MkdirAll` / mount work).

**Tests (tracked in PR)**

- Extend `TestSetupHugepages` for the new `os.Stat` guard.
- Add `TestSetupTmpfs` for the guard, nil mounter, mount detector errors, and the already-mounted memory case (idempotent path).
- Add `TestSetupDir` for permission verification and `os.Chmod` correction.

**User-facing impact**

None — cleanup / test coverage only.

**Related PR**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137227

title: SSA with force conflicts should update Service
body:
### What happened?

We have a controller in our clusters with a Service as an owned resource. A user (multi-tenant cluster) modified one of these services to simulate an application failure (chaos testing). The change triggered our controller, but the controller's attempt to correct the drift in the actual state was rejected by the API server. This error persisted until we manually corrected the Service.

Our controller is migrated to use SSA for all API operations and is configured to force conflicts (as controllers should do).

### What did you expect to happen?

The expected behavior is that the controller's SSA request (with force conflicts) should immediately revert the drift of the Service's actual state without any error.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Given the controller and user desired state of a Service:

````
$ cat controller-service.yaml 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  ports:
    - name: app
      protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
      targetPort: 8080

$ cat user-service.yaml 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  ports:
    - name: app
      protocol: UDP
      port: 8080
      targetPort: 8080

$ dyff between controller-service.yaml user-service.yaml --omit-header
spec.ports.app.protocol
  ± value change
    - TCP
    + UDP
````

First apply the Service as the controller:

````
$ k apply -f controller-service.yaml --field-manager controller --server-side --force-conflicts 
service/app serverside-applied
````

Then update the Service as the user:
````
$ k apply -f user-service.yaml 
Warning: resource services/app is missing the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation which is required by kubectl apply. kubectl apply should only be used on resources created declaratively by either kubectl create --save-config or kubectl apply. The missing annotation will be patched automatically.
service/app configured
````

Then try to apply the Service as the controller again:
````
$ k apply -f controller-service.yaml --field-manager controller --server-side --force-conflicts 
The Service "app" is invalid: spec.ports[1].name: Duplicate value: "app"
````

### Anything else we need to know?

[I asked about this on Slack](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EG7JC6T/p1739537899673079) before creating this issue.

title: Expose status.lastScheduleTime and status.lastSuccessfulTime to Downward API
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The CronJob status lastScheduleTime and lastSuccessfulTime timestamps would be a useful addition to the Downward API, i.e. being allowed as env > valueFrom > fieldRef > fieldPath and related options.

Example:

```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: {{ .name }}
spec:
  schedule: {{ .schedule }}
  timeZone: {{ $.Values.cronJobs.timeZone }}
  concurrencyPolicy: Replace
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      parallelism: 1
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: example
              image: ...
              env:
                - name: LAST_SCHEDULE_TIME
                  valueFrom:
                    fieldRef:
                      fieldPath: status.lastScheduleTime
status:
  lastScheduleTime: '2025-06-30T00:00:00Z'
  lastSuccessfulTime: '2025-06-30T00:01:14Z'
```

Note that there is a scenario where one or both is unset. In this case, the environment variable would need to be unset or empty.

### Why is this needed?

Cronjobs can use the timestamp for various purposes. For example, a job that scans a database every night can filter by some timestamp > LAST_SCHEDULE_TIME to get only rows that were changed since the last run.

Right now, this is possible by hardcoding (or having an environment variable for) the schedule interval into the app and calculating the schedule time. But this does not take potential startup delays for both the current and previous job.
Alternatively, the job can store its previous schedule or completion time in some form of database (e.g. key value store). But this requires a database to exist and the maintenance overhead that entails.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

The current context passed to the DryRunnableStorage lacks the request method, and the implementation has to fill in this gap of not having the request method in the context for further use. A common use case would be to call a common method from the Create/Delete/Get/GuaranteedUpdate methods to validate the request, and in some cases, the request method is useful to add additional validation.

How is this done in the code?

Create/Delete/Get/GuaranteedUpdate method adds the following to the context:
```
ctx = context.WithValue(ctx, "operation", "delete" or "get" or "create")
```

Getting the request method:
```
op, ok := ctx.Value("operation").(string)
```



### Why is this needed?

This helps to identify the type of request method in common validator methods called from Create/Delete/Get/GuaranteedUpdate methods.

title: GRPC healthprobe cannot handle TLS
body:
### What happened?

Since version 1.27 kubernetes supports the gprc healthserver for readyness and liveness probes. 
I now have several services that use grpc with self-signed tls certificates. The certificates are stored as secrets in the cluster. It took me quite a while to understand why my liveness probes always fail. So I rebuilt my service so that the endpoints are offered with TLS and the health server without. That works. 

### What did you expect to happen?

The grpc-health-probe also supports TLS connections. However, according to the documentation, parameters must be set for this.  Here is the link to Repo: [Health Checking TLS Servers](https://github.com/grpc-ecosystem/grpc-health-probe?tab=readme-ov-file#health-checking-tls-servers)

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A GRPC server with TLS and the corresponding code for the health probe should be sufficient. Here is a small example: 

```go
cer, err := tls.LoadX509KeyPair("tls/server/tls.crt", "tls/server/tls.key")
if err != nil {
  log.Println(err)
  return
}

creds := grpc.Creds(credentials.NewServerTLSFromCert(&cer))

addr := fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", "0.0.0.0", port)
listen, err := net.Listen("tcp", addr)
if err != nil {
  log.Panicln("Error while Listening to : ", addr, err)
}

grpcServer := grpc.NewServer(creds)
// Register health check service
healthServer := health.NewServer()
grpc_health_v1.RegisterHealthServer(grpcServer, healthServer)

// Set the health status to SERVING for your service
healthServer.SetServingStatus("APIServer", grpc_health_v1.HealthCheckResponse_SERVING)
fmt.Printf("[pid %d] GRPC server Listening on port %d\n", os.Getpid(), port)

// service connections
if err := grpcServer.Serve(listen); err != nil {
  log.Panicf("listen: %s\n", err)
}
```

### Anything else we need to know?

I think it would be easiest if you could tell the probe whether it is a TLS connection and, if in doubt, refer to a secret in the cluster where the CA certificate or similar is located.

title: Conditionally `Apply`ing with SSA
body:
This issue copies a slack thread to preserve it and continue discussion: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EG7JC6T/p1677203415388589. Note that our own use case is (mostly) handled, so I don't mind if this is a "won't fix"; I just wanted to at least make sure the discussion was preserved.

---

We want to essentially _conditionally_ SSA.

Use case: SimpleService resource "foo" as input, controller generates a Service "foo". But if the Service already existed and isn't owned by us, we don't want to mutate it (could cause outage on their end).
We want to "Apply only if we own it". The user could later modify it if they want, just not have existed before. We define ownership by a special label but could change (managedField, etc).

---

The best current way to do this is:
1. If object doesn't exist, just Apply as normal
2. If it does exist, set ResourceVersion to the existing object; if it has changed we will get a conflict (like Update).

Note for our use case this is actually largely fine, we just want to avoid taking over an existing thing since it may cause an outage; (1) only allows a tiny window where this could happen so its highly unlikely to cause an outage _practically_. But there may be cases where this is unacceptable as well

What doesn't work:
* tricks like setting UID=0, UID="", ResourceVersion=0, etc to ensure an object is "new".
* Owning metadata.name (can't)
* Force=false and always conflicting on some field (could work, but not a generalization for all use cases)

/sig api-machinery

title: Autoscaling a custom resource which does not create pods
body:
If someone has a custom resource which does not create pods but does have a scale subresource, it would be nice to be able to scale it based only on a custom metric. Currently this is not possible with HorizontalPodAutoscaler since it needs to list pods and does not just trust what the scale subresource tells it.

This would mean ignoring the implementation details of whatever the custom resource controller creates under the hood and just use the status of the scale subresource.

(obviously this means the "pod" in the hpa name wouldn't make much sense, but raising this so it could be considered if other changes happen around the area of counting pods)

/sig autoscaling
/cc @adrianmoisey

```go
2025-12-17T02:12:17.884482085Z 
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The getEventKey function should handle nil fields gracefully instead of panicking. It should either:
  1. Check for nil before accessing nested fields and use empty strings as defaults
  2. Return an error that can be handled by the caller
  3. Skip events with incomplete data

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

  This occurred in an OpenShift environment during operator installation/reconciliation. The logs before the panic show:
  - Multiple "resource name may not be empty" errors from the OperatorCondition controller
  - Conflict errors when updating Operator status
  - Rapid CSV reconciliation for servicemeshoperator3.v3.2.0 and kiali-operator.v2.17.2

  The panic happened in the event broadcaster goroutine, which runs independently from the main reconciliation loops.

### Anything else we need to know?

  The getEventKey function in events_cache.go constructs an event key by joining multiple fields:
```go
  The `getEventKey` function in `events_cache.go` constructs an event key by joining multiple fields:

  func getEventKey(event *v1.Event) string {
      return strings.Join([]string{
          event.Source.Component,      // panics if event is nil
          event.Source.Host,
          // ...
      }, "")
  }
```
  If `event` (which is a pointer `*v1.Event`) is nil, accessing `event.Source` causes
  a nil pointer dereference. The function lacks a nil check for the `event` parameter
  before accessing its fields.

title: Support resources overcommit for cpu memory
body:
Hi,

Currently Kubernetes retrieve CPU and MEMORY spec of nodes from cadvisor and use these phyiscal values as-is.
There is no way to do overcommit in Kubernetes from a cluster operator point of view.

Please reopen https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/44328

I think this issue is still relevant ! 

This would be very helpful to improve cpu utilisation on Kubernetes cluster used as compute plane for example for Spark.
It would also be very helpful for test platforms !
This is a standard feature in Openstack or VMware.

As explained in this Spark ticket, with Spark there is an assumption made that when you request N cores for parallel compute, that N cores would be 100% used.
In this way, Spark automatically cpu limits and cpu requests equal to N.
This is very inefficient, since most workload also do IO and are using effectively not more than 50% cpu usage.

https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-32744

From my experience as consultant on numerous projects, I see a lot of Kubernetes cluster used as Spark backend having really low CPU / memory real usage.

If we could set overcommit factors for memory and cpu on nodes spec that would be a very elegant and convenient way to improve resources usage.

title: [declarative-validation] Feature Request: `+k8s:monotonic` DV tag for enforcing non-decreasing integer fields
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add a `+k8s:monotonic` tag to `validation-gen` that enforces integer fields can only increase (never decrease) on update. This replaces the `apivalidation.IsDecremented` helper and equivalent handwritten comparison logic across 6 identified call sites.

### Motivation

Several Kubernetes API fields represent counters or generation numbers that must never go backwards. Today this is validated with handwritten Go code using `apivalidation.IsDecremented` or manual `<` comparisons against the old object.

This is a simple, mechanical pattern: compare `newValue` vs `oldValue`, reject if the value decreased. It is a natural fit for a declarative tag.

### Identified instances in the codebase

A scan of the codebase found 6 instances of monotonic increasing validation (value cannot decrease):

| File | Field | Handwritten code |
|------|-------|-----------------|
| `pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go` | `DaemonSetSpec.TemplateGeneration` | `if newSpec.TemplateGeneration < oldSpec.TemplateGeneration` |
| `pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go` | `DaemonSetStatus.CollisionCount` | `apivalidation.IsDecremented(ds.Status.CollisionCount, oldDS.Status.CollisionCount)` |
| `pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go` | `DeploymentStatus.CollisionCount` | `apivalidation.IsDecremented(update.Status.CollisionCount, old.Status.CollisionCount)` |
| `pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go` | `StatefulSetStatus.CollisionCount` | `apivalidation.IsDecremented(statefulSet.Status.CollisionCount, oldStatefulSet.Status.CollisionCount)` |
| `pkg/apis/batch/validation/validation.go` | `JobStatus.Failed` | `if job.Status.Failed < oldJob.Status.Failed` |
| `pkg/apis/batch/validation/validation.go` | `JobStatus.Succeeded` | `if job.Status.Succeeded < oldJob.Status.Succeeded` |

Note: There is also 1 instance of the reverse pattern (monotonic decreasing) on `PodSpec.ActiveDeadlineSeconds`, but that is out of scope for this proposal. A `+k8s:monotonic=decreasing` variant could be added in the future if needed.

### Proposed tag syntax

```go
// CollisionCount is a counter that is incremented on hash collisions.
// This value cannot be decremented.
// +optional
// +k8s:optional
// +k8s:monotonic
CollisionCount *int32 `json:"collisionCount,omitempty"`
```

The tag:
- Takes no arguments. `+k8s:monotonic` means "value cannot decrease on update" (monotonic non-decreasing).
- Applies only to integer-type fields (`int32`, `int64`, `*int32`, `*int64`, and unsigned variants)
- Only evaluated on update operations (create has no old value to compare)
- Handles nil pointers: if old is nil and new is non-nil (or vice versa), the semantics follow the same pattern as `+k8s:update=NoSet`/`NoUnset` for the nil transitions, and the monotonic check applies when both are non-nil
- A `+k8s:monotonic=decreasing` variant is out of scope for now but could be added later if the `ActiveDeadlineSeconds` case warrants it


### Implementation plan

#### 1. Add a runtime validation function

In `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/validate/`:

```go
// Monotonic validates that an integer value has not decreased on update.
func Monotonic[T constraints.Integer](ctx context.Context, op operation.Operation, fldPath *field.Path, obj, oldObj *T) field.ErrorList {
...
```

#### 2. Add a validator plugin

In `staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/monotonic.go`:

- Register for the `monotonic` tag name
- Validate that the field type is an integer type (reject with a lint error otherwise)
- Emit a call to `validate.Monotonic`
- Set `UpdateOnly: true` so the check is skipped on create

#### 3. Add output tests

In `cmd/validation-gen/output_tests/tags/monotonic/`

/sig api-machinery
/kind feature
/area declarative-validation


### Why is this needed?

Needed so that API authors can use declarative tags to express a value that can only increase monotonically on update.

title: [declarative validation] `+k8s:minimum` / `+k8s:maximum` do not correctly handle signedness and associated type bounds/boundary-values (ex: int32 vs int64)
body:
Declarative validation's `validation-gen`'s `ParseInt` returns Go `int` (64-bit) but does not validate that the parsed value fits in the target field's type. Values outside the target type's range are silently accepted at codegen time. For unsigned types, large values cannot be parsed at all. No boundary condition tests exist.

### Impact

**int32 vs int64:** All Kubernetes API integers are `int32` or `int64`. Writing `+k8s:minimum=-2147483649` on an `int32` field passes codegen without error but emits a literal that overflows `int32`.

**Unsigned types:** `strconv.Atoi` cannot parse values above `math.MaxInt64`, so `+k8s:maximum=18446744073709551615` on a `uint64` field fails. No kubernets native API types use unsigned integers today (from looking through `*/types.go` files), so this would be for library correctness currently.

**Untyped literal emission:** `toGolangSourceDataLiteral` uses `fmt.Sprintf("%v")` which emits untyped literals that may overflow or truncate near type boundaries.

### How to reproduce

1. Add `+k8s:minimum=-2147483649` to an `int32` field on a type with validation-gen enabled.
2. Run `hack/update-codegen.sh`.
3. Codegen succeeds, but the generated literal overflows `int32`.

Or:

1. Add `+k8s:maximum=18446744073709551615` to a `uint64` field.
2. Run `hack/update-codegen.sh`.
3. Codegen fails: `strconv.Atoi` cannot parse the value.

### What should happen

Codegen should reject values outside the target type's range with a clear error (e.g., "value -2147483649 does not fit in int32"). Values at the boundary (e.g., `-2147483648` for int32) should work correctly and emit properly typed Go literals.

### Fix outline

1. Split `ParseInt` into `ParseSignedInt` (returns `int64`) and `ParseUnsignedInt` (returns `uint64`).
2. In `minimumTagValidator`/`maximumTagValidator`, check the field's signedness, call the right parser, and validate the value fits the target type's range.
3. Emit typed literals (`int64(...)`, `uint64(...)`) in `toGolangSourceDataLiteral`.
4. Add boundary condition tests for int32 min/max, int64 min/max, uint32 max, uint64 max, and out-of-range rejection.

### Related PR // Background

Discovered via [PR #136589](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136589). @thockin noted from the PR there this issue as the PR there - specified +k8s:ifEnabled("WorkloadAwarePreemption")=+k8s:minimum=-2147483648 based on our guidance that all ints should spec min and max.

/sig api-machinery
/kind bug

title: [declarative validation] Support symbolic `MIN` / `MAX` values in `+k8s:minimum` / `+k8s:maximum`
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Allow `+k8s:minimum=MIN` and `+k8s:maximum=MAX` as symbolic values that resolve to the type-appropriate bound at code generation time. This avoids requiring authors to memorize raw integer literals like `-2147483648`.

### Motivation

Current guidance says all integer fields should specify min and max. For fields that use the full range of their type, this forces:

```go
// +k8s:minimum=-2147483648
// +k8s:maximum=2147483647
Priority *int32 `json:"priority,omitempty"`
```


### Proposed syntax

```go
// +k8s:minimum=MIN
// +k8s:maximum=MAX
Priority *int32 `json:"priority,omitempty"`
```

`MIN` and `MAX` resolve per the field's concrete type:

| Field type | `MIN` | `MAX` |
|-----------|-------|-------|
| `int32` | `-2147483648` | `2147483647` |
| `int64` | `-9223372036854775808` | `9223372036854775807` |
| `uint32` | `0` | `4294967295` |
| `uint64` | `0` | `18446744073709551615` |

Numeric literals remain supported. `MIN` and `MAX` are the only symbolic values.

## Depends on

The signedness/bounds parser fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/137965. The signed/unsigned parser split is the foundation that this symbolic resolution would build on.

## Alternative

Change guidance to not require min/max on type-bounded fields. See related discussion issue <link-TBD>

### Related PR // Background

Discovered via [PR #136589](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136589). @thockin noted from the PR there this issue as the PR there - specified +k8s:ifEnabled("WorkloadAwarePreemption")=+k8s:minimum=-2147483648 based on our guidance that all ints should spec min and max.

/sig api-machinery
/kind feature
/triage accepted

### Why is this needed?

This is needed, assuming we want all integer fields to have min and max boundaries, as an easy way to explain the boundary is the min/max value for the associated int type.  For example
```go
// +k8s:minimum=0
// +k8s:maximum=MAX
```

title: DRA: Explore sharing in-flight allocations when scheduling individual Pods
body:
ref. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137897#discussion_r2964817275

Currently, the DynamicResources scheduler plugin will reject a Pod as unschedulable if it references a ResourceClaim with an in-flight allocation: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/08d246509cdab7233196bc036d40c42b30e98ad2/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go#L479

This [breaks PodGroup scheduling](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/137617) and a fix for that is [in-progress](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137897).

A solution to that problem could potentially work both when scheduling PodGroups and individual Pods. The current approach taken by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137897 is only enabled for PodGroup scheduling, but we should investigate if there are ways to improve the non-PodGroup case based on that.

We might be able to simplify the logic by consolidating code paths and improve scheduler performance in some cases if we allow more Pods to share pending resource claims during scheduling.

More context in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137897#discussion_r2969442085:
> Note that the problem we're trying to solve is multi-layer:
> 
> 1. Scheduling Pods within a PodGroup in a single cycle
> 2. Re-scheduling the same PodGroups across many scheduling cycles (mainly Basic gang smaller minCount)
> 3. Scheduling different Pods (sharing the same Claim) across different cycles
> 4. Scheduling different PodGroups (sharing the same Claim) across different cycles

#137897 targets only the first scenario above. This issue is to address sharing in-flight allocations in cases 2-4 above.

/sig scheduling

title: kube-proxy's conntrack flushing of ready=false pods kills valid UDP flows
body:
### What happened?

## Setup
1) single cluster
2) Pod A talks to Pod B via Service B using the Service's ClusterIP. (Pod B is one of several in a Deployment).
3) A "connects" to B via UDP (sends an initial message).
4) kube-proxy on the Node of A sets up DNAT/conntrack/etc to make this work.
5) B responds on the UDP "connection", possibly multiple times, usually the first within milliseconds, and more following it over the next couple of seconds (the timing isn't important other than it's well below any timeout for the UDP pseuo-connection).
6) Some time during 5, pod B becomes ready=false via HTTP ready checks.

## Expected
- The responses of 5 should continue even after 6 happens, as long as pod B is actually healthy.

Actual behavior:
- kube-proxy on node A kills the UDP pseudo-connection by clearing the relevant conntrack entry.  This is done here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c35d03ce66ffc63099329adf9d8bb1dcaf398fe/pkg/proxy/conntrack/cleanup.go#L84 (and the surrounding code).
- Any subsequent messages from pod B are seen to successfully hit node A, but then aren't sent into the pod A's bridge network device (to get the packet into pod A's network namespace).  This is seen with a tcpdump on the Node of A.

## Possible fix
- Change the condition here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c35d03ce66ffc63099329adf9d8bb1dcaf398fe/pkg/proxy/conntrack/cleanup.go#L84 so that ready=false still is "true" for that conditional.  For example, only flush once the pod is actually terminated (no long phase=Running maybe?).

## Justification
Pod B needs to be able to go ready=false to load shed when the per pod load is too high.  When it does this, it needs to still process its existing connections.

While the UDP protocol described above maybe seems a bit silly and prone to issues, this is effectively how SIP over UDP works https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3261  and our customers depend upon it so we can't change it.  The client sends an initial `INVITE` request, then the server responds with an immediate `100 Processing`, follow up `180 Ringing`, and finally `200 OK`.  If this problem causes the `200 OK` to be lost then the user's call establishment is disrupted.

## Workaround

We put Envoy in place of Pod A and are pointing it at a headless Service that points at Pod B (and it's siblings in its Deployment).  Envoy is configured with very aggressive health checking of the HTTP ready endpoint.  This avoids the DNATing and conntrack dependency on Pod A associated with using a ClusterIP, and so obviously also avoids the problematic kube-proxy behavior that flushes the conntrack entries.

Another workaround is to try to get customers to use SIP over TCP, but not all of them can do this.

### What did you expect to happen?

Included above.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I think the steps to reproduce are described reasonably well above.  If you want me to spell out a testing approach more specifically I can.

title: Kubelet memory leak when a plugin is registered twice
body:
### What happened?

We found that the kubelet memory kept increasing，and we exported the pprof of the goroutine. The grpc goroutine leaks, causing memory leakage.
![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/54977497/76a1d622-2129-49e0-bd4c-79b6bad786b1)
We found out that the reason was because one of the pluginThe following code causes this situation. One client is lost.s kept registering twice and using the same name for both.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1dc30bf90fd6a729d226b4e942118110b0a73e65/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/plugin/v1beta1/handler.go#L90-L96
When two requests are registered at the same time, only one client is reserved in s.clients.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1dc30bf90fd6a729d226b4e942118110b0a73e65/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/plugin/v1beta1/handler.go#L106-L117
Therefore, after the c.Run () method in the runClient method is executed, s.getClient obtains only one registered client. As a result, the c.grpc.Close () method is not invoked, causing memory and coroutine leakage.


### What did you expect to happen?

Even in this case, kubelet should not leak memory.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1、The plug-in is registered every 5 seconds and two registration requests are sent at the same time.
2、The kubelet memory usage keeps increasing.
