https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128279#discussion_r1890549751 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128279/files?diff=unified&w=1#r1882520074 broke when bumping the master branch to 1.33 due to tests that depend on buildin APIs that meet specific graduation criteria of what is being tested, and stop working once the minor version of kubernetes increased to the point that the criteria falls out of our support/emulation windows.

We should instead modify these tests to depend on a test-only API that will stay valid forever, and don't depend on the k8s minor version.

This should be feasible to do.  Here's an existing test that has some test-only APIs that we could crib from:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9274a584b8a30262f05694f773a2523e4ec52920/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver_test.go#L184-L212

title: Kubelet should react more quickly to pod lifecycle transitions
body:
The Kubelet invokes pod setup, maintenance (collectively referred to as 'pod sync'), and teardown as synchronous functions from a per-pod goroutine.  The sync method in particular can run for seconds to minutes to hours if certain lifecycle actions like hooks are in use.  This means state transitions such as deletion (from API) and eviction (from Kubelet) can sometimes be significantly delayed.  Historically we had a number of asynchronous loops that raced against each other and provided sometimes incorrect behavior to pods - as we have tightened and improved the pod worker component to be more correct that has exacerbated the latency issues.

In general, we prefer to simplify the reasoning of adding new code to the pod's lifecycle and prefer to keep the bulk of pod setup, teardown, and cleanup synchronous.  Certain long running operations like pod start and volume attach/detach are asynchronous to the main pod loop, but others like pod lifecycle hooks are not.  In the long run, we should prefer to make those hooks asynchronous as well and use the pod sync methods to orchestrate hook invocation.  Even with perfect asynchronous logic we still must consider that our invocations of CRI functions may still hang or be delayed, and so at the pod worker level we must be able to interrupt the current invocation of SyncPod on transition.  For SyncTerminatingPod, we must be able to shorten (#113883) the wait before the pod is force killed - given the design of the CRI kill method we must interrupt the current call and make a new call with a shorter timeout in addition to any improvements on the CRI side.  Therefore the appropriate mechanism to reduce the wait is to interrupt the current sync method by cancelling a context passed to the worker.

A few PRs block resolving this issue:

* The pod worker is being improved to periodically resync missing pods - moderate refactor that must be completed #113145 
* If we were to propagate context into sync today, certain `wait` loops would return generic errors instead of context cancellation which would cause spurious errors - a refactor of the wait package that introduces new methods to handle this must be merged first #107826

After these two issues merge, we can propagate context into Sync methods and add tests that verify pods with long lifecycle hooks are terminated quickly and long grace period deletions can be reduced, as well as stress tests that verify that we do not generate excessive errors.  This issue tracks this final work.

In addition, we should continue to assess other sources of transition time, like evented PLEG and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/116617

#113591 took a slightly more scoped approach to plumbing context in Kubelet (in order to get tracing to work) than #107829 (which was trying to ensure sync*Pod would correctly cancel when pods transitioned to avoid very long latency of deletion requests).  As a consequence, the remaining issues that blocked #107829 in `syncPod` cancellation are unresolved, and those failures block #111591 from landing.  We can mitigate those by substituting a TODO context at the top of each sync method and then subsequently propagate those fixes (which also depends on #107826 for completeness).

#116032

This issue tracks adding that propagation.

/sig node

title: [Compatibility Version] Resource Lifecycle n+3
body:
We have prerelease-lifecycle tags that tags the releases when a resource is introduced, deprecated, and removed. With the introduction of compatibility versions, these versions become a bit more tricky. 

We currently use binary version to warn kubectl on with deprecation policies and this will need to be fixed to use emulation version: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/installer.go#L770

Because emulation can be 3 versions less than the binary version, one additional caveat is that we need to keep removed resources an extra 3 releases to be able to fully emulate the range of versions.

A resource available in 1.30, deprecated in 1.33 and removed in 1.36 (per resource lifecycle) must keep the resource in code until 1.39 because a 1.38 cluster can still emulate 1.35 when the resource is still available in the cluster.

One other point of consideration is testing. In the above example, if a resource is still able to be served with an emulation version toggle, it makes sense that tests should be kept. However,  the tests will fail if the resource is already removed for the latest emulation version. Upon an API being removed, would we lock the tests to the emulation version before the removal? These would then be removed 3 releases later when the resource is finally able to be removed?  We would need to communicate to feature owners not to delete tests and preserve them with a fixed compatibility version. Logically this solves our problems but the chore of bumping the compatibility version will have more nuanced things we need to do. (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/126977 was already quite involved with pushing removal back one release via `KUBE_APISERVER_SERVE_REMOVED_APIS_FOR_ONE_RELEASE`)

/cc @jpbetz @deads2k @aaron-prindle 
/sig api-machinery
/triage accepted

title: MemoryQoS does not set memory.high for BestEffort pods on cgroup v2
body:
### What happened?

With `MemoryQoS` enabled on a cgroup v2 node, BestEffort pods do not get a finite memory.high value. Instead, memory.high remains unset and reads as max.

This appears inconsistent with the [MemoryQoS KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/2570-memory-qos/README.md), which says that for BestEffort pods: _requests.memory = 0 limits.memory should be substituted with node allocatable memory in the memory.high formula:_
`memory.high = floor[ (memoryThrottlingFactor * node allocatable memory) / pageSize ] * pageSize`

In the current kubelet implementation, kubelet skips setting memory.high entirely when both memory requests, limits are 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

For a BestEffort pod on cgroup v2 with MemoryQoS enabled, memory.high is set to the value calculated as the formula defined in the KEP


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Prerequisites
- Linux node with cgroup v2 enabled
- kubelet with MemoryQoS=true

Pod manifests
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: memory-demo-besteffort
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
```

After the pod is running, inspect the pod/container cgroup files on the node.

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Pod CPU limit is not configured to cgroups as calculated if systemd cgroup driver is used
body:
### What happened?

As a result of #124216, which was introduced in v.1.32, a pod CPU limit calculated in `ResourceConfigForPod()` is rounded up to the nearest 10ms in `libcontainer` at resizing the pod:
- Resize a pod:
  ```
  $ kubectl patch pod resize-pod --subresource=resize --patch '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"resize-container", "resources":{"limits":{"cpu":"417m"}}}]}}'
  pod/resize-pod patched
  ```
- The container cgroup value is set with 1ms precision:
  ```
  $ kubectl exec resize-pod -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max
  41700 100000
  ```
- The pod cgroup value is rounded up:
  ```
  $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kubelet.slice/kubelet-kubepods.slice/kubelet-kubepods-burstable.slice/kubelet-kubepods-burstable-pod68a17b59_0d31_40b2_ba86_ea43f3b2f05c.slice/cpu.max
  42000 100000
  ```

When `systemd` cgroup driver is used, `libcontainer` passes the CPU Quota to `systemd` with rounding up:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a4b8a3b2e33a3b591884f69b64f439e6b880dc40/vendor/github.com/opencontainers/runc/libcontainer/cgroups/systemd/common.go#L304-L311

In addition, there seems to be a race in `libcontainer`. It directly writes values to the cgroup file without roundup after it passes the rounded value to `systemd`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a4b8a3b2e33a3b591884f69b64f439e6b880dc40/vendor/github.com/opencontainers/runc/libcontainer/cgroups/systemd/v2.go#L489-L493

So, there is also a case where the cgroup value is set as calculated. As far as I tried, decreasing CPU limits usually hits this case though I’m not sure why:
- Decrease the CPU limits:
  ```
  $ kubectl patch pod resize-pod --subresource=resize --patch '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"resize-container", "resources":{"limits":{"cpu":"365m"}}}]}}'
  pod/resize-pod patched
  ```

- Both the container and the pod cgroup values are set with 1ms precision:
  ```
  $ kubectl exec resize-pod -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max
  36500 100000
  $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kubelet.slice/kubelet-kubepods.slice/kubelet-kubepods-burstable.slice/kubelet-kubepods-burstable-pod68a17b59_0d31_40b2_ba86_ea43f3b2f05c.slice/cpu.max
  36500 100000
  ```


### What did you expect to happen?
This roundup looks like the intended behavior of `systemd` cgroup driver because CPU quota is also rounded up when a pod is just created with 1ms precision CPU limits. However, I have the following concerns:
- We might need to confirm this tiny gap doesn’t cause a similar issue to #128769 at resizing pods.
- We might need to clarify why the CPU quota of pod cgroup is sometimes not rounded up. This is especially necessary to complete #127192, which is going to add pod cgroup verification to resize tests.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

0. Use `systemd` cgroup driver and enable `InPlacePodVertialScaling`.
1. Resize CPU limits of a pod with 1ms precision.


### Anything else we need to know?

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Add additional E2E Burstable Pod QoS test cases for pods without resource limits
body:
### What would you like to be added?

It would be really great if  `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` could in-place resize cpu on containers that have requests only (no limits). 

Currently, `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` cannot successfully resize `cpu` against containers without limits.  e.g. given this pod: 
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sleeper
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - args:
    - -c
    - sleep infinity
    command:
    - /bin/sh
    image: registry.k8s.io/ubuntu-slim:0.1
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    name: sleeper
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 25m
        memory: 100Mi
```
If you change `cpu: 25m` to `cpu: 50m`, it will get stuck in `resize: InProgress` _forever_: 
```
  containerStatuses:
  - allocatedResources:
      cpu: 50m
      memory: 100Mi
    ...
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 25m
        memory: 100Mi
    restartCount: 0
    started: true
    state:
      running:
        startedAt: "2024-05-04T00:11:16Z"
  ...
  qosClass: Burstable
  resize: InProgress
```
### Why doesn't in-place work now without limits: 
- This looks like a result of this kubelet code [here](https://github.com/openshift/kubernetes/blob/258f1d5fb6491ba65fd8201c827e179432430627/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L556) not calculating the update if there are no limits (as in, if you do something naive like [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...jkyros:kubernetes:minimal-patch-fix-inplacepodverticalscaling-limits) it works, but probably has other consequences and I don't have enough background here to propose that as a proper fix )
- Memory looks like it "works" without limits, but it's [special](https://github.com/openshift/kubernetes/blob/258f1d5fb6491ba65fd8201c827e179432430627/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L592) and...doesn't really

### What additional tests do we need: 

- The [current test suite](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9791f0d1f39f3f1e0796add7833c1059325d5098/test/e2e/node/pod_resize.go#L664) includes some Burstable cases, but does not cover all corners, specifically: 
	- in-place increasing/reducing CPU requests on containers without limits 
	- in-place removing limits from a container that previously had them 
- Minimally could look something like this: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/72953418202f7d412072b2259e996efc8e14abbd

### Additional background: 
- This was discussed in the `sig-node` meeting on Apr 9, 2024, where I was encouraged to inquire via Slack

```CEL
// assume model is "model-a"
attribute["dra.example.com"].includes("model-a") --> true

// assume models is ["model-a", "model-b"]

test-namespaece        nodeagent-v9czm                                  0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   81 (61s ago)     6h46m  // OOM

### What did you expect to happen?

After the MemoryQoS capability is enabled,  containers whose memory request value is equal to the limit value can run properly and are not affected by OOM.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a container who memory request value is equal to the limit value
2. These containers need to frequently load some files, such as image repositories or database containers.

### Anything else we need to know?

1.My hypothesis is: when the request and limit values of a container's memory are equal, then memory.min == memory.max, which results in the cgroup not reclaiming the memory when the actual used memory is less than memory.min. However, when the actual used memory is greater than memory.min, which also means it is greater than memory.max, it directly triggers an OOM. Does this mean that after enabling MemoryQoS, Guaranteed pods or Burstable pods with memory request == limit will inherently be more likely to trigger an OOM? How does the Kubernetes community consider this issue, and what are the solutions?
2.When the request value of a container is set to a value less than the limit value, OOM will not occur. For example, if the request value is 239 Mi and the limit value is 240 Mi, OOM will not occur.

title: Feature Request: Native Deployment strategy to trigger rollout on referenced ConfigMap/Secret updates (Reviving #22368)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to propose a native mechanism within the `Deployment` (and `StatefulSet`/`DaemonSet`) spec to trigger a rollout when a referenced `ConfigMap` or `Secret` is modified.

This is a request to revive the discussion from **Issue #22368** with a focus on modern Platform Engineering requirements.

**Proposed Spec:**

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config
            # Proposed new field to handle the rollout logic natively
            policy:
              onUpdate: RollingUpdate # Options: Ignore, RollingUpdate, Recreate

```

**Justification for Core Inclusion:**

* **Safety:** The `kube-controller-manager` is the only component that can guarantee a safe rollout (respecting `maxUnavailable`/`maxSurge`) while ensuring the new config is actually available on the node before the pod starts.
* **Standardization:** This is a fundamental operational requirement for 90% of stateful and stateless applications. It should not require a third-party controller.

**Related Issues:**

* Relates to #22368 (Facilitate ConfigMap rollouts)

**Note for KEP**

I understand this is a significant change to the API and controller logic that would require a Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal (KEP). I am opening this issue to gauge community consensus on whether this logic belongs in upstream Kubernetes before attempting to draft a KEP.

### Why is this needed?

This is one of the most common operational pain points for Kubernetes users. While separating Configuration from Code is a best practice (12-Factor App), Kubernetes currently lacks a native way to reconcile the lifecycle of the two.

**Current Workarounds and their downsides:**

1. **Templating Hacks (Helm/Kustomize):** Users manually inject a checksum annotation (e.g., `checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}`) into the Pod template. This forces a rollout but requires complex templating logic and couples the CI/CD tool to the runtime behavior.
2. **External Controllers:** Users install third-party operators (like `Reloader` or `Wave`) solely to watch resources and delete Pods. This adds maintenance overhead, security surface area, and extra resource consumption to the cluster.
3. **Manual Toil:** Operators manually run `kubectl rollout restart` after applying config changes.

**Benefits of Native Support:**

* **Standardization:** Removes the need for every organization to "reinvent the wheel" for config reloads.
* **Safety:** The Kube Controller Manager is best positioned to handle this rollout safely, respecting `maxUnavailable` and `maxSurge` constraints better than external "pod killer" scripts.
* **GitOps Friendly:** Simplifies the reconciliation loop for tools like ArgoCD and Flux, ensuring that the running state always matches the configuration state defined in Git without extra glue code.

title: Memleak in client-go transport.tlsCache
body:
### What happened?

We're using a long-running process that connects to thousands of kubernetes cluster via client-go (not all simultaneously).
We noticed that the more kubernetes clusters we connect to and the longer the process runs, the more memory our process consumes over time.
An analysis with pprof confirmed that it looks like a memory leak in transport.tlsCache.

### What did you expect to happen?

Memory to be freed of clients that aren't used anymore, especially when the client object is not referenced anymore.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Connect to different k8s clusters with cert-base auth in a long-running process and watch memory usage grow.

### Anything else we need to know?

Reason for the leak:
We're using `kubernetes.NewForConfig` which eventually calls `transport.New(config)`
That transport calls `tlsCache.get`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3b5044fefd5a9a192b379236fac11ac8c41a7017/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/transport.go#L50

`tlsCache` is a non-exported global that implements a http transport cache. The `get` also stores the given transport in the cache if it's not there, yet.
However there are no mechanisms that would remove something from the cache. Neither explicitly, nor through expiration or anything.
The cache key includes k8s cert data which means every cluster we connect to will create a new cache entry that will then stay there indefinitely.

title: K8s volume mount race condition -  Failed to create subPath directory for volumeMount {volume} of container {container}
body:
**What happened**:
I have observed a race condition / issue with multiple pods creating the same subpath volume mount on the same node.

My understanding is that if you use a volume with a subpath that doesn't exist, Kubernetes will create it.

I believe what happens if that both pods observe that the subpath needs to be created as seen here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.15.11/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L200

Then, both pods try and create the subpath:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.15.11/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L212

However the "slower" pod gets the error that 
```
E0815 16:33:36.119849 19214 kubelet_pods.go:212] failed to create subPath directory for volumeMount "shared" of container "baf13717756c7b8a88829e6fb42022bc": cannot create directory /var/lib/kubelet/pods/1dab3c2f-0df9-4a1e-aedd-5a2a3e182774/volumes/kubernetes.io~glusterfs/XXXXXXXX-shared/XXX_XXXXX_XXXXXXXX_1_0_5_2020-08-15T16-33-30.421922_00-00: file exists
```

And finally:
```
E0815 16:33:36.119889 19214 kuberuntime_manager.go:779] container start failed: CreateContainerConfigError: failed to create subPath directory for volumeMount "shared" of container "baf13717756c7b8a88829e6fb42022bc"
```

**What you expected to happen**:
Instead of failing because the subpath already exists, it would be better if the code instead stopped trying to create it and simply use the subpath.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
* Schedule two new pods to the same node which use subpaths for a directory that does not yet exist.
* The pods will both try and create the subpath, one will work, the other will report the error:
`E0815 16:33:36.119889 19214 kuberuntime_manager.go:779] container start failed: CreateContainerConfigError: failed to create subPath directory for volumeMount "shared" of container "baf13717756c7b8a88829e6fb42022bc"`
The timing of these events needs to be very close as I believe this issue may only occur if both pods observe they need to create the subpath. 

**Anything else we need to know?**:
Airflow is being used to schedule these pods. The shared directory we are mounting is supposed to be shared across tasks in a DAG.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
v1.15.11-eks-065dce

EKS - r5.4xlarge

title: Add formats that are supported by CEL to CRDs
body:
Currently, Kubernetes [CRD formats](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4468565250c940bbf70c2bad07f2aad387454be1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/validation/formats.go#L26) lack consistent mapping to corresponding CEL types for commonly used data types like [CIDR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4468565250c940bbf70c2bad07f2aad387454be1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/cidr.go#L31), [Quantity](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4468565250c940bbf70c2bad07f2aad387454be1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/quantity.go#L37), and [Semver](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4468565250c940bbf70c2bad07f2aad387454be1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/semver.go#L34), despite CEL having native support for them.

This is inconsistent with types like "date" and "duration" that have a format that is [mapped to a CEL type](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4468565250c940bbf70c2bad07f2aad387454be1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/common/values.go#L137-L161).

For unmapped types, CRD authors must perform manual validation and casting within CEL expressions.

For mapped types, the fields are automatically validated against the format, and are typed according to the format in CEL expressions (without the need for a cast).

One way to think about this: Missing formats for CRD forces in "imperative" validation of fields, using CEL.  Adding formats makes "declarative validation" of field possible.

## Proposal

- Add new CRD formats: "cidr" "quantity" and "semver"
- Map these new formats to their corresponding CEL types.
- Somehow deal with cases where a format and CEL type both exist but are not mapped ("ipv4," "ipv6," and "uri.")
  - Consider introducing new, distinct formats (e.g. "ip4", "ip6", "url") to represent the desired CEL IP and URL types without breaking existing CRDs.

title: [InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Safer memory limit decrease
body:
Today, when memory limits are decreased, the kubelet performs a best-effort OOM-kill prevention by first checking whether the new limits are below the current usage, and blocking the resize if so. This is subject to a TOCTOU race condition.

We can reduce the TOCTOU race window by moving the check into the runtime.

See https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5368 for further discussion.

title: GracePeriod elegant delete  can only be set once
body:
### What happened? I checked the kubelet source code and found that after receiving a request to delete a pod, it will determine whether the pod is in the process of being updated, and if it is, it will store this update in the map of lastUndeliveredWorkUpdate. When this update is finished, it will be taken out from this map and put into the podUpdates pipeline for processing. However, if the gracePeriod is set for the first update, the podUpdates pipeline will block there. Because when the CRI is called, the container will not return the message immediately until the gracePeriod is up. In this case, I can only send the first gracePeriod valid, subsequent ones are invalid. There are business scenarios that require this feature. ### What did you expect to happen? If you delete a pod with the gracePeriod parameter, you should overwrite the last one with the latest gracePeriod time each time. I see in the source code comments that it is possible to overwrite the old time with the latest gracePeriod. But the actual business logic fails to implement this feature. pod_workers.go pod_workers.go ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1.kubectl delete pod name --grace-period=30 2.kubectl delete pod name --grace-period=10 The second operation is invalid ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version

title: serviceCIDRStrategy does not perform status wiping
Add a way to reschedule jobs upon failure rather than restart in place (via BackoffLimit)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

A possible idea is to provide something like BackOffLimit but on each iteration of the job we trigger a full rescheduling loop. 



### Why is this needed?

The more I'm reading https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9940 and https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/tree/main/keps/262-ConfigurableFailurePolicy#story-6-restartjob-and-restartjobandignoremaxrestarts.

I'm wondering if we need some kind of recreation on Failure for Job controller. It seems there is a need to relocate jobs upon failures but it seems we are missing upstream support for this in Job controller.

For JobSet we are adding quite a lot of code to force restarts of Jobs and tracking the individual jobs in the JobSet API. The goal is to enable recreation of the Jobs but JobSet is orchestrating this.

title: Pod with emptyDir fails to start after node reboot when LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring is enabled
body:
### What happened?

Hi, 
I am using an ext4 filesystem formatted and mounted with the prjquota.
When I create a Pod with emptyDir as shown below, the Pod fails to start after the node is rebooted.
```bash
$ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-pod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
  hostUsers: false
  containers:
  - name: test-container
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo Hello World && sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: test-storage
      mountPath: /mnt/temp
  volumes:
  - name: test-storage
    emptyDir: {}
EOF
$ kubectl exec test-pod -- mkdir /mnt/temp/dir
$ kubectl exec test-pod -- touch /mnt/temp/file
```
To further narrow down the issue, I made a small code change to capture the stderr output of the xfs_quota command when the error occurs, as shown below.
```diff
diff --git a/pkg/volume/util/fsquota/common/quota_common_linux_impl.go b/pkg/volume/util/fsquota/common/quota_common_linux_impl.go
index a9959662393..fa5bfc1ccd5 100644
--- a/pkg/volume/util/fsquota/common/quota_common_linux_impl.go
+++ b/pkg/volume/util/fsquota/common/quota_common_linux_impl.go
@@ -131,11 +131,11 @@ func doRunXFSQuotaCommand(mountpoint string, mountsFile, command string) (string
        klog.V(4).Infof("runXFSQuotaCommand %s -t %s -P/dev/null -D/dev/null -x -f %s -c %s", quotaCmd, mountsFile, mountpoint, command)
        cmd := exec.Command(quotaCmd, "-t", mountsFile, "-P/dev/null", "-D/dev/null", "-x", "-f", mountpoint, "-c", command)

-       data, err := cmd.Output()
+       data, err := cmd.CombinedOutput()
+       klog.V(4).Infof("runXFSQuotaCommand output:\n%s", string(data))
        if err != nil {
                return "", err
        }
-       klog.V(4).Infof("runXFSQuotaCommand output %q", string(data))
        return string(data), nil
 }
```
The relevant kubelet logs are as follows:
```text
Mar 17 21:58:08 ubuntu24-test kubelet[2984]: I0317 21:58:08.149043    2984 quota_common_linux_impl.go:131] runXFSQuotaCommand /sbin/xfs_quota -t /tmp/mounts1038897217 -P/dev/null -D/dev/null -x -f /var/lib/kubelet -c project -s -p /var/lib/kubelet/pods/91fd6e02-f0b4-45c6-a328-0fba789f2da6/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/test-storage 1048579
Mar 17 21:58:08 ubuntu24-test kubelet[2984]: I0317 21:58:08.150025    2984 quota_common_linux_impl.go:135] runXFSQuotaCommand output:
Mar 17 21:58:08 ubuntu24-test kubelet[2984]: xfs_quota: cannot set project on /var/lib/kubelet/pods/91fd6e02-f0b4-45c6-a328-0fba789f2da6/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/test-storage/file: Operation not supported

Mar 17 21:58:08 ubuntu24-test kubelet[2984]: Processed 1 (/dev/null and cmdline) paths for project 1048579 with recursion depth infinite (-1).

I observed that the "not supported" error occurs only when operating on the file `test-storage/file`, but not on the directory `test-storage/dir`. This may be related to the fact that the +P (project inheritance) flag can be applied to directory inodes, but not to file inodes.

In contrast, the issue does not occur on XFS, where the same Pod can be successfully created after a node reboot.


### What did you expect to happen?

Pods using emptyDir should start successfully after a node reboot when LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring is enabled.

title: No overflow validation when using MilliValue()
body:
### What happened?

There is a function called [`MilliValue()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b5e64567958aae5c2e5befae000d3186384c151b/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go#L817C1-L822C1) to represent values in milli units and its comment says "this could **overflow** an int64;  if that's a concern, call `Value()` first to verify the number is small enough." 
```go
// staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go
// MilliValue returns the value of ceil(q * 1000); this could overflow an int64;
// if that's a concern, call Value() first to verify the number is small enough.
func (q *Quantity) MilliValue() int64 {
	return q.ScaledValue(Milli)
}
```
But actually almost [all call to this function](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Akubernetes%2Fkubernetes%20MilliValue&type=code) don't verify the number is small enough first.

Here are a few unexpected behaviors caused by this overflow.

### 1. Pod with extremely large cpu request is treated as with 0 cpu request
**Trigger**: create a pod using the following yaml file, with the cpu resource request is set as a very large quantity.
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - name: test-container
    image: nginx
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 16Pi
      requests:
        cpu: 16Pi
# 16Pi = 2^4*2^50 = 2^54, 16Pi * 1000 > 2*63 > 2^63 - 1 = maxInt64, so represent this value in milli unit will cause a overflow
```

**Consequence:** The scheduler will treat this pod with 0 cpu request, so it can be scheduled to any nodes ignoring the node's cpu resource usage. 

**Cause**:  [type.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a28f14089cfa47ef9c57f9f283e1504a68f616d6/pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go#L854C1-L873C2)
The `noderesource` scheduler plugin uses `SetMaxResource()` to pre-calculate the pod resource request.
```go
// SetMaxResource compares with ResourceList and takes max value for each Resource.
func (r *Resource) SetMaxResource(rl v1.ResourceList) {
	if r == nil {
		return
	}

	for rName, rQuantity := range rl {
		switch rName {
		case v1.ResourceMemory:
			r.Memory = max(r.Memory, rQuantity.Value())
		case v1.ResourceCPU:
->			r.MilliCPU = max(r.MilliCPU, rQuantity.MilliValue())
		case v1.ResourceEphemeralStorage:
			r.EphemeralStorage = max(r.EphemeralStorage, rQuantity.Value())
		default:
			if schedutil.IsScalarResourceName(rName) {
				r.SetScalar(rName, max(r.ScalarResources[rName], rQuantity.Value()))
			}
		}
	}
}
```
1. In `SetMaxResource()`, calling `.MilliValue()` directly on a large `Quantity` without first validating it's small enough will lead to an overflow, causing `rQuantity.MilliValue()` to return a negative number.

2. `SetMaxResource()` iteratively compares the provided value with the existing one and retains the larger value (likely designed to handle cases that a resource is specified multiple times, retain the largest one). 
In this case, the CPU request is specified only once, and the default request value is `0`. 
Therefore, `max(0, negative_number)` returns `0`, resulting in the `noderesource` plugin considers this pod's cpu request is 0.

### 2. Pod with extremely large memory / ephemeral-storage request will trigger an unexpected warning
**Trigger**: create a pod using the following yaml file, with the ephemeral-storage resource request is a very large quantity.
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:latest
    resources:
      requests:
        ephemeral-storage: 9Pi
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: 9Pi

```
**Consequence:** When creating this pod, 
It's obvious here `9Pi` is an integer, but Kubernetes will output a confusing warning message: `fractional byte value "9Pi" is invalid, must be an integer.`
**Cause**:  [warning.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/175a5b9c4690c63b7d41c3c295402269780b3a27/pkg/api/pod/warnings.go#L237C3-L248C4)
```go
if value, ok := c.Resources.Limits[api.ResourceMemory]; ok && value.MilliValue()%int64(1000) != int64(0) {
    warnings = append(warnings, fmt.Sprintf("%s: fractional byte value %q is invalid, must be an integer", p.Child("resources", "limits").Key(string(api.ResourceMemory)), value.String()))
}
```
Because the quantity is very quite, calling `value.MilliValue()` will overflow and return a value that cannot be modded by 1000, triggers the warning.

### 3. Node with extremely large allocatable cpu becomes unschedulable.
**Trigger**: create a node using the following yaml file (in [KWOK](https://kwok.sigs.k8s.io/)), with the allocatable cpu resource is a very large quantity.
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Node
metadata:
  name: node-1
  namespace: default
status:
  allocatable:
    cpu: 1000Pi
  capacity:
    cpu: 1000Pi
```
**Consequence:** The node will be created but the scheduler thinks its allocatable cpu resource is negative, making this node unschedulable to any pod.

**Cause:** [types.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2caf4eddd8fc1ab7236ed608c1b548404dbc6bcf/pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go#L799C1-L820C2)
```go
// NewResource creates a Resource from ResourceList
func NewResource(rl v1.ResourceList) *Resource {
	r := &Resource{}
	r.Add(rl)
	return r
}

// Add adds ResourceList into Resource.
func (r *Resource) Add(rl v1.ResourceList) {
	if r == nil {
		return
	}

	for rName, rQuant := range rl {
		switch rName {
		case v1.ResourceCPU:
->			r.MilliCPU += rQuant.MilliValue()
		case v1.ResourceMemory:
			r.Memory += rQuant.Value()
		case v1.ResourcePods:
			r.AllowedPodNumber += int(rQuant.Value())
		case v1.ResourceEphemeralStorage:
			r.EphemeralStorage += rQuant.Value()
		default:
			if schedutil.IsScalarResourceName(rName) {
				r.AddScalar(rName, rQuant.Value())
			}
		}
	}
}
```
The call to `MilliValue` at the pointed line will cause an overflow, making the node's CPU resource negative. And `nodereourse` scheduler plugin will conclude this node is ineligible for any pod.


### What did you expect to happen?

Although it's unlikely that we will encounter these extremely large values in real world, there is no constraint on the range of this value. Therefore we expect no overflow happens regardless of the user's input.

1. Since most calls to `MilliValue()` do not verify that the number is small enough first, we think the simplest fix might be let `MilliValue()` or `ScaledValue()` handle overflow automatically. For example, capping the return value at maxInt64 when overflow occurs.

2. Another possible fix can be to add a range constraint of [MaxMilliValue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/847be850000a902bcd82fb4a02bada5d948595a0/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/resource/math.go#L49) for values will be interpreted as milli unit.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use the yaml file above.


### Anything else we need to know?

/sig scheduling api-machinery

title: Pod admission can fail due to webhooks + context deadline exceeded, even when all webhooks are set to failurePolicy = Ignore
body:
### What happened?

Pod admission failed with the error "Timeout: request did not complete within requested timeout - context deadline exceeded"

This occurred with Datadog's admission controller, when a default deny policy was applied and the network policy allowing ingress to Datadog's admission controller was missing. This is despite each of the webhook configurations specifying `failurePolicy: Ignore`. I can understand why they did that: failing pod admission basically kills the cluster.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod should be successfully admitted since all webhooks were set to `failurePolicy: Ignore`

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create 4 mutating or validating webhooks, each with a timeout of 10 seconds, and failurePolicy of Ignore. The webhooks should return an error.
2. Try admitting a Pod. It should work - failurePolicy is set to Ignore.
3. Add a default deny network policy to the webhook's namespace. This will cause connections from the kube-apiserver to the webhook admission controller to fail with a timeout. Overall, 10 seconds will be spent on each one, totaling 40 seconds.
4. Pod admission fails with "Timeout: request did not complete within requested timeout - context deadline exceeded"

### Anything else we need to know?

It seems that pod admission has a global 30 second timeout. By specifying 4 webhooks, each with a timeout of 10 seconds, it is possible to exceed that timeout and cause pod admission to fail, **even when all webhooks have failurePolicy set to Ignore**. This also results in a message that just says "context deadline exceeded", and doesn't name the offending webhooks, since they didn't actually cause the failure. This makes it super hard to debug, as you have to dig into the kube-apiserver looks to find the offending webhook. It also seems unintentional: my expectation was that having no webhooks set to `failurePolicy: Fail`, pod admission should not be able to fail due to webhooks.

title: Improve API serialization testdata fixtures for parameter-only encoded types
body:
Some types like GetOptions, ListOptions, PatchOptions are only encoded to parameter query strings

Because these types are registered into runtime.Scheme, they are currently tested as serialized to json, yaml, and proto (but *not* query parameters) in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/staging/src/k8s.io/api/testdata

That produced spurious proto diffs in PRs like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136657 for ListOptions

1. Identify the types we don't serialize to proto (GetOptions, ListOptions, PatchOptions, I think) and do serialize to query parameters
2. Exclude those from proto round-tripping and serialization
3. Add tests to cover the stability of their query parameter serializations

/sig architecture

/kind cleanup
/cc @deads2k

title: TopologySpreadConstraint should fail if labelSelector not provided
body:
So I've just recently realized, and folks can confirm - that if you create a TopologySpreadConstraint but do not list a `labelSelector`, it will be accepted - but will effectively do nothing since it matches nothing.

At least my observation was it was not respected until I added the `labelSelector`.

e.g. something like:
```
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/hostname
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
```

actually needs to be:
```
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/hostname
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: my-app
```

Unless I'm missing something, it seems clear to me that no one would want to specify a constraint without also having a `labelSelector` - and seems easy to miss.

I already missed it for my own application, and another application I use (cockroachDB), [also seems to have missed it](https://github.com/cockroachdb/helm-charts/blob/65fa4c6822b18d3cd8922cca60393199b7d95edb/cockroachdb-parent/charts/cockroachdb/values.yaml#L439) ([fix](https://github.com/cockroachdb/helm-charts/pull/584)).

While we are here - a related matter I find interesting, is that you can not specify `matchLabelKeys` without `labelSelector` (as per the [docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.34/#topologyspreadconstraint-v1-core)). Assuming I understand how it works, it seems like a pretty standard default to just want to match against key "app", whatever it is for my pod - and that's it.

Perhaps more generally, errors could be reported if labelSelector / matchLabelKeys ends up finding nothing (including itself!).

title: Cloud Controller Managers do not release leader election when shutting down
body:
### What happened?

When using the cloud controller manager libraries `k8s.io/cloud-provider` to build out a cloud controller manager, the libraries configure leader election.

They expose flags to configure this leader election, and, when these values are longer, can cause downtime when the pod restarts.

Other controller managers have the ability to release the leader election lease when they know they are shutting down, this minimises the time taken for a new leader to take over.

With the CCM, we have been configuring lease durations of 137s (some maths went into this but it doesn't matter right now), and so, in the worst case, we are seeing over 2 minutes of downtime when the pods are updated and switched over.

This is important to fix because, when the CCM isn't running, new nodes cannot be initialized and load balancer membership cannot be updated.

### What did you expect to happen?

The controller manager, on shutdown, should release the leader lease using the `ReleaseOnCancel` option in the configuration of the l[eader election config](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6e0cb243d57592c917fe449dde20b0e246bc66be/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/app/controllermanager.go#L570-L578).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run any cloud controller manager that uses the cloud-provider library, GCP or AWS are good candidates, and set the leader config to `--leader-elect-lease-duration=137s --leader-elect-renew-deadline=107s --leader-elect-retry-period=26`. Then change the deployment to create a rollout. During the rollout, you will notice it takes a long time for the leader election lease to be granted to the new pods.

### Anything else we need to know?

This was discussed on the sig-cloud-provider call on the 5th of July, 2023, and it was decided that this is something we should aim to fix, since the kube-controller-manager is also working towards this goal.
/sig cloud-provider

title: Run TestUpdateNominatedNodeName integration test with SchedulerPopFromBackoffQ feature enabled
body:
The TestUpdateNominatedNodeName scheduler integration test now runs with the  `SchedulerPopFromBackoffQ` feature gate disabled (see reason in the [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130772#discussion_r2005193048)). The feature is enabled in the Kubernetes by default, so it would be good to be able to verify this test with the feature enabled. It's non-trivial to do so, because the test relies on a pod staying in the backoffQ what is not easily possible now, because the pod would be popped from there quickly. 

/sig scheduling
/kind cleanup

title: "localhost NodePorts" (or equivalent), to better support local registries
body:
[**EDIT**: Originally this issue was a single idea ("fallback partial userspace proxy") for solving multiple unrelated kube-proxy problems (localhost nodeports, winkernel and ipvs limitations, etc), but it almost immediately got derailed into being a discussion of multiple ideas for solving _just_ the localhost nodeport problem. So I'm changing the title to reflect what the issue has become, but leaving the original comment below unchanged, so it no longer quite matches the title.)

----

There are people who really want localhost NodePorts, but there's no way to make them work in the ipvs proxy, and no way to make them work in iptables or nftables with IPv6, and we chose to not make them work in nftables with IPv4 because of the required terrible hacks (`route_localnet`). One way to make this work anyway would be to have kube-proxy fall back to doing userspace proxying _just_ for localhost NodePorts...

We've also just discovered that the winkernel proxy inherently can't support Services with named ports where the endpoints don't all have the same target port (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132647#discussion_r2198231875). That could potentially also be worked around by doing userspace proxying in that case?

I feel like this idea came up once before in some context (though maybe that was also just for localhost NodePorts). There are probably other edge cases that ipvs currently doesn't get quite right (eg #132689) that could be "fixed" in this way, but we're unlikely to actually fix them in ipvs at this point.

Note that this wouldn't mean resurrecting the entire userspace proxier; the necessary pieces are pretty small.

I can't decide if this is a terrible idea or not.

@aojea @BenTheElder

title: The pods of the StatefulSet were rebuilt during the upgrade from 1.31 to 1.34.
body:
### What happened?

We found that when Kubernetes was upgraded from 1.31 to 1.34, the pods of the StatefulSet were rebuilt. After comparing the YAML files before and after the upgrade, we found that the volumeClaimTemplates.metadata.creationTimestamp field was no longer available in version 1.34, which caused a rolling update of the StatefulSet.
1.31:
```
volumeClaimTemplates:
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
    metadata:
      annotations:
        deletePolicy: retain
        name: mydata
      creationTimestamp: null
      name: mydata
    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 100Gi
      storageClassName: localcsi
      volumeMode: Filesystem
```

1.34:
```
volumeClaimTemplates:
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
    metadata:
      annotations:
        deletePolicy: retain
        name: mydata
      name: mydata
    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 100Gi
      storageClassName: localcsi
      volumeMode: Filesystem
```
The **spec.volumeClaimTemplates.metadata.creationTimestamp** field is deleted.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod of the StatefulSet is not rebuilt.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1.31 -> 1.34 upgrade

title: [Scheduling] Enhance QueueSort plugin to co-locate pods from the same PodGroup
body:
## Problem Statement / Motivation

The current `QueueSort` plugin in the Kubernetes scheduler (e.g., `PrioritySort`) sorts pods solely based on pod priority and timestamp. However, this approach has several limitations in modern scheduling scenarios:

1. **Increased scheduling latency**: Pods belonging to the same PodGroup may be scattered across different positions in the scheduling queue, requiring multiple scheduling cycles to schedule all members of a PodGroup.

2. **Resource fragmentation**: Pods from the same PodGroup may be scheduled onto different nodes, reducing the efficiency of Gang Scheduling and leading to suboptimal resource utilization.

3. **Degraded user experience**: Users expect pods within the same PodGroup to be scheduled together as much as possible, especially for workloads that require gang semantics.

4. **Inability to leverage Workload Aware Scheduling optimizations**: Without PodGroup co-location in the queue, the scheduler cannot effectively apply Workload Aware Scheduling optimizations. The scheduler misses opportunities to make holistic scheduling decisions for related pods, such as:
   - Co-scheduling pods that need to communicate with each other
   - Optimizing resource packing for related workloads
   - Reducing cross-node traffic for distributed applications
   - Applying topology-aware placement strategies at the workload level

## Proposed Enhancement

We propose adding the capability to co-locate pods from the same PodGroup within the `QueueSort` plugin. The sorting strategy would be:

Sorting priority:
Pod priority (higher priority first)
PodGroup name (pods from the same PodGroup clustered together)
Timestamp (earlier created pods first)

### Implementation Approach

1. **Leverage existing PodGroup identification**: The `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/helper/podgroup.go` already provides the `MatchingSchedulingGroup` function to determine if two pods belong to the same PodGroup.

2. **Enhance the Less function**: Modify `PrioritySort.Less()` to include PodGroup comparison logic:
   - If two pods belong to the same PodGroup, sort by timestamp
   - If they belong to different PodGroups, sort by PodGroup name to cluster pods from the same group together

### Conceptual Code Example

```go
func (pl *PrioritySort) Less(pInfo1, pInfo2 fwk.QueuedPodInfo) bool {
    p1 := corev1helpers.PodPriority(pInfo1.GetPodInfo().GetPod())
    p2 := corev1helpers.PodPriority(pInfo2.GetPodInfo().GetPod())
    
    // First, sort by priority
    if p1 != p2 {
        return p1 > p2
    }
    
    pod1 := pInfo1.GetPodInfo().GetPod()
    pod2 := pInfo2.GetPodInfo().GetPod()
    
    // Get PodGroup information
    pg1 := getPodGroupName(pod1)
    pg2 := getPodGroupName(pod2)
    
    // Co-locate pods from the same PodGroup
    if pg1 != "" && pg2 != "" && pg1 != pg2 {
        return pg1 < pg2
    }
    
    // Finally, sort by timestamp
    return pInfo1.GetTimestamp().Before(pInfo2.GetTimestamp())
}

title: Non-SSA update of a map’s entry prevents deleting the map via SSA
body:
### What happened?

We’ve encountered this error in Kueue https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/6966. This issue reproduced both live and in an integration test.

In some situations, Kueue is modifying Workload's `status.admission.podSetAssignments[].resourceUsage.memory` and then performs SSA to remove the status.admission field, which fails like:

> Workload.kueue.x-k8s.io "job-sample-job-1-9qkhm-dfd40" is invalid: status.admission.podSetAssignments: Invalid value: "null": status.admission.podSetAssignments in body must be of type array: "null"

Importantly, `status.admission.podSetAssignments` uses `x-kubernetes-list-type: map`: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/blob/main/config/components/crd/bases/kueue.x-k8s.io_workloads.yaml#L8961

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected to be able to do SSA to remove the field.

The same scenario works as expected if the field is in a regular array.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a minimal CRD with a map field, e.g.
```
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: mycrds.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                arrayMap:
                  type: array
                  x-kubernetes-list-map-keys:
                  - key
                  x-kubernetes-list-type: map
                  items:
                    type: object
                    required:
                    - key
                    properties:
                      key:
                        type: string
                      foo:
                        type: string
                  
  scope: Cluster
  
  names:
    plural: mycrds
    singular: mycrd
    kind: MyCrd
    shortNames:
    - mc
EOF
```

Create the resource:
```
kubectl apply --server-side -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: "example.com/v1alpha1"
kind: MyCrd
metadata:
  name: repro
spec:
  arrayMap:
  - key: "0"
    foo: "1"
EOF
```

Patch the resource to update the map entry's field:
```
kubectl patch mc repro --type=json -p='[{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/arrayMap/0/foo", "value": "2"}]'
```

Server-side apply a change to remove the map:
```
kubectl apply --server-side -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: "example.com/v1alpha1"
kind: MyCrd
metadata:
  name: repro
spec:
EOF
```

Observe the error:
```
The MyCrd "repro" is invalid: spec.arrayMap: Invalid value: "null": spec.arrayMap in body must be of type array: "null"
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The initial resource creation doesn’t need to be SSA to repro as long as the last step uses SSA, but results in a slightly different (and potentially more misleading) output:

> Warning: failed to re-apply configuration after performing Server-Side Apply migration. This is non-fatal and will be retried next time you apply. Error: MyCrd.example.com "repro" is invalid: spec.arrayMap: Invalid value: "null": spec.arrayMap in body must be of type array: "null"
mycrd.example.com/repro serverside-applied

If I don’t use SSA in the last step, I’m able to apply the change.

If I use SSA instead of patch to update the map’s entry, I’m able to then remove the map with the `--force-conflicts` option.

If I use a regular array instead of a map, the operations succeed.

title: client-go/gentype: fake.go in production package disables Go linker dead code elimination (+52 MB binary bloat)
body:
## Summary

The `k8s.io/client-go/gentype` package includes `fake.go` in the same Go package as production code (`type.go`). Because Go compiles all non-test `.go` files in a package together, `fake.go`'s import of `k8s.io/client-go/testing` is included in every binary that uses typed Kubernetes clients — even when no fake/test code is used.

This transitively pulls in `google.golang.org/protobuf/internal/descfmt` and `google.golang.org/protobuf/internal/impl`, which use `reflect.MethodByName` with non-constant arguments. When the Go linker detects `reflect.MethodByName` is reachable, it [conservatively disables dead code elimination](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/25081) for **all exported methods on all reachable types**. This causes massive binary bloat for any program that also imports packages with large method sets, like `aws-sdk-go-v2/service/ec2`.

## Impact

Adding a blank import of `k8s.io/client-go/gentype` to a program that uses the AWS EC2 SDK increases binary size by **+52 MB** (from 13 MB to 65 MB), linking 2,273 `ec2.Client` methods instead of the 7 actually needed.

This affects **every consumer of typed Kubernetes clients** (`kubernetes/typed/*/v*`), since they all import `gentype`.

## Root Cause

The import chain:

```
k8s.io/client-go/gentype (fake.go)
  └─ k8s.io/client-go/testing
       ├─ k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields
       └─ k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/strategicpatch
            └─ ... (several hops) ...
                 └─ google.golang.org/protobuf/internal/descfmt
                      └─ reflect.ValueOf(vs).MethodByName("Get")  [stringer.go:44, 99]
                 └─ google.golang.org/protobuf/internal/impl
                      └─ reflect.PtrTo(t).MethodByName(...)  [message.go:198, 201]
```

The Go linker sees `reflect.MethodByName` is reachable and disables method pruning globally. See [golang/go#25081](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/25081) and [kubernetes/kubernetes#132216](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132216) for background.

## Reproduction

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
DIR=$(mktemp -d)
trap "rm -rf $DIR" EXIT
cd "$DIR"

go mod init gentype-dce-repro

cat > baseline.go << 'GOEOF'
//go:build baseline
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/config"
    "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/service/ec2"
)

type EC2API interface {
    DescribeInstances(ctx context.Context, params *ec2.DescribeInstancesInput, optFns ...func(*ec2.Options)) (*ec2.DescribeInstancesOutput, error)
}

func main() {
    cfg, _ := config.LoadDefaultConfig(context.Background())
    var client EC2API = ec2.NewFromConfig(cfg)
    out, _ := client.DescribeInstances(context.Background(), &ec2.DescribeInstancesInput{InstanceIds: []string{"i-test"}})
    fmt.Println(out)
}
GOEOF

cat > with_gentype.go << 'GOEOF'
//go:build with_gentype
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/config"
    "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/service/ec2"
    _ "k8s.io/client-go/gentype"
)

type EC2API interface {
    DescribeInstances(ctx context.Context, params *ec2.DescribeInstancesInput, optFns ...func(*ec2.Options)) (*ec2.DescribeInstancesOutput, error)
}

func main() {
    cfg, _ := config.LoadDefaultConfig(context.Background())
    var client EC2API = ec2.NewFromConfig(cfg)
    out, _ := client.DescribeInstances(context.Background(), &ec2.DescribeInstancesInput{InstanceIds: []string{"i-test"}})
    fmt.Println(out)
}
GOEOF

go mod tidy

echo "=== Go version ==="
go version

echo ""
echo "=== Baseline (EC2 SDK only) ==="
go build -tags baseline -o bin_baseline .
echo "Size: $(stat --format=%s bin_baseline) bytes ($(du -h bin_baseline | cut -f1))"
echo "ec2.Client methods linked: $(go tool nm bin_baseline | grep -c 'service/ec2\.(\*Client)\.')"

echo ""
echo "=== With gentype (blank import) ==="
go build -tags with_gentype -o bin_gentype .
echo "Size: $(stat --format=%s bin_gentype) bytes ($(du -h bin_gentype | cut -f1))"
echo "ec2.Client methods linked: $(go tool nm bin_gentype | grep -c 'service/ec2\.(\*Client)\.')"
```

### Results (Go 1.26.1 linux/amd64, client-go v0.35.2, ec2 v1.294.1)

| Build | Binary Size | `ec2.Client` methods linked |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline (EC2 SDK only) | 13 MB | 7 (just `DescribeInstances` + helpers) |
| + `k8s.io/client-go/gentype` (blank import) | 65 MB | 2,273 (all EC2 API operations) |
| **Difference** | **+52 MB** | **+2,266 dead methods** |

## Suggested Fix

Move `fake.go` out of the `gentype` package so that test fake infrastructure is not compiled into production binaries. Options:

1. **Move to a subpackage**: `k8s.io/client-go/gentype/fake` (analogous to how `k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/fake` is separate from `k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes`)
2. **Use a build tag**: Add a build constraint to `fake.go` to exclude it from production builds

Either approach would break the `gentype -> testing -> protobuf -> reflect.MethodByName` chain for production builds, allowing the Go linker to properly eliminate dead code.

## Related Issues

- [golang/go#25081](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/25081) — Enable linker dead code pruning when using reflect
- [golang/go#60221](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/60221) — There should be a way to determine why deadcode elimination was not performed
- [kubernetes/kubernetes#132216](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132216) — Allow linker to perform dead code elimination for kube-apiserver etc
- [kubernetes/kubernetes#127888](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/127888) — Make client-go lighter and easier to consume (Umbrella)

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

title: Add Prometheus metrics for Windows kube-proxy (winkernel) load balancer failures
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The Windows kube-proxy (winkernel proxier) currently lacks Prometheus metrics for load balancer operation failures. This makes it difficult to monitor and diagnose LB failures in production Windows clusters.

**Proposed metrics:**

Add three new `ALPHA` stability counter metrics:
- `kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_winkernel_lb_create_failures_total` - tracks LB creation failures
- `kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_winkernel_lb_update_failures_total` - tracks LB update failures  
- `kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_winkernel_lb_delete_failures_total` - tracks LB deletion failures

**Proposed labels for each metric:**

| Label | Values |
|-------|--------|
| `ip_family` | `IPv4`, `IPv6` |
| `lb_type` | `clusterip`, `nodeport`, `externalip`, `ingressip`, `healthcheck` |
| `error` | `network_not_found`, `port_already_exists`, `not_implemented`, `invalid_ip`, `other` |

The maximum cardinality per metric would be 50 (2 × 5 × 5), but in practice much lower since a proxier instance typically uses a single IP family and most error/lb_type combinations never fire.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Observability gap**: Linux kube-proxy modes (iptables, ipvs, nftables) have extensive metrics, but Windows winkernel proxier has none for LB failures.
2. **Production debugging**: Without these metrics, operators have no visibility into HCN/HNS failures until services become unavailable.
3. **Alerting**: Cannot set up proactive alerting on LB failure rates in Windows clusters.
4. **Parity**: Brings Windows kube-proxy closer to feature parity with Linux modes in terms of observability.

### Additional context

Example output from a real AKS Windows node:

```
kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_winkernel_lb_create_failures_total{error="other",ip_family="IPv4",lb_type="clusterip"} 222

title: Static pods that are rejected by admission should be periodically retried / preempt non-static pods
body:
### What happened?

A static pod is best thought of as a controller-driven API pod that should be continually restarted by the Kubelet.  Today, we pass static pods through admission and they can be rejected, which prevents the pod from being reconsidered until the kubelet is restarted.  Because status manager is the source of truth for "admission rejection" other code in the Kubelet can't tell the difference between pods that are truly terminal and those that were rejected for admission.

While working on #115331 we attempted to consistently set terminal phase on all pods that have completed - this should be fine for a mirror pod since the kubelet can restart it.  However, because a terminal phase in the status manager is indistinguishable from admission failure, the HandlePodCleanups method doesn't ever check to see whether it needs to be restarted.  If the admin were to make a config change, that *would* trigger a reassessment, but if that static pod had configured a static uid then the pod would not be reconsidered ever.

We should not require the Kubelet to be restarted to restart static pods, and a restart of the kubelet that caused a static pod to fail to be admitted should *probably* heal without a subsequent restart. 

/sig node

### What did you expect to happen?

1. We should be able to set a terminal phase on a mirror pod and not have it block the restart of a static pod
2. If a static pod fails admission we shouldn't have to restart the kubelet to get it to be retried
3. If a static pod is evicted (not sure if this is even possible) it should be reattempted without a kubelet restart

To do any of the above we probably have to have a better source of truth for admission rejection.  That might mean making the pod worker responsible for rejection during admission, since the pod worker should be the source of truth for admission anyway (#104824).  Until then, #115331 will ignore static pods as we can't safely assign a terminal phase to a static pod.

Also see #116483 which is also impacted by how we handle phase of mirror pods.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See description.

title: KEP-5304: DRA device metadata, add declarative validation for metadata types
body:
### What would you like to be added?

## Summary
The DRA device metadata API (introduced in KEP-5304) defines types in
`staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/api/metadata/` that are
serialized to JSON files mounted into containers. Currently, consumers
that parse these files get structural validation from Go's typed
deserialization (wrong types and unknown fields are caught), but there is
no field-level validation (e.g., required fields, length constraints).

## Proposal

Use the declarative validation to provide auto-generated code for go-clients
to validate the metadata generated by driver. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137086/changes/BASE..dc6f7cb81dd46ae5abb96062bf2501ff8fb0c696#r2934130825

### Why is this needed?

As of 1.36, consumers must either trust the producer or hand-roll
validation. Declarative validation markers on the metadata types would
let us generate validation code that consumers can call after parsing.

title: Move in-tree plugins to the staging repository
body:
Continued from #89930.

/sig scheduling
/kind feature
/cc @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-leads @ania-borowiec 

---

We moved all interfaces, types etc from k/k to the staging repo. 
The next discussion is whether we want to move our in-tree plugins to the staging repo. 
Some external components (such as descheduler, the cluster autoscaler, Kueue etc) run the scheduling simulation today, but, for example, descheduler implements the scheduling logic on their own. 
If we can publish in-tree plugins in the staging repo and make them easier to be imported, such components may want to use in-tree plugins to run their scheduling simulation. But, we, of course, first check if this motivation is big enough before starting this initiative.

On the technical side, as summarized in [this comment of mine](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/89930#issuecomment-2566236328), plugins still have some dependencies to k/k (e.g., feature flag package). We need to think about how we remove those dependencies to make in-tree plugins able to be moved outside.

title: Reduce the risk of waiting on the scheduling queue Pop(), despite having pods in backoffQ
body:
With SchedulerPopFromBackoffQ feature enabled, if activeQ is empty, but there is a pod in backoffQ, we try to schedule the pod from there. Because the backoffQ is locked with a different lock than activeQ, it is possible that between a check of backoffQ emptiness (line 260 below) and waiting on a condition (line 270), the pod might be added to the backoffQ in the meantime, leading to unnecessary waiting on condition (see [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130772#discussion_r2004381054)). It doesn't regress the scenario of popping pods from the activeQ, but might affect popping from the backoffQ. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/47a61c5c98822989d955e00d42f895234c1a1cb1/pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/active_queue.go#L255-L271

title: Kubernetes scheduler may preempt lower priority pods during deployment rollout
body:
### What happened?

Kubernetes scheduler may preempt lower priority pods during deployment rollout. I suspect https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-priority-preemption/#higher-priority-pods-are-preempted-before-lower-priority-pods partially explains why.  

### What did you expect to happen?

Pods belonging to the **same** deployment should not preempt each other in a manner that breaks a highly available app rollout involving priority class changes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply the following deployment on a 3 node cluster.  We are using 3 nodes here to simulate a multi zone cluster that spreads pods across zones.

```
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
description: high
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: high
value: 900000000
globalDefault: false
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
description: medium
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: medium
value: 500000000
globalDefault: false
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
description: low
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: low
value: 100000000
globalDefault: false
---
kind: Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
metadata:
  labels:
    app: alpine
  name: alpine
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: alpine
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 3
      maxUnavailable: 1
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: alpine
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - labelSelector:
              matchExpressions:
              - key: app
                operator: In
                values: ["alpine"]
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      containers:
      - image: alpine:latest
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        name: alpine
        command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 100000"]
```

Patch the deployment to set a priority class.  This will cause all pods to either be `Pending` or `Terminating` at the same time.
```
kubectl patch deployment alpine -p '{"spec": {"template": {"spec": {"priorityClassName": "low"}}}}'
```

Patch the deployment to increase priority.  This will cause all pods to either be `Pending` or `Terminating` at the same time.
```
kubectl patch deployment alpine -p '{"spec": {"template": {"spec": {"priorityClassName": "medium"}}}}'
```

Patch the deployment to increase priority.  This will cause all pods to either be `Pending` or `Terminating` at the same time.
```
kubectl patch deployment alpine -p '{"spec": {"template": {"spec": {"priorityClassName": "high"}}}}'
```

Patch the deployment to lower priority.  This will yield the expected rollout.
```
kubectl patch deployment alpine -p '{"spec": {"template": {"spec": {"priorityClassName": "low"}}}}'
```

### Anything else we need to know?

This issue is similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/108266 in that the deployment configuration impacts whether or not this problem occurs.

### Kubernetes version

Failure occurs on Kubernetes versions 1.20, 1.21, 1.22, 1.23 and 1.24.

N/A

IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service

title: Codegen tools need to ignore struct fields named `_`
body:
This is apparently a trick used by some Go devs to force fields to be named in struct initializing code (https://groups.google.com/g/Golang-Nuts/c/NSjVW82i0mY/m/qSshj0qIYxQJ).

From: https://github.com/kubernetes/gengo/issues/133

Running deepcopy-gen against structs that have `_` fields in them generates invalid go code.

Source struct:

```
type CreateBucketConfiguration struct {
	_ struct{} `type:"structure"`

	LocationConstraint BucketLocationConstraint `type:"string" enum:"true"`
}
type BucketLocationConstraint string
```

`doc.go` directives to deepcopy:

```
// +k8s:deepcopy-gen=package,register
```

deepcopy directives above structs that the above struct is a child of  (not sure if this makes a difference or not - this is autogenerated code from the operator sdk)

```
// +k8s:deepcopy-gen:interfaces=k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime.Object
```

Output by deepcopy-gen:
```
// DeepCopyInto is an autogenerated deepcopy function, copying the receiver, writing into out. in must be non-nil.
func (in *CreateBucketConfiguration) DeepCopyInto(out *CreateBucketConfiguration) {
	*out = *in
	out._ = in._
	return
}
```

Setting or accessing `_` fields is invalid. 

I applied the following patch locally and it outputs correct code (ie does not attempt to copy the `_` field).  No idea if this is the _correct_ way to solve the problem though.

```
diff --git a/vendor/k8s.io/gengo/examples/deepcopy-gen/generators/deepcopy.go b/vendor/k8s.io/gengo/examples/deepcopy-gen/generators/deepcopy.go
index 4548108..1d90578 100644
--- a/vendor/k8s.io/gengo/examples/deepcopy-gen/generators/deepcopy.go
+++ b/vendor/k8s.io/gengo/examples/deepcopy-gen/generators/deepcopy.go
@@ -823,6 +823,9 @@ func (g *genDeepCopy) doStruct(t *types.Type, sw *generator.SnippetWriter) {

 	// Now fix-up fields as needed.
 	for _, m := range ut.Members {
+		if m.Name == "_" {
+			continue
+		}
 		ft := m.Type
 		uft := underlyingType(ft)
```

After applying this patch, output is as expected:

```
// DeepCopyInto is an autogenerated deepcopy function, copying the receiver, writing into out. in must be non-nil.
func (in *CreateBucketConfiguration) DeepCopyInto(out *CreateBucketConfiguration) {
	*out = *in
	return
}
```

title: Clarify kubelet lifecycle semantics for node lease renewal during graceful shutdown
body:
## Summary

Kubelet currently keeps renewing the node lease during graceful node shutdown because lease renewal is started with `context.Background()`:

- `pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:1915`

At the same time, the node lifecycle controller treats a renewed lease as fresh health signal and refreshes its probe timestamp:

- `pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/node_lifecycle_controller.go:911-918`

This can delay the controller's transition to `Unknown` / `unreachable` during graceful shutdown by approximately the configured shutdown window.

The key technical detail is that `PrepareForShutdown(true)` does not cancel the shared kubelet `Run(ctx)` context today. The shutdown manager uses that context when it calls `syncNodeStatus(ctx)`, but it does not cancel it:

- `pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go:276-280`

## Why this matters

There is a direct user-facing impact around node failure detection timing for clusters that enable graceful node shutdown. With the current behavior, kubelet can continue renewing the node lease until final process exit even after graceful node shutdown has started. With current defaults, `NodeLeaseDurationSeconds = 40s`, the lease renew interval is `10s` (`40s * 0.25`), and `NodeMonitorGracePeriod = 50s`. If lease renewal continues during the graceful shutdown window, it can delay the controller's transition to `Unknown` / `unreachable` by an additional interval on the order of the shutdown window, depending on the lease renew cadence and the timing of the last renewal before kubelet exit. So this is not just a small timing detail; the effect can grow as the configured graceful shutdown duration grows.

This also makes context-wiring changes harder to reason about and harder to test. A change that looks like a simple cleanup, such as moving an individual loop from `context.Background()` to `Run(ctx)`, can change behavior differently depending on which shutdown path is active. In particular, `PrepareForShutdown(true)` and signal-driven process shutdown are not the same path today:

- `SIGTERM` / `SIGINT` cancel the shared kubelet `Run(ctx)` context
- `PrepareForShutdown(true)` runs graceful node shutdown handling, but does not itself cancel that shared context

Without stating that explicitly, it is easy to assume that switching a loop to `Run(ctx)` is enough to make it stop during graceful shutdown, which is not true in the current implementation.

## One possible narrow option

If the desired semantics are that node lease renewal should stop when graceful node shutdown begins, a narrow implementation option would be to manage lease renewal as its own kubelet-owned lifecycle instead of starting it directly with `context.Background()`.

Concretely, that could mean:

- kubelet creates and owns a dedicated lease-renewal context
- signal-driven process shutdown still stops lease renewal through normal kubelet shutdown
- `PrepareForShutdown(true)` explicitly stops lease renewal
- `PrepareForShutdown(false)` explicitly restarts lease renewal if shutdown is cancelled

That would keep the change scoped to lease renewal semantics without changing the lifecycle of unrelated kubelet loops.

However, this should be treated as a semantic change, not just a context cleanup, because it would change when the node stops sending lease heartbeats during graceful shutdown.

## Supporting material

I put together a small standalone simulator to make the current behavior easier to reason about:

- `https://github.com/hoteye/kubernetes/blob/issue-kubelet-shutdown-context-simulator/experiments/kubelet_shutdown_sim/main.go`
- `https://github.com/hoteye/kubernetes/blob/issue-kubelet-shutdown-context-simulator/experiments/kubelet_shutdown_sim/README.md`
- `https://github.com/hoteye/kubernetes/blob/issue-kubelet-shutdown-context-simulator/experiments/kubelet_shutdown_sim/sample-output.txt`

It is only meant as a reasoning aid for the current behavior split between signal shutdown and graceful node shutdown.

title: Default memory eviction-hard threshold in kubernetes should be set more than `vm.min_free_kbytes`
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Current default eviction threshold is hardcoded as 100MiB, this works for default linux default (66MiB). But this can be adjusted, and with swap use-cases, kubernetes environments will likely see this sysctl parameter adjusted to a higher value than default.

This proposal suggests to set the sysctl parameter based on the observed value instead:

`max( DefaultHardEvictionThresholdValue , NodeMinFreeKbytes + SafetyMargin )`

Where:
- `DefaultHardEvictionThresholdValue` is the current default (100MiB).
- `NodeMinFreeKbytes` is the value read from /proc/sys/vm/min_free_kbytes, converted to MiB.
- `SafetyMargin` is a buffer (e.g., 50MiB or a percentage of min_free_kbytes) to ensure eviction triggers comfortably before the kernel's absolute minimum is reached. 

Proposal discussed at SIG-Node: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qBkCuB7hPbCfCkTc7ilYwwDzyG_ykpP7losidyuOiTU/edit?usp=sharing
 

### Why is this needed?

This is required to ensure Kubernetes handles eviction before the OOM killer starts handling for memory pressure. This is particularly important for swap use-cases as the swap watermarks are directly influenced by this sysctl parameter.
