title: Kubelet retries NodeStageVolume indefinitely on NOT_FOUND
body:
### What happened?

When a CSI driver's `NodeStageVolume` returns `NOT_FOUND` (gRPC code 5), the kubelet continuously retries the operation with exponential backoff. However, the kubelet does not perform the recovery behavior specified in the CSI spec for this error code.

This results in pods being stuck in `ContainerCreating` state indefinitely, requiring manual intervention.

### What did you expect to happen?

According to the [CSI spec for NodeStageVolume errors](https://github.com/container-storage-interface/spec/blob/master/spec.md#nodestagevolume-errors), when `NOT_FOUND` is returned:

> **Condition:** Volume does not exist.
>
> **gRPC Code:** `5 NOT_FOUND`
>
> **Recovery Behavior:** "Caller MUST verify that the `volume_id` is correct and that the volume is accessible and has not been deleted before retrying with exponential back off."

The kubelet should follow this recovery behavior: **verify that the volume is accessible** before retrying.

Currently, the kubelet only retries `NodeStageVolume` without any verification step, which does not comply with the CSI spec.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

4. Observe:

The informer should expose metrics about queue/reflector/eventHandler.

title: add tag for "strategic merge is broken for this field"
body:
There are at least two GA API fields I know of where you cannot use strategic merge patch, because the declared strategy is incorrect and will result in data loss in some cases if you use it; `node.Status.Addresses` (#79391) and `pod.Spec.Ports` (#110564).

We can't fix the strategic merge tags on those fields, because the fields aren't broken in _all_ cases, and changing the merge tags would create an API break that would cause data loss in the cases that aren't currently broken.

It seems like it would be good to have a way to tag such fields to say "look, even though they have tags implying that they support strategic merge patch, you shoudn't do it", and have strategic merge patch fall back to non-strategic merging for those fields (as in #79391, but generic).

title: [LinuxOnly] is egregiously misused at least in sig-network tests
body:
In `test/e2e/network`, there are currently 45 tests marked `[LinuxOnly]`, of which it seems that 37 are incorrect or at least dubious:
- 15 claim that Windows does not support `SessionAffinity`, which [was implemented in `pkg/proxy/winkernel` 4 years ago](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/91701)
- 14 test dual-stack, which works on Windows but [is (was?) not fully supported by our CI environment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/100870)
- 3 need UDP support in agnhost, which the tests in question claim does not work, though I suspect this actually means "at [the time these tests were merged](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/98636), the windows agnhost image had not been rebuilt with the [recently-added udp client](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/98639) yet".
- 2 use `hostNetwork` pods, which [now exist in alpha on Windows](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3503), so we ought to at least optionally be running them there
- 1 uses pod hostPorts, which have been [supported on Windows since 2020](https://github.com/containernetworking/plugins/pull/475).
- 1 is skipped because "IPv6 is not supported on Windows", which is not true

The seemingly-correct ones:
- 5 use SCTP, which AIUI the Windows kernel does not implement and does not plan to implement.
- 3 test partial DNS names (`kubernetes.default.svc`) which apparently are not supported by the Windows resolver

cc @claudiubelu @knabben @MikeZappa87
/sig windows
/sig network

title: performance: prune non-preferred branches early in Topology Manager to avoid combinatorial explosion
body:
### What happened?


`Topology Manager`'s `iterateAllProviderTopologyHints` expands the full Cartesian product of all topology hint providers' hint sets. When a provider returns a large number of hints (e.g. Device Manager (GPU device plugin) calling `bitmask.IterateBitMasks` for all NUMA node power sets), this causes exponential time and memory blowup, making the kubelet unresponsive during pod admission. On an 8-NUMA-node system, a single provider can generate 255 (2^8-1) hints, leading to ~4.2 billion merges with 4 providers.

Measured on Apple M4 Pro (arm64):

**Before optimization:**

```bash
go test ./pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager \
  -run BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -bench BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -benchmem -count=1
```

```
goos: darwin
goarch: arm64
pkg: k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager
cpu: Apple M4 Pro
BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists-14    1    257951838000 ns/op    407509652776 B/op    12701401722 allocs/op
PASS
ok      k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager    258.551s
```

A single `Admit()` call took 258 seconds and allocated 407 GB of memory.


### What did you expect to happen?

`Admit()` completes in bounded time. The hint merging algorithm should not degrade to exponential complexity when providers return large hint sets.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To reproduce, first modify the function:

func (m HintMerger) mergePreferred() *TopologyHint {
}

Force it to return nil directly.

Then run the benchmark:

go test ./pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager \
  -run BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -bench BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -benchmem -count=1

The benchmark will run for ~4 minutes and consume several hundred GB of memory, reproducing the performance issue.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

main branch (as of 2026-03)


### Cloud provider

no


### OS version

darwin/arm64 (Apple M4 Pro)

title: Goroutine leak in filteredWatch
body:
### What happened?

I created a some ListWatches with filters to filter out uninteresting events before processing. And I did this by introducing the filteredWatch in the apimachinery.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/filter.go#45
```
type filteredWatch struct {
	incoming Interface
	result   chan Event
	f        FilterFunc
}
```
And then I stopped ListWatches. Of which I invoked the 'Stop' function to close filteredWatches.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/filter.go#56
```
// Stop stops the upstream watch, which will eventually stop this watch.
func (fw *filteredWatch) Stop() {
	fw.incoming.Stop()
}
```
I repeated the process many times. Then I noticed that my program memory was increasing.

After analysis, it is found that the problem is caused by incomplete resources release of filteredWatch.

I created the filteredWatch object using the Filter function. In which a blocking channel called 'result' and a goroutine called 'loop' were created.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/filter.go#35
```
func Filter(w Interface, f FilterFunc) Interface {
	fw := &filteredWatch{
		incoming: w,
		result:   make(chan Event),
		f:        f,
	}
	go fw.loop()
	return fw
}
```

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/filter.go#61
```
// loop waits for new values, filters them, and resends them.
func (fw *filteredWatch) loop() {
	defer close(fw.result)
	for event := range fw.incoming.ResultChan() {
		filtered, keep := fw.f(event)
		if keep {
			fw.result <- filtered
		}
	}
}
```

Assume that there were two events(A & B) in the incoming channel. They all meet the filter.

Time 1: A was popped from the fw.incoming.ResultChan() and was sent to the fw.result.
Time 2: B was just popped from the fw.incoming.ResultChan().
Time 3: The Stop function of the filteredWatch was invoked and the fw.incoming.ResultChan() was closed.

Since A has not been taken from the fw.result, the loop goroutine will stuck at line 'fw.result <- filtered' and leads to goroutine leaks.

### What did you expect to happen?

No goroutine leak when filteredWatch is closed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We can use a test case to reproduce the problem.
1. Add some observable points to the loop method.
```
var (
	PopFromIncoming = make(chan struct{}) // added
	ExitLoop = make(chan struct{}) // added
)

// loop waits for new values, filters them, and resends them.
func (fw *filteredWatch) loop() {
	defer close(fw.result)
	for event := range fw.incoming.ResultChan() {
		PopFromIncoming <- struct{}{} // added
		filtered, keep := fw.f(event)
		if keep {
			fw.result <- filtered
		}
	}
	ExitLoop <- struct{}{} // added
}
```
2. Add a test case.
```
func TestFilterLoopStuck(t *testing.T) {
	source := NewFake()
	filtered := Filter(source, func(e Event) (Event, bool) {
		return e, e.Object.(testType)[0] != 'b'
	})

	source.Add(testType("foo"))

	<-PopFromIncoming // Ensure event was popped from the fw.incoming.ResultChan()

	<-filtered.ResultChan() // Take out event

	filtered.Stop()
	<-ExitLoop
}
```
When we take out event from the filtered.ResultChan() before closing the filteredWatch, the test case do not stuck.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/112469714/197201261-df06ff9e-faac-4d7d-8a09-c2405fc220e5.png)
And when we directly close filteredWatch (Simulate the scenario where the ListWatch is closed without handling the event in a timely manner), the use case is stuck.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/112469714/197201874-64d4c11a-8cf5-4a49-9b54-ae2a21a41fba.png)

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

kubernetes GitVersion: v1.22.1

C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture

title: CEL Validation: permit hashing object fields to form object name
body:
Scenario: My CRD has fields x, y, and z. I want to ensure that within a given namespace, no two instances of this CRD have the same set of values for those fields.

Solution 1: Require that .metadata.name be x+y+z. (Add a x-kubernetes-validations to the root of the object, and do something like `"[self.metadata.name] == self.spec.x + self.spec.y + self.spec.z"`)
Problem 1: The fields might be too long, or not match the rules about names (contain "/" characters, etc)

Solution 2: Require that name be of the form sanitized_fields(x,y,z)+unique_hash(x,y,z). Where:
* sanitized_fields produces a string which contains as much of the given fields as possible, while removing forbidden characters and capping the length. This is to make the name human readable.
* unique_hash is some hash function which produces a fixed-length hash to ensure that the name is unique even if the sanitized_fields function collides.

The request here is to add a function or set of functions callable from CEL to do this sanitizing/hashing. Ideally we would like the code to be known ASAP so that people can use them in validating webhooks today and move to CEL when it is available.

For bonus points we would like to default the name to the correct value if it is blank, since it may be hard for clients to determine the correct value. (I suspect this isn't possible with our defaulting stack, but maybe I'm wrong.)

We need the error message to report the expected name, so that at least clients could e.g. send a dry-run POST request to figure out the correct name and then use it in the real request.

/sig api-machinery

title: AvailableConditionController escalatory check behaviour during network partitions
body:
### What happened? ### A Network Partition impacts our api extensions We experienced a network issue affecting our kubernetes apiservers which partitioned one or more of our apiservers from the back-end end pods which were providing api extensions. The issue affected the apiservice extensions “[v1.subresources.kubevirt.io](http://v1.subresources.kubevirt.io/)” and “[v1alpha3.subresources.kubevirt.io](http://v1alpha3.subresources.kubevirt.io/)” which were marked as unavailable, which are both extensions that hosted external to the apiservers through in-cluster services. We observed a high frequency of work being queued by the three controllers associated with the kube-aggregator, “APIServiceRegistrationController”, “autoregister” and “AvailableConditionController” as seen in this graph of the rate of workqueue_adds_total metric emitted by these controllers: - ￼ We also saw a high volume of discovery URL requests, e.g. “/apis/subresources.kubevirt.io/v1” on the backend and so looked into the behaviour of the “AvailableConditionController” to learn more. The “AvailableConditionController” is running on all apiservers running the kube-aggregator and sharing a status condition which is stored in the apiservice object in the kubernetes api. If the condition is toggled between “Available” or “Unavailable” by an apiserver this will trigger a round of immediate tests across all of the apiservers. If one or more of the apiservers are in disagreement as to the condition (i.e. some see it down and some it up) then they will toggle the condition back and forth between “Available” and “Unavailable” and trigger more checks as they go. The number of times that the condition is toggled to “Unavailable” is recorded by the metric aggregator_unavailable_apiservice_total, but we can’t see the toggling back to “Available” because this is specifically not recorded: - ￼ We can see from the graph above a lot a changes of state from “Available” to “Unavailable” (especially towards the end of the issues) and that a single apiserver instance can be responsible for much or all of the toggling to “Unavailable”. We might say that the apiservers are fighting over the status of the service because of the number of times the condition is changing and the number of re-checks being performed (across all of the apiservers). ### Rate-limiting Not Reducing Check Frequency It is clear from the metrics that the failing apiservers are performing a great many checks despite the use of a rate limiting workqueue (workqueue.rateLimitingType) for the checks, and an exponential rate limiter (workqueue.ItemExponentialFailureRateLimiter) for handling retries. See (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/619f1cf55208212893504338f18c69f3dcfcdc66/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/controllers/status/available_controller.go#L165) We observe that, whilst the controller adds an exponential backoff to slow retries for failing checks (by calling AddRateLimited() after a failing check to requeue it), it does not apply any limit to the rate of new checks being scheduled through Informer events. If a check is in the process of running or waiting the in the delayed queue a new check can be immediately added through the call to Add(): - ![unknown](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1453938/185146839-56a48d91-04c0-4b98-9974-cf6365e83407.png) ￼ Please note that in this example all updates are for the same object ‘X’, i.e. the same apiservice. 1. Informer event 1 triggers an Add() which adds X into the queue. 2. Informer event 2 triggers an Add() which does not add X into the queue because it is already queued. 3. Processing of event 1 starts and X is moved from the queue to processing. 4. Informer event 3 triggers Add() and is queued in the dirty set (but not the queue) because this is the behaviour of the queue. A new request can be queued for an item if it is being processed. 5. Processing of event 1 succeeds and it is marked Done() and Forgot() by the controller. The action of Done() means that event 3 is now added to the active queue. 6. Processing of event 3 starts from the queue. 7. Processing of event 3 fails and so both Done() and AddRateLimited() are called. The call to AddRateLimited() put the item on the delayed queue. 8. Informer event 4 triggers an Add() which immediately queues X whilst the retry is still waiting in the delayed queue. This queue behaviour explains why even with ratelimiting we are still seeing a large number of checks being queued and performed per-apiserver. In the the scenario where the condition is changing often the exponential rate limiter is providing no value at all because all of the rechecks are being triggered by the apiservice changes. We will absolutely be working to preventing the network partition from re-occurring, but feel that the “AvailableConditionController” could be improved to better handle this kind of failure scenario, rather than actively making matters worse through the increased load on the service. ### What did you expect to happen? ### Possible Improvements Whilst we want to recover quickly, we don’t want to hammer a service that is failing. In the context of the “AvailableConditionController” there is no difference between a retry and a new check, they both amount to the same thing. Both will re-read the apiservice from the apiServiceLister and so will get the latest condiguration and perform the test of the backend. We believe that the rate limiting aspect can take advantage of the knowledge that retries and new checks amount to the same thing and perform additionally rate limit the checks to reduce the load. ### Option 1: Only check on .spec changes We could compare the “.spec” of the apiservice object triggering the check if the new value does not reflect.DeepEqual() the existing value. This would require us to implement an alternative mechanism for performing the checks every 30 seconds because the resyncs from the Informer would be filtered out. This behaviour would be restricted to just the “apiservice” informer and changes to “services” and “endpoints” would continue to be checked immediately (so that we can quickly react to change which may restore service). ### Option 2: Block new checks whilst failing checks are retried Also only targeting changes sent by the “apiservice” informer and not to “service” or “endpoints”. Use the NumRequeues() method on the ratelimiting work queue to check whether the specific apiservice is in a failure-retry state and ignore new events if it is. All existing triggers remain the same, including the periodic 30 second re-checks and checks caused by Condition changes, we are effectively restricting all incoming apiservice changes when the service is known to be failing. We rely on the delayed retry with exponential back-off in order to give the backend a chance to stableize. Even in maximum backoff it will be re-checked every 30 seconds. When an apiservice check succeeds the call to Forget() will mean that all apiservice updates will trigger checks again. This will slow down failing apiservers from toggling the condition to Unavailable which in turn will reduce the amount of fighting over the status and prevent the constant stream of rechecking. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Not so easy, you need to be able to force a partition in your apiservers. You might achieve this by configuring a proxy for apiserver outbound traffic and then configuring it to return 503 to each request so that it fails fast with an error. ### Anything else we need to know? https://github.com/google/capslock -- Something GKE Security folks have mentioned.

> Capslock is a capability analysis CLI for Go packages that informs users of which privileged operations a given package can access. This works by classifying the capabilities of Go packages by following transitive calls to privileged standard library operations.

> The recent increase in supply chain attacks targeting open source software has highlighted that third party dependencies should not be inherently trusted. Capabilities indicate what permissions a package has access to, and can be used in conjunction with other security signals to indicate which code requires additional scrutiny before it can be considered trusted.

title: Patching stateful set not updating statefulset
DRA: DBC - scheduler behavior after binding failure
body:
## Summary

The `DRADeviceBindingConditions` feature requires that both `BindingConditions` and `BindingFailureConditions` are set as its specification. If the BindingFailureConditions are met, the scheduler will re-execute scheduling.

BindingFailureConditions are typically met when device preparation fails. Considering that such failures may be temporary, @dom4ha suggested allowing this feature to control scheduler's behavior so that, after re-scheduling, it can attempt to schedule the same device again.

In this issue, we will discuss the necessity of this enhancement and how it should be implemented.

Discussion link: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5487#discussion_r2412008129

## Scenario

The following is the scenario assumed in this issue:

1. ResourceClaim is allocated to a device with BindingConditions.
2. An external controller detects this and performs device provisioning.
3. The provisioning fails for some reason and a BindingFailureConditions is marked on the ResourceClaim.
4. The scheduler initiates re-scheduling.

## **Proposed implementation ideas**

Introduce a well-known error status on binding failure and enable the scheduler to execute predefined actions based on that status. Specifically, implement the following statuses and behaviors in this statement.

- `retried` (on reschedule keep using the same device(s) if only they are still available as the failure could be transient),
- `reconsidered` (reassess all possible node options - the default behavior) or
- `avoided` (the same device can be still chosen but as the last option)

When `retried` is specified among the above, we could preserve the allocated resources for the next cycle but it's unclear how we'd grab the attached devices in the next cycle and needs further discussion.

## Necessity of This Enhancement

If a BindingFailure occurs and we want to reschedule on the same device, we need to preserve the allocation information for the next scheduling cycle; otherwise, we risk that the released resource will be taken by other pods, whether CPU, memory, or other required DRA resources.

@dom4ha  
I have summarized the points you suggested in the discussion link above. Please let me know if there is anything missing or that should be added. 

Also, I would like to discuss with other maintainers, including @pohly and @johnbelamaric, whether this enhancement is necessary or not.

title: DRA drivers: helper code for checking device allocations
body:
### What would you like to be added?

A DRA driver has to check in NodePrepareResources whether the devices are a) already prepared for other claims and b) really currently available.

If so, it has to refuse to prepare them again. This is a sanity check that acts as last line of defense against unintended concurrent usage of a device (case a) or race conditions. DRA tries hard to avoid such situations, but at least the ["device became unhealthy"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/128979) is inherently racy. Allocating the same device for different claims could be the result of a bug or allocation by different schedulers without [coordination](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/128980#issuecomment-2500948711).

DRA driver authors might forget to implement this check. Perhaps we can move it into [k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/kubeletplugin](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/kubeletplugin) with such an API change that the driver authors are forced to do something?


### Why is this needed?

Higher quality of DRA drivers.

title: Support for expanded 'operators' (e.g. In) in field selectors
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Support for selecting objects using 'set operations' (notably 'In') with field selectors, bringing parity with labelSelectors.

More specifically, I'd like to be able to select over the `metadata.namespace` field, so I can establish multi-namespace watches with consistent RV semantics.

### Why is this needed?

To perform a multi-namespace list/watch today, a user must fetch objects at the cluster-scope and then filter down the response client-side. This is expensive and doesn't scale well as the size of the cluster grows (and various permissions/authZ boundaries are put in place).

Forcing the apiserver to perform this sort of filtering has typically been avoided in the past, as etcd does not natively support something like this, meaning apiservers have to establish a cluster-scoped watch for each client and perform filtering in memory, leading to high amounts of decoding objects from etcd (only to throw them away again after).

Recent work within the apiserver I believe enables us to reduce the impact of these kinds of requests, namely:

* https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2340 (consistent reads from cache)
* https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4568 (resilient watch cache initialization)

Combined, these allow us to ensure we serve list/field selectors from the watch cache, allowing us to optimise and index (similar to how we index certain field selectors and label selectors today).

I believe this feature would complement https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4601 (authorise with selectors) well, as it'd allow end-users to authorise field selector usage as well.

---

For this feature, I think it'll be important to ensure we also index watches and probably also list operations that utilise fieldSelectors, at the very least for `metadata.namespace`. For watches, this is relatively simple as we can add the `cacheWatcher` for the request to the `indexedWatchers` structure multiple times (by generating multiple namespaceName/scope entries): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/06a15c5cf96131faaf44f93f1be228a013ae5c0d/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L135-L163. I've hacked together a quick PoC of the sort of change needed for watches here: https://github.com/munnerz/kubernetes/commit/ae075a0d30906a7218fdc123dd11cc96748bc20d - please do note that this relies on stuffing a `kubernetes.io/metadata.namespace` label into GetAttr funcs to emulate fieldSelector 'In' support, but it demonstrates the performance optimisation technique somewhat :)

Optimising LIST operations is a bit more complex today (as far as I can tell!) due the underlying Store/Indexer implementations in `k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache` not supporting indexed 'set operations' natively.

title: response_sizes metrics for verb=WATCH is only present for built in resources.
body:
### What happened?

The `apiserver_response_sizes` correctly report `GET` and `LIST` metrics for all resources. However, for `WATCH`, its only present for built in resources. This means resources defined in CustomResourceDefinitions are not present.

Its not 100% clear to me what the expected behavior was when it was introduced (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/49117), and if the plan was to not have `watch` metrics here - but we have seen it useful in practice. The verb definition here has changed a bit as well, and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/93523 + https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/81660 split the definition of `verb` and `reportedVerb`. And given this metric is treated as STABLE now, it feels wrong to me to remove the existing `WATCH` metrics here.

Here is an example of how it works today;

```bash
$ kubectl get --raw /metrics | egrep 'apiserver_response_sizes_sum\{component="apiserver",group="(cilium.io)?",resource="(pods|ciliumnetworkpolicies)",scope="cluster"'
apiserver_response_sizes_sum{component="apiserver",group="",resource="pods",scope="cluster",subresource="",verb="LIST",version="v1"} 1.00624648e+08
apiserver_response_sizes_sum{component="apiserver",group="",resource="pods",scope="cluster",subresource="",verb="WATCH",version="v1"} 2.6141637319e+10
apiserver_response_sizes_sum{component="apiserver",group="cilium.io",resource="ciliumnetworkpolicies",scope="cluster",subresource="",verb="LIST",version="v2"} 1.723691e+06
```

As seen both resources have `LIST` metrics, but only the built in resource `pods` has `WATCH`.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect the above request to also contain WATCH for the custom type as well;
```bash
$ kubectl get --raw /metrics | egrep 'apiserver_response_sizes_sum\{component="apiserver",group="(cilium.io)?",resource="(pods|ciliumnetworkpolicies)",scope="cluster"'
apiserver_response_sizes_sum{component="apiserver",group="",resource="pods",scope="cluster",subresource="",verb="LIST",version="v1"} 1.00624648e+08
apiserver_response_sizes_sum{component="apiserver",group="",resource="pods",scope="cluster",subresource="",verb="WATCH",version="v1"} 2.6141637319e+10
apiserver_response_sizes_sum{component="apiserver",group="cilium.io",resource="ciliumnetworkpolicies",scope="cluster",subresource="",verb="LIST",version="v2"} 1.723691e+06
apiserver_response_sizes_sum{component="apiserver",group="cilium.io",resource="ciliumnetworkpolicies",scope="cluster",subresource="",verb="WATCH",version="v2"} 1.090217513e+09
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Install a CRD, have at least one watcher on it, and use `kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep 'apiserver_response_sizes_sum'` and look for the `WATCH` metric of that resource.

title: CEL: enable size validations based on observed sizes, not worst case sizes
body:
I would like the ability to express size limits in my API based on the observed sizes of nested objects/arrays, rather than the worst case.

For example, consider an API like so (this is a real API we have):

```yaml
rules:
- from:
  -  serviceAccounts:
    - foo/bar
```

As you can see, we have 3 tiers of lists, then a string.

In order to write any meaningful validation on this to pretty small sizes (~64 max length on the lists). This is, presumably, since the theoretical max size is `rules * from * serviceAccounts * len(sa)`. With 64 each and 320 length on the string we may have a total `83886080` size, so the validator rejects us.

In practice, this is not happening. No one is writing 64 `rules` AND 64 `froms`  AND 64 `serviceAccounts` in one rule.. but they may have >64 of any individual elements based on their use case.

It would be ideally to be able to express something like 'total cardinality', to take into account the nesting nature. Without this, a large portion of our APIs are forced out of using CEL entirely.

title: [Compatibility Version] Verify there is no orphaned feature gate
body:
## What would you like to be added?

Add tests to verify every existing feature gate in `versioned_feature_list.yaml` (including `*/features/kube_features.go` files):

- [ ] used somewhere in the code
- [ ] has test coverage for the default and non-default values.

## Why is this needed?
To improve code health and developer experience wrt Compatibility Version.

Currently we aggregate all feature gate status in `versioned_feature_list.yaml` file, and require approvals from `feature-approvers` for changes of the file. We rely on the reviewers to ensure proper practice for compatibility version. But one could just keep the definition of the feature gate (orphaned) and remove everything else without triggering the review requirements. If this happens, we would not be able to emulate that feature in compatibility version mode. 

In addition, it is risky to always rely on the reviewers to look out for test coverage. 

We should have better mechanisms to detect and avoid deviations from the correct procedure.
